menus.Name: acne
menus.Text:
## ACNE
Acne is an inflammatory skin condition caused by excess sebum production, gland
obstruction and infection with Cutibacterum acnes. Early disease manifests with
black heads and white heads and little inflammation. Small papules and pustules
are present in mild disease. Severe disease occurs when comedones, papules,
pustules and less often cysts are present.
The goal of treatment is prevention and reeducation of new comedones and
creating an environment that is inhibitory for C. acnes. General skin care
treatment measures include utilizing gentle skin cleansers, avoiding aggressive
scrubbing, using non-comedogenic skin products, and avoiding picking of lesions.
Diet's role in therapy remains uncertain.
Non-Antimicrobial therapy includes benzoyl peroxide topical/wash, salicylic acid
topical, and tretinoin topical. These agents can be used as monotherapy in early
disease and in addition to antimicrobial treatment in mild to severe disease.
## Early Disease:
Clindamycin 1% lotion topically q12h ($) [M]
< OR >
Erythromycin 2% gel topically q12h ($) [DI]
## Mild Disease:
Erythromycin 2% gel topically q12h ($) [DI]
< OR >
Doxycycline 50 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for 12 weeks
< OR >
Minocycline 50 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for 12 weeks
## Severe Disease:

topically q12h
< OR >
Minocycline 100 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for 12 weeks <AND> erythromycin 2% gel
topically q12h

menus.Name: acute-bact-prostatitis
menus.Text:
## ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS
Acute bacterial prostatitis typically presents with fever, dysuria, chills,
malaise, myalgia, pelvic or perianal pain. On exam, the prostate gland is tense,
boggy, and extremely tender. The urinalysis reveals pyuria, and the urine
culture is positive. Men with dysuria and fever but without pyuria and/or
bacteriuria should be seen by a urologist. If there is any suspicion of abscess,
especially in men older than 40 years, the patient should be seen by a urologist
and transurethral prostate resection for drainage should be considered.
Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract
instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated
with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 and those who
are at high risk of sexually transmitted infections are associated with N.
gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if the
patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course of
antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to
ciprofloxacin.
A urine Gram stain and culture should be performed in all patients to guide
antimicrobial therapy:
Lab menu
## Duration
There is limited data on duration of antimicrobial treatment for prostatitis. 14
days minimum is required. 4 to 6 weeks may be necessary to completely eradicate
bacteria in the prostate to ensure patient does not progress to chronic
bacterial prostatitis.
## _____________________________________________________________________________
## Empirical treatment
Hydration, bed rest and analgesics are recommended along with antimicrobials
treatment.
## Age < 35 years and those at high risk of sexually transmitted infections
Patient weighing less than 300 lbs:
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once ($) [M] <AND> doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for
14 days
Patients weighing 300 lbs or greater:
Ceftriaxone 1 gm IM once ($) [M] <AND> doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for
14 days
## Age >/= 35 years ## Inpatient
Preferred:
Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h ($) [R, DI] for 14 days
< OR >
Levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h ($) [R, DI] for 14 days

## Outpatient Non-VA order for above

menus.Name: acute-sinusitis
menus.Text:
## ACUTE SINUSITIS
Most cases of acute sinusitis are viral and resolve within 10 days. Symptoms
(nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, and tooth or facial pain) can be
treated with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline. Diagnosis of acute
sinusitis is based on the presence of at least 2 major or 1 major and at least 2
minor symptoms.
## Major Symptoms
1. Purulent anterior nasal discharge
2. Purulent or discolored posterior nasal discharge
3. Nasal congestion or fullness
4. Facial pain or pressure
5. Hyposmia or anosmia
6. Fever
## Minor Symptoms
1. Headache
2. Ear pain, pressure or fullness
3. Halitosis
4. Dental pain
5. Cough
6. Fatigue
If patient meets criteria above for acute sinusitis, treat with antimicrobials
according to the following criteria for mild to moderate or severe bacterial
sinusitis.
## Mild to moderate bacterial sinusitis
1. Symptoms persisting beyond 10 days
< OR >
2. Double-sickening - Symptoms typical of viral upper respiratory infection
initially improving for 5-6 days then worsening with new development of fever,
headache or increased nasal discharge.
for treatment of mild to moderate bacterial sinusitis
## Severe bacterial sinusitis
Severe signs or symptoms of high fever (>/= 102 degrees Fahrenheit, >/= 39
degrees Celsius) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4 consecutive days or facial
pain lasting for at least 3-4 consecutive days at the beginning of illness.
for treatment of severe bacterial sinusitis

menus.Name: antiviral-immunosuppressive-malignancy
menus.Text:
## PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
## Severly Immunosuppressive Chemo-immunotherapy
## Purine Analogues
Chemotherapy with purine analogues such as fludarabine, cladribine, or
pentostatin results in major cellular-immunodeficiency that may outlast the
exposure by months and enhances the risk for viral infections.
Recommend antiviral prophylaxis for patients treated with purine analogues,
if at least one of the following risk factors is present:
a) Second-line chemotherapy
b) Treatment with corticosteroids
c) CD4 cell count <50/ul
d) Age >65 years
e) Prolonged Mild or Moderate Neutropenia: Mild<1000 Neutrophils /
ï¿½L (Grade III neutropenia) OR Moderate: <500 Neutrophils/ï¿½L
(Grade IV neutropenia)
## Recommendations:
Duration: Antiviral prophylaxis should be initiated in the first week of
therapy and continued until 2 months after completion of therapy.
Acyclovir 800 MG PO q12h ($) [R]
## Alemtuzumab Therapy:
Alemtuzumab is a potent reactivator of latent intracellular pathogens,
including CMV. Chemotherapy with alemtuzumab results in major cellular-
immunodeficiency that may outlast the exposure by months and enhances the
risk for viral infections. The risk of viral disease increases with the
intensity and duration of functional T-cell suppression experienced with
recipients of alemtuzumab.
## Recommendations:
Duration: Initiate antiviral prophylaxis with alemtuzumab therapy and
continue therapy for at least 2 months after last dose or until CD4 counts
are greater than or equal to 200 cells/ul, whichever is later.
Acyclovir 800 MG PO q12h ($) [R]
## References:
Taplitz RA Journal of Clinical Oncology 2018, 36:3043
Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in
Cancer Patients
Up-to-Date website
Sandherr M Annals of Oncology 2006, 17:1051

## Outpatient

Guidance
## Recommendations:
Acyclovir 800 MG PO BID ($0.40/day) [R]

menus.Name: antiviral-infection-malignancy
menus.Text:
## PREVENTION OF VIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
## Prophylaxis for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV)
Select for recommendations for antiviral prophylaxis
## Prophylaxis for Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses
Yearly influenza vaccination with inactivated vaccine is recommended for all
patients receiving chemotherapy for malignancy and all family and household
contacts and health care providers.
Optimal timing of vaccination for patients being treated for cancer is not
established, but serologic responses may be best between chemotherapy cycles
(greater than 7 days after the last treatment) or greater than 2 weeks
before chemotherapy starts.
Patients with active malignant disease are at higher risk for upper
respiratory infections due to influenza, parainfluenza or respiratory
syncytial virus (RSV). Although response to vaccination with the attenuated
influenza vaccine in patients on chemotherapy is variable, ranging
from 24-75%, immnunoprophylaxis with the influenza vaccine is recommended for
patients with active malignant disease or chemotherapy, lymphoproliferative
disease, or multiple myeloma. In areas and seasons where influenza is
endemic, chemoprophylaxis can be considered in addition to vaccination in
exposed patients with a high risk of influenza complications.
## Recommendations:
[Seasonal Influenza Recommendations](orzid2-gmenu-abx-influenza-recommendations)
## Prophylaxis for Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
Prophylaxis and monitoring for CMV reactivation is not recommended unless the
patient has received an allogeneic HSCT. Usually the recommendations for
surveillance and prophylaxis of CMV infections from the institution
performing the HSCT will be followed.
## Recommendations:
Consult Infectious Disease
## Prophylaxis for Chronic Hepatitis B
Reactivation of chronic hepatitis B in patients undergoing immunosuppressive
or antineoplastic treatment is a severe complication. Patients with positive
HBsAg, chronic hepatitis B infection, or a previous episode of HBV
reactivation who will receive immunosuppressive therapy should receive
prophylaxis.
Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B prior to initiating Rituximab
(Anti-CD20 antibody) therapy in patients.
## Recommendations:
[Hepatitis B Evaluation Anti-CD20 Antibody](orzid3-gmenu-hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody)
Consult Infectious Disease
## References:
Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in
Cancer Patients
Taplitz RA Journal of Clinical Oncology 2018, 36:3043
Up-to-Date website
Sandherr M Annals of Oncology 2006, 17: 1051-1059, 2006

menus.Name: antiviral-treatment
menus.Text:
## INFLUENZA ANTIVIRAL THERAPY RECOMMENDATIONS
## Who to Treat:
The decision to treat should be based on clinical symptoms and/or presence of a
high-risk condition and should NOT be delayed until laboratory test results are
available.
It is important to use antiviral drugs early to treat influenza in people who
are very sick with influenza (for example hospitalized people) and people who
are sick with influenza and have a greater chance of getting severe
complications. If a patient is not in a high-risk group or is not hospitalized,
healthcare providers should use clinical judgment to guide treatment decisions.
## People who have a greater chance of serious influenza complications include:
*Adults aged 65 years or older
*Persons who have chronic pulmonary (including
asthma) or cardiovascular (except isolated hypertension), renal, hepatic,
hematologic, metabolic disorders (including diabetes mellitus), neurologic and
neuro-developmental disorders
*Persons who are immunocompromised due to any
cause (including immunosuppression caused by medications or by HIV infection)
*Pregnant women and women up to 2 weeks after the end of pregnancy
*Persons younger than 19 years of age who are receiving long-term aspirin- or
salicylate-containing medications and who might be at risk for experiencing Reye
syndrome after influenza virus infection *Residents of nursing homes and other
long-term care facilities
*Non-Hispanic Black persons, Hispanic or Latino persons, and American Indian or
Alaska Native persons
*Persons who are extremely obese (BMI greater than or equal to 40)
## Antiviral Treatment:
If indicated, antivirals should be started as soon as possible. Maximal benefit
occurs when treatment is started within 48 hours of symptom onset. However,
antivirals should not be withheld if symptoms begin more than 48 hours prior and
the patient meets criteria for treatment and remains severely ill.
## Treatment Dosing:
Zanamivir is not recommended for patients with chronic respiratory diseases such
as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. These patients may have
bronchospasm with zanamivir. If zanamivir must be used, and patients are using
an inhaled bronchodilator, zanamivir should be taken just after the
bronchodilator.
Extending the duration of treatment for oseltamivir or peramivir may be needed
for those patients with prolonged illness or who are immunosuppressed.
## Preferred:
Oseltamivir 75 mg po bid [R] for 5 days
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## **Below is for information only, quick orders are not available
## Alternative:
 Requires Infectious Disease Approval ##Inpatient/Outpatient
Zanamivir 2 inhalations (2 x 5 mg) BID [O] for 5 days
< OR >
Baloxavir 80 mg PO x1 dose patients wt 80 kg or greater, 40 mg PO x 1 dose for
patients wt < 80 kg [DI]
## Alternative for patients unable to tolerate or absorb oral oseltamivir:
Peramivir may not be available. Contact ID for more information.
Requires Infectious Disease Approval
Hospitalized, high risk:
Peramivir 600 mg IV q24h [R] for 5 days
Acute, uncomplicated:
Peramivir 600mg IV Once [R]

menus.Name: antiviral-type-of-malignancy
menus.Text:
## PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
## **Solid Tumors**
## No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended
Solid tumors do not significantly compromise the cellular immune system.
Therefore, patients are at low risk for opportunistic viral infections.
Documented invasive viral infections are very rare. Coincidental
mucocutaneous infections by herpes simplex are easily treated and do not
result in life-threatening invasive infections. Reactivation of
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is rarely observed.
## **Acute Leukemia**
## Herpes simplex virus-seronegative patients
No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended
In patients with acute leukemia, treatment is highly aggressive and consists
of a combination of various cytotoxic agents administered in sequential
cycles as induction, consolidation and maintenance therapy. Persistent, i.e.
>10 days and profound neutropenia (<500 neutrophils) regularly occurs and
correlates with the risk of developing fever and infections. Almost all viral
infections during neutropenia constitute reactivations of herpes viruses.
None of the available studies demonstrated an effect of antiviral prophylaxis
on the initiation of antibiotic treatment, number of febrile days, duration
of antibiotic treatment, and onset of opportunistic infections. Therefore, no
recommendation for antiviral prophylaxis in patients with acute leukemia can
be given.
## Herpes simplex virus-seropostive patients
Patients undergoing leukemia induction therapy should receive prophylaxis.
Acyclovir 800 MG PO q12h ($) [R]
## **Lymphoma**
## No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended
Rituximab is a monoclonal anti-CD-20 antibody used for treatment of
lymphomas. It leads to a profound depletion of circulating B-cells. B-cells
recover usually within 3-6 months after treatment. Prolonged administration
of rituximab (e.g., maintenance treatment >12 months) may result in a
significant decrease of levels of immunoglobulin M. Parvovirus B19 and JC-
papovavirus infections have been reported with maintenance rituximab therapy,
but drugs that would prevent these infections are not available. There is no
substantial increase in risk of reactivation of herpes viruses (including
HSV, VZV, and CMV).
Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B virus prior to initiating Rituximab
therapy in patients.
Hepatitis B information page
[Hepatitis B Evaluation Anti-CD20 Antibody](orzid3-gmenu-hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody)
## References:
Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in
Cancer Patients
Up-to-Date
Sandherr,M et al, Annals of Oncology 17: 1051-1059, 2006

## APPENDICITIS WITHOUT PERFORATION
Oral step-down treatment
Patients with an acutely inflamed appendix and no gangrene or perforation are
considered to have uncomplicated appendicitis. Patients with gangrene,
perforation, peritonitis, or abscess have complicated appendicitis. Treatment
with antibiotics is an option for patients who are unfit for surgery or refuse
surgery. Treatment with antibiotics should not be used routinely as an
alternative to surgery.
## Select for treatment of complicated appendicitis
Link to appendicitis with perforation menu
## Treatment of uncomplicated appendicitis
Surgical management: Administer prophylaxis regimen below prior to surgery
only. Stop antibiotics after the surgery.
Surgical prophylaxis:
Cefazolin weight-based dosing preop < AND > metronidazole 500 mg IV once
Post-surgical: antibiotics not recommended after appendectomy
## Interval appendectomy or no appendectomy
Duration of therapy: Treat with antibiotics for 7 days total
Preferred:
## Inpatient

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h [M] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]

## ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA

When a larger than usual volume of orogastric content is aspirated,
mechanical/chemical irritation occurs. Some of these develop into bacterial
pneumonia.
It is reasonable to wait before starting antimicrobials to see if respiratory
impairment improves or worsens before starting bacterial pneumonia treatment, in

Therapy directed towards anaerobic pathogens is usually unnecessary.

## ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in women and elderly people, especially in
those with chronic medical problems (e.g., diabetes, spinal cord injury,
institutionalized patients, catheterized patients). Most patients have no
adverse outcomes and receive no benefit from treatment of asymptomatic
bacteriuria.
Patients who have no symptoms of cystitis (i.e., no dysuria, pain, urgency)
should not be treated. The presence of pyuria (>7 wbc/hpf) or positive leukocyte
esterase, urine nitrate, or urine bacteria is not a sufficient indication for
antibiotic treatment. Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is
indicated for pregnant women and patients who will have urological procedures
and may be indicated in patients < 1-month post-renal transplant. If an
indwelling catheter is in place and can be removed safely, it should be done as
the bacteriuria may clear.
Bacteriuria in pregnant women is associated with pyelonephritis, premature
delivery, and lower birth weight. Screening for bacteriuria is recommended at
least once early in pregnancy. If bacteriuria is not found upon initial testing,
further screening cultures are not needed. If bacteriuria (>10,000 CFU/mL) is
present, the patient should be treated. Testing should be repeated throughout
the pregnancy to detect recurrences.

menus.Text:
## AZITHROMYCIN FOR PREVENTION OF EXACERBATIONS IN ADVANCED COPD
## Eligibility Criteria:
*Age >40 years
*Clinical diagnosis of COPD (>= 10 pack-years cigarette smoking, a ratio of
postbronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1] to forced vital
capacity of <70%, and a postbronchodilator FEV1 of <80% of the predicted value),
*AND*
*Were either using continuous supplemental oxygen or had received systemic
glucocorticoids within the previous year, *OR*
*Had gone to an emergency room or had been hospitalized for an acute
exacerbation of COPD.
## Exclusion criteria:
*Asthma
*People with hearing impairments
*Congestive heart failure
*Resting heart rate > 100 beats per minute
*Use of medications that are associated with torsades de pointes (except for
amiodarone)
*Prolonged QTc interval (>450 msec)
*Use of medications that prolong the QTc interval
Please Click Here for Resource for Drugs that Cause QTc Prolongation
If, after trying all the standard treatments, patients are still having acute
exacerbations of COPD, long-term antibiotic treatment with Azithromycin may be
considered. Note: Guidelines for COPD can be found on the CPRS Tools Menu.
## Select below for Inpatient COPD order sets for comprehensive management:
## Inpatient

Inpatient COPD Exacerbation Orders
If the patient meets the criteria and is willing to have audiometric testing and
an electrocardiogram, please place a Pulmonary Consult for long-term
Azithromycin therapy for the prevention COPD exacerbations.

menus.Text:
## BALANITIS AND BALANOPOSTHITIS
Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis and is often associated with
erythema and pruritis. When the foreskin is also involved, the condition is
known as balanoposthitis (also referred to as balanitis in this discussion).
There are a variety of causes of balanitis, but most are due to poor hygiene of
the foreskin in uncircumcised men resulting in candida infection. Other, less
common causes, include bacterial infection (typically sexually transmitted or
anaerobic bacteria), dermatologic conditions, malignancy as well as others. Men
with Candidal balanitis often have a white curd-like exudate compared to a thick
foul-smelling purulent exudate in menu with anaerobic bacterial balanitis.
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
treatment:
Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure

menus.Text:
## BELL'S PALSY

Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster are possible causes of Bell's palsy. Others
include Borrelia burgdorferi or trauma. Some cases are idiopathic. Risk factors
Bell's Palsy include pregnancy, diabetes, obesity, hypertension, and upper
respiratory infections. Neurology consult is encouraged.
If Lyme disease is suspected, refer to the Lyme disease treatment page:
[Lyme Disease](lyme-disease)
Treatment with prednisone and an antiviral within 72 hours of symptoms onset
improves the chances of a complete recovery.

## Treatment #Preferred:

## Inpatient

Prednisone 60 mg q24h PO for 7 days <AND> valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h ($) [R]
for 7 days
Alternative:
Prednisone 60 mg q24h PO for 7 days <AND> acyclovir 400 mg PO 5X/day ($) [R]
for 10 days

## Outpatient

Prednisone 60 mg q24h PO for 7 days <AND> valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h ($) [R]
for 7 days
Non-VA order for above
Alternative:
Prednisone 60 mg q24h PO for 7 days <AND> acyclovir 400 mg PO 5X/day ($) [R]
for 10 days
Non-VA order for above

## BITE WOUNDS
Bite wounds are prone to infection because of the pathogenic oral flora carried
into tissues by teeth. Clean wounds with soap and water as soon as possible.
Consult Orthopedic surgery for bite wounds involving the hand.
## Antibiotic Prophylaxis Indications:
Severe injury less than 8 hours, Crush injury, Bone or joint penetration, Wound
of the face or hands or genitals, Immunocompromised host, Asplenia, Advanced
liver disease
*Routine use of prophylactic antibiotics for non-immunocompromised patients with
superficial wounds with no puncture that do not involve the face/ genitals/hands
is not recommended.
## Antimicrobial Treatment:
Empiric treatment for suspected or established infection following bite wound In
these cases, therapy should be directed against pathogen identified by Gram
stain and culture whenever possible.
## Rabies Prophylaxis:
Consider rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for all animal bite cases. Contact
Infectious diseases for assistance.
## Consider tetanus immunization status:
If immunization is up to date, nothing more needs to be done to prevent tetanus.
If immunization is lacking, and: wound IS NOT tetanus prone, bring immunization
up to date with Td wound IS tetanus prone, bring immunization up to date with Td
< AND > Human Tetanus Immune Globulin Inject 250 units deeply into muscle (deep
IM)

## BODY LICE (PEDICULOSIS CORPORIS)
Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood.
Body lice proliferate in places where crowding of persons with poor hygiene is
common, especially homeless persons.
Infested clothing and bed linen should be heat washed or discarded.
Itching is the most common symptom, but some patients present only with
excoriations and inflammation on the neck and trunk.

menus.Text:
## CANDIDA URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS
A positive urine culture for candida usually reflects colonization. Treat
cystitis only if the patient has symptoms of urinary tract infection (e.g.
dysuria, frequency, urgency, and/or suprapubic tenderness) or if the patient
will undergo invasive urological manipulation
Asymptomatic candiduria in a patient with a urinary catheter should not be
treated without an additional indication. Removal of catheter is strongly
recommended. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.
Neutropenic patients with asymptomatic candiduria should be assessed for
candidemia because they are at risk of dissemination. Obtain blood cultures and
assess potential sources of candidemia such as central venous catheters. Refer
to fungemia page for treatment recommendations.
[Fungemia Associated with Candida spp.](orzid2-gmenu-bacteremia-candida-spp)
## Treatment
## Inpatient

menus.Name: candida-vulvo-vaginitis
menus.Text:
## CANDIDA VULVOVAGINITIS
Candida vulvovaginitis typically presents with valvular irritation, burning or
pruritus. Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined
under the microscope for clue cells (epithelial cell coated with bacteria) to
exclude bacterial vaginosis. In candida vulvovaginitis, the vaginal pH is
typically normal (4-4.5) and vaginal discharge is typically thick and curdy with
white plaques on vaginal mucosa. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying fungus or
yeast with KOH prep.
Most non-C. albicans species respond to fluconazole treatment except C. krusei
and C. glabrata. C. krusei can be treated with topical agents as for complicated
candida vulvovaginitis below. C. glabrata treatment is complicated and azole
therapy is frequently unsuccessful. Consult Infectious Diseases in patients with
C. glabrata vulvovaginitis.
Recurrent candida vulvovaginitis is treated as complicated candida
vulvovaginitis for induction treatment, followed by maintenance regimen for 6
months.
## Candida vulvovaginitis in pregnancy:
## Inpatient

Clotrimazole vaginal cream 1% 1 applicatorful qhs for 7 days
## Treatment of uncomplicated candida vulvovaginitis
Fluconazole 150 mg PO once ($) [R,DI]
< OR >
Clotrimazole vaginal 1% cream 1 applicator full qhs ($) [M] for 7 to 14 days
< OR >
Terconazole 0.4% vaginal cream 1 applicator full qhs ($) [M] for 7 days
## Treatment of complicated candida vulvovaginitis (e.g. immunocompromised, severe
## disease) or recurrent infection induction treatment
Fluconazole 150 mg PO q72h for 7 days (3 doses) ($) [R,DI]
< OR >
Clotrimazole vaginal 1% cream 1 applicator full qhs ($) [M] for 10-14 days
< OR >
Terconazole 0.4% vaginal cream 1 applicator full qhs ($) [M] for 10-14 days
## Recurrent candida vulvovaginitis maintenance regimen following induction
## treatment above
Fluconazole 150 mg PO every 7 days ($) [R,DI] for 6 months
## Treatment of C. glabrata vulvovaginitis
Failure of azole therapy is common, alternative topical treatments below require
compounding by a pharmacist. Please call pharmacy to order.
Topical boric acid capsule 600 mg intravaginal qhs for 14 days
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Clotrimazole vaginal 1% cream 1 applicator full qhs ($) [M] for 7 days
## Treatment of uncomplicated candida vulvovaginitis

Non-VA order for above

Non-VA order for above

menus.Text:
## NON-SEVERE COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA TREATED IN AN INPATIENT SETTING
Common alternative explanations include heart failure, thromboembolic disease,
COPD exacerbation, viral pneumonitis, aspiration pneumonitis, or tumor. Most of
the latter conditions do NOT benefit from antimicrobials.
## Duration of therapy
Patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of 5 days, should be afebrile
for 48-72 hours, and should have no more than 1 CAP- associated sign of clinical
instability before discontinuation of therapy.
## Criteria for clinical stability
Temperature less than/equal to 100 degrees F Heart rate less than/equal to 100
beats/minute Respiratory rate less than/equal to 24 breaths/minute Systolic
blood pressure greater than/equal to 90 mm Hg Arterial oxygen saturation greater
than/equal to 90% --OR-- PO2 greater than/equal to 60 mm Hg on room air Ability
to maintain oral intake Normal mental status
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Stepdown empiric treatment for CAP (Intravenous to Oral conversion)
[Stepdown empiric treatment for CAP with oral antibiotics](cap-oral-treatment)
Note: These regimens may also be used to convert patients to oral medications
prior to discharge.
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Inpatient

## Preferred
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h for 5 days [M] <AND> azithromycin 500 mg PO x1 on
day 1, then 250 mg PO Q24H for 4 days [M]

menus.Text:
## SEVERE Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) Treated in Intensive Care Unit (ICU)
## Criteria for Defining SEVERE Community-acquired Pneumonia
Validated definition includes either one major or three or more minor criteria
MAJOR CRITERIA:
Septic shock with need for vasopressors
Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
MINOR CRITERIA:
Respiratory rate greater than or equal to 30 breaths/minute
PaO2/FiO2 ratio less than or equal to 250
Multilobar infiltrates
Confusion/disorientation
Uremia (blood urea nitrogen level greater than 20 mg/dl)
Leukopenia* (WBC less than 4,000 cells/microliter)
*Due to infection alone (i.e., not chemotherapy induced)
Thrombocytopenia (platelet count less than 100,000 microliters)
Hypothermia (core temperature less than 36 degrees C)
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation
## Recommendation for duration of antibiotic therapy for CAP:
Patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of 5 days, should be
afebrile for 48-72 hours, and should have no more than 1 CAP-
associated sign of clinical instability before discontinuation
of therapy.
## Criteria for clinical stability:
Temperature less than/equal to 100 degrees F
Heart rate less than/equal to 100 beats/minute
Respiratory rate less than/equal to 24 breaths/minute
Systolic blood pressure greater than/equal to 90 mm Hg
Arterial oxygen saturation greater than/equal to 90% --OR--
PO2 greater than/equal to 60 mm Hg on room air
Ability to maintain oral intake
Normal mental status

menus.Text:
## CERVICITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES
The main diagnostic signs that characterize cervicitis are 1)women who present
with purulent or mucopurulent exudate in the endocervical canal or on an
endocervical swab specimen and 2)sustained endocervical bleeding induced by
gentle passage of cotton swab through the cervical os. One or both signs may be
present.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the two most common sexually
transmitted cervicitis pathogens. Nucleic acid amplification tests for these
pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients at
risk for sexually transmitted cervicitis.
Chlamydia & GC PCR/LCR test
## For patients who have recently been treated for cervicitis
Treatment of recurrent or persistent cervicitis
When diagnosed with sexually transmitted cervicitis, the patient's sexual
partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually
transmitted infection. If diagnostic tests for the cause of cervicitis are not
feasible, therapy for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be given to
partners.
## Initial treatment of patients and sex partners
Patients and partners are often infected with both N. gonorrhoeae and C.
trachomatis. Treat for both pathogens unless one is ruled out by lab test.
Treatment for chlamydial or non-gonococcal cervicitis
Treatment for gonorrhea cervicitis

menus.Name: cholangitis
menus.Text:
## CHOLANGITIS
Oral step-down treatment
Most cases are due to common bile duct obstruction. Obstruction (if present)
must be relieved with an endoscopical, transcutaneous, or surgical procedure.
The most common pathogens isolated are E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus and
Enterobacter. Pseudomonas coverage is recommended in severe (grade 3)
cholangitis. Anaerobic coverage is recommended if biliary-enteric abnormality
is present.
Antimicrobials' role in cholangitis is to allow patients to have elective and
not emergently scheduled drainage procedures.
Due to increasing resistance, fluoroquinolones are only recommended in cases of
severe penicillin and cephalosporin allergy.
## Inpatient

## Treatment of patients on ward without systemic symptoms of infection
Treat for 4-7 days after source control
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h [M]
Biliary structural abnormality, including stent:
<ADD> Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI] to above regimen
## Treatment of patients in ICU with systemic symptoms of infection
Treat for 4-7 days after source control
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h [R]
Alternative:
Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
Alternative for severe beta-lactam reaction:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h [R,DI] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

## Treatment of patients on ward without systemic symptoms of infection
Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS
## Treatment of patients in ICU with systemic symptoms of infection
Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## ER

## Treatment of patients on ward without systemic symptoms of infection
Treat for 4-7 days after source control
Ceftriaxone 2 gm once STAT [M]
Biliary structural abnormality, including stent:
<ADD> Metronidazole 500 mg IV once STAT [DI] to above regimen
## Treatment of patients in ICU with systemic symptoms of infection
Treat for 4-7 days after source control
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV once STAT [R]
Alternative:
Cefepime 2 gm IV once STAT [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV once STAT [DI]
Alternative for severe beta-lactam reaction:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV once STAT [R,DI] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV once STAT
[DI]
## ________________________________________________________________________ References:

Cholangitis, Cholecystitis)

Solomkin et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2010, 50:133-64

menus.Name: cholecystitis
menus.Text:
## CHOLECYSTITIS
Oral step-down treatment
Adequate biliary drainage is the definitive treatment. Antimicrobials should be
prescribed only if signs of infection like leukocytosis or fever are present or
if the patient is elderly. Surgery and Gastroenterology involvement are
essential.
For acute cholecystitis in grade 1 disease, antimicrobials are primarily
prophylactic. For moderate to severe disease grades 2-3, antimicrobials should
be continued for 4-7 days.
Most cases are associated with E. coli, Enterococcus, Klebsiella, and
Enterobacter. Anaerobic coverage is not indicated unless a biliary-enteric
abnormality is present. For community-acquired acute cholecystitis, enterococcal
coverage is not required because Enterococcus has not been shown to be
pathogenic in these patients
Due to increasing resistance, fluoroquinolones are only recommended in cases of
severe penicillin and cephalosporin allergy.
## Treatment of patient on ward without systemic symptoms of infection
Duration of Therapy: Antimicrobials should be discontinued within 24 hours of
drainage procedure
Cefazolin 2 gm IV q8h [R]
Biliary structural abnormality, including stent:
< ADD > Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI] to above regimen
## Treatment of patient on ward with systemic symptoms of infection
Duration of Therapy: Treat for 4-7 days after source control
Preferred:
Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 gm IV q6h [R]
Alternative:
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h [M]
Biliary structural abnormality, including stent:
< ADD > Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI] to one of the regimens above
Alternative for severe beta-lactam reaction:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h [R,DI] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
## Treatment of ICU patients
## Inpatient

Duration of Therapy: Most can be treated for 4-7 days after source control.
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h [R]
< OR >
Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q12h [DI]
< OR >
Meropenem 1 gm IV q8h [R,O]
## Outpatient

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS ## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Sanford Guide article: Gallbladder Infections, Acute Cholecystitis
J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci (2018) 25:3-16 "Tokyo Guidelines"

menus.Text:
## CHRONIC PROSTATITIS / CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME
This syndrome presents with intermittent perineal and/or low back pain,
obstructive voiding symptoms, relatively normal examination, and negative urine
cultures. Antimicrobial therapy is not indicated.
Consult urology for non-antimicrobial therapy recommendations (e.g.
alpha-adrenergic antagonists, anti-inflammatory medications) to reduce symptoms.
## Anti-inflammatory treatment
## Inpatient

Ibuprofen 400 mg PO q8h for 2 to 3 weeks
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Ibuprofen 400 mg PO q8h for 2 to 3 weeks
Non-VA order for above
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Mandell chapter: Prostatitis, Epididymitis and Orchitis

menus.Name: chronic-bact-prostatitis
menus.Text:
## CHRONIC BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS
Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually presents as recurrent urinary tract
infections with the same bacterial etiology. Pain, tenderness, and fever may
accompany intermittent episodes of cystitis, but men are usually asymptomatic
between episodes and the prostate examination may be normal. Non-steroidal anti-
inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) often relieve pain. If the diagnosis is uncertain or
if the patient's symptoms do not respond to therapy, consult urology. The
presence of hematuria may be a sign of carcinoma, especially in older men, and a
urology consult should be requested.
A urine culture should be performed in all patients to guide antimicrobial
therapy.
Chronic prostate pain syndrome should be considered in patients who have
symptoms of prostatitis but have negative urine cultures. Chronic prostate pain
syndrome is discussed elsewhere:
Chronic prostate pain syndrome
 ## Duration
4 weeks minimum and up to 6 weeks of treatment is required. Durations longer
than 6 weeks may be needed in treatment of resistant organisms. Treatment with
trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole requires a treatment duration of 1 to 3 months.
## Empirical treatment
Preferred:
## Inpatient

Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h ($) [R,DI] for 4 weeks
< OR >
Levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h ($) [R,DI] for 4 weeks
Alternative:
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h ($) [R,DI] for 4 weeks
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h ($) [R,DI] for 4 weeks
Non-VA order for above
Alternative:
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h ($) [R,DI] for 4 weeks
Non-VA order for above
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Rees et al., BJU Int, 2015,116.509-525
Lipsky et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2010, 50(12)1641-1652
Mandell chapter: Prostatitis, Epididymitis and Orchitis

menus.Name: cmv-colitis-or-esophagitis
menus.Text:
## CMV COLITIS OR ESOPHAGITIS
Infection in immunocompetent patients is rare and usually associated with
minimal or no symptoms. Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased
include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving
prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease
indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter. Treatment is complex
and requires Infectious Diseases consultation.
## Duration of therapy
Treat for 3-6 weeks. Patients may be converted to oral therapy after initial
intravenous therapy and after clinical improvement of severe disease.
## Treatment of mild to moderate disease or following clinical improvement of
## severe disease
## Inpatient

Valganciclovir 900 mg PO q12h [R,O]
## Treatment of severe disease
Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h [R,O]
< OR >
Foscarnet 90 mg/kg IV q12h [R,O]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Valganciclovir 900 mg PO BID ($$$) [R,O]
Non-VA order for above
## Treatment of severe disease
Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.
References:
Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in HIV
Infected Adults and Adolescents. AIDSinfo (2015) 1-282
Mandell chapter: Cytomegalovirus
Sanford keyword: Cytomegalovirus
Up-to-Date article: Epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and treatment of
cytomegalovirus infection in immunocompetent adults

menus.Name: cmv-pneumonia
menus.Text:
## CMV PNEUMONIA
CMV pneumonia occurs almost exclusively in bone marrow transplant recipients,
usually within the first 120 days after transplantation. In these patients, CMV
pneumonia is severe and requires aggressive treatment. Treatment is complex and
requires Infectious Diseases consultation.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Induction therapy is indicated for 3 to 6 weeks, followed by maintenance
therapy. Duration of maintenance therapy is not well established.
## Treatment
## Inpatient

Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h ($$$$) [R,O] <AND> intravenous immune globulin
0.5 grams/kg IV every other day
## Maintenance therapy
Valganciclovir 900 mg PO Q24h ($$$) [R,O]
## Outpatient

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS. ##References:
Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in HIV
Infected Adults and Adolescents. AIDSinfo (2015) 1-282

menus.Name: cmv-retinitis
menus.Text:
## CMV RETINITIS AND ACUTE RETINAL NECROSIS
Infection in immunocompetent patients is rare and usually associated with
minimal or no symptoms. Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased
include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving
prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease
indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter. Treatment is complex
and requires Infectious Diseases consultation.
For sight threatening lesions (lesions within 1500 microns of the fovea)
intravitreal infections of ganciclovir or foscarnet are recommended in addition
to systemic treatment. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Treat retinitis for 14 to 21 days. Patients may be converted to oral therapy
after initial intravenous therapy and after clinical improvement of severe
disease. Treat acute retinal necrosis with IV therapy for at least 7 days and
until disease stabilizes then oral therapy for a minimum of 6 weeks. Maintenance
therapy after completion of treatment is indicated when CD4 count <100.
Discontinue maintenance therapy when CD4 count is >100 for 6 months.
## Treatment acute retinal necrosis or severe disease
Intravitreal antiviral in addition to systemic antiviral may provide added
therapeutic efficacy.
## Inpatient

Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h ($$$$) [R,O]
< OR >
Foscarnet 90 mg/kg IV q12h ($$$$) [R,O]
Optional add-on therapy for acute retinal necrosis
Ganciclovir 4mg/0.1mL intravitreal injection STAT ($$$$) [R,O]
< OR >
Foscarnet 2.4mg/0.1 mL intravitreal injection STAT ($$$$) [R,O]
## For cases not responsive to Intravenous therapy with foscarnet and ganciclovir
## used alone
Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h ($$$$) [R,O] <AND> foscarnet 90 mg/kg IV q12h
($$$$) [R,O]
In cases not responsive to first-line therapy, second-line therapies may be
effective. Their use is highly specialized and must be done by someone
experienced with HIV/AIDS medicine.
## Treatment of mild to moderate retinitis or after clinical improvement of severe
## retinitis/acute retinal necrosis
Valganciclovir 900 mg PO q12h($$$) [R,O]
## Maintenance therapy
Valganciclovir 900 mg PO q24h ($$$) [R,O]
## Outpatient

## Treatment acute retinal necrosis or severe disease
Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy
## Treatment of mild to moderate retinitis or after clinical improvement of severe
## retinitis/acute retinal necrosis Valganciclovir 900 mg PO q12h ($$$) [R,O]
Non-VA order for above
## Maintenance therapy
Valganciclovir 900 mg PO q24h ($$$) [R,O]
Non-VA order for above

menus.Name: colonized-respiratory-tract-ventilator
menus.Text:
## COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT IN A PATIENT ON A VENTILATOR
The respiratory tracts of persons who are intubated, have a
tracheostomy, or have other abnormalities of the larynx or trachea are
usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. The bacteria can be of
relatively low virulence (e.g. coagulase negative staphylococci, streptococci,
candida) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus,
enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida and enterococci are common
respiratory tract colonizers and they almost never cause pneumonia. There is
no benefit from treatment of patients with systemic antimicrobials simply
because the respiratory tract is colonized with a potential pathogen and there
is no evidence of an infiltrate. Systemic antimicrobial therapy will select for
resistant organisms and may lead to other adverse effects.
## Inpatient

See below for ventilator-associated pneumonia treatment recommendations in
patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and at least one of the following:
fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis, leukopenia or purulent bronchial
secretions.
Nosocomial Pneumonia
## Outpatient

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for ventilator-associated pneumonia
treatment recommendations in patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and
at least one of the following: fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis,
leukopenia or purulent bronchial secretions.
References
Kalil et al. Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 63(5): e61-e111.

menus.Name: conjunctivitis
menus.Text:
## CONJUNCTIVITIS
Conjunctivitis is associated with viral or bacterial pathogens. Viral
conjunctivitis presents with watery discharge. Bacterial infections are more
likely to present with thick exudate and conjunctival injection. Allergic
conjunctivitis typically presents with stringy mucus. If there is pus
(hypopion), corneal involvement, possible bacterial conjunctivitis, or
keratitis, consult ophthalmology.
Viral conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by adenovirus. It is self-limited
and antivirals provide no benefit. Symptomatic treatment with ophthalmic
antihistamine/decongestants and warm or cool compresses may relieve symptoms.
Bacterial conjunctivitis is most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus,
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus spp., Moraxella catarrhalis,
Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria spp. or enteric gram-negative rods. It is
generally self-limited, but topical antimicrobials reduce duration of symptoms
and limit person-to-person spread of infection. If symptoms do not improve after
2 days of antimicrobial therapy, the patient should be seen by an
ophthalmologist.
## Treatment for acute bacterial conjunctivitis
Trimethoprim/polymixin B ophthalmic solution 1 drop in affected eye(s)
q3h for 7 days ($) [M]
## Treatment for severe cases of bacterial conjunctivitis involving suppuration or
## contact lens wearers
Consult ophthalmology and begin topical antimicrobials.
Ofloxacin 0.3% ophthalmic solution 2 drops in affected eye q2h while awake for 2
days then 2 drops QID for 5 days ($) [M]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Trimethoprim/polymixin B ophthalmic solution 1 drop in affected eye(s)
q3h for 7 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above
## Treatment for severe cases of bacterial conjunctivitis involving suppuration or
## contact lens wearers
Consult ophthalmology and begin topical antimicrobials.
Ofloxacin 0.3% ophthalmic solution 2 drops in affected eye q2h while awake for 2
days then 2 drops QID for 5 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above

IDSA Guidelines Treatment/Management Patients with COVID-19
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## HOSPITALIZED DUE TO COVID-19
Refer to COVID-19 Pharmacological Inpatient Treatment Guidelines to determine
whether monotherapy or combination therapy with remdesivir and dexamethasone is
appropriate. For patients on dexamethasone with rapidly increasing oxygen needs
and systemic inflammation, add a second immunomodulatory drug (see
Immunomodulatory Treatment below)
Minneapolis VAHCS COVID Pharmacologic Inpatient Treatment Guidelines
## Remdesivir (IV):
Remdesivir 200mg IV once on day 1, then 100mg IV daily for 4 additional days
< AND >
Lab orders for monitoring remdesivir treatment (CMP, CBC with diff, INR)
## Dexamethasone (PO/IV):
Dexamethasone 6 MG PO q24h for up to 10 days
< OR >
Dexamethasone 6 MG IV q24h for up to 10 days
## Immunomodulatory Treatment
MVAHCS recommends baricitinib over tocilizumab in patients on high flow nasal
cannula oxygen or non-invasive ventilated patients that can take PO or NG. For
patients who cannot take PO or NG, or for those who are mechanically ventilated,
we recommend tocilizumab. These treatments are to be added on to dexamethasone,
with or without remdesivir. Consult Infectious Diseases for more details.
[Baricitinib PO/NG/GT](orzid2-gmenu-abx-baricitinib-eua-covid-19)
<OR>
Tocilizumab IV

Treatment is recommended for patients with confirmed mild to moderate COVID-19
and are at high risk of progressing to severe COVID-19.

## DECUBITUS ULCERS
Decubitus ulcers are colonized with bacteria. Antimicrobial therapy is
unnecessary unless the patient has infection of surrounding tissues signified by
erythema, warmth, local tenderness, or purulent discharge. Rectal or groin

Ulcers located in other sites are usually treated with antimicrobials for
staphylococci and streptococci.
## Duration of therapy: 5 - 7 days, but adjust to clinical response

osteomyelitis if managed without plastic surgery. Treatment with prolonged
antibiotics for osteomyelitis is typically reserved for when patients are
managed with surgical debridement, bone biopsy, and/or wound closure. ID consult
recommended.

menus.Name: deep-orophar-infect
menus.Text:
## DEEP OROPHARYNGEAL INFECTIONS
Deep oropharyngeal infections may threaten life and must be treated immediately.
Assess the risk of airway compromise and monitor the airway if it is threatened.
These infections are more common in people with diabetes mellitus and are caused
by mixed organisms including streptococcus sp., Staphylococcus aureus and
anaerobes . Perform CT scan to diagnose abscess. ENT and Infectious Diseases
consults are essential.
## Duration of therapy
If the patient's condition worsens or does not improve during the first 48 hours
of antimicrobial therapy, surgical drainage is indicated. If surgical drainage
is done, antimicrobials are usually continued for 48 hours after the procedure.
If surgical drainage is not done, 2 weeks of antimicrobial therapy until
clinical improvement is observed (e.g. resolution of fever and leukocytosis) is
appropriate.
## Empiric Treatment
## Inpatient

Preferred:
Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 gm IV q6h for 7 days ($) [R]
Alternative: [Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) [M] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h ($) [DI]
## Risk factors for MRSA or gram-positive cocci in clusters on gram stain, in
## addition to one of the above antimicrobial regimens
< ADD > vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12 hours ($) [R]
## Immunocompromised patient or severe infection
Immunocompromised patients require additional coverage for Staphylococcus aureus
and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Preferred:
< AND > vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
Alternative:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Cefepime 2 gm IV q12h ($$) [R] < AND > vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q 12 hours ($) [R]
for 7 days
## Step-down treatment after initial intravenous therapy. Adjust duration based on
## criteria above.
Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) [R]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy
## Step-down treatment after initial intravenous therapy. Adjust duration based on
## criteria above.
Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
## _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
## DISSEMINATED MYCOBACTERIUM AVIUM DISEASE TREATMENT
Many of these patients have HIV/AIDS. Management is complex. Consult
Infectious Diseases.
Rifabutin is optional for disseminated disease. Rifabutin can improve cure
rates, but may decrease blood concentrations of many drugs. Consult Infectious
Diseases or Pharmacy for more information.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Treatment is continued for 12 months and until CD4 count is >100 cells per
microliter for at least 6 months.
## Two-drug treatment
Preferred treatment
## Inpatient

Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h ($) [R,DI] <AND> ethambutol 15 mg/kg PO q24h
($$) [R]
Alternative
Azithromycin 250 mg PO q24h ($) [M] <AND> ethambutol 15 mg/kg PO q24h [R]
## Three-drug treatment
Preferred treatment
Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h($) [R,DI] <AND> ethambutol 15 mg/kg PO q24h
($$) [R] <AND> rifabutin 300 mg PO q24h ($$) [R,DI]
Alternative
Azithromycin 250 mg PO q24h ($) M <AND> ethambutol 15 mg/kg PO q24h [R]
<AND> rifabutin 300 mg q24h ($$) [R,DI]
## Outpatient

($$) [R]

## Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)
Antibiotic therapy is not required for mild to moderate disease caused by these
organisms because diarrhea often resolves on its own. Do not use antimotility
agents in patients with bloody stool. Antimicrobial treatment in patients with
AIDS Treatment is complex, consult Infectious Diseases
Primary treatment: Hydration and electrolyte replacement
Antimicrobial treatment of severe diarrhea

## Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) and Shiga Toxin-producing E. coli (STEC)
EHEC and STEC disease often presents as bloody diarrhea.
Treatment includes supportive measures such as volume repletion and
administering appropriate nutrition. Do not use antimotility or antimicrobial
agents as they can increase shiga-toxin release and increase the risk of
hemolytic uremia syndrome (HUS).
## Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)
EIEC disease typically presents as watery diarrhea, sometimes progressing to
bloody diarrhea. Refer to Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment
recommendations.

## ECTHYMA GANGRENOSUM
Ecthyma gangrenosum lesions commonly begin as painless red macules which
rapidly evolve into areas of induration that develop into pustules and-or
bullae. Ultimately, these become gangrenous ulcers. Ecthyma lesions
typically progress rapidly within 12 to 18 hours. They are often associated
with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia, especially in neutropenic patients.
Recommend blood cultures and culture of skin exudates.
#Inpatient Infectious disease consult is suggested.
Consider combination therapy in patients with severe infections.
Treat for 7 days.
## Preferred treatment
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h ($$) [R]
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q8h ($) [R,DI]
Gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV q24h ($) [R,O]

5 mg/kg IV q24h ($) [R,O]

IV q24h ($) [R,O]

menus.Text:
## ENDOPHTHALMITIS
Endophthalmitis is a medical emergency and presents with eye pain and visual
loss. It may be associated with gram positive or gram-negative bacteria,
including Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or with fungi.
Consult ophthalmology immediately. The ophthalmologist will obtain an aqueous or
vitreous fluid sample for gram stain and culture and begin intravitreal
antimicrobials.
## Inpatient

## Treatment with intravitreal antimicrobials
Vancomycin 1 mg/0.1 mL intravitreal injection STAT ($) [R] < AND > ceftazidime
2.25 mg/0.1 mL intravitreal injection STAT ($$) [M]
< OR >
Vancomycin 1 mg/0.1 mL intravitreal injection STAT ($) [R] < AND > amikacin 0.4
mg/0.1 mL intravitreal injection STAT ($$) [M]

menus.Name: epididymitis
menus.Text:
## EPIDIDYMITIS AND EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS
Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved
is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common
cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and
edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually
unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma
and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before
treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract
instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated
with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated
with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if
the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course
of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to
ciprofloxacin.
A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting
treatment to guide therapy:
Lab menu
Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for
treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more
information.
Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve
within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal
pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.
Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men
should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is
elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely
to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

## ERYSIPELAS
In contrast to cellulitis, erysipelas has sharply demarcated borders and a
characteristic raised, orange-peel appearance. Most cases are associated with
streptococcus. In a minority of cases, especially those involving the face,
Staphylococcus aureus is also a potential pathogen. In severe cases,
methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage must be provided
until microbiology results are available.
Treat for 5 to 10days, longer if patient is bacteremic.

## ERYSIPELOID (ERYSIPELOTHRIX RHUSOPATHIAE INFECTION)
Erysipeloid is a localized cutaneous infection with Erysipelothrix rhusopathiae.
It is a zoonotic infection of fisherman, fish handlers, and butchers acquired by
direct animal contact, most commonly with fish, but also with other animals
(e.g., swine). It usually affects the hand or fingers and is characterized by
throbbing pain and a red rash with a purple center and an elevated border.
Localized infections can be treated with oral antimicrobials.
Severe, diffuse cutaneous infections or systemic infections with E.
rhusopathiae occur rarely after ingestion of undercooked pork or contaminated
seafood in immunosuppressed individuals. These infections are treated
initially with intravenous antimicrobials.

menus.Name: esophagitis
menus.Text:
## ESOPHAGITIS
Esophagitis is usually associated with non-infectious diseases like
gastroesophageal reflux disease, mucositis, and pill-induced esophagitis.
Esophageal infection occurs primarily in immunosuppressed individuals (e.g.
chemotherapy, transplantation, HIV) and rarely in healthy individuals. Most of
the infectious esophagitis is caused by Candida albicans, cytomegalovirus (CMV)
and herpes simplex virus. Aphthous ulceration of the esophagus is common in HIV
infection. HIV screening is recommended.
## Inpatient/Outpatient

Candidiasis
CMV Esophagitis

## FIRST RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)
Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic
therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide,
etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved
or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the
diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to
antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial
therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.
## First Recurrence CDI: *The REGIMEN should be different from initial treatment.*
## Inpatient

Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days [M]
< OR >
Vancomycin Extended-Pulse Taper Regimen [M]
(Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days, then taper and pulse with 125 mg po q12h
for 7 days, then 125mg po qday for 7 days, then 125mg every other day for 6
weeks)
< OR >

< OR >

(Fidaxomicin 200mg po bid x5days, then 200mg every other day x 20days)

menus.Name: folliculitis
menus.Text:
## FOLLICULITIS
Folliculitis is an infection of the hair follicle with purulent exudate in the
epidermis. It is usually associated with Staphylococcus aureus. In patients
exposed to swimming pools or hot tubs, folliculitis may be associated with
Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Candida albicans can cause folliculitis in patients
receiving antimicrobials and/or corticosteroids. For folliculitis in patients
with severe acne, consult Dermatology. For extensive folliculitis or in
patients with HIV, consult Infectious Diseases.
## Treatment
Usually self-limiting. For most cases, treat with daily saline compresses until
symptoms resolve.
## Inpatient

## For moderate to severe cases associated with Staphylococcus aureus:
Mupirocin ointment to affected area q8h for 7 days ($) [M]
## For cases associated with Candida albicans
Clotrimazole cream q8h for 7 days ($) [M]
## Outpatient

## For moderate to severe cases associated with Staphylococcus aureus:
Mupirocin 2% ointment topical to affected area TID for 7 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above
## For cases associated with Candida albicans
Clotrimazole cream to affected area TID for 7 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above
References
Up-to-Date website
Sanford keyword: Folliculitis
Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014 59: 147

menus.Name: fungi-candida-albicans
menus.Text:
## CANDIDA ALBICANS
Avoid using fluconazole empirically to treat candidal infections in patients who
have received an imidazole in the previous year.
## Treatment of thrush or oropharyngeal candidiasis
Oropharyngeal candidal disease may present in different patterns, like white
plaques in the oropharyngeal area, erythematous macules (often in patients with
dentures), or as pseudomembranes. Thrush infection often recurs, especially in
patients with AIDS. Consult MRTC clinic or Infectious Diseases (MRTC may also be
consulted in the MVAHCS) for more information on treatment of recurrent
infection. Mild disease:
#Inpatient Nystatin swish and swallow q6h for 7-14 days [M]
< OR >
Clotrimazole troche 10 mg PO 5X/day for 7-14 days [M]
Moderate to severe disease:
Fluconazole 200 mg PO q24h for 7-14 days [R,DI]
## Esophageal candidiasis
Esophageal infection requires systemic therapy.
Preferred:
Fluconazole 400 mg PO q24h for 14-21 days [R,DI]
Alternative for patient who cannot swallow tablets:
Fluconazole 400 IV q24h for 14-21 days [R,DI]
<OR>
Micafungin 100-150mg IV q24h for 14-21 days
## Systemic candidal infection
Fluconazole is preferred empirical therapy in most cases. Amphotericin B should
be used empirically in patients who have received an azole antifungal drug
recently, or in patients who are critically ill.
Duration of Therapy: Duration of therapy is dependent upon location, severity of
infection, and response to therapy. Consult Infectious Diseases for more
information.
Preferred:
Fluconazole 800 mg PO once then 400 mg PO q24h [R,DI]
< OR >
Fluconazole 800 mg IV once then 400 mg IV q24h [R,DI]
Recent azole antifungal treatment:
Liposomal amphotericin (Ambisome) 3-5 mg/kg IV q24h [R,O]
< OR >
Micafungin 100-150 mg IV q24h [H,DI]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient
Nystatin swish and swallow QID for 7-14 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above
< OR >
Clotrimazole troche 10 mg PO 5X/day for 7-14 days ($) [M]
Non-VA order for above
Moderate to severe disease
Fluconazole 200 mg PO QDay for 7-14 days ($) [R,DI]
Non-VA order for above
## Esophageal candidiasis
Esophageal infection requires systemic therapy.
Preferred treatment
Fluconazole 400 mg PO QDay for 14-21 days ($) [R,DI]
Non-VA order for above
Alternative for patient who cannot swallow tablets
Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

menus.Name: furuncles-and-carbuncles
menus.Text:
## FURUNCLES AND CARBUNCLES
Localized purulent infections include furuncles, carbuncles and cutaneous
abscesses. Nearly all are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. A furuncle is an
inflamed nodule that usually develops as a complication of folliculitis. A
carbuncle is a more extensive lesion that extends further into the subcutaneous
tissue. Contact a wound care nurse for more information.
Incision and drainage is the mainstay of therapy for carbuncles, cutaneous
abscesses, and large furuncles.
The decision to administer antibiotics directed against S. aureus as an adjunct
to incision and drainage should be made based on the presence of systemic
inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) or in patients with markedly impaired
host defenses.
## For recurrent skin abscesses in addition to culture and antibiotic therapy
## recommended consider a decolonization regimen.
[Select here for Staphylococcus aureus Decolonization](orzid2-gmenu-abx-staphylococcus-aureus-decolonization)
## Mild infection: Purulent infection without systemic signs of infection
Recommend incision and drainage. No antibiotic indicated.
## Moderate Infection: Purulent infection with signs of systemic infection.
Recommend incision and drainage. Culture material and use results to guide
therapy.
Treat for 5 days and extend/modify treatment if not improved in this time.
## Preferred treatment:
## Inpatient

Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h ($) [R,DI]
## Alternative:
Doxycycline 100 mg po q12h ($) [DI]
## If methicillin-RESISTANT Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is suspected or proved
Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h ($) [DI]
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h ($) [R,DI]
## Severe Infections:
Patients who have failed incision and drainage along with oral antibiotics
or those with SIRS or for infections in those with neutropenia or diminished
neutrophil function.
Recommend incision and drainage. Culture material and use results to guide
therapy.
Treat for 5 days. Reevaluate patient and extend or modify treatment if not
improved in this time.
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
## Outpatient

Treat for 5 days and extend/modify treatment if not improved in this time.
## Preferred treatment

menus.Text:
## GENITAL HERPES
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Immunocompetent patients
## _______________________________________________________________________________
Treatment of the initial episode decreases the duration of pain, lesions, and
viral shedding by 1 to 2 days. Treatment of the initial episode does not
decrease likelihood of recurrent episodes.
Treatment
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7-10 days ($) [R]
Alternative
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h for 7-10 days ($) [R]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Episodic therapy for relapses
## _______________________________________________________________________________
Treatment of recurrent episodes must be started within 24 hours of symptom
onset. Treatment decreases the duration of pain and lesions, and viral shedding
by 1 to 2 days. Consider suppressive treatment for patients with more than 6
episodes per year.
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 5 days ($) [R]
< OR >
Acyclovir 800 mg PO q8h for 2 days ($) [R]
< OR >
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO q12h for 3 days ($) [R]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Immunocompromised patients
## _______________________________________________________________________________
Immunocompromised patients in whom genital herpes simplex disease is often
severe include: patients with HIV infection, organ transplants, malnourishment,
eczema or severe burns, and in patients receiving immunosuppressive
chemotherapy.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Treat mild to moderate disease for 10 days. In severe disease, treat with
intravenous acyclovir for 2 to 7 days based on clinical response, then treat
with an oral antiviral for a total duration of 10 days.
## Treatment for mild to moderate disease or after clinical improvement of severe
## disease
## Inpatient

Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h ($) [R]
Alternative
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h ($) [R]
## Treatment for severe disease
Infectious Diseases consult encouraged.
Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV q8h ($$) [R]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Chronic suppressive therapy
## _______________________________________________________________________________
Suppressive therapy is indicated in patients with more than 6 episodes per
year, or in patients with less frequent episodes who are desiring to minimize
risk of transmission. Some patients may find episodic treatment more
convenient. The frequency of recurrences can decrease after 1 to 5 years,
and suppressive therapy may be stopped every few years to see if it is
still needed.
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q12h ($) [R]
Alternative
*Note: Recommend increasing dose to 1000 mg per day for patients that have
breakthrough on the 500 mg dose. See recommendation below.
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO Q24h ($) [R]
## For patients with 10 or more episodes/year or breakthrough on lower dose:
Valacyclovir 1000 mg PO Q24h ($) [R]
## Outpatient

Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID for 7-10 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
Alternative
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO BID for 7-10 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
## _______________________________________________________________________________

## DIARRHEA WITH GIARDIA
Treatment can be offered when the patient has symptomatic disease.
Treatment of asymptomatic patients can be considered if they have contact with
immunocompromised or pregnant people or live or work in settings where there is
risk of spreading infection to others (e.g., food handlers, daycare, nursing
home).
## Primary treatment
## Inpatient

Hydration and electrolyte replacement
## Antimicrobial treatment
Metronidazole 250 mg PO q8h for 5 to 7 days [DI]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

## HEAD LICE (PEDICULOSIS CAPITIS)
Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood. To
make a diagnosis, use a nit comb, bright light, or lens to find a louse living
on the scalp. Dead nits may remain for months after successful treatment. Dead
nits are usually located more than 6 mm from the scalp.
Lice are often transmitted by infected clothing and bedclothes but not by
ordinary furniture that is not typically in contact with hair or scalp. Refer
to the following for advice on household cleaning for lice infestations:
https://www.cdc.gov/lice/treatment/index.html
## Treatment
Repeat if live lice are seen 7-10 days after treatment.
## Inpatient

Permethrin 1% lotion Apply to affected area for 10 minutes then comb out nits
[M]

Permethrin 1% lotion Apply to affected area for 10 minutes then comb out nits
[M]

menus.Name: hepatitis-a
menus.Text:
## HEPATITIS A
## Disease Management
Most acute disease is self-limited, and the virus does not cause chronic
disease. No specific antiviral therapy is available.
Patients who appear to be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with
mental status changes should receive supportive treatment.
## Inapatient ## Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease
[Hepatitis A Vaccine Information Page (outpatient orders only)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-hepa-vaccine-information-page)
## Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure
Post-exposure prophylaxis, including immune globulin and vaccination, should be
offered to persons with substantial exposure to hepatitis A.. Post exposure
prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of exposure. Vaccine can be given at
the same time as immune-globulin.
Consult GI for treatment recommendations
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

## Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease
Vaccine should be offered to persons at high risk of hepatitis A infection: men
who have sex with men, travelers to endemic areas likely to be exposed, illegal
drug users, persons at occupational risk of disease, persons with chronic liver
disease or clotting factor disorders.
Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months
## Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure
Post-exposure prophylaxis should be offered to persons with substantial exposure
to hepatitis A. Specifically, persons exposed to acute hepatitis through
household or sexual contact, persons who attend or work in a day care center
with a recent case, or employee or patron of a restaurant with a food handler
with hepatitis. Post exposure prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of
exposure. Vaccine can be given at the same time as immune-globulin.
Immune globulin 0.02 ml/kg IM x 1 <AND>
Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months
References:
Mandell chapter: Acute viral hepatitis
Sanford keyword: Hepatitis A, Acute, Treatment

## HEPATITIS B
## Acute disease management
Most acute hepatitis B disease is mild and self-limited. Patients who appear to
be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with mental status changes
should receive supportive treatment. ##Inpatient Antiviral therapy is not indicated.
Consult Gastroenterology and Infectious Diseases
## Chronic disease management
Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B is a complicated, highly specialized
task.
Consult Gastroenterology and Infectious Diseases
## Prevention
[Hepatitis B Vaccine Information Page](orzid3-gmenu-abx-hepb-vaccine-information-page)
## Select below for [Hepatitis B evaluation](orzid3-gmenu-hepatitis-b-evaluation-anti-cd20-antibody) for patients receiving Anti-CD20
## Antibody Treatment
Hepatitis B Evaluation
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Fulminant hepatitis is suggested by
increased prothrombin time, cholestasis, ascites, decreased liver size, or
decreasing serum albumin. Supportive treatment includes maintenance of fluid
and electrolyte balance, monitoring and possible correction of coagulation
defects, treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, and good nutrition with a low-
protein diet. Antiviral therapy is not indicated. Gastroenterology consult
encouraged.
## Chronic disease management
Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B is a complicated, highly specialized
task. Consult with gastroenterology and infectious diseases.
## Prevention
Vaccinate persons at high risk of disease including men who have sex with men,
illegal drug users, and health care workers with substantial exposure to blood
or body fluids.
Give Hepatitis B vaccine 1 dose IM in deltoid at 0, then 1 or 2 months, and
again at 4 to 6 months.

menus.Name: herpes-keratitis
menus.Text:
## HERPES KERATITIS
Ocular herpes infection can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. The majority of
cases are caused by HSV-1. The recurrence rate of ocular herpes is 40% over a 5
year period, less than that of oral or genital herpes. Ocular herpes is a
major cause of blindness and typically presents as infection of the epithelium
of the cornea but can also rarely involve the stroma and endothelium.
Ophthalmology consultation is recommended.
Involvement of the stroma or endothelium requires treatment with topical
steroid and close monitoring. For these cases, start oral antiviral and consult
ophthalmology for management.
Antiviral prophylaxis is recommended for patients with multiple recurrences,
recurrent episodes with ulceration, recurrent inflammation with
scar/vascularization approaching visual axis, patients who have had keratoplasty
for HSV-related scarring/astigmatism, and patients who have had HSV keratitis
while on immunosuppressive therapy. Post-surgical prophylaxis is not discussed
here. Please consult ophthalmology for more information.
## Treatment of acute infection
Without epithelial ulceration
## Inpatient

Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7-10 days ($) [R]
<OR>
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO q12h for 7-10 days ($) [R]
Ulceration of epithelium (Geographic ulcer)
Acyclovir 800 mg PO 5x/day for 14-21 days ($) [R]
<OR>
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q8h for 14-21 days ($) [R]
## Infection prophylaxis for prevention of recurrence
Reassess need for prophylaxis every 12 months
Acyclovir 400 mg PO Q12h for 12 months ($) [R]
<OR>
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO Q24h for 12 months ($) [R]
## Outpatient

Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID for 7-10 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
<OR>
Valacyclovir 500 mg PO BID for 7-10 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
Ulceration of epithelium (Geographic ulcer)
Acyclovir 800 mg PO 5x/day for 14-21 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
<OR>
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO TID for 14-21 days ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
## Infection prophylaxis for prevention of recurrence
Reassess need for prophylaxis every 12 months
Acyclovir 400 mg PO BID for 12 months ($) [R]
Non-VA order for above
<OR>

Non-VA order for above

menus.Name: herpes-simplex-esophagitis
menus.Text:
## HERPES SIMPLEX ESOPHAGITIS
HSV infection of the esophagus usually occurs in patients who are
immunocompromised, typically solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients.
In healthy patients HSV esophagitis occurs occasionally, usually in men under
the age of 40.
Patients usually present with odynophagia and dysphagia. Fever, epigastric
pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn are less frequent. Some patients may have
coexistent herpes labialis or oropharyngeal ulcers. Diagnosis is usually
established with an upper endoscopy. Suggestive findings may also be seen during
a barium swallow.
## Immunocompetent patients
Spontaneous resolution usually occurs in immunocompetent patients after one to
two weeks. Patients may respond more quickly if treated with a short course of
oral acyclovir.
## Duration of therapy
Treat for 7-10 days
## Treatment
## Inpatient

Acyclovir 400 mg PO 5x/day [R]
