menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT VENTILATOR
menus.Term1: Colonized respiratory tract in patient on a ventilator
menus.Text:
# COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT IN A PATIENT ON A VENTILATOR

The respiratory tracts of persons who are intubated, have a

tracheostomy, or have other abnormalities of the larynx or trachea are

usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. The bacteria can be of

relatively low virulence (e.g. coagulase negative staphylococci, streptococci,

candida) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus,

enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida and enterococci are common

respiratory tract colonizers and they almost never cause pneumonia. There is

no benefit from treatment of patients with systemic antimicrobials simply

because the respiratory tract is colonized with a potential pathogen and there

is no evidence of an infiltrate. Systemic antimicrobial therapy will select for

resistant organisms and may lead to other adverse effects.

See below for ventilator-associated pneumonia treatment recommendations in

patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and at least one of the following:

fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis, leukopenia or purulent bronchial

secretions.

[Nosocomial Pneumonia](orzid2-gmenu-abx-noso-pneumonia-new)

References

Kalil et al. Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 63(5): e61-e111.

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX COLONIZED WOUNDS
menus.Text:
# COLONIZED WOUNDS

Open wounds are usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. This is true of

ulcers (see below), post-operative wounds, traumatic wounds, and others. Then

bacteria can be of relatively low virulence (eg, coagulase negative

staphylococci, diphtheroids) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus

aureus, enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida is commonly present on wounds

that are moist or covered. There is no need to treat patients with systemic

antimicrobials simply because a wound culture is positive for a potential

pathogen. Topical antimicrobials are not effective in nearly all circumstances

and can select for resistant organisms or lead to other adverse effects.

Systemic antimicrobial therapy may be indicated if there are signs of infection.

[Decubitus ulcers](orzid2-gmenu-decubitus-ulcers)

[Diabetic foot ulcers](orzid2-gmenu-foot-ulcer-with-dm)

References

Lipsky et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2012, 54(12): e132-e173

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX COMPLICATED UTI CATHETER ASSOCIATED
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# CATHETER ASSOCIATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

# Rule out obstruction.

When patients who require parenteral therapy are afebrile, clinically stable,

and can take oral medication, convert to oral therapy based on the

identification and susceptibility of the isolate.

# Duration

Treat for 5 days with fluoroquinolones or 7 days with non-fluoroquinolone

antibiotics.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment

# PO therapy options

Preferred:

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h R,DI for 7 days](psjzid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-tab-bid)

*Avoid trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in the first and third trimesters

< OR >

[Nitrofurantoin SA 100 mg PO q12h R,O, CrCl =/>30mL/min, for 7 days](psjzid-nitrofurantoin-sa-100-mg-po-bid)

*Avoid nitrofurantoin in the third trimester

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

Primary alternatives:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psjzid-amoxicillin-clavulanate-875-125-mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Fosfomycin 3 gm sachet PO every other day M x 3 doses](psjzid-fosfomycin-3gm-po-qod-3-doses)

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

< OR >

[Cefpodoxime 400 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psjzid-cefpodoxime-400mg-po-q12h)

Secondary alternative:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h R,DI for 5 days](psjzid-ciprofloxacin-500mg-po-q12h)

# IV therapy options

Preferred:

[Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h M for 7 days](psjizid-ceftriaxone-2gm-iv-q24h)

History of ESBL or severe beta-lactam allergy:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Ertapenem 1 gm IV q24h R,O for 7 days](psjizid-ertapenem-1gm-iv-q24h)

History of Pseudomonas or Gram-negative MDR bacteria:

[Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h R for 7 days](psjizid-pip-taz-4-5gm-iv-q6h-ne-extinf-ci-cefep-metro)

< OR >

[Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h R for 7 days](psjizid-cefepime-2-gm-iv-q8h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Treatment for specific pathogens based on susceptibilities

# Enterobacteria including E. coli, Klebsiella, and Proteus

Preferred:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psjzid-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h M for 7 days](psjizid-ceftriaxone-2gm-iv-q24h)

Alternative:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h R,DI for 7 days](psjzid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-tab-bid)

*Avoid trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in the first and third trimesters

# Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is an uncommon urinary tract pathogen and presence in the urine may be

due to hematogenous seeding from another site. Blood cultures are indicated to

rule out bacteremia in patients who have S. aureus isolated from the urine.

Consult Infectious Diseases for more information.

# Pseudomonas

[Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q12h R,DI for 5 days](psjzid-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h R for 7 days](psjizid-pip-taz-4-5gm-iv-q6h-ne-extinf-ci-cefep-metro)

< OR >

[Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h R for 7 days](psjizid-cefepime-2-gm-iv-q8h)

# Enterococcus

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO q8h R for 7 days](psjzid-amoxicillin-1000-mg-po-bid)

< OR >

[Ampicillin 2 gm IV q4h R for 7 days](psjizid-ampicillin-2-gm-iv-q4h)

Alternatives:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Fosfomycin 3 gm sachet PO every other day M x 3 doses](psjzid-fosfomycin-3gm-po-qod-3-doses)

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

< OR >

[Nitrofurantoin SA 100 mg PO q12h R,O, CrCl =/>30 mL/min, for 7 days](psjzid-nitrofurantoin-sa-100-mg-po-bid)

*Avoid nitrofurantoin in the third trimester

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

< OR >

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h R for 7 days](orz-set-abx-vanco-new-start-15mg-kg-q12h-mrsa-nares-screening)

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX COMPLICATED UTI NO CATHETER
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# COMPLICATED UTI (NO CATHETER)

# Complicated UTI is an infection beyond the bladder accompanied by symptoms

# including fever/other signs of systemic illness, flank pain, and costovertebral

# tenderness. This includes pyelonephritis and febrile or bacteremic UTI.

NOT signs or symptoms: abnormal urinalysis alone, pyuria, falls, change in urine

odor or color, delirium (acute mental status change, confusion) without systemic

signs of infection. These may occur in patients with a UTI but alone are

inadequate for diagnosis and empiric treatment.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

For patients without signs or symptoms of UTI:

[Asymptomatic bacteriuria](orzid2-gmenu-abx-asymp-bacteriuria)

For patients presenting with septic shock from a suspected urinary tract

infection:

[Sepsis or Shock with Suspected Urinary Tract Infection](orzid2-gmenu-sepsis-suspected-uro-sepsis)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Duration

Treat for 5 days with fluoroquinolones or 7 days with non-fluoroquinolone

organisms, presence of obstruction, underlying renal disease, immunosuppression,

and neurologic or structural abnormality in some cases. Often therapy can be

completed with an oral agent pending clinical stability and susceptibility

testing.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment

# Preferred

[Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h M for 7 days](psjizid-ceftriaxone-2gm-iv-q24h)

# History of Pseudomonas

# Treatment for specific pathogens

# Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is an uncommon urinary tract pathogen and presence in the urine may be

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# EXACERBATION OF CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE (COPD)

Exacerbation of COPD (ECOPD): dyspnea and/or cough and sputum worsening over

< 14 days. An acute change in one or more of the following:

- Increased cough frequency and severity

- Increased sputum volume and/or changes in character

- Increased dyspnea

Available evidence is limited but suggests antibiotics are beneficial for COPD

exacerbations in hospitalized patients. Antibiotics are strongly recommended for

all patients admitted to the ICU for COPD exacerbation and those with sputum

purulence (new or increased from baseline).

Antibiotics are not routinely recommended for non-critically ill patients with

clear non-infectious causes for exacerbations (e.g. medication non-adherence,

environmental exposures) or known viral infections.

Dyspnea differential: acute coronary syndrome, worsening heart failure,

pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, medication non-adherence

Test for influenza and COVID

# General Ward patients

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h R for 5 days](psjzid-amox-clav-875-125mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h DI for 5 days](psjzid-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Azithromycin 500mg PO once, then 250mg q24h days 2-5 O](orz-set-abx-azithromycin-po-500-250-once-q24h-x4days)

Unable to tolerate oral antibiotics:

[Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 gm IV q6h R for 5 days](psjizid-ampicillin-sulbactam-3gm-iv-q6h)

History of Pseudomonas in a respiratory isolate in the past year:

[Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h R for 5 days](psjizid-cefepime-2-gm-iv-q8h)

# NOTE: Fluoroquinolones are not listed as a choice because of the risk of serious

# side effects outweigh the benefits.

[Fluoroquinolones FDA Serious Adverse Reactions](orz-gtx-abx-idp-fluoroquinolones-fda-warnings)

# ICU patients

Preferred:

[Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h R for 5 days](psjizid-ceftriaxone-2gm-iv-q24h)

History of Pseudomonas in a respiratory isolate in the past year or

immunosuppression:

[Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h R for 5 days](psjizid-cefepime-2-gm-iv-q8h)

< OR >

[Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h R for 5 days](psjizid-pip-taz-4-5gm-iv-q6h-ne-extinf-ci-cefep-metro)

menus.Text:
# ANTIMICROBIAL COST INFORMATION

Cost is represented as dollar ($) signs in parenthesis following the antibiotic.

The number of $ signs represent the cost ranges below:

$ = Less than 10 dollars per day

$$ = 10-50 dollars per day

$$$ = 51-100 dollars per day

$$$$ = 101-400 dollars per day

$$$$ = Greater than 400 dollars per day

The displayed cost of an antibiotic is an estimate based on usual daily doses

for an 80kg patient. Costs may change frequently due to VA contract negotiations

as well as supply and demand effects. Antibiotic cost and formulary are reviewed

by members of the Antimicrobial Subcommittee annually.

# INPATIENT COVID-19 ANTIMICROBIAL TREATMENT GUIDELINES

Refer to the Minneapolis VAHCS COVID-19 SharePoint site for additional info.

[Minneapolis VAHCS COVID-19 SharePoint Site](orz-gtx-abx-url-minneapolis-covid-sharepoint-site)

# ***COVID-19 therapy is a rapidly evolving field, including the widespread

# dissemination of therapies with little or no evidence for benefit. Therapies and

# dosages not specifically listed here or in the IDSA treatment guidelines

# should be discussed with the infectious diseases service. ***

[Click here IDSA Guidelines Treatment/Management Patients with COVID-19](orz-gtx-abx-url-idsa-covid-guidelines-2024)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# HOSPITALIZED DUE TO COVID-19

Refer to COVID-19 Pharmacological Inpatient Treatment Guidelines to determine

whether monotherapy or combination therapy with remdesivir and dexamethasone is

appropriate. For patients on dexamethasone with rapidly increasing oxygen needs

and systemic inflammation, add a second immunomodulatory drug (see

Immunomodulatory Treatment below)

[Minneapolis VAHCS COVID Pharmacologic Inpatient Treatment Guidelines](orz-gtx-abx-covid-19-pharmacologic-inpt-treatment-guidelines)

# Remdesivir (IV):

[Remdesivir 200mg IV once on day 1, then 100mg IV daily for 4 additional days](orz-set-abx-remdesivir-200mg-load-then-100mg-q24h-5days)

< AND >

[Lab orders for monitoring remdesivir treatment \(CMP, CBC with diff, INR\)](lrtz-set-remdesivir-x5-days)

# Dexamethasone (PO/IV):

[Dexamethasone 6 MG PO q24h for up to 10 days](psjzid-dexamethasone-6mg-po-qday-for-10days-covid)

< OR >

[Dexamethasone 6 MG IV q24h for up to 10 days](psjzid-dexamethasone-6mg-iv-push-q24h-for-10days-covid)

# Immunomodulatory Treatment

MVAHCS recommends baricitinib over tocilizumab in patients on high flow nasal

cannula oxygen or non-invasive ventilated patients that can take PO or NG. For

patients who cannot take PO or NG, or for those who are mechanically ventilated,

we recommend tocilizumab.  These treatments are to be added on to dexamethasone,

with or without remdesivir.  Consult Infectious Diseases for more details.

[Baricitinib PO/NG/GT](orzid2-gmenu-abx-baricitinib-eua-covid-19)

<OR>

[Tocilizumab IV](orzid2-gmenu-abx-tocilizumab-for-treatment-of-covid-19)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# HOSPITALIZED FOR REASONS OTHER THAN COVID-19

Treatment is recommended for patients with confirmed mild to moderate COVID-19

and are at high risk of progressing to severe COVID-19.

[Interaction checker for COVID-19 medications website link](orz-gtx-abx-url-covid-19-med-interaction-checker)

# Preferred treatment, within 5 days of symptom onset:

Paxlovid order sets below contain both inpatient and outpatient orders.

NORMAL RENAL FUNCTION (eGFR =/> 60 mL/min)

[Paxlovid \(Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir\) 300mg/100mg PO BID for 5 days](orz-set-abx-paxlovid-inpt-and-opt-orders)

MODERATE RENAL IMPAIRMENT (eGFR 30 to < 60 mL/min)

[Paxlovid \(Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir\) 150mg/100mg PO BID for 5 days](orz-set-abx-paxlovid-renal-dosing-pharmacy-info)

SEVERE RENAL IMPAIRMENT including hemodialysis (eGFR < 30 mL/min)

[Paxlovid \(Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir\) 300mg/100mg once on day 1 then](orz-set-abx-paxlovid-severe-renal-dosing-pharmacy-info)

150mg/100mg daily for 4 days

# Alternative, within 7 days of symptom onset:

[Remdesivir 200mg IV once on day 1, then 100mg IV daily for 2 additional days](orz-set-abx-remdesivir-200mg-iv-load-then-100mg-q24hh-3days)

< AND >

[Lab orders for monitoring remdesivir treatment \(CMP, CBC with diff, INR\)](lrtz-set-remdesivir-x3-days)

# HIGH RISK FOR SURGICAL SITE INFECTIONS ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS

Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for prevention of infection for the listed

high risk conditions:

1. Extensive inflammatory skin disease (e.g. high tension)

2. Groin or Lower Extremities

3. Skin flaps and grafts

4. Wedge excision of lip or ear

Contaminated, dirty or infected wound may warrant antibiotic prophylaxis if

patient is not currently on an antimicrobial for treatment of infection at the

surgical site. Surgical prophylaxis is covered by antimicrobials for treatment

of infection at time of surgery. No additional antimicrobials are necessary.

# Preferred

[Cephalexin 2 GM PO ONCE - 1 hour prior to procedure \($\) R](psjzid-cephalexin-2gm-po-once-c)

# MRSA risk factor

[Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO 60 minutes before incision \($\)](orz-set-abx-op-tmp-smx-1-ds-tab-po-once-penvk-500mg-po-once)

[R,DI] < AND > penicillin VK 500 mg PO 60 minutes before incision ($) [R]

# Unable to take oral medications

[Cefazolin Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-cefazolin-weight-based-dosing)

# MRSA risk factors and unable to take oral medications

# DERMATOLOGIC SURGERY POST-OPERATIVE ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS

# RECOMMENDATIONS

Conditions that may warrant dermatologic surgery post-operative antibiotic

prophylaxis:

1. Large wound (>5cm)

2. Long procedure where wound is open for a long time

3. Wound near cartilage or bone (e.g. some nose, scalp or ear sites)

If patient received pre-operative antibiotics, select the same antibiotic for

post-operative prophylaxis. Duration of antimicrobial prophylaxis should not

exceed 24 hours. Durations longer than 24 hours have not been shown effective in

preventing surgical site infections.

menus.Text:
# ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS AND DERMATOLOGIC SURGERY

Antibiotics are used to prevent infections in patients undergoing surgery in

certain well-defined circumstances. They are used to prevent surgical site

infection or to prevent endocarditis in circumstances where the risk of

endocarditis is high. For many low-risk surgeries, the risks associated with

antibiotic use, which can be severe or cause death, outweigh the benefits. The

following recommendations are consistent with guidelines published by the

American Heart Association and Infectious Disease Society of America.

In general, antibiotics are used to prevent post-operative wound infection

in clean-contaminated surgery. Most dermatological surgery involves clean

sites, and the risks of antibiotics outweigh potential benefits. Antibiotics

are used to prevent endocarditis and hematogenous joint infection in procedures

involving infected skin structures. Antibitic prophylaxis is also

recommended to prevent surgical site infections in procedures involving high

risk surgical sites and conditions.

When they are used, prophylactic oral antimicrobial agents should be

administered 30-60 minutes before the first tissue manipulation or incision.

Intravenous antimicrobials should be administered 60 minutes (120 minutes for

vancomycin) prior to procedure.

Antimicrobials should not be used to prevent infections in patients with

vascular grafts or orthopedic prostheses because the risk of bacteremia or

infection of these devices is tiny and antibiotic risks outweigh any theoretical

benefit.

A full course of antibiotics should be used to treat skin infections where

infection is already present at the time of surgery.

Suggested antibiotic prophylaxis regimens should be targeted against the typical

pathogens likely to be present. A risk-based approach for coverage of MRSA

should be taken in patients with specific risk factors for MRSA.

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# DIAGNOSIS OF ENDOCARDITIS

Diagnosis and management are complex. Cardiology, Infectious Disease, and

Surgery services should all be involved in diagnosis and management of infective

endocarditis.

Endocarditis is the result of growth of microorganisms on endothelium of the

heart. The integrity of the endothelial surface must be compromised in order to

allow microorganisms to attach and proliferate. Often such lesions are caused by

abnormal blood flow or thrombi resulting from heart valvular disease, prosthetic

heart valves, or from foreign material or microorganisms introduced to the

bloodstream as byproducts of illicit intravenous drug use.

Endocarditis should be considered a possible diagnosis in a patient with

persistent bacteremia without an identifiable focal infection, especially when

the patient has a structural heart abnormality, prosthesis, or has a recent

history of intravenous illicit drug use.

Diagnosis of endocarditis can be based on several combinations of signs and

symptoms. The Duke criteria help categorize cases as definite or possible

endocarditis based on major and minor criteria. The Duke criteria also indicate

when a diagnosis of endocarditis can be excluded.

[Modified Duke Diagnostic Criteria](orzid2-gmenu-abx-duke-criteria)

# Severity of Disease

Endocarditis is categorized by time course and severity of symptoms of illness

into acute and subacute. These classifications help suggest which pathogens may

be more likely associated with symptoms.

# Acute

Acute endocarditis is a rapidly progressing illness that often causes fever. It

can be associated with spread of infection to other parts of the body and can

cause death within a matter of weeks. In patient with suspected acute

endocarditis, three sets of blood cultures should be obtained with the first and

last cultures separated by at least one hour. Empiric antimicrobial therapy

should then be initiated as soon as possible.

# Subacute

Subacute endocarditis follows an indolent course. Generally, patients have had

some symptoms for at least 2 weeks. Symptoms are more subtle and spread of

infection to other systems is uncommon. In patients with suspected subacute

endocarditis, every attempt should be made to identify a pathogen prior to

initiating antimicrobial therapy. These patients should be observed carefully

for signs of heart failure or embolic complications, and if signs are noted,

surgery should be consulted immediately.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
# DRUG ALLERGIES

# Importance of history

The nature and circumstances of a possible previous reaction including the

timing should be considered. In many cases, previous reactions are clearly

not due to drug allergy.

# Types of reactions

*Immediate - within one hour of starting drug administration.

Type I reactions present with urticaria, hypotension, angioedema, bronchospasm,

or anaphylaxis and occur within an hour of exposure. These reactions are

immunoglobulin E (IgE) and mast cell and/or basophil mediated.

*Delayed - After one hour of starting administration (usually after 6 days)

1) Type II reactions manifest as hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and

neutropenia. They are caused by antibody (usually IgG)- mediated cell

destruction.

2) Type III reactions can manifest as serum sickness, vasculitis or Arthus

reaction, and are caused by IgG:drug immune complex deposition and complement

activation.

3) Type IV reactions typically manifest as contact dermatitis, morbilliform

reactions, severe exfoliative dermatoses (Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic

epidermal necrolysis) and other presentations. They are T-cell mediated.

Repeated exposures lead to reactions that are of the same type.

# Beta-lactam allergies

Approximately 10% of patients report a beta-lactam allergy. Up to 90% of these

patients can tolerate penicillin and have been designated penicillin allergic

unnecessarily. Patients allergic to cephalosporins will have a cross-reaction to

penicillins 3% to 5% of the time. Overall, patients with a history of penicillin

allergy can tolerate cephalosporins although there are rare reports to severe,

sometimes fatal anaphylactic reactions. Neither penicillin- or cephalosporin-

allergic patients will react to aztreonam. The degree of cross-reactivity of

penicillins and cephalosporins with carbapenems appears to be low.

# Therapeutic implications

If a patient has had an immediate reaction to a drug in the past, an allergy

specialist should evaluate the patient before a drug of the same class is

administered to the patient. Patients with delayed onset reactions causing

fever, systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement should also be evaluated by an

allergy specialist before a drug of the same class is administered.

# Desensitization

A patient with previous Type I reaction to a beta-lactam can be desensitized and

then receive therapeutic doses of the same class within a day. Severe

reactions during desensitization are uncommon. Pharmacy service must be

contacted for assistance and drug preparation. Infectious Disease consultation

strongly recommended.

[Link to penicillin desensitization protocol](orzid2-gmenu-abx-penicillin-desens-protocol)

# MODIFIED DUKE DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA

The Modified Duke criteria are used to diagnose endocarditis on clinical

grounds. Endocarditis may also be diagnosed by pathology results.

[Modified Duke Criteria Diagnostic Listing](orzid2-gmenu-abx-duke-listing)

# Requirements for definite diagnosis of endocarditis

Two major criteria

< OR >

One major criterion and three minor criteria

< OR >

Five minor criteria

# Requirements for possible diagnosis of endocarditis

One major criterion and one minor criterion

< OR >

Three minor criteria

# Requirements for rejection of diagnosis of endocarditis

Firm alternative diagnosis explaining evidence of endocarditis

< OR >

Resolution of endocarditis syndrome with antibiotic therapy for less than 4 days

< OR >

No pathological evidence of endocarditis at surgery or autopsy, with antibiotic

therapy for less than 4 days

< OR >

Does not meet criteria for possible endocarditis as above.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Baddour et al., Circulation 2015, 132:1-52

Mandell chapter: Endocarditis and intravascular infections

Sanford keyword: Endocarditis

Up-To-Date article: Overview of management of infective endocarditis in adults

Wang et al., JAMA 2018, 320.1:72-83

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA DIAGNOSTIC LISTING

# Major criteria

# Blood culture positive

*Typical microorganisms consistent with IE from 2 separate blood cultures:

Viridans streptococci, Streptococcus bovis, HACEK group organisms (Haemophilus

species, Aggregatibacter species, Cardiobacterium species, Eikenella corrodens,

and Kingella species), Staphylococcus aureus, or community-acquired enterococci

in the absence of a primary focus, or microorganisms consistent with IE from

persistently positive blood cultures defined as follows: at least 2 positive

cultures of blood samples drawn >12h apart or all 3 or a majority of >/= 4

separate cultures of blood (with first and last sample drawn at least 1 h apart)

*Single culture positive for Coxiella burnetii or anti-phase 1 IgG antibody

titer greater than or equal to 1:800

# Echocardiogram positive for endocarditis

*Echocardiographic evidence for endocarditis, defined as:

An echo dense, intracardiac mass attached to valve or supporting structures, in

the path of regurgitant jets, or a mass present on implanted material in the

absence of an alternative anatomic explanation

< OR >

Paravalvular abscess

< OR >

New partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve or new valvular regurgitation

(worsening or changing or preexisting murmur is not sufficient for a major

criterion)

Note: Echocardiography should be performed in all patients suspected of having

endocarditis. Transesophageal echocardiograph (TEE) is recommended for patients

with prosthetic valves. Transthoracic echocardiograph (TTE) is often adequate

for patients suspected of having native valve endocarditis, especially on the

aortic valve, but TEE may be needed for these patients as well. Contact

infectious diseases or cardiology for more information.

# Minor criteria

# Predisposing heart condition or intravenous drug user

# Fever

Temperature over 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit)

# Vascular phenomena

Major arterial embolus, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm,

intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, or Janeway's lesions

# Immunologic phenomena

Glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth's spots, or rheumatoid factor

# Microbiological evidence

A case with a positive blood culture, but with results that don't meet the major

criterion blood culture criteria listed above or serological evidence of active

infection with organism consistent with endocarditis. Microbiological evidence

is not intended to include all positive blood cultures. For example, a single

positive culture for coagulase-negative staphylococci or a culture yielding an

organism that is not a cause of endocarditis would not support a diagnosis of

endocarditis.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Baddour et al., Circulation 2015, 132:1-52

Mandell chapter: Endocarditis and intravascular infections

Sanford keyword: Endocarditis

Up-To-Date article: Overview of management of infective endocarditis in adults

Wang et al., JAMA 2018, 320.1:72-83

menus.Text:
# DURATION OF ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY

In general, duration of therapy is based on multiple factors, including

infection severity, rapidity of improvement, and pathogen susceptibility. For a

few diseases guidelines are established based on available evidence and opinion.

For many more diseases, guidelines have not been established.

For outpatient prescriptions, when a range is recommended by CDSS, the

prescription order will default to the lowest dose and day supply. For inpatient

orders, durations are listed in the recommendations but are not included in the

quick order. The provider must select a duration, if desired, when completing an

inpatient quick order.

For all cases clinical judgment is important. More information is given within

specific diagnoses or syndromes sections.

# DIARRHEA WITH ESCHERICHIA COLI

# Enteroaggretive E. coli (EAEC), Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), and

# Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)

Antibiotic therapy is not required for mild to moderate disease caused by these

organisms because diarrhea often resolves on its own. Do not use antimotility

agents in patients with bloody stool. Antimicrobial treatment in patients with

AIDS Treatment is complex, consult Infectious Diseases

Primary treatment: Hydration and electrolyte replacement

Antimicrobial treatment of severe diarrhea

[Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h for 3 days R,DI](psjzid-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-q24h-for-3-days)

Alternative

[Rifaximin 200 mg q8h for 3 days M](orz-set-abx-rifaxamin-200mg-po-q8h-for-3-days)

# Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) and Shiga Toxin-producing E. coli (STEC)

EHEC and STEC disease often presents as bloody diarrhea.

Treatment includes supportive measures such as volume repletion and

administering appropriate nutrition. Do not use antimotility or antimicrobial

agents as they can increase shiga-toxin release and increase the risk of

hemolytic uremia syndrome (HUS).

# Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)

EIEC disease typically presents as watery diarrhea, sometimes progressing to

bloody diarrhea. Refer to Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment

recommendations.

[Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment recommendations](orzid2-gmenu-abx-shigella-species)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

65(12):45-80

menus.Term2: Elements of a CDSS advice page
menus.Text:
# ELEMENTS OF A CDSS ADVICE MENU

Advice menus are comprised of the following elements:

# _____________________________________

# TYPICALLY present on an advice menu

# _____________________________________

1) Diagnosis or condition label-at the top of each advice menu.

2) Treatment. Empirical treatment as well as treatment for selected pathogens

is presented with links to antimicrobial quick orders unless stated otherwise.

In addition to the drug, dose, and route, each quick order text includes the

drug's approximate cost per day and coding for important drug properties of

note. Drugs clustered together are considered equivalent.

3) Help. At the top of each advice menu. There are links to a variety of

resources (susceptibilities, important drug properties, section-specific

consults, etc.).

4) References. At the bottom on each advice menu. These are key references for

the recommendations on the menu.

# _____________________________________

# DISCRETIONARY advice menu components

# _____________________________________

1) (Treatment) Alternative. Following the (preferred) Treatment section with

quick orders for common alternative antimicrobials. Antimicrobial listed under

each alternative header are equivalents among those listed. A broader selection

of medications can be accessed through the Need an alternative menu within the

help section. For some conditions we recommend alternative antimicrobials when

recommended drugs are not suitable for an individual patient. Unless otherwise

stated drugs clustered together under Alternatives are considered equivalent.

If none of the recommended or alternative drugs is suitable you can find more

drugs by clicking on the Need an alternative link at the top of the menu.

2) Consults. At the top of the menu, these are consultation requests pertinent

to the clinical problem addressed by the menu. Links to context-specific

consults can be found on advice menus, as appropriate. For example, the herpes

simplex encephalitis menu contains a link to a request for neurology consult.

3) Resources. Pertinent to the clinical problem and addressed by the menu is

provided for example. For some menus, supplemental resources have been

identified (e.g., PORT score calculator for Community Acquired Pneumonia,

diagnostic tools, Epidemiology, etc.) the information is included on the advice

menu.

# EMPYEMA/LUNG ABSCESS

Empyema is usually a complication of pneumonia. Diagnostic thoracentesis is

recommended in most cases. Pulmonary or Infectious Diseases consultation is

essential.

The duration of antibiotic therapy for bacterial empyema is not well defined but

generally 4-6 weeks

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# EPIDIDYMITIS AND EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS

Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved

is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common

cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and

edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually

unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma

and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before

treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract

instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated

with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated

with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if

the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course

of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to

ciprofloxacin.

A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)

should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting

treatment to guide therapy:

[Lab menu](orzid2-gmenu-abx-lab-menu)

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for

treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more

information.

Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve

within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal

pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.

Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men

should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is

elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely

to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment in men who practice insertive anal intercourse

[Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once \($\) M < AND > levofloxacin 500 mg PO q24h](orz-set-abx-ceftriaxone-500mg-im-once-levoflox-500mg-po-q24h)

for 10 days ($) [R, DI]

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Age >/= 35 years or

# Recent urinary tract instrumentation or urinary tract surgery (e.g., prostate

# biopsy, vasectomy):

# EPIGLOTTITIS

Maintaining the airway is the key to management. Call ENT service and ask them

to see the patient immediately. Blood cultures and epiglottal cultures (in

intubated patients) should be used to direct antimicrobial therapy. Empirical

therapy should be initiated prior to results of cultures as infection is life

threatening and cover for likely pathogens (Moraxella catarrhalis, penicillin

resistant S. pneumonia, beta-hemolytic streptococci and possibly Staph. aureus)

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX ESBL KPC ETC
menus.Text:
# Gram-Negative Bacilli Drug Resistance

In some Gram-negative bacilli, potent bacterial enzymes have emerged that

inactive many newer broad-spectrum beta lactam drugs. These include extended-

spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), serine carbapenemases, metallo-beta-

lactamases, AmpC beta-lactamases and oxacillinases. These enzymes are most

common in strains of Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Escherichia coli,

Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella, and Serratia

marcescens. The enzymes can be latent under many circumstances. However, in

patients receiving beta lactam antibiotics, the enzymes can be expressed and

contribute to treatment failure. Because of this, and since the enzymes continue

to evolve, they are difficult to detect in clinical microbiology laboratories.

Bacteria carrying these enzymes are often also resistant to many other commonly

used antimicrobials, including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, and

others, through different mechanisms. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas and

Acinetobacter are increasingly resistant to all antimicrobials.

Clinicians must be aware that these enzymes may not be detected in all strains

that carry them. If a Gram-negative infection is not responding to therapy with

a beta lactam drug, consider adding or switching to a drug that is not a beta

lactam and appears active in the susceptibility report.

If a patient is suspected of having a Gram-negative infection and is likely to

be colonized with bacteria carrying these enzymes, empirical therapy with

alternative drugs that are not inactivated by them should be considered.

# Risk factors for colonization or infection with resistant gram-negative bacilli

1. Travel to Asia

2. Central venous catheters and other indwelling tube and drains

3. Recent surgical procedures

4. Recent antibiotic therapy

5. Long-term care facility residence

6. Multiple, severe chronic illnesses

7. Ventilator assistance

8. Hemodialysis

9. Long hospital or ICU stay.

# AmpC beta-lactamases alternative antimicrobials

Inactivate many cephalosporins, most penicillins, and beta-lactam inhibitor

combinations. Alternatives include aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cefepime and

colistin.

# ESBLs alternative antimicrobials

Inactivate most cephalosporins, monobactams, and penicillins. Alternatives

include aminoglycosides, carbapenems and colistin.

# Serine carbapenemases, metallo-beta-lactamases and oxacillinases alternative

# antimicrobials

Confer resistance to all beta-lactams. Most strains are also resistant to most

other antibiotic classes. Alternatives include aminoglycosides and colistin.

Infectious Diseases consultation is recommended.

# Additional alternative antimicrobials

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and quinolones are non-beta-lactam alternative

antimicrobials, especially useful for IV to PO conversion. Gram negative bacilli

co-resistance to these antimicrobials is common however. Tigecycline (restricted

to ID) and ceftazidime-avibactam (non-formulary) are also potential options for

susceptible isolates. Infectious Diseases consultation is required for their

use.

References

Mandell chapter: Molecular Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance in Bacteria

Up-to-Date article: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases

Up-to-Date article: Overview of carbapenemase-producing gram-negative bacilli

Rodrï¿½guez-Bano et al. Clinical microbiology reviews, 2018, 31(2): e00079-17

Sanford guide keyword: Gram Negative Bacilli, Drug Resistance, Overview

# ESOPHAGITIS

Esophagitis is usually associated with non-infectious diseases like

gastroesophageal reflux disease, mucositis, and pill-induced esophagitis.

Esophageal infection occurs primarily in immunosuppressed individuals (e.g.

chemotherapy, transplantation, HIV) and rarely in healthy individuals. Most of

the infectious esophagitis is caused by Candida albicans, cytomegalovirus (CMV)

and herpes simplex virus. Aphthous ulceration of the esophagus is common in HIV

infection. HIV screening is recommended.

# FIRST RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic

therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide,

etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved

or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the

diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to

antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial

therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.

# First Recurrence CDI: *The REGIMEN should be different from initial treatment.*

[Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days M](psjzid-vancomycin-125mg-po-q6h-x10days-cdiff)

< OR >

[Vancomycin Extended-Pulse Taper Regimen M](psjzid-vancomycin-taper-and-pulse-dosing)

(Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days, then taper and pulse with 125 mg po q12h

for 7 days, then 125mg po qday for 7 days, then 125mg every other day for 6

weeks)

< OR >

[Fidaxomicin 200 mg po q12h for 10 days M](psjzid-fidaxomicin-200mg-q12h-10d)

< OR >

[Fidaxomicin Extended-Pulse Regimen M](psjzid-fidaxomicin-extended-pulse-regimen)

(Fidaxomicin 200mg po bid x5days, then 200mg every other day x 20days)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# Diabetes-Related Foot Infections (Diabetic Foot Infections-DFI)

# Wound Cultures:

Do NOT:

-Culture a wound that appears uninfected

-Swab the wound to obtain a culture

-Culture without first cleaning and debriding a wound

-Order blood cultures in patients with mild-moderate DFI

Do:

-Obtain culture by deep tissue biopsy after cleaning and debriding the wound

-Obtain blood culture in patiens with signs of sepsis or severe DFI

# Imaging:

-An x-ray is recommended for all new foot ulcers in patiens with diabetes

to evaluate for deformity, bony destruction, soft tissue gas, and/or

foreign bodies.

-An MRI is preferred when more specific imaging is needed to evaluate for

either soft tissue abscess or osteomyelitis.

[<Click here> Osteomyelitis Evaluation](orzid3-gmenu-osteomyelitis-evaluation)

# Infection Severity (IWGDF/IDSA Classification)

# Uninfected DFI (Class 1/Uninfected): Chronic ulceration without s/s infection

-Do not culture wound

-Do not treat with antibiotics

If osteomyelitis identified arrange for bone biopsy --hold antibiotics

# _________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 2/Mild):

At least two of the following are present:

-Local swelling or induration

-Erythema >0.5cm but <2cm around wound

-Local tenderness or pain

-Local increased warmth

-Purulent drainage

# Primarily Outpatient Treatment:

Duration of therapy: 1-2 weeks

# Preferred Regimens:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h x 7days \($\) R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 7 days \($\) R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

# Treatment with MRSA Risk Factors and/or Severe PCN allergy:

[Beta-lactam Allergy Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO bid x 7days \($\) R,DI](psozid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-po-bid-7ds)

< OR >

[Linezolid 600 mg PO BID for 7 days \($\) DI,O](psozid2-linezolid-600mg-po-bid-x7days)

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 3/Moderate):

Infection with no systemic manifestations and envolving:

-Erythema extending >2cm from the wound margin, and/or

-Tissue deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissues

(e.g., tendon, muscle, joint, and bone)

# Outpatient/Often Hospitalized Treatment:

Oral or IV with change to PO with improvement

***See CDSS Inpatient for IV treatment***

Duration of therapy: 1-3 weeks

# Preferred Treatments:

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125mg po bid \($\) R for 14 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-14ds-po-bid)

# Treatment with MRSA risk factors:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg po BID \($\) R <AND> Doxycycline 100mg](orz-set-abx-op-amox-clav-875-doxy-14days)

1 tablet po bid ($) [DI] for 14 days

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg po bid \($\) R <AND> Trimethoprim-sulfa](orz-set-abx-op-amox-clav-875-bid-tmp-sulfa-14days)

1 tablet PO bid ($) [R,DI] for 14 days

# Treatment with Penicillin allergy:

[Beta-lactam Allergy Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h \($\) R,DI <AND> metronidazole 1000 mg PO q12h \($\)](orz-set-abx-levofl-750mg-po-q24h-metro-1-gm-po-q12h)

[DI,H]

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 4/Severe):

Infection with associated systemic manifestations as indicated by 2 or

more of the following:

-Fever, Tachycardia, Leukocytosis, Hypotension, Sepsis, Necrotizing infection

# Managed exclusively in the Inpatient setting

***See CDSS Inpatient for treatment recommendations***

# __________________________________________________________________

Reference:

Senneville Diabetes Metab Res Rev. (2024) 40(3):e3687

Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59:147

Lipsky BA Clin Infect Dis 2012, 54:e132

# Diabetes-Related Foot Infections (Diabetic Foot Infections-DFI)

# Wound Cultures:

Do NOT:

-Culture a wound that appears uninfected

-Swab the wound to obtain a culture

-Culture without first cleaning and debriding a wound

-Order blood cultures in patients with mild-moderate DFI

Do:

-Obtain culture by deep tissue biopsy after cleaning and debriding the wound

-Obtain blood culture in patiens with signs of sepsis or severe DFI

# Imaging:

-An x-ray is recommended for all new foot ulcers in patiens with diabetes

to evaluate for deformity, bony destruction, soft tissue gas, and/or

foreign bodies.

-An MRI is preferred when more specific imaging is needed to evaluate for

either soft tissue abscess or osteomyelitis.

[<Click here> Osteomyelitis Evaluation](orzid3-gmenu-osteomyelitis-evaluation)

# Infection Severity (IWGDF/IDSA Classification)

# Uninfected DFI (Class 1/Uninfected): Chronic ulceration without s/s infection

-Do not culture wound

-Do not treat with antibiotics

If osteomyelitis identified arrange for bone biopsy --hold antibiotics

# _________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 2/Mild):

At least two of the following are present:

-Local swelling or induration

-Erythema >0.5cm but <2cm around wound

-Local tenderness or pain

-Local increased warmth

-Purulent drainage

# Primarily Outpatient Treatment:

Duration of therapy: 1-2 weeks

# Preferred Regimens:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h x 7days \($\) R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 7 days \($\) R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

# Treatment with MRSA Risk Factors and/or Severe PCN allergy:

[Beta-lactam Allergy Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO bid x 7days \($\) R,DI](psozid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-po-bid-7ds)

< OR >

[Linezolid 600 mg PO BID for 7 days \($\) DI,O](psozid2-linezolid-600mg-po-bid-x7days)

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 3/Moderate):

-Erythema extending >2cm from the wound margin, and/or

-Tissue deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissues

(e.g., tendon, muscle, joint, and bone)

# Outpatient/Often Hospitalized Treatment:

Oral or IV with change to PO with improvement

***See CDSS Inpatient for IV treatment***

Duration of therapy: 1-3 weeks

# Preferred Treatments:

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125mg po bid \($\) R for 14 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-14ds-po-bid)

# Treatment with MRSA risk factors:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg po BID \($\) R <AND> Doxycycline 100mg](orz-set-abx-op-amox-clav-875-doxy-14days)

1 tablet po bid ($) [DI] for 14 days

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg po bid \($\) R <AND> Trimethoprim-sulfa](orz-set-abx-op-amox-clav-875-bid-tmp-sulfa-14days)

1 tablet PO bid ($) [R,DI] for 14 days

# Treatment with Penicillin allergy:

[Beta-lactam Allergy Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h \($\) R,DI <AND> metronidazole 1000 mg PO q12h \($\)](orz-set-abx-levofl-750mg-po-q24h-metro-1-gm-po-q12h)

[DI,H]

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 4/Severe):

Infection with associated systemic manifestations as indicated by 2 or

more of the following:

-Fever, Tachycardia, Leukocytosis, Hypotension, Sepsis, Necrotizing infection

# Managed exclusively in the Inpatient setting

***See CDSS Inpatient for treatment recommendations***

# __________________________________________________________________

Reference:

Senneville Diabetes Metab Res Rev. (2024) 40(3):e3687

Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59:147

Lipsky BA Clin Infect Dis 2012, 54:e132

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX GENITAL HERPES
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# GENITAL HERPES

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompetent patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Treatment of the initial episode decreases the duration of pain, lesions, and

viral shedding by 1 to 2 days. Treatment of the initial episode does not

decrease likelihood of recurrent episodes.

Treatment

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7-10 days \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-q8h)

Alternative

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h for 7-10 days \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-1gm-po-q12h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Episodic therapy for relapses

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Treatment of recurrent episodes must be started within 24 hours of symptom

onset. Treatment decreases the duration of pain and lesions, and viral shedding

by 1 to 2 days. Consider suppressive treatment for patients with more than 6

episodes per year.

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 5 days \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-q8h)

< OR >

[Acyclovir 800 mg PO q8h for 2 days \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-800mg-po-tid)

< OR >

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO q12h for 3 days \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-500mg-po-bid)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompromised patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Immunocompromised patients in whom genital herpes simplex disease is often

severe include: patients with HIV infection, organ transplants, malnourishment,

eczema or severe burns, and in patients receiving immunosuppressive

chemotherapy.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat mild to moderate disease for 10 days. In severe disease, treat with

intravenous acyclovir for 2 to 7 days based on clinical response, then treat

with an oral antiviral for a total duration of 10 days.

# Treatment for mild to moderate disease or after clinical improvement of severe

# disease

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-q8h)

Alternative

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-1gm-po-q12h)

# Treatment for severe disease

Infectious Diseases consult encouraged.

[Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV q8h \($$\) R](psjizid-acyclovir-5-mg-kg-iv-q8h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Chronic suppressive therapy

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Suppressive therapy is indicated in patients with more than 6 episodes per

year, or in patients with less frequent episodes who are desiring to minimize

risk of transmission. Some patients may find episodic treatment more

convenient. The frequency of recurrences can decrease after 1 to 5 years,

and suppressive therapy may be stopped every few years to see if it is

still needed.

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO q12h \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-bid)

Alternative

*Note: Recommend increasing dose to 1000 mg per day for patients that have

breakthrough on the 500 mg dose. See recommendation below.

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO Q24h \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-500mg-po-q24h)

# For patients with 10 or more episodes/year or breakthrough on lower dose:

[Valacyclovir 1000 mg PO Q24h \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-1000-mg-po-q24h)

References:

Center for Disease Control and Prevention. MMWR (2021) 70:1-192

Mandell chapter: Herpes simplex virus

Sanford keyword: Herpes simplex

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# Antibiotic Prophylaxis for GI Endoscopic Ultrasound FNA Procedures

The purpose of antibiotic prophylaxis during GI endoscopy is to reduce the

risk of iatrogenic infectious complications.

# Cystic lesions along GI tract including mediastinum:

Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended before a FNA for cystic lesions along

the GI tract to prevent cyst infection.

# Recommendation:

# INPATIENT:

[Levofloxacin 500 mg PO q24h for 4 days, beginning 60 minutes before](psjzid-levofloxacin-500mg-po-qday-4days-procedure)

endoscopic procedure ($) [R,DI]

# OUTPATIENT:

[Levofloxacin 500 mg PO q24h for 4 days, beginning 60 minutes before](psozid-levofloxacin-500mg-po-once-then-qday-3days)

endoscopic procedure ($) [R,DI]

# Solid Lesions along the upper or lower GI tract:

Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended before a diagnostic EUS or EUS-FNA

of solid lesions along the upper or lower GI tract.

# References:

Up-to-Date website

Guideline: Antibiotic prophylaxis for GI endoscopy, Gastrointestinal

Endoscopy 2008, 67:791-795

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# DIARRHEA WITH GIARDIA

Treatment can be offered when the patient has symptomatic disease.

Treatment of asymptomatic patients can be considered if they have contact with

immunocompromised or pregnant people or live or work in settings where there is

risk of spreading infection to others (e.g., food handlers, daycare, nursing

home).

# Primary treatment

Hydration and electrolyte replacement

# Antimicrobial treatment

[Metronidazole 250 mg PO q8h for 5 to 7 days DI](psjzid-metronidazole-250-mg-po-q8h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

DOI: 10.1136/bmj.i5369-Minetti et al, BMJ, 2016, 355.i5369

Sanford Guide article: Giardiasis

DOI: 10.1093/cid/cix669-Shane et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases 2017,

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# Gonococcal Infections:

-When diagnosed with sexually transmitted disease, the patient's sexual

partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually

transmitted infection.

# Uncomplicated gonococcal infections of the pharynx, cervix, urethra, or rectum:

-If chlamydial infection has not been excluded, recommend to treat for

chlamydia.

-A test-of-cure is unnecessary for uncomplicated urogenital or rectal

gonorrhea for patients treated with the recommended or alternative regimen.

-A test-of-cure is recommended for patients with pharyngeal gonorrhea.

Obtain nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) 7 to 14 days after initial

treatment, regardless of regimen used for pharyngeal gonorrhea.

# Lab test:

[Click here Place order for gonorrhea/chlamydia lab NAAT test](lrtzid-chlamydia-gc-urine-naat)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Chlamydial infection and no co-infection:

[Click here Chlamydial infection and no co-infection](orzid2-gmenu-abx-chlamydia-urethritis-cervicitis-or-proctitis)

# _____________________________________________________________________________

# Preferred treatment for patients and no chlamydial co-infection:

# Patients weighing less than 150 kg:

[Ceftriaxone 500 MG IM x1 dose \($\) M](psjizid-ceftriaxone-500mg-im-x1-gonococcal)

# Patients weighing 150 kg or greater:

[Ceftriaxone 1 GM IM x1 dose \($\) M](psjizid-ceftriaxone-1gm-im-x1-gonococcal)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Preferred treatment with chlamydial co-infection or chlamydial infection has

# not been excluded:

# Patient weighing less than 150 kg:

[Ceftriaxone 500mg IM Once \($\) M <AND> Doxycycline 100mg PO bidx7days \($\) DI](orz-set-abx-ceftriaxone-500mg-im-x1-doxy-100mg-po-bidx7d-gonoc)

# Patients weighing 150 kg or greater:

[Ceftriaxone 1 GM IM Once \($\) M <AND> Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7days\($\) DI](orz-set-abx-ceftriaxone-1gm-imx1-doxy-100mg-bid-x7d)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Alternative treatment for beta-lactam allergy for cervix, urethra, or rectum:

For persons with a history of a beta-lactam allergy, a thorough assessment

of the reaction is recommended.

[Gentamicin 240 MG IM Once \($\) R <AND> Azithromycin 2000 mg PO Once \($\) DI](orz-set-abx-gentamicin-240mg-im-x1-azith-2000mg-x1-gonococcal)

# Alternative treatment for beta-lactam allergy for pharynx:

No reliable alternative treatments are available for pharyngeal gonorrhea.

For persons with a history of a beta-lactam allergy, a thorough assessment

of the reaction is recommended. For persons with an anaphylactic or other

severe reaction to ceftriaxone, consult Infectious Disease for alternative

treatment recommendation.

References:

St. Cyr S, et al. MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020, 69:1911-1916.

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX H PYLORI INFECTION
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# HELICOBACTER PYLORI INFECTION

H. pylori infection is associated with peptic ulcers, gastritis, gastric

adenocarcinoma, and gastric lymphoma. Antimicrobials should be given to patients

with confirmed H. pylori infection. Antisecretory therapy should be given

concurrently.

Test of cure should be completed at least 4 weeks after completion of therapy

(recommended within 4-8 weeks after completion). Any PPI therapy must be

held for 2 weeks prior to testing.

[Click here Lab H.pylori, stool](lrtz-h-pylori-ag-stool)

Note: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) advises adult household

members of individuals who have a positive non-serological test for

H. pylori to seek testing trough their provider.

# First line treatment:

[Bismuth subsalicylate 524 mg PO q6h <AND> Tetracycline 500 mg q6h DI](orz-set-abx-bis-subsal-metro-tcn-omep-h-pylori)

<AND> metronidazole 500mg PO q6h [DI] <AND> omeprazole 20mg po q12h. Take

all for 14 days.

# Alternative treatments:

Alternatives may have lower efficacy and higher resistances rates. Test of

cure extremely important.

***Consider referring patients who cannot take first line therapy to

GI pharmacist for treatment management and follow-up testing.***

[Click here Gastroenterology \(Inpatient\) Consult - Pharmacists](gmrctz-gastroenterology-ip)

# Rifabutin triple (Talicia):

Note: place medication order and PADR using order below

[Amoxicillin/Omeprazole/Rifabutin \(250/10/12.5MG\) 4 cap po tid x14days DI,H](orz-set-abx-rifabutin-triple-hyplori-14days-padr)

< OR >

# PCAB dual (Voquezna DualPak-Amoxicillin+Vonoprazan - dispensed individually)

Note: place medication order and PADR using order below

[Amoxicillin 500mg po q8h + Vonoprazan 20mg po q12h +PADR x14 days DI](orz-set-abx-voquezna-dualpak)

< OR >

# Clarithromycin Quadruple:

Resistance to clarithromycin is increasing. Do not use for patients with prior

exposure to macrolides. Consider susceptibility testing prior to use.

[Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h R,DI <AND> Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO q12h R](orz-set-abx-clarith-amox-metro-omepro-h-pylori)

<AND> metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h [DI] <AND> omeprazole 20 mg PO q12h. Take all

for 14 days.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Chey et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection.

Am J Gastroenterol, 2024, 119(9):1730-1753.

VA PBM Clinical Recommendations November 2024. Use of newer combination products

in the treatment of H.pylori infections.

menus.Text:
# HEPATITIS A

# Disease Management

Most acute disease is self-limited, and the virus does not cause chronic

disease. No specific antiviral therapy is available.

Patients who appear to be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with

mental status changes should receive supportive treatment.

# Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease

[Hepatitis A Vaccine Information Page \(outpatient orders only\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-hepa-vaccine-information-page)

# Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure

Post-exposure prophylaxis, including immune globulin and vaccination, should be

offered to persons with substantial exposure to hepatitis A.. Post exposure

prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of exposure. Vaccine can be given at

the same time as immune-globulin.

Consult GI for treatment recommendations

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Mandell chapter: Acute viral hepatitis

Sanford Guide article: Hepatitis A

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX HERPES KERATITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# HERPES KERATITIS

Ocular herpes infection can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. The majority of

cases are caused by HSV-1. The recurrence rate of ocular herpes is 40% over a 5

year period, less than that of oral or genital herpes. Ocular herpes is a

major cause of blindness and typically presents as infection of the epithelium

of the cornea but can also rarely involve the stroma and endothelium.

Ophthalmology consultation is recommended.

Involvement of the stroma or endothelium requires treatment with topical

steroid and close monitoring. For these cases, start oral antiviral and consult

ophthalmology for management.

Antiviral prophylaxis is recommended for patients with multiple recurrences,

recurrent episodes with ulceration, recurrent inflammation with

scar/vascularization approaching visual axis, patients who have had keratoplasty

for HSV-related scarring/astigmatism, and patients who have had HSV keratitis

while on immunosuppressive therapy. Post-surgical prophylaxis is not discussed

here. Please consult ophthalmology for more information.

# Treatment of acute infection

Without epithelial ulceration

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7-10 days \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-q8h)

<OR>

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO q12h for 7-10 days \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-500mg-po-bid)

Ulceration of epithelium (Geographic ulcer)

[Acyclovir 800 mg PO 5x/day for 14-21 days \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-800mg-po-5x-d)

<OR>

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q8h for 14-21 days \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-1gm-po-q8h)

# Infection prophylaxis for prevention of recurrence

Reassess need for prophylaxis every 12 months

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO Q12h for 12 months \($\) R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-bid)

<OR>

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO Q24h for 12 months \($\) R](psjzid-valacyclovir-500mg-po-q24h)

References:

Baratz, Arch Ophthalmology, (2012) 130.1: 108-110

Guess et al, The Ocular Surface, (2007) 5.3:240-250

Wilhelmus, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (2015), 1:CD002898

Miserocchi et al, Efficacy of Valacyclovir vs Acyclovir for the Prevention of

Recurrent Herpes Simplex

Virus Eye Disease: A Pilot Study, American Journal of Ophthalmology, 2007

144:547-551

White et al, Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group and American Academy of

Ophthalmology, (2014)

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX HERPES SIMPLEX ESOPHAGITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# HERPES SIMPLEX ESOPHAGITIS

HSV infection of the esophagus usually occurs in patients who are

immunocompromised, typically solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients.

In healthy patients HSV esophagitis occurs occasionally, usually in men under

the age of 40.

Patients usually present with odynophagia and dysphagia.  Fever, epigastric

pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn are less frequent. Some patients may have

coexistent herpes labialis or oropharyngeal ulcers.  Diagnosis is usually

established with an upper endoscopy. Suggestive findings may also be seen during

a barium swallow.

# Immunocompetent patients

Spontaneous resolution usually occurs in immunocompetent patients after one to

two weeks. Patients may respond more quickly if treated with a short course of

oral acyclovir.

# Duration of therapy

Treat for 7-10 days

# Treatment

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO 5x/day R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-5x-days)

< OR >

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h R](psjzid-valacyclovir-1gm-po-q12h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompromised patients

# Treatment for mild to moderate disease

Duration of therapy: Treat for 14-21 days

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO 5x/day R](psjzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-5x-days)

< OR >

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h R](psjzid-valacyclovir-1gm-po-q12h)

# Treatment for severe disease

Duration of Therapy: Treat for 7-14 days

[Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV q8h R](psjizid-acyclovir-5-mg-kg-iv-q8h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

John Hopkin's Guides article: Herpes simplex virus

Mandell chapter: Herpes simplex virus

Sanford Guide article: Herpes simplex

# HIV

HIV infection and AIDS are associated with several host defense defects. Cell-

mediated immune defects render a patient more susceptible to opportunistic

infections with pathogens like Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis

carinii), Toxoplasma gondii, cytomegalovirus, mycobacterium-avium intracellulare

complex, and Candida spp.

Contact ID or HIV service for assistance.

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX HOW TO FIND ALT ABX
menus.Text:
# HOW TO FIND AN ALTERNATIVE ANTIMICROBIAL WITHIN THE CDSS

The CDSS has been developed locally with input from a broad, representative

group of clinicians. All antimicrobial recommendations within the Antimicrobial

CDSS are reviewed by a clinical pharmacist and an Infectious Diseases Medical

Specialist. Recommendations provided are based on local susceptibility patterns,

clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines. In rare cases,

the recommended antimicrobials and listed alternatives may not be preferred for

the patient you are treating (e.g. isolate resistance, allergies, etc.). In

these cases, a broader set of alternative antimicrobials may be ordered through

the Antimicrobial CDSS. Like other antimicrobial orders in the CDSS,

antimicrobials ordered through the Alternative Antimicrobials menu do on require

a prior authorization or ID approval.

To access the Alternative Antimicrobials menu, navigate to the menu containing

antimicrobial recommendations for the infectious disease you are treating.

At the top of the menu, select:

#2 Help legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more

Then select- Alternative Antimicrobials to CDSS Recommendations

Select the reason an alternative antimicrobial is required then the Alternative

Antimicrobial menu will display.

The Alternative Antimicrobial menu contains antimicrobial regimens that have

been deemed appropriate for use as alternatives to recommended antimicrobials by

the Antimicrobial P&T Subcommittee. If the list does not contain the preferred

antimicrobial, contact or consult Infectious Diseases.

The regimens provided in the Alternative Antimicrobial menu are not tailored for

a specific infectious disease. The dose, frequency, and duration must be changed

based on the infectious disease you are treating as well as for patient specific

factors. The usage of alternative antimicrobials are monitored by the

Antimicrobial CDSS team for appropriateness and to identify infectious diseases

for addition to the system.

menus.Text:
# HOW TO USE THE CDSS

The CDSS has been designed to offer antimicrobial prescribing advice quickly and

efficiently. Since inpatient and outpatient drugs are ordered differently, the

CDSS has both and inpatient and outpatient versions for prescribing.

The Antimicrobial CDSS is located within CPRS. When CPRS is open, click on the

Orders tab at the bottom left hand side of the CPRS window.

# For inpatients

On the left-hand side of the "Orders" tab, click on the "Medicine Inpt Orders."

option.  In the right-hand column of the window that pops up, select "#77

Antimicrobials (CDSS).". The main menu of the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS will

now be open.

# For outpatients

On the left-hand side of the "Orders" tab, click on the "Medicine Outpt Orders."

option.In the right-hand column of the window that pops up, select "#55

Antimicrobial (CDSS).". The main menu of the Outpatient Antimicrobial CDSS will

now be open.

# Navigating Within the CDSS

*Using the decision tree

The main menu of the Antimicrobial CDSS contains links to categories of

infectious diseases based on syndrome/organ system (e.g. cardiovascular,

genitourinary, etc.), organisms (e.g. gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative

bacteria, viruses, etc.) and other special cases. To navigate to specific

infectious disease, select the category the infectious disease is associated

with. Within the category menu, select the specific infectious disease sub-menu

for recommendations, quick orders and pertinent resources (e.g., section-

specific consults, important drug properties, CDSS system help resources, etc.).

*Using the Index

The Index is in the main menu at the top of the left-hand column under the

header Index of Antimicrobial CDSS content. The Index contains an alphabetized

list of Antimicrobial CDSS content. Find the infectious disease, organism or

other topic you are looking for by scrolling down the list. When you locate the

term you are looking for, click on it to be linked to the menu containing

specific recommendations, quick orders and pertinent resources.

# Quick Orders

Quick orders are preprogrammed with the usually recommended antimicrobial dose,

frequency and solution for the specific infectious disease.

[More information on duration of antimicrobial therapy](orzid2-gmenu-abx-duration-of-abx-therapy)

Quick orders are not tailored to specific patient factors such as renal

insufficiency, comorbidities, contraindications, weight, allergies, etc. The

provider must assess every patient closely for these factors and modify

recommended antimicrobials if needed. To assist the provider, additional drug

information is provided within specific infectious diseases recommendation menus

and a link to more in depth information is provided at the top of these menus.

Alternatives to preferred antimicrobials quick orders are often provided in

recommendations, a broader selection of alternative antimicrobials is provided

in the Alternative Antimicrobial menu (see What if a Preferred Antimicrobial is

not Provided in the Recommendations?).

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# HERPES SIMPLEX ENCEPHALITIS

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 is the leading cause of sporadic fatal

encephalitis worldwide and should be suspected in patients who have symptoms

unexplained by other causes. Typical symptoms include acute alteration of

consciousness for more than 24 hours, fever, new onset seizures and/or focal

neurologic deficits. Patients taking natalizumab are at increased risk of HSV

encephalitis. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to achieve resolution

of infection and symptoms. If diagnosis is not certain and there is little

likelihood of herniation, obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample for HSV

polymerase chain reaction (PCR). MRI without contrast nearly always show

abnormal signs in patients with HSV encephalitis. Neurology and Infectious

disease consultations are strongly encouraged.

# Treatment, Initiate Immediately When HSV Encephalitis is Suspected

[Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h \($$\) R,DI for 14 to 21 days](psjizid-acyclovir-10-mg-kg-iv-q8h)

*If BMI > 35, use IBW to dose

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX IDP CIPROFLOXACIN PO
menus.Text:
# ________________________________________

# Ciprofloxacin PO

# ________________________________________

# Usual dose:

250-500 mg q12h

# Dose adjustments for renal or hepatic insufficiency:

# Creatinine clearance (ml/min) Dose adjustment

< 30250 mg q12h

Hemodialysis  250-500 mg q24h

# Drug Interactions:

Hypoglycemia that can lead to coma especially in diabetics taking

oral hypoglycemic medicine or insulin.

Calcium, dairy products, iron, zinc, magnesium, aluminum  inhibit the absorption

of oral ciprofloxacin.  Give ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after these

drugs.

Increases effects of caffeine and theophylline by inhibiting  metabolism.

Monitor the patient for signs of agitation or anxiety.

Increases the effect of warfarin.  Monitor international normalized ratio (INR)

ratio (INR) frequently in patients taking warfarin.

# Adverse Drug Reactions:

# FDA Drug Safety Communication

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration advised that the serious

side effects associated with fluoroquinolone antibacterial drugs

generally outweigh the benefits for patients with acute sinusitis, acute

bronchitis, and uncomplicated urinary tract infections who have other

treatment options. For patients with these conditions, fluoroquinolones should

be reserved for those who do not have alternative treatment options.

An FDA safety review has shown that fluoroquinolones when used systemically

are associated with disabling and potentially permanent serious side effects

that can occur together. These side effects can involve the tendons,

muscles, joints, nerves, and central nervous system.

FDA identified cases of hypoglycemic coma, resulting in death in some

instances. Most pateints had risk factors for hypoglycemia such as older age,

diabetes, renal insufficiency, and concomitant use of hypoglycemic drugs,

especally sulfonylureas.  FDA also identified reports of additional mental

health side effects, and requires that all fluoroquinolones include six

psychiatric adverse reactions (disturbance in attention, memory impairment,

delirium, nervousness, agitation and disorientation).

# Other adverse reactions:

Nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, confusion, CNS

stimulation, rare seizures, rare QT interval prolongation, and

tendinitis/tendon rupture. Six psychiatric adverse reactions

including disturbance in attention, memory impairment, delirium,

nervousness, agitation and disorientation.

Hypoglycemia that can lead to coma, occuring more frequently in

the elderly and those with diabetes.

# Pregnancy Risk Factor Category: C

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU ABX IMPETIGO
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

Impetigo and Ecthyma

Impetigo is a superficial skin infection that rarely causes systemic

symptoms. Ecthyma is a skin infection characterized by crusted sores

beneath which ulcers form. It is a deep form of impetigo, as the same

bacteria causing the infection are involved. Ecthyma causes deeper

erosions of the skin into the dermis.

Gram stain and culture of the pus or exudates from skin lesions of

impetigo and ecthyma are recommended to help identify whether

Staphylococcus aureus and/or beta-hemolytic Streptococcus is the cause.

Bullous and non-bullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical

antimicrobials, but oral therapy is recommended for patients with

numerous lesions or in outbreaks affecting several people to help

decrease transmission of infection. Treatment for ecthyma should be an

oral antimicrobial.

# Treatment for impetigo with few lesions

[Mupirocin ointment to affected area q8h for 5 days \($\) M](psjzid-mupirocin-2-oint-top-to-affect-area-q8h)

# Treatment for ecthyma and for impetigo with numerous lesions or

# whose symptoms have not responded to topical treatment

Treat orally for 7 days

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h \($\) R](psjzid-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-q12h)

# Alternative for penicillin allergy

[Doxycycline 100MG PO q12h \($\) DI](psjzid-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h)

# IF MRSA confirmed or suspected:

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h \($\) R,DI](psjzid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-tab-bid)

[Doxycycline 100MG PO q12h \($\) DI](psjzid-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h)
