menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for most clean procedures,

including knee, hand or foot procedures, arthroscopy, or other procedures

without implantation of foreign materials.

Prophylaxis is indicated for internal fixation of fracture, total joint

replacement, and any implanted foreign body. Open fractures should be treated

as infected.

Cefazolin is preferred for prophylaxis, as it is more active than vancomycin

against susceptible staphylococci, the most common surgical pathogens.

Vancomycin should be used in patients who are colonized or recently infected

with methicilin-resistant Staphlococcus aureus (MRSA).

Prophylaxis beyond 24 hours is not supported by current data and guidelines.

Longer durations provide no additional benefit and are associated with

side effects, increased costs, and bacterial resistance.

Also, there is no evidence of benefit of antimicrobial administration until

all drains or catheters are removed.

# Clean procedures of hand, knee, and foot:

[Click here No antimicrobial prophylaxis recommended for procedure](orz-gtx-abx-pre-op-url-nurse-generic-order)

# Prophylaxis recommendations for the following surgeries:

Internal fixation of fracture, total joint replacement, any implanted

foreign body

# Preferred:

[Cefazolin Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-cefazolin-weight-based-dosing)

Prophylaxis recommendation includes q8h for 2 doses post-op. Please place

post-op antimicrobial prophylaxis order from orthopedic standing post-op orders

AFTER patient is admitted.

# Alternative for patients with beta lactam allergy:

[Vancomycin 15mg/kg Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-vancomycin-weight-based-dosing)

Prophylaxis recommendation includes q12h for 1 dose post-op. Please place

post-op antimicrobial prophylaxis order from orthopedic standing post-op orders

AFTER patient is admitted.

# Known MRSA colonization:

[Vancomycin 15mg/kg Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-vancomycin-weight-based-dosing)

Prophylaxis recommendation includes q12h for 1 dose post-op. Please place

post-op antimicrobial prophylaxis order from orthopedic standing post-op orders

AFTER patient is admitted.

References:

Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis

in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013, vol 70 pages 195-283

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

POST-OPERATIVE WOUND INFECTION

Surgical site infections are categorized by the extent of tissues involved.

Superficial incisional infections involve only the subcutaneous space and occur

within 30 days of operation.  Deep incisional infections involve deep layers of

soft tissue, such as fascia and muscle, and occur within 30 days of operation,

or within 1 year of operation if prosthetic material was inserted.  Organ/space

infections involve anatomical areas other than the incisional wound that were

opened or manipulated during operation.  Organ/space infections should be

treated as infections of the relevant area of the anatomy.  Return to the main

page and choose the pertinent organ system for advice on management of these

infections.

Post-operative wound infections usually occur between 2 and 30 days after the

operation.  Infections within 48 hours of the surgery are uncommon, but are

serious when they do occur.  Symptoms commonly begin to appear no sooner than 5

days after the operation and may take up to 2 weeks to appear.

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

SURGICAL PROPHYLAXIS COMMON PRINCIPLES

Potential pathogens are introduced into normally sterile areas of the body

during most surgical procedures.  The purpose of antimicrobial prophylaxis is to

reduce the intraoperative microbial burden so that local host defenses can

eliminate microorganisms and prevent disease.  Prophylaxis cannot be expected to

sterilize tissues.

Antimicrobial agent for surgical prophylaxis should be:

1. active against the pathogens most likely to contaminate the surgical site

2. given in an appropriate dosage and at a time that ensures adequate serum

and tissue concentrations during the period of potential contamination

3. safe, and

4. administered for the shortest effective period to minimize adverse

effects, the development of resistance, and costs.

# References:

Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis

in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283

Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The

Medical Letter 2012 Vol 10 pages 73-77

# THORACIC SURGERY POST-OPERATIVE ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS RECOMMENDATIONS

Place post-op IV antimicrobial prophylaxis orders after admission to ward.

Duration of antimicrobial prophylaxis should not exceed 24 hours. Durations

longer than 24 hours have not been shown effective in preventing cardiothoracic

surgical site infections. There is no benefit to continuing antimicrobial

prophylaxis until all indwelling drains and intravascular catheters are removed.

For CIED surgery postoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis click link below:

[CIED Surgery Postoperative Prophylaxis](orzid2-gmenu-surg-vascular-surg-postop)

For CV surgery (Open Heart) postoperative prophylaxis click link below:

[CV Surgery Postoperative Prophylaxis](orzid2-gmenu-surg-cv-postop)

# Non-Esophageal Thoracic Procedures Postoperative Prophylaxis

Includes video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) and non-cardiac procedures

including lobectomy, pneumonectomy, lung resection and thoracotomy.

No postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

TIMING AND DOSING (INCLUDING RE-DOSING) OF PROPHYLACTIC ANTIMICROBIALS

For optimal prevention, antimicrobial concentrations should be above the minimal

inhibitory concentration (MIC) of potential pathogens from initial incision

until closure.

There is no advantage to giving post-operative doses. Despite a lack of

demonstrated benefit, post-operative doses are sometimes given in clinical

practice.  If post-operative doses are given, they should be discontinued by 24

hours after closure of the incision.

When prophylaxis consists of a single dose as should be the case in the majority

of procedures, adjustment for renal or hepatic dysfunction is not necessary.

The optimal time for administration of preoperative doses is 30 to

60 minutes before surgical incision for most antimicrobials.

Infusions of drugs like fluoroquinolones and vancomycin that require longer

infusion times should begin 60 to 120 minutes before first incision.

During procedures that last so long that concentrations might fall below the

MICs of potential pathogens, repeated doses of antimicrobials should be given.

Re-dosing may also be warranted if prolonged or excessive bleeding

occurs.

[Doses and Redosing Recommendations for Common Antimicrobials](orzid2-gmenu-surg-prophylaxis-doses-and-redosing)

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

VASCULAR SURGERY

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for some procedures, including

brachiocephalic procedures (e.g., carotid endarterectomy, brachial artery

repair) without implantation of prosthetic material.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended in vascular procedures that involve

implantation of prosthetic material and procedures for which there is greater

risk of infection, such as aneurysm repair, thromboendarterectomy and vein

bypass. Longer duration of antimicrobial prophylaxis therapy is warranted for

graft placement.

# If no antimicrobial prophylaxis recommended, select below:

[Click here No antimicrobial prophylaxis recommended for procedure](orz-gtx-abx-pre-op-url-nurse-generic-order)

# Prophylaxis for vascular procedures OTHER THAN graft placement* and procedures

# involving the groin** (see below for graft placement and involving groin)

# Preferred:

[Cefazolin Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-cefazolin-weight-based-dosing)

# Alternative for beta-lactam allergy or MRSA colonization:

[Click here Beta-lactam reaction assessment](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Vancomycin 15mg/kg Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-vancomycin-weight-based-dosing)

# *Prophylaxis for graft placement procedures:

# Preferred:

[Cefazolin Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-cefazolin-weight-based-dosing)

Post-op prophylaxis include q8h x2doses.

Please plase post-op antimicrobial prophylaxis order after admission.

Please place post-op antimicrobial prophylaxis order after admission.

# Rifampin vascular graft soak for INFECTED graft

[Rifampin Vascular Graft Soak \(600mg\)](psjizid-rifampin-600-mg-vial-for-vascular-surgery)

# **Prophylaxis for procedures that involve the abdominal aorta or groin incision

# due to the potential for gastrointestinal flora:

# Preferred:

[Cefazolin Weight Based Dosing Preop R](orzid2-gmenu-surg-cefazolin-weight-based-dosing)

# Alternative for beta lactam allergy:

[Click here Beta-lactam reaction assessment](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Vancomycin 15mg/kg weight based dosing + Gentamicin 5mg/kg weight based dosing](orz-set-abx-vancom-15-mg-kg-iv-60min-gent-5mg-kg-iv-once)

# Alternative for MRSA colonization:

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU SURG W/I 48HRS PROCEDURE
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

PATIENTS WITH SIGNS OF INFECTION WITHIN 48 HOURS OF PROCEDURE

Fever within 48 hours of procedure is usually due to anesthesia or other non-

infectious factors but Clostridium species and Streptococcus pyogenes can cause

early infections.  Examine the wound of any patient with systemic signs of

infection, like fever, within 48 hours of surgery.  If there are signs of

infection consider opening the wound.  Obtain a STAT Gram stain and culture of

any drainage. If the Gram stain shows evidence of streptococci or clostridia

refer to the section on necrotizing infections.  If signs of wound infection are

absent seek an alternative source of the fever.

[Necrotizing infections](orzid2-gmenu-necrotizing-infections)

[References](orzid2-gmenu-abx-references)

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU SURG WND CLASS PROPHYL REC
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

SURGICAL WOUND CLASSIFICATION AND ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS RECOMMENDATIONS

# >>  Clean  <<

A wound resulting from a procedure in which no inflammation or infection was

encountered and the respiratory, alimentary, genital, or uninfected urinary

tract was not entered.  Clean wounds are closed at the end of surgery and if

drainage is necessary wounds are closed with drains in place.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is usually not indicated.  Exceptions are procedures

in which prosthetic material will be inserted or for operations in which a

surgical site infection would be catastrophic.  These exceptions include most

cardiac operations, joint replacement, revascularization procedures in legs, and

most neurosurgical operations.

# >>  Clean contaminated  <<

Clean-contaminated wounds are those in which the respiratory, alimentary,

genital, or urinary tracts are entered but there is no evidence of infection and

there is no major break in technique.  These include operations on the biliary

tract, appendix, vagina, and oropharynx.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is indicated for most of these procedures.

# >>  Contaminated  <<

Contaminated wounds include an open, fresh, accidental wound, or operations with

major breaks in sterile technique, gross spillage from the gastrointestinal

tract, or incisions in which acute, non-purulent inflammation is encountered.

Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.

# >>  Dirty-Infected  <<

Dirty-infected wounds are old traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue and those

that involve existing infection or perforated viscera.  The organisms usually

have been present in the operative field since before the operation.

Antimicrobials are therapeutic and not prophylactic.

[References](orzid2-gmenu-abx-references)

Bratzler DW, et al.  Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial

in surgery, Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013 Vol 70 page 195-283

Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery, Treatment Guidelines from The

Medical Letter 2012 Vol 10 pages 73-77

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU TINEA CAPITIS (RINGWORM)
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# TINEA CAPITIS (RINGWORM)

Tinea capitis is a common fungal infection of the scalp and hair. It is

characterized by itchy, red, raised, scaly patches often sharply defined. Redder

margins than centers create impression of ring. Tinea capitis primarily affects

prepubescent children but can affect people of any age.

Baseline liver function test monitoring recommended. Repeat LFTs if treating for

longer than 6 weeks and there were baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver

disease, or other risks for hepatotoxicity.

# Treatment:

Treat for 4 weeks.

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO QDAY R,H,DI,O](psjzid-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday)

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU TINEA PEDIS (ATHLETE'S FOOT)
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# TINEA PEDIS (ATHLETE'S FOOT), TINEA CORPORIS, TINEA MANUUM, OR TINEA CRURIS

Dermatophyte fungal infections are common worldwide. Dermatophytes metabolize

and subsist upon keratin in the skin, hair, and nails. Most tinea infections can

often be cured with topical therapy alone.  Systemic therapy is reserved for

severe or refractory infection, recurrent infection, or in immunocompromised

patients.

Treatment should continue for at least one week after clinical curing of

infection.

# Treatment

[Terbinafine 1% cream apply to affected area BID x 2-4 weeks M](psjzid-terbinafine-1-cream-top-bid)

# Alternative

[Clotrimazole 1% cream apply to affected area BID x 4 weeks M](psjzid-clotrimazole-1-cream-topical-bid)

# Systemic treatment

[Fluconazole 150 mg q week x 2-4 weeks R,DI](psjzid-fluconazole-150mg-po-qweek)

< OR >

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO QDAY x 2 weeks R,H,DI,O](psjzid-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU TINEA UNGUIUM (ONYCHOMYCOSIS)
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# TINEA UNGUIUM (ONYCHOMYCOSIS)

Obtain a fungal stain of nail sample prior to initiating treatment. Using large

nail clippers, remove as much of the unattached dystrophic nail as possible.

Place the piece of clipped nail plate in formalin jar and send to pathology for

fungal stain (PAS). Treatment should only be initiated if stain is positive for

fungal elements. Fungal culture is NOT recommended.

Systemic therapy is most likely to achieve a cure, especially with more nail

involvement. If <25% involvement topical therapy may be considered. If >50-75%

involvement systemic therapy should be considered.

Toenails take 12-18 months to grow out completely, so improvement should not be

expected to be observed for at least 6-9 months.  Continued improvement can be

experienced following treatment completion.

# Oral Treatment:

Terbinafine works about 70% of the time to cure the fungus, and reinfection is

common, so many patients will need to do more than one course of treatment.

Fluconazole pulse dosing response rate is approximately 50%. May consider

retreatment with oral therapy after one year.

Recommend Dermatology Consult for retreatment after failure of 2 courses of

terbinafine or fluconazole.

# Preferred Terbinafine first-line oral:

Toenail infections treat for 12 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to

starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were

baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for

hepatotoxicity.

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 12 weeks \(R,H,DI,O](psjzid-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday)

Fingernail infections treat for 6 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to

starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were

baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for

hepatotoxicity.

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 6 weeks R,H,DI,O](psjzid-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday)

# Alternative oral therapy:

Toenail infections treat for at least 6 months

[Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for total of 6 months R,DI](psjzid-fluconazole-300mg-po-qweek-for-nail-infection)

Fingernail infections treat for 3 months

[Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for 3 months R,DI](psjzid-fluconazole-300mg-po-qweek-for-nail-infection)

# Topical Treatment:

Ciclopirox is a topical first-line treatment for both fingernails and toenails.

Complete resolution occurs in approximately 7 percent of patients treated daily

for 48 weeks.  Ciclopirox is a well-tolerated treatment. Potential side effects

include temporary nail changes and local skin irritation.

[Ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer: Apply once daily to affected nail\(s\)](psjzid-ciclopirox-8-nail-lacquer-qday-remove-q7days)

Remove with rubbing alcohol every 7 days. [M] See accompanying medication

pamphlet for specific instructions. Treatment is continued until nail clearance

or up to 48 weeks.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Gupta AK, et al. Br J Dermatol 2020 182(2): 287-299

Ameen M, et al. Br J Dermatol 2014 171: 937

# TINEA VERSICOLOR

Topical antifungals can be used for limited disease.  For disease that involves

nails or does not respond to topical therapy, use oral antifungals.

Return of normal skin color often takes several weeks after the treatment course

is finished.

# Treatment limited disease:

[Ketoconazole 2% shampoo apply to the affected area QDAY for 3 days. Apply to](psjzid-ketoconazole-2-shampoo-qday)

damp skin, lather, leave on 5 minutes, and rinse.

< OR >

[Ketoconazole 2% cream to affected area QDAY for 14 days M](psjzid-ketoconazole-2-cream-top-qday)

< OR >

[Terbinafine 1% cream apply to affected area QDAY for 7 days M](psjzid-terbinafine-1-crm-top-qday)

< OR >

[Selenium sulfide lotion 2.5% apply to affected area, leave on for 10 minutes,](psjzid-selenium-sulfide-lot-2-5-10min)

then rinse/shower thoroughly QDAY for 7 days [M]

# Treatment extensive disease:

[Fluconazole 300 MG PO weekly for 2 weeks R](psjzid-fluconazole-300mg-po-weekly-x2-weeks)

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) can be associated with either staphylococci or

streptococci.  Antimicrobial treatment and supportive care is urgent.  Click one

of the links below for diagnostic criteria.

[Link to Diagnosis of Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome](orzid2-gmenu-strep-toxic-shock-syndrome)

[Link to Diagnosis of Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome](orzid2-gmenu-staph-toxic-shock-syndrome)

# _________________________________________________

# Treatment of Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome

# _________________________________________________

# Preferred treatment

[Penicillin 4 million units IV q4h \($\) R <AND> clindamycin 900 mg](orz-set-abx-penici-4mu-iv-q4h-clinda-900mg-iv-q8h)

IV q8h ($$) [H,O]

# Alternative for penicillin allergy

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> Clindamycin 900 mg IV](orz-set-abx-vanco-15mg-kg-and-clinda-900mg-iv-q8h)

q8h ($$) [H,O]

# _________________________________________________

# Treatment of Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome

# _________________________________________________

Use vancomycin initially in case methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is

present.  If cultures reveal methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus

(MSSA), change to nafcillin or cefazolin for better antimicrobial activity.

# Empirical treatment

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h \($$\) H,O](orz-set-abx-vanco-15mg-kg-and-clinda-900mg-iv-q8h)

# Treatment if MSSA is isolated

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU TOXOPLASMA SPP.
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# TOXOPLASMA SPP.

If patient is immunocompetent and not pregnant, treatment is usually not needed

as disease is usually self-limited. Patients who are immunocompromised, pregnant

or have severe disease should be treated. Consult Infectious Diseases in all

cases.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Non-pregnant patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat immunocompetent patients for 2-4 weeks. Treat immunocompromised patients

for 6 weeks or longer if radiologic disease is extensive or response is

incomplete at 6 weeks.

# Preferred treatment

Patients weighing <60 kg

[Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO once \($$$\), then 50 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND>](orz-set-abx-pyrim200mgthen50mgq24h-sulfdiaz1gmq6h-leuco10mgq24h)

sulfadiazine 1 gm PO q6h ($$) [DI,O] <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h($) [M]

Patients weighing >60kg

[Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO once \($$$\), then 75 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND>](orz-set-abx-pyrim200mgthen75mgq24h-sulfad1-5gmq6h-leuco10mgq24h)

sulfadiazine 1.5 gm PO q6h ($$) [DI,O] <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h($) [M]

# Preferred alternative for sulfa allergy

Patients weighing <60 kg

[Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO once \($$$\), then 50 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND>](orz-set-abx-pyrim200mgthen50mgq24h-clinda600mgq6h-leuco10mgq24h)

clindamycin 600 mg PO q6h ($) [H,O] <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h ($) [M]

Patients weighing >60 kg

[Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO once \($$$\), then 75 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND>](orz-set-abx-pyrim200mgthen75mgq24h-clinda600mgq6h-leuco10mgq24h)

clindamycin 600 mg PO q6h ($) [H,O] <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h ($) [M]

# Secondary alternatives

[Trimethoprim 5 mg/kg-sulfamethoxazole 25 mg/kg IV q12h \($$\) R,DI](psjizid-trimethoprim-sulfameth-5-25-mg-kg-iv-q12h)

< OR >

[Trimethoprim 5 mg/kg-sulfamethoxazole 25 mg/kg PO q12h \($\) R,DI](psjzid-trimeth-sulfa-5-25-mg-kg-po-q12h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Chronic Maintenance therapy for immunocompromised patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Discontinue maintenance therapy if patient has remained asymptomatic and CD4 >

200 cells per microliter.

# Maintenance therapy

[Pyrimethamine 50 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND> sulfadiazine 0.5-1 gm PO q6h](orz-set-abx-pyrim-50mg-q24h-sulfadiaz-0-5gm-q6h-leuco-10mg-q24h)

($$) <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h ($) [M]

# Preferred alternative for sulfa allergy

[Pyrimethamine 50 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND> clindamycin 600 mg PO q8h \($\)](orz-set-abx-pyrim-50mg-q24h-clinda-600mg-q8h-leuco-10mg-q24h)

[H,O] <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h ($) [M]

# Secondary alternatives

[Pyrimethamine 25 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND> atovaquone 750-1500 mg PO](orz-set-abx-pyrime-25mg-q24h-atova-750mg-q12h-leuco-10mg-q24h)

q12h ($) [M] <AND> leucovorin 10-25 mg PO q24h ($) [M]

< OR >

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1DS tablet PO q24h \($\) R,DI](psjzid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-tablet-po-q24h)

< OR >

[Atovaquone 750-1500 mg PO q12h \($\) M](psjzid-atovaquone-750mg-po-q12h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Pregnant patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Patient diagnosed <16-18 weeks of gestation

*Contact Infectious Diseases, non-formulary consult is required for spiramycin

Spiramycin 1 gm po q8h until week 18 of gestation

# Patient diagnosed >16-18 weeks of gestation

[Pyrimethamine 50 mg q12h for 2 days, then 50 mg PO q24h \($$\) DI,O <AND>](orz-set-abx-pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin-pregnancy)

sulfadiazine 75mg/kg once, then 50mg/kg q12h ($$) [DI,O] <AND> leucovorin 10-25

mg PO q24h ($) [M] for 4 weeks or duration of pregnancy if ultrasound evidence

of fetal distress

menus.Name: ORZID2 GMENU TRANSPLANTATION
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

TRANSPLANTATION

Organ transplantation is associated with many host defense defects.  Early on,

surgical wounds may become infected.  Preparation for transplantation and anti-

rejection drugs can induce neutropenia.  Later, CMI defects predominate.

Patients become infected with exogenous pathogens and also endogenous pathogens

like cytomegalovirus that might have been present in latent or subclinical form.

Cell-mediated immune defects caused by anti-rejection drugs cause patients to be

especially susceptible to infections with organisms that infrequently cause

disease in healthy people.  They include: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly

Pneumocystis carinii), mycobacteria, salmonella, candida, aspergillus,

Toxoplasma gondii, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus,

and cryptosporidia.

The approach to fever or other signs or symptoms suggesting the possibility of

an infectious disease depends on the specific defects present in the patient,

the nature of the presenting signs and symptoms and a bedside assessment of the

severity of illness.  Empirical antimicrobials are usually not indicated for

fever alone unless the patient has a host defense defect that predisposes to

rapid progression of illness like severe neutropenia or splenectomy.  Contact

Infectious Diseases for more information.

[References](orzid2-gmenu-abx-references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology

Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# UVEITIS

Most cases are non-infectious. Most infectious cases are associated with a

pathogen causing systemic or central nervous system infection. Diagnosis of

uveitis usually must be made presumptively due to the technical difficulty of

sampling the uvea. Cases have been associated with fungi, bacteria, viruses, and

protozoa like Toxoplasma gondii.

# For treatment of posterior uveitis (retinitis) or acute retinal necrosis (ARN)

# due to Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) or herpes simplex virus (HSV) or

# Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

[VZV or HSV retinitis and ARN](orzid2-gmenu-retinitis)

[CMV retinitis and ARN](orzid2-gmenu-abx-cmv-retinitis)

# Treatment of uveitis involves treating the underlying infection and is usually

# systemic. Refer to specific pathogen recommendations for treatment of underlyin

# infection. Contact Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases for assistance.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# DISKITIS AND VERTEBRAL OSTEOMYELITIS

When possible, obtain diagnostic cultures before starting empiric therapy.

Obtain blood cultures and image guided aspirates or surgical bone biopsy.

Definitive therapy is based on culture and susceptibility test results.

# Recommended duration of therapy:

Treat for at least 6 weeks of pathogen directed IV/PO therapy for high risk

including MRSA infection, ESRD, or undrained abscess or device implantation.

Once culture and susceptibility testing is available switch to pathogen directed

therapy.

# Empiric therapy if patient is systemically ill:

Preferred:

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h R <AND> ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h M](orz-set-abx-vanco-15-mg-kg-iv-q12h-ceftriax-2gm-iv-q24h)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX ACNE
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ACNE

Acne is an inflammatory skin condition caused by excess sebum production, gland

obstruction and infection with Cutibacterum acnes. Early disease manifests with

black heads and white heads and little inflammation. Small papules and pustules

are present in mild disease. Severe disease occurs when comedones, papules,

pustules and less often cysts are present.

The goal of treatment is prevention and reeducation of new comedones and

creating an environment that is inhibitory for C. acnes. General skin care

treatment measures include utilizing gentle skin cleansers, avoiding aggressive

scrubbing, using non-comedogenic skin products, and avoiding picking of lesions.

Diet's role in therapy remains uncertain.

Non-Antimicrobial therapy includes benzoyl peroxide topical/wash, salicylic acid

topical, and tretinoin topical. These agents can be used as monotherapy in early

disease and in addition to antimicrobial treatment in mild to severe disease.

# Early Disease:

[Clindamycin 1% lotion topically q12h \($\) M](psozid-clindamycin-1-lotion-topically-q12h)

< OR >

[Erythromycin 2% gel topically q12h \($\) DI](psozid-erythromycin-2-gel-topically-q12h)

# Mild Disease:

[Erythromycin 2% gel topically q12h \($\) DI](psozid-erythromycin-2-gel-topically-q12h)

< OR >

[Doxycycline 50 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks](psozid2-doxycycline-12wks-50mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Minocycline 50 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks](psozid2-minocylcine-12wks-50mg-po-q12h)

# Severe Disease:

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h  \($\) DI for 12 weeks <AND> erythromycin 2% gel](orz-set-abx-op-doxy-100mg-po-bid-12wks-erythromycin-2-gel-q12h)

topically q12h

< OR >

[Minocycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks <AND> erythromycin 2% gel](orz-set-abx-op-mino-100mg-po-bid-12wks-erythromycin-2-gel-q12h)

topically q12h

________________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# APPROACH TO URINARY TRACT INFECTION (UTI)

# IDSA 2025 complicated and uncomplicated UTI definition updates:

Uncomplicated UTI is an infection confined to the bladder in afebrile women or

men without urinary catheter.

[Uncomplicated urinary tract infection](orzid3-gmenu-abx-uncomp-uti)

Complicated UTI is an infection beyond the bladder and accompanied by symptoms

including fever/other signs of systemic illness. Complicated UTI includes

pyelonephritis, febrile or bacteremic UTI, catheter-associated (CAUTI).

[Complicated UTI without catheter](orzid3-gmenu-abx-complicated-uti-no-catheter)

[Complicated UTI catheter associated](orzid3-gmenu-abx-complicated-uti-catheter-associated)

[Acute prostatitis](orzid3-gmenu-acute-bact-prostatitis)

For patients presenting with septic shock from a suspected urinary tract

infection: Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

Asymptomatic bacteriuria occurs in patients who have bacteria in the urine but

do not have symptoms of a urinary tract infection.

[Asymptomatic bacteriuria](orzid3-gmenu-asymp-bacteriuria)

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for

treatment:

[Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure](orzid3-gmenu-sexually-transmitted-infections-sti)

Candida urinary tract infections are discussed elsewhere:

[Candida urinary tract infections](orzid3-gmenu-abx-candida-uti)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX BALANITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# BALANITIS AND BALANOPOSTHITIS

Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis and is often associated with

erythema and pruritis. When the foreskin is also involved, the condition is

known as balanoposthitis (also referred to as balanitis in this discussion).

There are a variety of causes of balanitis, but most are due to poor hygiene of

the foreskin in uncircumcised men resulting in candida infection. Other, less

common causes, include bacterial infection (typically sexually transmitted or

anaerobic bacteria), dermatologic conditions, malignancy as well as others. Men

with Candidal balanitis often have a white curd-like exudate compared to a thick

foul-smelling purulent exudate in menu with anaerobic bacterial balanitis.

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for

treatment:

[Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure](orzid3-gmenu-sexually-transmitted-infections-sti)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CANDIDA URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS

A positive urine culture for candida usually reflects colonization. Treat

cystitis only if the patient has symptoms of urinary tract infection (e.g.

dysuria, frequency, urgency, and/or suprapubic tenderness) or if the patient

will undergo invasive urological manipulation

Asymptomatic candiduria in a patient with a urinary catheter should not be

treated without an additional indication. Removal of catheter is strongly

recommended. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

Neutropenic patients with asymptomatic candiduria should be assessed for

candidemia because they are at risk of dissemination. Obtain blood cultures and

assess potential sources of candidemia such as central venous catheters. Refer

to fungemia page in the Inpatient Antimicrobialc CDSS for treatment

recommendations.

# Treatment

Patient undergoing invasive urological manipulation:

[Fluconazole 400 mg \(6 mg/kg\) PO q24h \($\) R,DI for 3 days before and 3 days](psozid2-fluconazole-400mg-po-qday-6days)

after procedure

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-400mg-po-qday-6days)

Symptomatic candida cystitis:

[Fluconazole 200 mg \(3 mg/kg\) PO q24h \($\) R,DI for 14 days](psozid2-fluconazole-200mg-qday-14-days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-200mg-qday-14-days)

Pyelonephritis:

[Fluconazole 400 mg \(6 mg/kg\) PO q24h \($\) R,DI for 14 days](psozid2-fluconazole-400mg-qday-14-days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-400mg-qday-14-days)

Resistant candida:

Consult Infectious Diseases for treatment options

pathogenesis

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CYTOMEGALOVIRUS (CMV)

# Antiviral toxicity information

The major toxicities of both ganciclovir and valganciclovir are neutropenia.

Nephrotoxicity is the major toxicity associated with foscarnet, which may be

reduced by concomitant saline administration (generally 0.5-1L).

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompetent patient

Infection is rare and usually associated with minimal or no symptoms.

Mononucleosis can be associated with CMV, but is more commonly associated with

Epstein Barr virus. Antiviral treatment is not usually necessary as most

patients recover without intervention.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompromised patient

Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased include solid organ and

bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving prolonged immunosuppressive

chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease indicated by a CD4 count of

less than 50 cells/microliter.

# CMV treatment recommendations

[Colitis or esophagitis](orzid3-gmenu-cmv-colitis-esophagitis)

[Encephalitis](orzid3-gmenu-cmv-encephalitis)

[Polyradiculopathy](orzid3-gmenu-cmv-polyradiculopathy)

[Retinitis](orzid3-gmenu-cmv-retinitis)

[Pneumonia](orzid3-gmenu-cmv-pneumonia)

References:

Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in HIV

Infected Adults and Adolescents. AIDSinfo (2015) 1-282

Sanford keyword: Cytomegalovirus

cytomegalovirus infection in immunocompetent adults

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT VENTILATOR OP
menus.Text:
# COLONIZED RESPIRATORY TRACT IN A PATIENT ON A VENTILATOR

The respiratory tracts of persons who are intubated, have a

tracheostomy, or have other abnormalities of the larynx or trachea are

usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. The bacteria can be of

relatively low virulence (e.g. coagulase negative staphylococci, streptococci,

candida) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus aureus,

enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida and enterococci are common

respiratory tract colonizers and they almost never cause pneumonia. There is

no benefit from treatment of patients with systemic antimicrobials simply

because the respiratory tract is colonized with a potential pathogen and there

is no evidence of an infiltrate. Systemic antimicrobial therapy will select for

resistant organisms and may lead to other adverse effects.

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for ventilator-associated pneumonia

treatment recommendations in patients with a new or progressive infiltrate and

at least one of the following: fever greater than 100.4F, leukocytosis,

leukopenia or purulent bronchial secretions.

References

Kalil et al. Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 63(5): e61-e111.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX COLONIZED WOUNDS OP
menus.Text:
# COLONIZED WOUNDS

Open wounds are usually colonized with bacteria and often fungi. This is true of

ulcers (see below), post-operative wounds, traumatic wounds, and others. Then

bacteria can be of relatively low virulence (eg, coagulase negative

staphylococci, diphtheroids) or of potentially greater virulence (Staphylococcus

aureus, enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas). Candida is commonly present on wounds

that are moist or covered. There is no need to treat patients with systemic

antimicrobials simply because a wound culture is positive for a potential

pathogen. Topical antimicrobials are not effective in nearly all circumstances

and can select for resistant organisms or lead to other adverse effects.

Systemic antimicrobial therapy may be indicated if there are signs of infection.

[Decubitus ulcers](orzid3-gmenu-decubitis-ulcers)

[Diabetic foot ulcers](orzid3-gmenu-foot-ulcer-in-pt-w-dm)

References

Lipsky et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2012, 54(12): e132-e173

Up-to-Date article: Clinical assessment of chronic wounds

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX COMPLICATED UTI CATHETER ASSOCIATED
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CATHETER ASSOCIATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION

# Rule out obstruction.

When patients who require parenteral therapy are afebrile, clinically stable,

and can take oral medication, convert to oral therapy based on the

identification and susceptibility of the isolate.

# Duration

Treat for 5 days with fluoroquinolones or 7 days with non-fluoroquinolone

antibiotics.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment

# PO therapy options

Preferred:

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h R,DI for 7 days](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

*Avoid trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in the first and third trimesters

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

< OR >

[Nitrofurantoin SA 100 mg PO q12h R,O, CrCl =/>30mL/min, for 7 days](psozid-nitrofurantoin-sa-7ds-100-mg-po-bid)

*Avoid nitrofurantoin in the third trimester

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-nitrofurantoin-sa-7ds-100-mg-po-bid)

Primary alternatives:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

< OR >

[Fosfomycin 3 gm sachet PO every other day M x 3 doses](psozid-fosfomycin-3gm-po-qotherday-for-3doses)

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-fosfomycin-3gm-po-qotherday-for-3doses)

< OR >

[Cefpodoxime 400 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psozid2-cefpodoxime-400mg-po-bid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefpodoxime-400mg-po-bid-7ds)

Secondary alternative:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h R,DI for 5 days](psozid2-ciprofloxacin-5ds-500mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-5ds-500mg-po-bid)

# IV therapy options

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Treatment for specific pathogens based on susceptibilities

# Enterobacteria including E. coli, Klebsiella, and Proteus

Preferred:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

Alternative:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h R,DI for 7 days](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

*Avoid trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in the first and third trimesters

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

# Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is an uncommon urinary tract pathogen and presence in the urine may be

due to hematogenous seeding from another site. Blood cultures are indicated to

rule out bacteremia in patients who have S. aureus isolated from the urine.

Consult Infectious Diseases for more information.

# Pseudomonas

[Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q12h R,DI for 5 days](psozid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-5ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-5ds)

# Enterococcus

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO q8h R for 7 days](psozid2-amoxicillin-1000mg-po-tid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amoxicillin-1000mg-po-tid-7days)

Alternatives:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Fosfomycin 3 gm sachet PO every other day M x 3 doses](psozid-fosfomycin-3gm-po-qotherday-for-3doses)

*Not for infections outside of the bladder

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# COMPLICATED UTI (NO CATHETER)

# Complicated UTI is an infection beyond the bladder accompanied by symptoms

# including fever/other signs of systemic illness, flank pain, and costovertebral

# tenderness. This includes pyelonephritis and febrile or bacteremic UTI.

NOT signs or symptoms: abnormal urinalysis alone, pyuria, falls, change in urine

odor or color, delirium (acute mental status change, confusion) without systemic

signs of infection. These may occur in patients with a UTI but alone are

inadequate for diagnosis and empiric treatment.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

For patients without signs or symptoms of UTI:

[Asymptomatic bacteriuria](orzid3-gmenu-asymp-bacteriuria)

For patients presenting with septic shock from a suspected urinary tract

infection: Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Duration

Treat for 5 days with fluoroquinolones or 7 days with non-fluoroquinolone

organisms, presence of obstruction, underlying renal disease, immunosuppression,

and neurologic or structural abnormality in some cases. Often therapy can be

completed with an oral agent pending clinical stability and susceptibility

testing.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment

Preferred:

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet q12h R,DI for 7 days](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

*Avoid trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in the first and third trimesters

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

< OR >

[Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q12h R,DI for 5 days](psozid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-5ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-5ds)

Alternative or isolate resistant to preferred antimicrobials:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

< OR >

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Treatment for specific pathogens

# Enterobacteria including E. coli, Klebsiella, and Proteus

Preferred:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h R for 7 days](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-7days-1ds-tab-bid)

# Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is an uncommon urinary tract pathogen and presence in the urine may be

due to hematogenous seeding from another site. Blood cultures are indicated to

rule out bacteremia in patients who have S. aureus isolated from the urine.

Consult Infectious Diseases for more information.

# Pseudomonas

Preferred:

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-5ds)

# COPD Exacerbations

Exacerbation of COPD (ECOPD): dyspnea and/or cough and sputum worsening

over <14 days. An acute change in one or more of the following:

-Increased cough frequency and severity

-Increased sputum volume and/or changes in character

-Increased dyspnea

Patients at risk for poor outcomes are most likely to benefit from early,

appropriate antibiotics and close follow-up. Risk factors: age > 65,

FEV1 < 50% predicted, 2 or more exacerbations in the past year, hospitalization

for exacerbation in the past year, continuous supplemental oxygen, ischemic

heart disease or heart failure.

Dyspnea differential: acute coronary syndrome, worsening heart failure,

pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, medication non-adherence

A home action plan with on demand oral corticosteroids and antibiotic is

recommended if a patient with moderate or severe COPD had an exacerbation

requiring treatment (outpatient, ER, or inpatient) in the previous 12 months.

# COPD Management & Respiratory Symptom Treatment

[Acute Respiratory Infection \(ARI\) Symptomatic Therapy](orzid3-gmenu-ari-symptomatic-therapy)

# Antibiotics:

Antibiotics recommended for patients with moderate or severe chronic COPD

plus an exacerbation with 2 or more of the following:

- Increase or change in sputum purulence

- Increased sputum volume

- Increased dyspnea

[Doxcycline 100 mg PO BID for COPD exacerbation 5 days \($\) DI](psozid2-doxycycline-5ds-100mg-po-bid-copd-exacerbation)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX DENTAL SOP ANTIBIOTIC CHOICE
menus.Text:
# Dental SOP for Antibiotic Prophylaxis

# Antibiotic choice considerations:

a. See links below for recommendations

b. Amoxicillin is preferred over Penicillin as it is more effective against

gram negative anaerobes and is associated with lower incidence of GI

adverse effects.

c. If a patient reports a Penicillin allergy, conduct an allergy assessment

to determine if it is a true allergy. If not, consider prescribing

Cephalexin.

d. In the unusual case where a patient cannot take Penicillin or Cephalexin,

Doxycycline or Azithromycin would be first choice. Clindamycin is no longer

recommended by the ADA, due to the side effects--it increases the risk

of developing Clostridioides difficile Infection (CDI), even after a

single dose. Clindamycin also gives suboptimal prophylactic coverage.

e. If patient is taking an antibiotic with the same spectrum as the one

indicated for antibiotic prophylaxis, additional antibiotics do not need

to be prescribed.

f. Consider intramuscular antibiotic therapy for patients with GI disorders.

# Select indication below for recommendations:

[Dental Infections](orzid3-gmenu-supp-odontogenic-infect)

[Periodontal Disease](orzid3-gmenu-periodental-disease)

[Tooth Abscess and other Suppurative Odonotogenic Infections](orzid3-gmenu-supp-odontogenic-infect)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX DENTAL SOP BACKGROUND INFORMATION
menus.Text:
a. Compared to previous recommendations, there are currently few patient

subpopulations who would benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis prior to

designated dental procedures.

b. Cumulative, low grade bacteremias (triggered by normal daily activities,

such as tooth brushing, flossing and chewing) are a greater risk factor in

developing Infective Endocarditis (IE), more so than sporadic, high grade

bacteremias (caused by invasive dental procedures). Maintenance of oral

health to reduce bacteremia from daily activities is more important than

antibiotic prophylaxis.

c. Adverse events associated with inappropriate antibiotic use include

antimicrobial resistance, C. difficile associated disease (CDI), allergic

reactions and disruptions in normal flora.

d. Some conditions that may warrant antibiotic prophylaxis are:

i. Heart conditions (risk of developing IE)

1. Artificial heart valve

2. History of IE

3. Certain specific congenital heart conditions--highly recommend

Cardiology consult

4. Cardiac transplant that develops a problem in the heart valve

ii. These conditions are NOT recommended for prophylaxis:

1. Coronary artery stents, history of coronary artery bypass

graft (CABG).

e. Presence of prosthetic joints is no longer an indication to provide

# ESOPHAGITIS

Esophagitis is usually associated with non-infectious diseases like

gastroesophageal reflux disease, mucositis and pill-induced esophagitis.

Esophageal infection occurs primarily in immunosuppressed individuals (e.g.

chemotherapy, transplantation, HIV) and rarely in healthy individuals. The

majority of infectious esophagitis is caused by Candida albicans,

cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus. Aphthous ulceration of the

esophagus is common in HIV infection. HIV screening is recommneded.

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HEPATITIS A

# Disease Management

Most acute disease is self-limited, and the virus does not cause chronic

disease. No specific antiviral therapy is available.

Patients who appear to be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with

mental status changes should receive supportive treatment. Fulminant hepatitis

is suggested by increased prothrombin time, cholestasis, ascites, decreased

liver size, or decreasing serum albumin. Supportive treatment includes

maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance, monitoring and possible correction

of coagulation defects, treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, and good nutrition

with a low-protein diet.

# Prevention for persons with continuing high risk of disease

Vaccine should be offered to persons at high risk of hepatitis A infection: men

who have sex with men, travelers to endemic areas likely to be exposed, illegal

drug users, persons at occupational risk of disease, persons with chronic liver

disease or clotting factor disorders.

Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months

# Prevention for persons with a specific, defined exposure

Post-exposure prophylaxis should be offered to persons with substantial exposure

to hepatitis A. Specifically, persons exposed to acute hepatitis through

household or sexual contact, persons who attend or work in a day care center

with a recent case, or employee or patron of a restaurant with a food handler

with hepatitis. Post exposure prophylaxis must be given within 2 weeks of

exposure. Vaccine can be given at the same time as immune-globulin.

Immune globulin 0.02 ml/kg IM x 1 <AND>

Give Hepatitis A vaccine 1 ml IM x 2, separated by 6 to 12 months

References:

Mandell chapter: Acute viral hepatitis

Sanford keyword: Hepatitis A, Acute, Treatment

Up-to-date article: Hepatitis A virus infections: Treatment and prevention

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HEPATITIS B

# Acute disease management

Most acute hepatitis B disease is mild and self-limited. Patients who appear to

be developing fulminant hepatitis, including those with mental status changes

should receive supportive treatment. Fulminant hepatitis is suggested by

increased prothrombin time, cholestasis, ascites, decreased liver size, or

decreasing serum albumin. Supportive treatment includes maintenance of fluid

and electrolyte balance, monitoring and possible correction of coagulation

defects, treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, and good nutrition with a low-

protein diet. Antiviral therapy is not indicated. Gastroenterology consult

encouraged.

# Chronic disease management

Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B is a complicated, highly specialized

task. Consult with gastroenterology and infectious diseases.

# Prevention

Vaccinate persons at high risk of disease including men who have sex with men,

illegal drug users, and health care workers with substantial exposure to blood

or body fluids.

Give Hepatitis B vaccine 1 dose IM in deltoid at 0, then 1 or 2 months, and

again at 4 to 6 months.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HERPES KERATITIS

Ocular herpes infection can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. The majority of

cases are caused by HSV-1. The recurrence rate of ocular herpes is 40% over a 5

year period, less than that of oral or genital herpes. Ocular herpes is a

major cause of blindness and typically presents as infection of the epithelium

of the cornea but can also rarely involve the stroma and endothelium.

Ophthalmology consultation is recommended.

Involvement of the stroma or endothelium requires treatment with topical

steroid and close monitoring. For these cases, start oral antiviral and consult

ophthalmology for management.

Antiviral prophylaxis is recommended for patients with multiple recurrences,

recurrent episodes with ulceration, recurrent inflammation with

scar/vascularization approaching visual axis, patients who have had keratoplasty

for HSV-related scarring/astigmatism, and patients who have had HSV keratitis

while on immunosuppressive therapy. Post-surgical prophylaxis is not discussed

here. Please consult ophthalmology for more information.

# Treatment of acute infection

Without epithelial ulceration

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID for 7-10 days \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-7days-400mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-7days-400mg-po-tid)

<OR>

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO BID for 7-10 days \($\) R](psozid2-valacyclovir-500mg-bid-7d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-valacyclovir-500mg-bid-7d)

Ulceration of epithelium (Geographic ulcer)

[Acyclovir 800 mg PO 5x/day for 14-21 days \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-800mg-5x-day-14d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-800mg-5x-day-14d)

<OR>

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO TID for 14-21 days \($\) R](psozid2-valacyclovir-1gm-tid-14d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-valacyclovir-1gm-tid-14d)

# Infection prophylaxis for prevention of recurrence

Reassess need for prophylaxis every 12 months

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO BID for 12 months \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-400mg-bid-1yr)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-400mg-bid-1yr)

<OR>

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO QDay for 12 months \($\) R](psozid2-valacyclovir-1yr-500mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-valacyclovir-1yr-500mg-po-qday)

References:

Baratz, Arch Ophthalmology, (2012) 130.1: 108-110

Guess et al, The Ocular Surface, (2007) 5.3:240-250

Wilhelmus, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (2015), 1:CD002898

Miserocchi et al, Efficacy of Valacyclovir vs Acyclovir for the Prevention of

Recurrent Herpes Simplex

Virus Eye Disease: A Pilot Study, American Journal of Ophthalmology, 2007

144:547-551

White et al, Ocular Microbiology and Immunology Group and American Academy of

Ophthalmology, (2014)

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

HERPES SIMPLEX ESOPHAGITIS

HSV infection of the esophagus usually occurs in patients who are

immunocompromised, typically solid organ and bone marrow transplant

recipients. In healthy patients HSV esophagitis occurs occasionally,

usually in men under the age of 40.

Patients usually present with odynophagia and dysphagia. Fever

epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn are less frequent.

Some patients may have coexistent herpes labialis or oropharyngeal

ulcers. Diagnosis is usually established with an upper endoscopy.

Suggestive findings may also be seen during a barium swallow.

# Immunocompetent patients

Spontaneous resolution usually occurs in immunocompetent patients after

one to two weeks. Patients may respond more quickly if treated with a

short course of oral acyclovir.

# Treatment

Treat for 7-10 days

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO 5x/day for 7 days \($\) R](psozid-acyclovir-400mg-po-5x-day-7d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-acyclovir-400mg-po-5x-day-7d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-valacyclovir-7ds-1gm-po-bid)

menus.Term1: Haemophilus influenza Type B vaccine information
menus.Text:
## Vaccine route, orders, names
## __________________________
## Route: IM
## Outpatient Hib orders:
[One dose](orz-set-abx-op-haemophilus-b-vaccine-one-dose)
HSCT Pts only:
[3 dose series](orz-set-abx-op-haemophilus-b-vaccine-3-dose-series)
## CPRS name:
HAEMOPHILUS B VACCINE
INJ,LYPHL
## Stocked brand name:
Hiberix
## Other names:
Haemophilus influenzae
type b
(Hib)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*Not routinely recommended
for healthy adults.
*Those adults at highest
risk of serious Hib
disease include people who
1) have anatomic or
functional asplenia,
2) are undergoing an
elective splenectomy, or
3) are recipients of
hematopoietic stem cell
transplant (HSCT).
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 1 dose to adults in
categories 1 or 2 (see 2nd
bullet in column to left)
if no history of previous
Hib vaccine.
*For HSCT patients,
regardless of Hib vacci-
nation history, give 3
doses, at least 4wks
apart, beginning 6-12
months after transplant.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
## Precautions:
Moderate or severe acute
illness with or
without fever.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HIV

HIV infection and AIDS are associated with several host defense defects. Cell-

mediated immune defects render a patient more susceptible to opportunistic

infections with pathogens like Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly Pneumocystis

carinii), Toxoplasma gondii, cytomegalovirus, mycobacterium-avium intracellulare

complex, and Candida spp.

Contact ID or HIV service for assistance.

[HIV Clinic Consult](gmrctz-mrtc-outpt)

References:

Rich RR, et al, eds. Clinical Immunology

Roitt l, et al, eds. Immunology

## Vaccine route, orders, names

## Route: IM
## Outpatient HPV orders:

## CPRS name:
PAPILLOMAVIRUS HUMAN
VACCINE INJ,SUSP
## Stocked brand name:
Gardasil 9
## Other names:
Human papillomavirus
(HPV)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*For unvaccinated or
partially vaccinated
adults through age 26yrs:
Complete a 3-dose series
of HPV.
*Unvaccinated adults age
27 through 45yrs may be
vaccinated based on
shared clinical decision-
making.
*Other guidance: Pregnancy
is neither a
contraindication nor a
precaution
to HPV vaccine.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 3 doses on a 0, 1-2,
6-month schedule.
*There must be at least
4wks between doses #1 and
#2 and at least 12wks
between doses #2 and #3.
Overall, there must be at
least 5 months between
doses #1 and #3
*If the type of HPV
vaccine previously given
is not known or not
available, any available
HPV vaccine should be used
to complete the series.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
## Precautions:
Moderate or severe acute
illness with or
without fever.

menus.Term1: Initial treatment for peritonitis with dialysis
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# PERITONITIS ASSOCIATED WITH PERITONEAL DIALYSIS

# Peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis usually presents with abdominal

# pain, fever, nausea or vomiting, and cloudy effluent. The leukocyte

# concentration is greater than 100 cells/microliter of dialysate, with more than

# 50% neutrophils.

# Obtain Gram stain, culture, and cell count with differential of dialysate before

# antimicrobials are given.

Nephrology consultation is essential. If cultures show Gram-negative or mixed

bacterial infection, a gastrointestinal tract infectious source is more likely.

Gram-positive organisms like staphylococci usually result from external

contamination. Fungal peritonitis is rare and requires immediate catheter

removal.

**Antimicrobial recommendations are for empirical therapy only. Regimens should

be tailored according to patient response and microbiology results in

consultation with Nephrology and/or Infectious Diseases for more information.

If vancomycin is used, trough serum concentrations should be kept above 15

mcg/ml to ensure adequate intraperitoneal levels. Usually vancomycin must be

given every 3 to 7 days. Contact Nephrology and/or Pharmacy for more

information.

# Consult Nephrology in all cases.

[Peritonitis labs](orz-set-peritonitis-labs)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Antimicrobial therapy

# Duration

Duration of therapy depends on the pathogen identified. Treat staphylococcal and

streptococcal infections for 2 weeks and all other gram-positive infections for

3 weeks. In patients who have Staphylococcus isolated and had a previous

staphylococcal infection, treat for 3 weeks

# All antimicrobials below are administered via 2.5% dextrose 2000 mL peritoneal

# dialysate bag over 6 hours with heparin 1000 units, unless contraindicated

# Empirical treatment while waiting for results of gram stain

[Vancomycin 30 mg/kg PD LD \($\) R <AND>](orzid3-gmenu-pd-init-cefepime-1gm-q24h-vanco-15-30mg-kg-q5-7d)

cefepime 1 gm PD  ($) [R]

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Antifungal prophylaxis:

Antifungal prophylaxis may be used for the duration of antimicrobial therapy to

possibly reduce the risk of fungal peritonitis. *Order if previous peritonitis*

[Fluconazole 200 mg PO every other day \($\) R,DI](psozid-fluconazole-200mg-po-qod)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-fluconazole-200mg-po-qod)

<OR>

[Fluconazole 100 mg PO q24h \($\) R,DI](psozid-fluconazole-100mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-fluconazole-100mg-po-qday)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

De Vin et al, Peritoneal Dialysis International, 2009, Vol. 39, pp. 5-15

Li et al, Peritoneal Dialysis International, 2016, Vol. 36, pp. 481-508

# MALARIA TREATMENT

Consider malaria in any febrile person who has traveled to a malaria-endemic

area in preceding months

Search "CDC malaria countries" for malaria endemic areas

[Link to open internet browser and Google search "CDC Malaria Countries"](orz-gtx-abx-url-google-cdc-malaria-countries)

Obtain malaria smear and call ID on-call in ALL cases when a malaria test is

sent

[Malaria Smear lab order](lrtz-mb-malaria-smear)

[ID on call schedule](orz-min-on-call-schedule)

# Treatment

[Coartem + prior auth bundle: artemether 80 mg/lumefantrine 480 mg twice daily](orz-set-abx-op-malaria-treatment-and-prior-auth)

for 3 days, the first 2 doses should be administered 8 hours apart

Artesunate is appropriate in certain situations e.g. severe malaria - contact

ID on call

## CPRS name:
MENINGOCOCCAL
OLIGOSACCHARIDE
CONJ. VACC INJ,SUSP
## Stocked brand name:
Menveo
## Other names:
Meningococcal conjugate
(MenACWY)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*People with anatomic or
functional asplenia, HIV
infection, or persistent
complement component
deficiency, or complement
inhibitor use.
*People who travel to or
reside in countries in
which meningococcal
disease is hyperendemic or
epidemic (e.g., the
meningitis belt of Sub-
Saharan Africa).
*Microbiologists routinely
exposed to isolates of N.
meningitidis.
*For first year college
students living in a
residence hall, regardless
of age,
>> if unvaccinated, give 1
dose.
>> if history of 1 dose
given when younger than
age 16, give dose #2.
>> if most recent dose
given after 16th birthday
and more than 5 years
have elapsed, give 1 dose.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 2 initial doses of
MenACWY separated by 2m to
adults with risk factors
listed in 1st bullet in
column to left.
*Give 1 initial dose of
MenACWY to all other
adults with risk factors
(see 2nd-4th bullets in
column to left).
*Give booster doses of
MenACWY every 5yrs to
adults with continuing
risk (see the 1st-3rd
bullets in column to
left).
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
## Precautions:
Moderate or severe acute
illness with or
without fever.

## CPRS name:
MEASLES/MUMPS/RUBELLA
VIRUS VACCINE INJ
## Stocked brand name:
M-M-R II
## Other names:
Measles, mumps, rubella
(MMR)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*People born in 1957 or
later (especially those
born outside the U.S.)
should receive at least 1
dose of MMR if they have
no laboratory evidence of
immunity to each of the 3
diseases or documentation
of a dose given on or
after the first birthday.
*People in high-risk
groups, such as healthcare
personnel (paid, unpaid,
or volunteer), students
entering college and other
post-high school
educational institutions,
and international
travelers, should receive
a total of 2 doses.
*HIV infection with CD4
count >/=200 cells/mm3 for
at least 6 months and no
evidence of immunity to
measles, mumps, or rubella
should receive a total of
2 doses. MMR
contraindicated for HIV
infection with CD4 count
<200 cells/mm3
*People born before 1957
are usually considered
immune, but evidence of
immunity (serology or
documented history of 2
doses of MMR) should be
considered for healthcare
personnel.
*Women of childbearing age
who do not have acceptable
evidence of rubella
immunity or vaccination.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 1 or 2 doses (see
criteria in 1st and 2nd
bullets in box to left).
*If dose #2 is
recommended, give it no
sooner than 4wks after
dose #1.
*If woman of childbearing-
age is found to be rubella
susceptible and is not
pregnant, give 1 dose of
MMR. If she is pregnant,
the dose should be given
postpartum. This includes
women who have already
received 1 or 2 doses of
rubella-containing
vaccine.
*If 2 or more of the
following live virus
vaccines are to be given -
MMR, LAIV, Var, ZVL,
and/or yellow fever - they
should be given on the
same day. If they are not
given on the same day,
space them by at least 28d
(30d for yellow fever).
May use as post-exposure
prophylaxis if given
within 3d of exposure.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications:
*History of severe allergic
reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or a vaccine
component.
*Pregnancy or possibility
of pregnancy within 4wks.
*Severe immunodeficiency
(e.g., hematologic and
solid tumors, receiving
chemotherapy, congenital
immunodeficiency, long-
term immunosuppressive
therapy, people with human
immunodeficiency virus
(HIV) infection who are
severely
immunocompromised (CD4
count <200 cells/mm3).)
## Precautions
*Moderate or severe acute
illness with or without
fever.
*If blood, plasma, and/or
immune globulin were given
in past 11m, see ACIP's
[Best Practices Guidance](orz-gtx-abx-url-acip-best-practices-guidance)
regarding time to wait
before vaccinating.
*History of
thrombocytopenia or
thrombocytopenic purpura.
*Need for tuberculin skin
testing (TST) or
interferon-gamma release
assay (IGRA) testing.
note: If TST or IGRA and
MMR are both needed but
not given on same day,
delay TST or IGRA for at
least 4wks after MMR.

menus.Text:
# BACTERIURIA, CANDIDURIA, AND PYURIA

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (>= 100,000 bacteria per ml of urine) is common in

middle aged and older people, especially those who have chronic medical

conditions. Pyuria is common in persons with bacteriuria and individuals with

indwelling catheters in place. By itself, the presence of pyuria is not

sufficient to diagnose bacteriuria, and the presence or absence of pyuria does

not differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic urinary infection. Candiduria is

less common than bacteriuria, but the implications of candiduria are similar to

those of bacteriuria.

Many studies, including randomized clinical trials have shown that

treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria and candiduria, with or without pyuria is

of no benefit, except in certain well-defined circumstances. Antimicrobial

therapy is always accompanied by risk of harms, including drug reactions,

Clostridium difficile colitis, anaphylaxis and death. Except in circumstances

specified below, it is best to not order urinalysis or urine culture in

asymptomatic persons. If bacteriuria, candiduria or pyuria is discovered in an

asymptomatic person for some reason, antimicrobial therapy should not be given

except as specified below.

# Pregnant women or patients undergoing urological procedures with bacteriuria

[Treatment of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria](orzid3-gmenu-asymp-bacteriuria)

# Patients undergoing urological procedures or neutropenic patients with

# candiduria

[Treatment of Candida Urinary Tract Infections](orzid3-gmenu-abx-candida-uti)

References

Pappas et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2016, 62.409

Nicolle et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2005, 40:643

# CONDITIONS NOT BENEFITTED BY ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY

Several common conditions associated with inflammation or

microorganisms do not benefit from antibiotic therapy in most or all cases.

Yet, antimicrobials are frequently prescribed for these conditions leading to

unnecessary toxicity and costs, rare deaths, and the relentless increase in

antimicrobial resistance. Please review these conditions and do not give

antimicrobials for these conditions unless there are extraordinary

circumstances that make your situation different. If you have any questions,

please contact the infectious disease physician on call.

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# PAROTITIS

Infection of salivary tissue is a relatively common disease. It is usually

caused by a stone in the parotid duct, dehydration, or a viral infection.

Sialolithiasis in elderly patients often leads to ductal obstruction and

secondary infection. Other predisposing factors for ductal occlusion include

dehydration, anticholinergic medications such as tricyclics and diphenhydramine,

general disability and trauma. Once culture results are available adjust

antimicrobial therapy based on specific etiologic organism.

For more information click on the link below

[More information on Parotitis](orzid3-gmenu-abx-parotitis-more-information)

# Suppurative Parotitis or Chronic Bacterial Parotitis Exacerbation Empiric

# Treatment

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Viral Parotitis

Suspect mumps parotitis if there is fever, malaise, earache and bilateral tender

swelling of the parotid glands. For mumps parotitis treat with warm compresses

and analgesics and maintain good hydration to prevent secondary bacterial

infection. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Wilson et al., Am Fam Physician. 2014, 89(11)882-888

Mandell chapter:  Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases

Sanford keyword: Parotitis

Up-To-Date  article: Suppurative parotitis in adults

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX PAROTITIS MORE INFORMATION
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# MORE ABOUT PAROTITIS

Suppurative Parotitis. Acute bacterial parotitis affects primarily elderly,

malnourished, dehydrated or post-operative patients. Symptoms include fever,

toxicity, and tender swelling along the mandible with purulent drainage from the

parotid duct. Suppurative parotitis is usually unilateral whereas viral

parotitis is usually bilateral. Pain is intense and aggressive, analgesic

therapy is required. Progression of infection may lead to massive swelling of

the neck, respiratory obstruction, septicemia and osteomyelitis of adjacent

facial bones. Empiric antibiotics are required for coverage of Staphylococcus

aureus if bacterial, and surgical drainage is usually necessary.

Chronic Parotitis. Parotitis is recurrent with intermittent acute exacerbations.

Chronic, low-grade bacterial infection results in functional destruction of the

salivary gland. It may be confused with Sjogren's syndrome, a noninfectious

illness. Therapy includes systemic antibiotics. Parotidectomy may eventually be

required for patients with long-standing infection.

Viral Parotitis. Mumps parotitis is characterized by the rapid, painful swelling

of one or both parotid glands within 2 to 3 weeks after exposure to the mumps

virus. Mumps usually involves both parotid glands whereas bacterial parotitis is

unilateral. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.

Mumps parotitis usually resolves spontaneously in 5 to 10 days. Provide

symptomatic relief of pain and fever and maintain hydration to prevent secondary

bacterial infection.

# PERIANAL/ANORECTAL ABSCESS

Antibiotics should typically be reserved for patients with an anorectal abscess

complicated by cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, underlying

immunosuppression, or failure to improve with drainage alone.

Cultures of abscess fluid are not routinely recommended. Consider in patients

who will be treated with adjunctive antibiotic treatment for systemic signs of

infection, recurrent infection or nonhealing wounds, or underlying

immunosuppression.

# Primary therapy: abscess drainage

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Adjunctive antimicrobial treatment for patients with above complications.

# Duration of treatment

5 days of antibiotics after incision and drainage is recommended. In the absence

of source control, recommended duration is 7-14 days based on severity of

infection, underlying immunosuppression, and clinical response.

# Mild disease, outpatients, oral transition

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX POSITIVE BLOOD CULTURE OP COAG NEG STAPH
menus.Text:
# BLOOD CULTURE POSITIVE FOR COAGULASE NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CNS)

CNS are the most common contaminants isolated from blood cultures. When CNS

isolated from blood cultures represent true bacteremia, the blood is usually

obtained from a patient with plastic or metal in the body. The most common

source of coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia is an infected

intravascular catheter.

When CNS are isolated from blood, the physician should carefully assess the

patient to decide whether the isolation represents disease or colonization.

Colonization is more likely if a single bottle is positive or both bottles from

a single blood draw are positive. If multiple bottles are positive from separate

blood draws, it is more likely that the isolates reflect disease or colonization

of an intravascular device. Isolates from contaminated bottles often take

several days to become positive. If the patient has risk factors for true

coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia, catheter-related blood stream

infection and/or the patient is severely ill, antimicrobials should be given. If

there is a plastic or metal prosthesis in the body, the physician should

evaluate the site for possible infection. If the isolates are likely to

represent contamination and the patient does not seem ill with CNS,

antimicrobial therapy would not be helpful and should not be given.

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for treatment CNS bacteremia and infected

intravascular catheters treatment recommendations

References

Mandell chapter: Staphylococcus epidermis and Other Coagulase-Negative

Staphylococci

Mermel et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2009, 49
