# RABIES POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS

Patients are given post-exposure prophylaxis based upon their risk including

type of exposure, epidemiology of rabies in the area where contact occurred,

circumstances of the exposure incident, species and the availability of animal

involved. The Minnesota Department of Health has staff available 24/7 to consult

health care providers on risk-status of individuals. They can be contacted by

phone at 651-201-5414. Refer to link below for more information.

[Minnesota Department of Health Guide on Animal Bites and Rabies Risk](orz-gtx-abx-mdh-animal-bites-and-rabies-risk)

Discussion with Infectious Diseases inpatient attending by phone is highly

recommended. Use the link below to obtain the pager number for on-call staff.

[Infectious Diseases On-Call Schedule](orz-min-on-call-schedule)

# Wound cleansing

All post-exposure prophylaxis should begin with immediate thorough cleansing of

all wounds with soap and water. After cleansing, use povidine-iodine solution to

irrigate the wounds.

[Povidine-iodine irrigation solution](psczid-povidine-iodine-soln-wound-cleanse-one-time-dose)

# Patients without history of rabies vaccination

After wound cleansing, administer rabies immune globulin and first dose of

rabies vaccine series immediately.

[Rabies immune globulin STAT < AND > rabies vaccine STAT](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-igg-and-vaccine-series)

Administer second, third and fourth doses of rabies vaccine series on days 3, 7,

and 14. An additional dose is given on day 28 for immunocompromised patients.

# Patients with history of rabies vaccination

Patients with a history of complete pre-exposure vaccination regimen and a

documented antibody response to the rabies virus, do not require rabies immune

globulin administration. If the patient does not meet these criteria, treat as a

patient without history of rabies vaccination above. If patient does meet these

criteria, after wound cleansing, administer first dose of rabies vaccine series.

[Rabies vaccine STAT](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-stat-and-vaccine-series)

Administer second dose of rabies vaccine series on day 3.

# Tetanus Prophylaxis

In bite wounds that break the skin, tetanus vaccine is indicated if patient has

received <3 doses of tetanus vaccine or immunization history is unknown. Tetanus

immune globulin is also indicated in these patients if they have a tetanus prone

wound. For patients with 3 or more documented tetanus vaccine doses, tetanus

vaccine is indicated if >5 years since last booster in tetanus prone wounds and

indicated if >10 years since last booster in non-tetanus-prone wounds.

[Tetanus and Diphtheria \(Td\) vaccine booster dose STAT](psczid-tetanus-diptheria-vaccine-one-dose-stat)

# Treatment of infection

[Bite wounds recommendations \(outpatient\)](orzid3-gmenu-bite-wounds)

# ORDER RABIES POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS SUBSEQUENT VACCINE DOSES

A second dose of the rabies vaccine is required on day 3 for patients with a

history of documented rabies vaccination. To order the second dose of the rabies

vaccination, follow these two steps:

# 1) Select vaccine series below based on administration location

# 2) Click the [Next] button at the top right of this window when finished

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# If second dose will be administered at MVAMC ED

[CLICK HERE to place clinic order for second dose](psczid-rabies-post-exposure-vaccine-2nd-dose-of-2-dose-series)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# If second dose will be administered at a CBOC

Complete the following 4 steps:

1) Complete rabies vaccination plan in the EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT STAFF NOTE and

attach patient's primary care provider for follow up.

2) Ensure the CBOC is open on day 3.

[CLICK HERE for CBOC open hours and contact information](orz-gtx-abx-cboc-info)

3) Order vaccine dose and place return to clinic (RTC) order.

[CLICK HERE to place clinic order and RTC order](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-vaccine-post-exp-dose-2-of-2-dose-series)

4) Call inpatient pharmacy at ext 31-3128 to ensure vaccine dose is mailed over

night to the CBOC for administration.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Manning SE, Rupprecht CE, Fishbein D, et al. Human rabies prevention-United

States, 2008: recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization

Practices. MMWR Recomm Rep 2008, 57:1.

Rupprecht, Charles E., et al. Use of a reduced (4-dose) vaccine schedule for

postexposure prophylaxis to prevent human rabies: recommendations of the

advisory committee on immunization practices. MMWR Recomm Rep 59.RR-2 (2010): 1-

9

# ORDER RABIES POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS SUBSEQUENT VACCINE DOSES

In patients without documented rabies vaccination, subsequent doses of the

rabies vaccine are required on days 3, 7, and 14. An additional dose is given on

day 28 for immunocompromised patients. To order subsequent rabies vaccinations,

follow these two steps:

# 1) Select vaccine series below based on administration location and immune

# status

# 2) Click the [Next] button at the top right of this window when finished

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# If all subsequent rabies vaccine doses will be administered at the MVAMC ED

[CLICK HERE for immunocompetent patients](psczid-rabies-post-exposure-vaccine-2-4-series)

[CLICK HERE for immunocompromised patients](psczid-rabies-post-exposure-vaccine-2-5-series)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# If at least one subsequent rabies vaccine dose will be administered at a CBOC

Complete the following 4 steps:

1) Complete rabies vaccination plan in the EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT STAFF NOTE and

attach patient's primary care provider for follow up.

2) Ensure CBOC is open on days when vaccine is scheduled to be given there. The

rabies vaccine is given on a 3, 7, 14-day schedule, an additional dose is given

on day 28 for immunocompromised patients

[CLICK HERE for CBOC open hours and contact information](orz-gtx-abx-cboc-info)

3) Order vaccine doses and return to clinic (RTC) order

[CLICK HERE for immunocompetent patients](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-post-exposure-vaccine-2-4-series)

[CLICK HERE for immunocompromised patients](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-post-exposure-vaccine-2-5-series)

4) Call inpatient pharmacy at ext 31-3128 to ensure vaccine dose is mailed over

night to the CBOC for administration.

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# RABIES PRE-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS

For patients exposed to a rabid animal, refer to the Rabies Post-Exposure

Prophylaxis recommendations in the emergency department CDSS.

[Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis](orzid3-gmenu-abx-rabies-post-exposure-prophylaxis)

# Rabies Vaccination

People in Risk Category Groups 1-4 (see below for full descriptions) should be

vaccinated against rabies.

[Rabies vaccine, 2-dose series \(0, 7 days\)](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-vaccine-2-dose-series)

# Rabies Booster

A booster vaccination is given for groups 1 through 3 (not 4 or 5).  For groups

1 and 2, this is dictated by rabies serum titer levels.  For group 3, a one-time

booster is recommended at a specific time interval.  For those in risk category

1, check titer every 6 months.  For those in risk category 2, check titer every

2 years).  See below for information regarding timing of the one-time booster

for risk category 3.

[Rabies virus rapid fluorescent focus inhibition test](lrtzid-rabies-virus-rapid-fluorescent-inhibition-test)

[Rabies booster vaccine](orz-set-abx-op-rabies-booster-vaccine-one-dose)

# CDC guidelines categorize patients into five categories based on exposure risk

Risk Category 1 (Highest risk): People who work with live or concentrated rabies

virus in laboratories

Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Check titer every 6 months and give

booster dose if titer is low

Risk Category 2: People who frequently do at least one of the following: handle

bats, have contact with bats, enter high-density bat environments like caves, or

perform animal necropsies

Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Check titer every 2 years and give

booster dose if titer is low

Risk Category 3: People who interact with, or are at higher risk to interact,

with mammals other than bats that could be rabid, for a period longer than three

years after they receive PrEP. This group includes:

Most veterinarians, veterinary technicians, animal control officers, wildlife

biologists, rehabilitators, trappers, and spelunkers (cave explorers). Certain

travelers to regions outside of the United States where rabies in dogs is

commonly found.

Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Either a one-time titer check after 1

and up to 3 years following the first 2-dose vaccination < OR > 1-dose booster

between 3 weeks and 3 years following the first vaccine in the 2-dose

vaccination

Risk Category 4: Same population as risk category 3, but at a higher risk for ?

three years after they receive PrEP.

Recommendation: Give rabies vaccination. Routine boosters not recommended.

Risk Category 5:

People who do not have special occupational risks.

Recommendation: Rabies vaccination and boosters not recommended.

_______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Rao et. Al., MMWR. Morbidity and mortality weekly report 71 (2022)

https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-care/pre-exposure-prophylaxis.html

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# RABIES RISK CATEGORIES

# Continuous

Rabies research laboratory workers, rabies biologics production workers

# Frequent

Rabies diagnostic laboratory workers, cavers, veterinarians and staff and

animal-control and wildlife workers in areas where rabies is enzootic. All

persons who frequently handle bats.

# Infrequent

Veterinarians and animal-control staff working with terrestrial animals in areas

where rabies is uncommon to rare. Veterinary students. Travelers visiting areas

where rabies is enzootic and immediate access to appropriate medical care

including biologics is limited.

# Rare

U.S. population at large, including persons in areas where rabies is epizootic.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Manning SE, Rupprecht CE, Fishbein D, et al. Human rabies prevention-United

States, 2008: recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization

Practices. MMWR Recomm Rep 2008, 57:1.

Rupprecht, Charles E., et al. Use of a reduced (4-dose) vaccine schedule for

postexposure prophylaxis to prevent human rabies: recommendations of the

advisory committee on immunization practices. MMWR Recomm Rep 59.RR-2 (2010): 1-

9

# CDC Recommended Adult Immunization Schedule

[Click Here for link to PDF of CDC Recommended Adult Immunization Schedule](orz-gtx-abx-cdc-adult-immunization-schedule)

# Please note:

*A vaccine series does not need to be restarted, regardless of the time that has

elapsed between doses.

*For calculating intervals between doses, 4 weeks = 28 days. Intervals of 4

months or greater are determined by calendar months.

*Any vaccine can be given with another unless otherwise noted on the specific

vaccine page.

*Mild illness is not a contraindication to receiving any vaccine.

# RESPIRATORY PAPILLOMATOSIS

Respiratory papillomas are usually associated with human papillomavirus

infection. The papillomas are found in the pharynx, usually in the

larynx.  They can be surgically removed, but they often recur.

removed to prevent recurrences.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# ROSACEA

Rosacea is an inflammatory skin condition resulting in erythema and

telangiectasia of nose, cheeks, eyelids, and forehead. It typically occurs in

mid-life and the etiology is unknown. Erythematous rosacea is the early stage of

the disease and usually manifests with flushing reactions and persistently

erythematous skin. Late-stage disease is known as papulopustular rosace.

Symptoms include papular, pustular, cysts and nodules. Severe disease results in

tissue atrophy and rhinophyma (bulbus nose).

The goal of treatment is control of symptoms, not cure. General treatment

measures include avoiding triggers (e.g. spicy food, alcohol), skin care (e.g.

moisturizing, gentle cleansing, avoiding topical irritants) and using sun

screen. Medical treatment includes topical agents as first line therapy and oral

treatment for refractory disease.

# Papulopustular rosacea

Preferred:

[Metronidazole 0.75% cream topically q24h \($\) DI](psozid-metronidazole-0-75-cream-topically-q24h)

Alternative:

[Doxycycline 50 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks](psozid2-doxycycline-12wks-50mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Minocycline 50 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks](psozid2-minocylcine-12wks-50mg-po-q12h)

________________________________________________________________________________

**FOR DERMATOLOGY USE ONLY, REQUIRES DERMATOLOGY CONSULT PRIOR TO TREATMENT**

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS DECOLONIZATION

From 10% to 40% of adults are colonized with Staphylococcus aureus, and the

anterior nares is the most common site of colonization. A majority of people

never have disease with S. aureus, but a tiny fraction of people develop

clinical infections with the S. aureus that has colonized their skin or anterior

nares. Steps to decolonize the skin and anterior nares can transiently diminish

or eradicate S. aureus colonization and can prevent post-operative wound

infection in certain high-risk circumstances. For people who have other forms of

recurrent S. aureus disease, not associated with an operation, results with

decolonization have been disappointing, and decolonization is not routinely

recommended. Colonization typically reappears in most patients within a few days

or weeks after decolonization has been attempted. Clinicians occasionally wish

to attempt decolonization for patients with frequent, troublesome recurrences.

The procedure here is one of several that have been studied, but none have been

particularly effective over the long run.

Consultation with Infectious Diseases is recommended.

# Decolonization Order Set:

[Mupirocin 2% ointment topically BID M <AND> chlorhexidine 4% liquid](orz-set-abx-op-chlorhexidine-mupirocin-decolonization)

topically qday [M] for 5 days

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-chlorhexidine-mupirocin-decolonization)

# Instructions

* Patient must wear clean clothes after bathing to prevent recontamination

* Bedding and linens must be changed/cleaned daily until the end of the

decolonization protocol.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Bradley S Clin Infect Dis 2007, 44: 186

Lonneke G NEJM 2010, 362: 9

Schweizer et al, JAMA 2015, 313.212:162-2171

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX STASIS DERMATITIS OP
menus.Text:
# STASIS DERMATITIS

Stasis dermatitis is a common condition that is often confused with

bacterial cellulitis. Stasis dermatitis does not benefit from antimicrobial

therapy. It is important to distinguish between the two. The provider

should be mindful of the fact that bacterial cellulitis can occur on skin

with underlying stasis dermatitis. (See link below for bacterial cellulitis)

Common risk factors for venous stasis include advancing age, family

history of venous disease, increased body mass index, smoking, a history of

trauma, prior venous thrombosis and pregnancy. Chronic venous disease and

arterial vascular disease have some common risk factors (eg, smoking,

obesity) and pathophysiological processes. The most common symptoms reported

by patients with chronic venous disease are limb discomfort (tired, heavy

legs), pain, and limb swelling. Swelling is often worse with prolonged

standing and improves with leg elevation and walking. The skin of the

anterior surfaces of the lower legs often has brown or blue-grey

hyperpigmentation.

People with venous stasis are prone to develop stasis dermatitis which

is one of the most common and earliest dermatologic signs of chronic venous

insufficiency. Stasis dermatitis is an inflammatory process that presents as

an eczematous rash characterized by itching, erythema, scaling, weeping,

erosions, and crusting. Longstanding cases may develop lipodermatosclerosis

a fibrosing panniculitis of the subcutaneous tissue. Lipodermatosclerosis

typically starts with a firm area of induration at the medial ankle. As the

process progresses, the entire leg lower leg can become involved with

extension up to the mid leg in more advanced cases. The skin overlying the

panniculitis is typically heavily pigmented and bound down to the

subcutaneous tissues. Brawny edema above the fibrotic area and on the foot

below is seen in advanced cases. Leukocytosis and fever are common in people

with stasis dermatitis.

Chronic venous disease is the most common cause of leg ulcers. They

are usually found low on the medial ankle over a perforating vein, or along

the course of the great or small saphenous veins. They occur more proximally

if precipitated by trauma. Venous ulcers are not found on the forefoot or

above the level of the knee. Venous ulcers can be multiple or single, and

can be exquisitely tender, shallow, exudative and have a granulation base.

The ulcer borders are usually irregular but not undermined. They can extend

circumferentially around the leg if left untreated.

Arterial ulcers are typically painful, and punched out or stellate. The

surrounding skin is red and taut. Some arterial ulcers are pale - others have

a black or yellow eschar. They are often associated with trauma and commonly

occur on the foot over pressure points. There may be other signs of arterial

insufficiency on the lower limb including thin atrophic or hairless skin,

poor pedal pulses, diminished capillary refill, or hypertrophic deformed

nails.

Patients with stasis or lipodermatosclerosis are prone to bouts of

bacterial cellulitis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or encapsulated

streptococci. Typically, stasis dermatitis develops slowly, over a week or

more. It is often bilateral. The onset of bacterial cellulitis is usually

abrupt, typically developing over 1 or 2 days. Bacterial cellulitis often

starts in one area and spreads to adjacent areas. Bacterial cellulitis is

unilateral. Both can present with fever and leukocytosis.

In a patient with stasis and cellulitis and the physician is uncertain

about whether bacterial cellulitis is present, the physician should consider

a trial of bed rest, leg elevation, and if there is fluid overload, diuresis

If the cellulitis improves in 24-48 hours, antibacterial therapy and the

attendant adverse reactions can be avoided. If it is clear that bacterial

cellulitis has occurred, antimicrobial therapy should be given.

[Bacterial Cellulitis](orzid3-gmenu-cellulitis)

References

Stevens et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2014, 59(2): e10-52

Up-to-Date article: Stasis dermatitis

acellular pertussis

References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*All people who lack
written documentation of a
primary series consisting
of at least 3 doses of
tetanus- and diphtheria-
toxoid-containing vaccine.
*A booster dose of Td or
Tdap may be needed for
wound management, so
consult ACIP
recommendations.
*Adults who have not
received Td or Tdap in the
past 10 years or whose
Tdap history is not known.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*For people who are
unvaccinated or behind,
complete a 3-dose series
with Tdap as the first
dose, followed by Td or
Tdap (observe intervals of
1-2m between dose #1 and
#2, and an interval of 6-
12m between dose #2 and
#3).
*Give Tdap to pregnant
women during each
pregnancy (preferred
during the early part of
gestational weeks 27
through 36), regardless of
the interval since prior
Td or Tdap.
*Give Td or Tdap booster
every 10yrs after the
primary series has been
completed.
*If Tdap is indicated,
Tdap should be given
regardless of interval
since previous Td.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications
*History of severe
allergic reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or to a vaccine
component.
*For Tdap only, history of
encephalopathy not
attributable to an
identifiable cause, within
7d following DTP/DTaP, or
Tdap.
## Precautions
*Moderate or severe acute
illness with or without
fever.
*History of Guillain-Barre
syndrome within 6wks
following previous dose of
tetanus-toxoid containing
vaccine.
*History of Arthus-type
reaction following a prior
dose of tetanus or
diphtheria-toxoid
containing vaccine
(including MenACWY): defer
vaccination until at least
10yrs have elapsed since
the last tetanus toxoid-
containing vaccine.
*For pertussis-containing
vaccines only, progressive
or unstable neurologic
disorder, uncontrolled
seizures, or progressive
encephalopathy until a
treatment regimen has been
established and the
condition has stabilized.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CDC MPOX TREATMENT WITH TPOXX

# Eligibility:

o Consent: Must have documented consent by patient or legally authorized

representative in paper or i-Med consent

o Primary/empiric treatment: Confirmed diagnosis or suspected infection based

on exposure and/or symptoms while testing is pending.

o Secondary Treatment: Complications from replication competent vaccinia

infection from vaccination, secondary transmission, or other exposure. TPOXX may

be used after VIGIV treatment or in conjunction with VIGIV and/or with other

therapies based on clinical judgement.

o Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): May be considered on a case-by-case basis in

consultation with the CDC. Eligibility for PEP use depends on high risk exposure

confirmed or probable case and alternative or complement to PEP vaccination

is needed based on clinical judgment (e.g. vaccine allergy, immunocompromise).

o Dosage and duration: Weight based dosing for 14 days. But it may be longer

based on clinical progress but not to exceed 90 days. Oral tecovirimat capsule

should be taken by mouth with a full glass of water within 30 minutes after

eating a full meal of moderate or high fat (ideally about 600 calories and 25

grams of fat).

o CDC Case Reports Forms:  To be completed and returned to CDC by treating

physicians per IND protocol.

[CLICK HERE for link to required documents \(MPox Taskforce Teams group\)](orz-gtx-abx-tpoxx-documents-link)

# Exclusions:

o Patient or legally authorized representative unwilling to sign an informed

consent and refuse tecovirimat treatment

o  Known allergy to tecovirimat and/or excipients of tecovirimat

o  Upon negative test results for orthopoxvirus whose treatment was initiated

based on clinical manifestations prior to laboratory results.

o For IV tecovirimat only: patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine

clearance <30 mL/min)

# Oral Treatment:

Patients 40kg to < 120 kg

# UNCOMPLICATED URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS

# Uncomplicated UTI is an infection confined to the bladder in afebrile women or

# men without urinary catheter. Symptoms include dysuria, lower abdominal pain,

# and urgency.

NOT signs or symptoms: abnormal urinalysis alone, pyuria, falls, change in urine

odor or color, delirium (acute mental status change, confusion) without systemic

signs of infection. These may occur in patients with a UTI but alone are

inadequate for diagnosis and empiric treatment.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

For patients without signs or symptoms of UTI:

[Asymptomatic bacteriuria](orzid3-gmenu-asymp-bacteriuria)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
# UPPER RESPIRATORY INFECTION (URI)

Upper respiratory infections include several common syndromes including

the common cold, bronchitis (see below), pharyngitis (see below) and sinusitis

(see below). Most are caused by viruses and there is no benefit from

antimicrobial therapy. If a patient presents with a URI, consider specific

infections that do respond to antimicrobial therapy like herpes simplex

stomatitis, pertussis or thrush. If no condition that benefits from

antimicrobial therapy is present, antimicrobials will almost certainly not help

but will likely select for antimicrobial resistance and may lead to other

adverse effects.

[Bronchitis](orzid3-gmenu-bronchitis-new)

[Sinusitis](orzid3-gmenu-acute-sinusitis-opt)

[Pharyngitis](orzid3-gmenu-pharyngitis)

References

Kogawa et al, General medicine, 2009, 10:7-15

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ABX VAR VACCINE INFORMATION PAGE
menus.Text:
## Vaccine route, orders, names
## __________________________
## Route: Subcutaneous
## Outpatient VAR orders:
[2 dose series](orz-set-abx-op-varicella-vaccine-2-dose-series)
## CPRS name:
VARICELLA VIRUS VACCINE
INJ
## Stocked brand name:
Varivax
## Other names:
Varicella
(Chickenpox, VAR)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*All adults without
evidence of immunity.
NOTE: Evidence of immunity
is defined as written
documentation
of 2 doses of varicella
vaccine, a history of
varicella disease or
herpes zoster (shingles)
based on healthcare-
provider diagnosis,
laboratory evidence of
immunity or confirmation
of disease, and/or birth
in the U.S. before 1980,
with the exceptions that
follow:
>>Healthcare personnel
(HCP) born in the U.S.
before 1980 who do not
meet any of the criteria
above should be tested or
given the 2-dose vaccine
series. If testing
indicates they are not
immune, give the 1st dose
of varicella vaccine
immediately. Give the 2nd
dose 4-8 wks later.
>>Pregnant women born in
the U.S. before 1980 who
do not meet any of the
criteria above should
either 1) be tested for
susceptibility during
pregnancy and if found
susceptible, given the 1st
dose of varicella vaccine
postpartum before hospital
discharge, or 2) not be
tested for susceptibility
and given the 1st dose of
varicella vaccine post-
partum before hospital
discharge. Give the 2nd
dose 4-8wks later.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 2 doses.
*Dose #2 is given 4-8wks
after dose #1.
*If dose #2 is delayed, do
not start over. Just give
dose #2.
*If 2 or more of the
following live virus
vaccines are to be given -
MMR, LAIV, Var, ZVL,
and/or yellow fever - they
should be given on the
same day. If they are not
given on the same day,
space them by at least 28d
(30d for yellow fever).
*May use as post exposure
prophylaxis if given
within 5d of exposure.
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications
*History of severe
allergic reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or to a vaccine
component.
*Pregnancy or possibility
of pregnancy within 4wks.
*People on long-term
immunosuppressive therapy
or who are
immunocompromised
because of malignancy and
primary or acquired
immunodeficiency,
including HIV/AIDS
(although vaccination
may be considered if CD4+
T-lymphocyte counts are
greater than or equal to
200 cells/mm3)
*People with isolated B-
lymphocyte deficiency may
receive varicella vaccine.
## Precautions:
*Moderate or severe acute
illness with or without
fever.
*If blood, plasma, and/or
immune globulin (IG or
VZIG) were given in past
11m, see ACIP's Best
Practices Guidance
regarding time to wait
before vaccinating.
*Receipt of specific
antivirals (i.e.,
acyclovir, famciclovir, or
valacyclovir) 24hrs before
vaccination, if possible.
Delay resumption of these
antiviral drugs for 14d
after vaccination.
*Use of aspirin or
aspirin-containing
products.

menus.Text:
## Vaccine route, orders, names
## __________________________
## Route: IM
## Outpatient RZV (Shingrix)
## Orders:
[2 dose series](orz-set-abx-op-zoster-recombinant-vaccine-2-dose-series)
## CPRS name:
ZOSTER VACCINE INJ,LYPHL
## Stocked brand name:
Shingrix
## Other names:
Zoster, Shingles
(RZV)
References:
Immunization Action
Coalition,
Summary of Adult
Immunizations, 2021, P2011
Freedman et al., Annals of
internal medicine, 2021,
174(3)374-384.
<!-- COLUMN 2 -->
## Recommended populations
## __________________________
*People age 50yrs and
older
>>NOTE: Do not test people
age 50yrs or older for
varicella immunity prior
to zoster vaccination.
Persons born in the U.S.
prior to 1980 can be
presumed to be immune to
varicella for the purpose
of zoster vaccination,
regardless of their
recollection of having had
chickenpox.
*People age
18 years and
older who are
or will be at
increased risk
of zoster due to
immunodeficiency
or immunosuppression
caused by known
disease or
therapy.
<!-- COLUMN 3 -->
## Administration Schedule
## __________________________
*Give 2 doses of RZV,
separated by 2-6m,
regardless of previous
history of herpes zoster
(shingles) or chickenpox.
*If previously vaccinated
with ZVL (Zostavax), give
2 doses of RZV at least 2m
after ZVL.
*A 1-time dose of ZVL may
be given to previously
unvaccinated
immunocompetent adults age
60y and older: however,
RZV is preferred.
*If 2 or more of the
following live virus
vaccines are to be given -
LAIV, MMR, Var, ZVL,
and/or yellow fever - they
should be given on the
same day. If they are not,
space them by at least 28d
(30d for yellow fever).
<!-- COLUMN 4 -->
## Contraindications/Precautions
## __________________________
## Contraindications
*History of severe
allergic reaction (e.g.,
anaphylaxis) to a previous
dose or to a vaccine
component.
## Precautions
*Moderate or severe acute
illness with or without
fever.
*Consider delaying
vaccination in pregnant
or lactating women

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ACUTE BACT PROSTATITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS

Acute bacterial prostatitis typically presents with fever, dysuria, chills,

malaise, myalgia, pelvic or perianal pain. On exam, the prostate gland is tense,

boggy, and extremely tender. The urinalysis reveals pyuria, and the urine

culture is positive. Men with dysuria and fever but without pyuria and/or

bacteriuria should be seen by a urologist. If there is any suspicion of abscess,

especially in men older than 40 years, the patient should be seen by a urologist

and transurethral prostate resection for drainage should be considered.

Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract

instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated

with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 and those who

are at high risk of sexually transmitted infections are associated with N.

gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if the

patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course of

antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to

ciprofloxacin.

A urine Gram stain and culture should be performed in all patients to guide

antimicrobial therapy:

[Lab menu](orzid2-gmenu-abx-lab-menu)

# Duration

There is limited data on duration of antimicrobial treatment for prostatitis. 14

days minimum is required. 4 to 6 weeks may be necessary to completely eradicate

bacteria in the prostate to ensure patient does not progress to chronic

bacterial prostatitis.

# _____________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment

Hydration, bed rest and analgesics are recommended along with antimicrobials

treatment.

# Age < 35 years and those at high risk of sexually transmitted infections

Patient weighing less than 300 lbs:

[Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once \($\) M <AND> doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for](orz-set-abx-op-ceftr-500mg-im-x1-doxyc-14ds-100-po-bid)

14 days

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-ceftr-500mg-im-x1-doxyc-14ds-100-po-bid)

Patients weighing 300 lbs or greater:

[Ceftriaxone 1 gm IM once \($\) M <AND> doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for](orz-set-abx-op-ceftr-1gm-im-x1-doxyc-14ds-100-po-bid)

14 days

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-ceftr-1gm-im-x1-doxyc-14ds-100-po-bid)

# Age >/= 35 years

Preferred:

[Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h \($\) R, DI for 14 days](psozid2-levofloxacin-14ds-750mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-levofloxacin-14ds-750mg-po-qday)

Alternative:

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet q12h \($\) R,DI for 14 days](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-14days-1ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-14days-1ds-po-bid)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Lipsky et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2010, 50(12)1641-1652

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ACUTE SINUSITIS (OPT)
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ACUTE SINUSITIS

Most cases of acute sinusitis are viral and resolve within 10 days. Symptoms

(nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, and tooth or facial pain) can be

treated with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline. Diagnosis of acute

sinusitis is based on the presence of at least 2 major or 1 major and at least 2

minor symptoms.

# Major Symptoms

1. Purulent anterior nasal discharge

2. Purulent or discolored posterior nasal discharge

3. Nasal congestion or fullness

4. Facial pain or pressure

5. Hyposmia or anosmia

6. Fever

# Minor Symptoms

1. Headache

2. Ear pain, pressure or fullness

3. Halitosis

4. Dental pain

5. Cough

6. Fatigue

If patient meets criteria above for acute sinusitis, treat with antimicrobials

according to the following criteria for mild to moderate or severe bacterial

sinusitis.

# Mild to moderate bacterial sinusitis

1. Symptoms persisting beyond 10 days

< OR >

2. Double-sickening - Symptoms typical of viral upper respiratory infection

initially improving for 5-6 days then worsening with new development of fever,

headache or increased nasal discharge.

[CLICK HERE for treatment of mild to moderate bacterial sinusitis](orzid3-gmenu-acute-sinusitis-mild-to-mod)

# Severe bacterial sinusitis

Severe signs or symptoms of high fever (>/= 102 degrees Fahrenheit, >/= 39

degrees Celsius) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4 consecutive days or facial

pain lasting for at least 3-4 consecutive days at the beginning of illness.

[CLICK HERE for treatment of severe bacterial sinusitis](orzid3-gmenu-acute-sinusitis-severe)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Chow et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012, 54(8) e72-e112

Mandell chapter: Sinusitis

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# MILD TO MODERATE SINUSITIS

Community-acquired bacterial sinusitis is most often due to Streptococcus

pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis. Streptococci,

Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes are isolated less frequently.

# Treatment for first 10 days of illness

Treat with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline spray.

[CLICK HERE to go to acute respiratory infection symptomatic treatment menu](orzid3-gmenu-ari-symptomatic-therapy)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Treatment of cases that have not improved in 10 days despite

# treatment with decongestants, analgesics, and nasal saline.

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h \($\) R for 5 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

Alternatives:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Cefdinir 300 mg PO q12h \($\) R for 5 days](psozid2-cefdinir-300mg-po-bid-5days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefdinir-300mg-po-bid-5days)

< OR >

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 5 days](psozid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d)

# Treatment Failure

If symptoms worsen despite 72 hours or  fail to improve after 3-5 days of

initial empirical antimicrobial therapy, broaden coverage, switch to different

antimicrobial class and treat 7-10 days. If symptoms continue to worsen or there

is no improvement after 3-5 more days of treatment, obtain CT to investigate

non-infectious or suppurative causes. ENT consultation is recommended. If

sinuses are aspirated, specimens should be cultured.

[Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h \($\) R,DI for 7 days](psozid2-levofloxacin-7ds-750mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-levofloxacin-7ds-750mg-po-qday)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# SEVERE SINUSITIS

Community-acquired bacterial sinusitis is most often due to Streptococcus

pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza or Moraxella catarrhalis. Group A

Streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes are isolated less frequently.

For patients who present with severe symptoms (high fever (>/= 102 degrees

Fahrenheit, >/= 39 degrees Celsius) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4

consecutive days or facial pain lasting for at least 3-4 consecutive days at the

beginning of illness), initiate empiric antimicrobials and obtain CT of sinuses

to determine the extent of infection. If the CT shows extension of sinusitis

infection into surrounding structures (i.e. the cranium or orbit) consult ENT

immediately. Closely monitor all patients who present with severe signs and

symptoms to ensure that signs and symptoms improve within 72 hours.

# Outpatient Treatment

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h \($\) R for 7 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

Alternatives:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Cefdinir 300 mg PO q12h \($\) R for 7 days](psozid2-cefdinir-300mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefdinir-300mg-po-bid-7days)

< OR >

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID\($\) DI for 7 days](psozid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-7ds)

# Treatment of hospitalized patient

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Treatment failure

If symptoms worsen or no improvement is seen after 3-5 days of treatment,

broaden coverage, switch to different antimicrobial class and treat 10 days. If

symptoms continue to worsen or there is no improvement after 3-5 more days of

treatment, obtain CT to investigate non-infectious or suppurative causes. ENT

consultation is recommended. If sinuses are aspirated, specimens should be

cultured.

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS (SBP)

[Oral step-down treatment](orzid3-gmenu-abx-step-down-treatment)

SBP is infection of the peritoneal cavity in the absence of apparent trauma or

other obvious cause. SBP occurs primarily in people with end-stage liver disease

and ascites. The diagnosis is made when a peritoneal fluid sample has >/= 250

polymorphonuclear leukocyte cells per microliter, or when bacterial pathogens

are isolated.

Long-term SBP prophylaxis is indicated for patients who experience a first

episode of SBP.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ANTIVIRAL IMMUNOSUPPRESIVE MALIGNANCY
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

# Severly Immunosuppressive Chemo-immunotherapy

# Purine Analogues

Chemotherapy with purine analogues such as fludarabine, cladribine, or

pentostatin results in major cellular-immunodeficiency that may outlast the

exposure by months and enhances the risk for viral infections.

Recommend antiviral prophylaxis for patients treated with purine analogues

if at least one of the following risk factors is present:

a) Second-line chemotherapy

b) Treatment with corticosteroids

c) CD4 cell count <50/ul

d) Age >65 years

e) Prolonged Mild or Moderate Neutropenia: Mild<1000 Neutrophils /

ï¿½L (Grade III neutropenia) OR Moderate: <500 Neutrophils/ï¿½L

(Grade IV neutropenia)

# Recommendations:

Duration: Antiviral prophylaxis should be initiated in the first week of

therapy and continued until 2 months after completion of therapy.

[Acyclovir 800 MG PO BID \($0.40/day\) R](psozid-acyclovir-800-mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-acyclovir-800-mg-po-bid)

# Alemtuzumab Therapy:

Alemtuzumab is a potent reactivator of latent intracellular pathogens,

including CMV. Chemotherapy with alemtuzumab results in major cellular-

immunodeficiency that may outlast the exposure by months and enhances the

risk for viral infections. The risk of viral disease increases with the

intensity and duration of functional T-cell suppression experienced with

recipients of alemtuzumab.

Duration: Initiate antiviral prophylaxis with alemtuzumab therapy and

continue therapy for at least 2 months after last dose or until CD4 counts

are greater than or equal to 200 cells/ul, whichever is later.

[Acyclovir 800 MG PO BID \($0.40/day\) R](psozid-acyclovir-800-mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-acyclovir-800-mg-po-bid)

# References:

Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in

Cancer Patients

Up-to-Date (accessed 6-10-12)

Sandherr,M et al, Annals of Oncology 17: 1051-1059, 2006

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

# Prophylaxis for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV)

[Select for recommendations for antiviral prophylaxis](orzid3-gmenu-antiviral-immunosuppresive-malignancy)

# Prophylaxis for Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses

Patients with active malignant disease are at higher risk for upper

respiratory infections due to influenza, parainfluenza or respiratory

syncytial virus (RSV). Although response to vaccination with the attenuate

influenza vaccine in patients on chemotherapy is variable, ranging

from 24-75%, immnunoprophylaxis with the influenza vaccine is recommended

patients with active malignant disease or chemotherapy, lymphoproliferative

disease, or multiple myeloma. In areas and seasons where influenza is

endemic, chemoprophylaxis can be considered in addition to vaccination in

exposed patients with a high risk of influenza complications.

# Recommendations:

[Seasonal Influenza](orzid3-gmenu-influenza-recommendations-outpatient)

# Prophylaxis for Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

Prophylaxis and monitoring for CMV reactivation is not recommended unless

patient has received an allogeneic HSCT. Usually the recommendations for

surveillance and prophylaxis of CMV infections from the institution

performing the HSCT will be followed.

# Recommendations:

[Consult Infectious Disease](gmrctz-infectious-disease-inpt)

# Prophylaxis for Chronic Hepatitis B

Reactivation of chronic hepatitis B in patients undergoing immunosuppressive

or antineoplastic treatment is a severe complication. Patients with positive

HBsAg, chronic hepatitis B infection, or a previous episode of HBV

reactivation who will receive immunosuppressive therapy should receive

prophylaxis.

Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B prior to initiating Rituximab

therapy in patients.

# Recommendations:

[Consult Infectious Disease](gmrctz-infectious-disease-inpt)

# References:

Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in

Cancer Patients

Up-to-Date website

Sandherr, M et al, Annals of Oncology 17: 1051-1059, 2006

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

Viral infections reactivate in a small percentage of people with malignancy

Most viral infections in patients with hematologic malignancies or solid

tumors result from reactivation of asymptomatic latent infections,

predominantly of herpes viruses, including herpes simplex virus (HSV),

varicella zoster virus (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Exogenous

respiratory tract infections caused by influenza, parainfluenza

or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are less common.

The main risk factor for clinically relevant reactivation is profound

disruption of cellular immune response, usually due to chemotherapy.

The duration and severity of neutropenia are of lesser importance.

The risk of viral disease increases with the intensity and duration

of functional T-cell suppression. Patients receiving conventionally

dosed chemotherapy regimens for solid tumors experience no major

T-cell suppression and do not have a higher incidence of

invasive viral infections.

# This section is organized mainly by type of malignancy.

There are separate sections for purine analogues (fludarabine,

cladribine, pentostatin), alemtuzumab and rituximab.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# INFLUENZA ANTIVIRAL THERAPY RECOMMENDATIONS

# Who to Treat:

The decision to treat should be based on clinical symptoms and/or presence of a

high-risk condition and should NOT be delayed until laboratory test results are

available.

It is important to use antiviral drugs early to treat influenza in people who

are very sick with influenza (for example hospitalized people) and people who

are sick with influenza and have a greater chance of getting severe

complications. If a patient is not in a high-risk group or is not hospitalized,

healthcare providers should use clinical judgment to guide treatment decisions.

# People who have a greater chance of serious influenza complications include:

*Adults aged 65 years or older

*Persons who have chronic pulmonary (including

asthma) or cardiovascular (except isolated hypertension), renal, hepatic,

hematologic, metabolic disorders (including diabetes mellitus), neurologic and

neuro-developmental disorders

*Persons who are immunocompromised due to any

cause (including immunosuppression caused by medications or by HIV infection)

*Pregnant women and women up to 2 weeks after the end of pregnancy

*Persons younger than 19 years of age who are receiving long-term aspirin- or

salicylate-containing medications and who might be at risk for experiencing Reye

syndrome after influenza virus infection *Residents of nursing homes and other

long-term care facilities

*Non-Hispanic Black persons, Hispanic or Latino persons, and American Indian or

Alaska Native persons

*Persons who are extremely obese (BMI greater than or equal to 40)

# Antiviral Treatment:

If indicated, antivirals should be started as soon as possible.  Maximal benefit

occurs when treatment is started within 48 hours of symptom onset.  However,

antivirals should not be withheld if symptoms begin more than 48 hours prior and

the patient meets criteria for treatment and remains severely ill.

# Treatment Dosing:

Zanamivir is not recommended for patients with chronic respiratory diseases such

as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. These patients may have

bronchospasm with zanamivir. If zanamivir must be used, and patients are using

an inhaled bronchodilator, zanamivir should be taken just after the

bronchodilator.

Extending the duration of treatment for oseltamivir or peramivir may be needed

for those patients with prolonged illness or who are immunosuppressed.

# Preferred:

[Oseltamivir 75 mg po bid for 5 days R](psozid2-oseltamivir-75mg-po-bid-5-days-treat)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid3-oseltamivir-75mg-po-bid-5-days-treat)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# **Below is for information only, quick orders not available

# Alternative:

Requires Infectious Diseases Approval.

Zanamivir 2 inhalations (2 x 5 mg) BID for 5 days [O]

< OR >

Baloxavir 80 mg PO x1 dose patients wt 80kg or greater, 40mg PO x1dose for

patients wt <80kg [DI]

# Alternative for patients unable to tolerate or absorb oral oseltamivir:

Peramivir may not be available. Contact ID for more information.

Requires Infectious Disease Approval.

# Hospitalized, high risk:

Peramivir 600 mg IV q24h for 5 days [R]

# Acute, uncomplicated:

Peramivir 600mg IV Once [R]

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# References:

Centers for Disease Control (CDC) (Accessed 9/20/23)

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/professionals/antivirals/summary-clinician

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ANTIVIRAL TYPE OF MALIGNANCY
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# PREVENTION OF ANTIVIRAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY

# Solid Tumors

# No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended

Solid tumors do not significantly compromise the cellular immune system.

Therefore, patients are at low risk for opportunistic viral infections.

Documented invasive viral infections are very rare. Coincidental

mucocutaneous infections by herpes simplex are easily treated and do not

result in life-threatening invasive infections. Reactivation of

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is rarely observed.

# Acute Leukemia

# No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended

In patients with acute leukemia, treatment is highly aggressive and consists

of a combination of various cytotoxic agents administered in sequential

cycles as induction, consolidation and maintenance therapy. Persistent, i.e.

>10 days and profound neutropenia (<500 neutrophils) regularly occurs and

correlates with the risk of developing fever and infections. Almost all viral

infections during neutropenia constitute reactivations of herpes viruses.

None of the available studies demonstrated an effect of antiviral prophylaxis

on the initiation of antibiotic treatment, number of febrile days, duration

of antibiotic treatment, and onset of opportunistic infections. Therefore,

recommendation for antiviral prophylaxis in patients with acute leukemia can

be given.

# Lymphoma

# No Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommended

Rituximab is a monoclonal anti-CD-20 antibody used for treatment of

lymphomas. It leads to a profound depletion of circulating B-cells. B-cell

recover usually within 3-6 months after treatment. Prolonged administration

of rituximab (e.g., maintenance treatment >12 months) may result in a

significant decrease of levels of immunoglobulin M. Parvovirus B19 and JC-

papovavirus infections have been reported with maintenance rituximab therapy

but drugs that would prevent these infections are not available. There is

substantial increase in risk of reactivation of herpes viruses (including

HSV, VZV, and CMV).

Recommend routine testing for Hepatitis B prior to initiating Rituximab

therapy in patients.

# References

Mandel Chapter: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy of Infection in

Cancer Patients

Up-to-Date (accessed 6-10-11)

Sandherr,M et al, Annals of Oncology 17: 1051-1059, 2006

# Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) Symptomatic Therapy

[Contact the CDSS Team](orzid2-gmenu-abx-additional-assistance)

# Per CDC: Antibiotics Aren't Always the Answer. Be Antibiotics Aware.

Antibiotics do not work on viruses, such as colds and flu, or runny noses,

even if the mucus is thick, yellow or green. Antibiotics also won't help

some common bacterial infections including most cases of bronchitis, many

sinus infections, and some ear infections. When antibiotics aren't needed,

they won't help you, and the side effects could still hurt you. Reactions

from antibiotics cause 1 out of 5 medication-related visits to ED.

# Select links below to print educational material for patient:

[<Link> CDC Print Pamphlet-Symptomatic RX for Acute Respiratory Infections](orz-gtx-abx-url-rx-prescription-for-viruses)

Antibiotics do not work on viruses, such as colds and flu, or runny noses,

# ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA

When a larger than usual volume of orogastric content is aspirated,

mechanical/chemical irritation occurs.  Some of these develop into bacterial

pneumonia.

It is reasonable to wait before starting antimicrobials to see if respiratory

impairment improves or worsens before starting bacterial pneumonia treatment, in

hemodynamically stable patients.

Therapy directed towards anaerobic pathogens is usually unnecessary.

Antimicrobial treatment is warranted if pneumonia is confirmed.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ASYMP BACTERIURIA
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in women and elderly people, especially in

those with chronic medical problems (e.g., diabetes, spinal cord injury,

institutionalized patients, catheterized patients). Most patients have no

adverse outcomes and receive no benefit from treatment of asymptomatic

bacteriuria.

Patients who have no symptoms of cystitis (i.e., no dysuria, pain, urgency)

should not be treated. The presence of pyuria (>7 wbc/hpf) or positive leukocyte

esterase, urine nitrate, or urine bacteria is not a sufficient indication for

antibiotic treatment. Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is

indicated for pregnant women and patients who will have urological procedures

and may be indicated in patients < 1-month post-renal transplant. If an

indwelling catheter is in place and can be removed safely, it should be done as

the bacteriuria may clear.

Bacteriuria in pregnant women is associated with pyelonephritis, premature

delivery, and lower birth weight. Screening for bacteriuria is recommended at

least once early in pregnancy. If bacteriuria is not found upon initial testing,

further screening cultures are not needed. If bacteriuria (>10,000 CFU/mL) is

present, the patient should be treated. Testing should be repeated throughout

the pregnancy to detect recurrences.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Pregnant women, empirical treatment

Preferred:

[Nitrofurantoin SA 100 mg PO q12h \($\) R,O, CrCl >30 mL/min, for 5 days](psozid2-nitrofurantoin-sa-100mg-bid-5ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-nitrofurantoin-sa-100mg-bid-5ds)

*Avoid nitrofurantoin in the third trimester

Alternatives:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h \($\) R for 5 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

< OR >

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg q12h \($\) R for 5 days](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-x5days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-x5days)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Patients having urological procedures

[Antimicrobial prophylaxis for urological procedures](orzid2-gmenu-surg-urology-preop)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Renal transplant recipients < 1 month after transplant

Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria may be indicated. Consult

nephrology for recommendations.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU AZITHROMYCIN PREVENTION OF COPD
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# AZITHROMYCIN FOR PREVENTION OF EXACERBATIONS IN ADVANCED COPD

# Eligibility Criteria:

*Age >40 years

*Clinical diagnosis of COPD (>= 10 pack-years cigarette smoking, a ratio of

postbronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1] to forced vital

capacity of <70%, and a postbronchodilator FEV1 of <80% of the predicted value),

*AND*

*Were either using continuous supplemental oxygen or had received systemic

glucocorticoids within the previous year, *OR*

*Had gone to an emergency room or had been hospitalized for an acute

exacerbation of COPD.

# Exclusion criteria:

*Asthma

*People with hearing impairments

*Congestive heart failure

*Resting heart rate > 100 beats per minute

*Use of medications that are associated with torsades de pointes (except for

amiodarone)

*Prolonged QTc interval (>450 msec)

*Use of medications that prolong the QTc interval

[Please Click Here for Resource for Drugs that Cause QTc Prolongation](orz-gtx-abx-resource-qtc)

If, after trying all the standard treatments, patients are still having acute

exacerbations of COPD, long-term antibiotic treatment with Azithromycin may be

considered. Note: Guidelines for COPD can be found on the CPRS Tools Menu.

# Complete Outpatient COPD Order set is available in the Pulmonary Orders... menu

# (#35) in the Medicine Outpt Orders... menu of CPRS.

If the patient meets the criteria and is willing to have audiometric testing and

an electrocardiogram, please place a Pulmonary Consult for long-term

Azithromycin therapy for the prevention COPD exacerbations.

# Pulmonary is the only approved provider for ordering long-term Azithromycin

# therapy for COPD.

[Azithromycin 250 mg po daily long-term for COPD DI](psozid-azithromycin-longterm-copd-pulm)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-azithromycin-longterm-copd-pulm)

Journal of Medicine

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS

Vaginitis usually presents with discharge, itching, irritation, odor, or pain.

Bacterial vaginosis is the most common form of vaginitis. Normal hydrogen

peroxide and lactic acid producing vaginal flora, including Lactobacillus

species, is reduced and high concentrations of anaerobic bacterial pathogens are

present. Pathogenic bacteria commonly include Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma

hominis, Nobiluncus, Prevotella and other Gram-negative anaerobes.

Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the

microscope for identification of clue cells (epithelial cell coated with

bacteria). In bacterial vaginosis the vaginal pH is high (> 4.5), the discharge

is homogenous and gray-white, and the specimen has a positive amine or whiff

test characterized by a fishy odor before or after addition of 10% KOH.

Bacterial vaginosis nucleic acid amplification tests are available for common

pathogens to aide in identification of pathogen(s).

Bacterial vaginosis may be transmitted sexually. Patients at risk of sexually

transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment.

[Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure](orzid3-gmenu-sexually-transmitted-infections-sti)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# Concurrent Male Partner Treatment for Recurrent, Symptomatic Bacterial Vaginosis

In monogamous relationships where the female partner has confirmed symptomatic,

recurrent bacterial vaginosis (defined as three or more episodes within a

12-month period), concurrent treatment of the male partner is recommended to

to reduce the risk of recurrence. Concurrent treatment should be considered

when the male partner is willing to complete a full 7-day treatment course.

Couples should agree to sexual abstinence or consistent condom use until both

partners have completed therapy. Additionally, continued condom use for at

least three months following treatment is advised to further minimize

the risk of reinfection.

# Treatment

[Metronidazole 500mg po bid x7days DI <AND> Clindamycin 2% cream apply](orz-set-abx-op-metro-500-bid-clindamycin-cream-2-male-partner)

topically to penile skin bid x 7days [M]

# BELL'S PALSY

Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster are possible causes of Bell's palsy. Others

include Borrelia burgdorferi trauma. Some cases are idiopathic. Risk factors for

Bell's Palsy include pregnancy, diabetes, obesity, hypertension, and upper

respiratory infections. Neurology consult is encouraged.

If Lyme disease is suspected, refer to the Lyme disease treatment page:

[Lyme Disease](orzid3-gmenu-lyme-disease)

Treatment with prednisone and an antiviral within 72 hours of symptoms onset

improves the chances of a complete recovery.

Preferred:

[Prednisone 60 mg q24h PO for 7 days <AND> valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h \($\) R](orz-set-abx-op-pred-60mg-qid-po-7d-valacyc-1000mg-po-q8h-7d)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# BITE WOUNDS

Bite wounds are prone to infection because of the pathogenic oral flora carried

into tissues by teeth. Clean wounds with soap and water as soon as possible.

Consult Orthopedic surgery for bite wounds involving the hand.

# Antibiotic Prophylaxis Indications:

Severe injury less than 8 hours, Crush injury, Bone or joint penetration, Wound

of the face or hands or genitals, Immunocompromised host, Asplenia, Advanced

liver disease

*Routine use of prophylactic antibiotics for non-immunocompromised patients with

superficial wounds with no puncture that do not involve the face/ genitals/hands

is not recommended.

# Antimicrobial Treatment:

Empiric treatment for suspected or established infection following bite wound In

these cases, therapy should be directed against pathogen identified by Gram

stain and culture whenever possible.

# Rabies Prophylaxis:

Consider rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for all animal bite cases. Contact

Infectious diseases for assistance.

# Consider tetanus immunization status:

If immunization is up to date, nothing more needs to be done to prevent tetanus.

If immunization is lacking, and: wound IS NOT tetanus prone, bring immunization

up to date with Td wound IS tetanus prone, bring immunization up to date with Td

< AND > Human Tetanus Immune Globulin Inject 250 units deeply into muscle (deep

IM)

# Select below for Tetanus vaccination information page:

[Tetanus, Diphtheria and Acellular Pertussis Vaccine Information Page](orzid3-gmenu-abx-tdap-vaccine-information-page)

# Prophylaxis:

Duration 3 to 5 days:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 5 days R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

Alternative for patients with penicillin allergy:

depends on the bite: call ID if further questions

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 5 days < AND > metronidazole 500 mg PO](orz-set-abx-op-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d-metro-500mg-bid-5d)

BID for 5 days

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d-metro-500mg-bid-5d)

# Empiric treatment for suspected or established infection:

Duration 7 to 14 days:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 10 days R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-10ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-10ds-po-bid)

Alternative for patients with penicillin allergy:

depends on the bite, call ID if further questions

[Moxifloxacin 400 MG PO qday for 10 days R,DI](psozid2-moxifloxacin-10ds-400mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-moxifloxacin-10ds-400mg-po-qday)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU BODY LICE (PEDICULOSIS CORPORIS)
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

BODY LICE (PEDICULOSIS CORPORIS)

Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood.

Body lice proliferate in places where crowding of persons with poor hygiene

common, especially homeless persons.

Infested clothing and bed linen should be heat washed or discarded.

Itching is the most common symptom, but some patients present only with

excoriations and inflammation on the neck and trunk.

# Treatment

A repeat application may be used if live lice are seen 7-10 days after

treatment.

[Permethrin 1% lotion Apply to affected area for 10 minutes then comb out](psozid2-permethrin-1-lot-10min-7days)

nits ($) [M]

# BRONCHITIS

Acute bronchitis should not be treated with antimicrobials except in specific

circumstances. If pneumonia is suspected, order a chest x-ray.  If an infiltrate

is not present, the patient does not have bacterial pneumonia and need not be

treated for it. If a patient has chronic pulmonary disease, see COPD

exacerbation menu.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU CANDIDA VULVO-VAGINITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CANDIDA VULVOVAGINITIS

Candida vulvovaginitis typically presents with valvular irritation, burning or

pruritus. Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined

under the microscope for clue cells (epithelial cell coated with bacteria) to

exclude bacterial vaginosis. In candida vulvovaginitis, the vaginal pH is

typically normal (4-4.5) and vaginal discharge is typically thick and curdy with

white plaques on vaginal mucosa. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying fungus or

yeast with KOH prep.

Most non-C. albicans species respond to fluconazole treatment except C. krusei

and C. glabrata. C. krusei can be treated with topical agents as for complicated

candida vulvovaginitis below. C. glabrata treatment is complicated and azole

therapy is frequently unsuccessful. Consult Infectious Diseases in patients with

C. glabrata vulvovaginitis.

Recurrent candida vulvovaginitis is treated as complicated candida

vulvovaginitis for induction treatment, followed by maintenance regimen for 6

months.

# Candida vulvovaginitis in pregnancy:

[Clotrimazole vaginal 1% cream 1 applicator full qhs \($\) M for 7 days](psozid2-clotrimazole-vag-1-crm-1-app-qhs-7ds)

# Treatment of uncomplicated candida vulvovaginitis

[Fluconazole 150 mg PO once \($\) R,DI](psozid2-fluconazole-150mg-po-once)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-150mg-po-once)

< OR >

[Clotrimazole vaginal 1% cream 1 applicator full qhs \($\) M for 7 days](psozid2-clotrimazole-vag-1-crm-1-app-qhs-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-clotrimazole-vag-1-crm-1-app-qhs-7ds)

< OR >

[Terconazole 0.4% vaginal cream 1 applicator full qhs \($\) M for 7 days](psozid2-terconazole-0-4-vag-crm-qhs-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-terconazole-0-4-vag-crm-qhs-7ds)

# Treatment of complicated candida vulvovaginitis (e.g. immunocompromised, severe

# disease, pregnancy) or recurrent infection induction treatment

[Fluconazole 150 mg PO q72h for 7 days \(3 doses\) \($\) R,DI](psozid2-fluconazole-150-mg-po-q72h-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-150-mg-po-q72h-7ds)

< OR >

[Clotrimazole vaginal 1% cream 1 applicator full qhs \($\) M for 10 days](psozid2-clotrimazole-vag-1-crm-1-app-qhs-10ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-clotrimazole-vag-1-crm-1-app-qhs-10ds)

< OR >

[Terconazole 0.4% vaginal cream 1 applicator full qhs \($\) M for 10 days](psozid2-terconazole-0-4-vag-crm-qhs-10ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-terconazole-0-4-vag-crm-qhs-10ds)

# Recurrent candida vulvovaginitis maintenance regimen following induction

# treatment above

[Fluconazole 150 mg PO every 7 days \($\) R,DI for 6 months](psozid2-fluconazole-150mg-po-qweek-6mo)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-150mg-po-qweek-6mo)

# Treatment of C. glabrata vulvovaginitis

Failure of azole therapy is common, alternative topical treatments below require

compounding by a pharmacist. Enter Outpatient Rx for CPD-BORIC ACID CAP,VAG.

Topical boric acid capsule 600 mg intravaginal qhs for 14 days

# COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA (CAP) TREATED WITH ORAL ANTIBIOTICS

Empirical regimens listed here cover the usual pathogens associated with CAP,

including atypical pathogens. Specific therapy should be guided by culture

results.

# Diagnosis

Use the CAP Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) to assist with level of care decision

[CAP Pneumonia Severity Index \(PSI\) Calculator](orz-gtx-abx-cap-psi)

# Previously healthy patients (i.e. no comorbidities):

(WITHOUT chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, renal failure,

congestive heart failure, malignancy, alcoholism, asplenia, immunosuppressing

conditions, or use of immunosuppressing drugs)

Preferred:

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO Q12H for 5 days DI](psozid2-pna-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-pna-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5days)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO Q8H for 5 days R](psozid2-pna-amoxicillin-1000mg-po-tid-x5days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-pna-amoxicillin-1000mg-po-tid-x5days)

# Patients with comorbidities:

(WITH chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, renal failure, congestive

heart failure, malignancy, alcoholism, asplenia, immunosuppressing conditions or

use of immunosuppressing drugs)

Preferred:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO Q12H for 5 days R <AND> azithromycin po](orz-set-abx-op-pna-amox-clav-875-125-bid-azith-500-then-250)

once on day 1, then 250 mg PO QDAY for 4 days [M]

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-pna-amox-clav-875-125-bid-azith-500-then-250)

< OR >

[Cefdinir 300 mg PO Q12H for 5 days R <AND> azithromycin once on day 1, then](orz-set-abx-op-pna-cefdinir-300mg-po-bid-azith-500-then-250)

250 mg PO QDAY for 4 days [M]

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-pna-cefdinir-300mg-po-bid-azith-500-then-250)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO Q12H for 5 days R <AND> doxycycline 100](orz-set-abx-op-pna-amox-clav-875-125-bid-doxy-100mg-bid)

mg PO Q12H for 5 days [DI]

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-pna-amox-clav-875-125-bid-doxy-100mg-bid)

< OR >

[Cefdinir 300 mg PO q12h for 5 days R <AND> doxycycline 100 mg PO Q12H for 5](orz-set-abx-op-pna-cefdinir-300mg-bid-doxy-100mg-bid)

days [DI]

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

# Initial CDI diagnosis (all are required)

(1) Unexplained diarrhea (e.g., no laxative or increase in tube feed)

(2) New onset diarrhea (e.g., 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours)

(3) Laboratory confirmation of CDI

[Click here Information on C. difficile lab testing](orzid2-gmenu-abx-c-difficile-2-step-testing)

The Infectious Disease service is available to discuss CDI testing and results.

# Recurrence

Typically defined as symptomatic, laboratory confirmed CDI within 12 weeks after

a prior episode. Recurrence rates are up to 25%. Recurrence is usually due to

failure of normal colonic flora to re-establish itself, rather than

antimicrobial treatment failure.

# Fulminant CDI

Hypotension, shock, ileus, megacolon: General Surgery consult is essential for

ileus or megacolon.

# Treatment

[Initial Episode](orzid3-gmenu-ini-episode-abx-assoc-colitis)

[First Recurrence](orzid3-gmenu-first-recurrence-abx-associated-colitis)

[Second Recurrence](orzid3-gmenu-second-recurrence-cdiff-colitis)

# Fulminant CDI: Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# Third Recurrence: Consult Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Disease

# CELLULITIS & ERYSIPELAS

Skin and soft tissue infections without abscess or other sign of purulence.

MRSA coverage is typically unnecessary when there is no purulence, even in

patients with a history of MRSA colonization or infection. It may be considered

for specific patients with the considerations listed below but is not

recommended as the default choice.

Elevation, good skin hygiene, and support stockings are recommended.

# Duration: 5 days

# Empirical outpatient treatment for cellulitis

[Beta-lactam reaction assessment](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO bid for 5 days \($\) R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-x5days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-x5days)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID for 5 days \($\) R](psozid2-amoxicillin-5ds-500mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amoxicillin-5ds-500mg-po-tid)

# Alternative for penicillin allergy or with MRSA considerations

Consider MRSA coverage for cellulitis associated with penetrating trauma

(including injection drug use), neutropenia, or infections not improving on

first line beta-lactams, history of MRSA skin infection.

[Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet BID for 5 days \($\) R,DI](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-5days-1ds-tab-bid)

BACTERIAL CELLULITIS

Cellulitis refers to inflammation of the skin and subcutaneous tissue and is

often associated with bacterial pathogens.

Mild cases can be treated with oral antimicrobials.  Moderate to severe cases

should be treated initially with intravenous antimicrobials.  Switch to oral

drugs after clinical improvement.

Consider MRSA coverage for cellulitis associated with penetrating trauma,

history of MRSA infection, injection drug use, or infections not responding

to first line beta-lactams.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU CERVICITIS ASSOC STD
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CERVICITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES

The main diagnostic signs that characterize cervicitis are 1)women who present

with purulent or mucopurulent exudate in the endocervical canal or on an

endocervical swab specimen and 2)sustained endocervical bleeding induced by

gentle passage of cotton swab through the cervical os. One or both signs may be

present.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the two most common sexually

transmitted cervicitis pathogens. Nucleic acid amplification tests for these

pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients at

risk for sexually transmitted cervicitis.

[Chlamydia & GC PCR/LCR test](lrtzid-chlamydia-gc-urine-naat)

# For patients who have recently been treated for cervicitis

[Treatment of recurrent or persistent cervicitis](orzid3-gmenu-recurrent-persistent-urethritis)

When diagnosed with sexually transmitted cervicitis, the patient's sexual

partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually

transmitted infection. If diagnostic tests for the cause of cervicitis are not

feasible, therapy for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be given to

partners.

# Initial treatment of patients and sex partners

Patients and partners are often infected with both N. gonorrhoeae and C.

trachomatis.

[Treatment for Gonococcal and Chlamydial trachomatis co-infections](orzid3-gmenu-gonococcal)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU CHOLANGITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CHOLANGITIS

[Step down treatment](orzid3-gmenu-abx-step-down-treatment)

Most cases are due to common bile duct obstruction. Obstruction (if present)

must be relieved with an endoscopical, transcutaneous, or surgical procedure.

The most common pathogens isolated are E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus and

Enterobacter. Pseudomonas coverage is recommended in severe (grade 3)

cholangitis.  Anaerobic coverage is recommended if biliary-enteric abnormality

is present.

Antimicrobials' role in cholangitis is to allow patients to have elective and

not emergently scheduled drainage procedures.

Due to increasing resistance, fluoroquinolones are only recommended in cases of

severe penicillin and cephalosporin allergy.

# Treatment of patients on ward without systemic symptoms of infection

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# Treatment of patients in ICU with systemic symptoms of infection

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# CHRONIC PROSTATITIS / CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME

This syndrome presents with intermittent perineal and/or low back pain,

obstructive voiding symptoms, relatively normal examination, and negative urine

cultures. Antimicrobial therapy is not indicated.

Consult urology for non-antimicrobial therapy recommendations (e.g.

alpha-adrenergic antagonists, anti-inflammatory medications) to reduce symptoms.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU CHRONIC BACT PROSTATITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CHRONIC BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS

Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually presents as recurrent urinary tract

infections with the same bacterial etiology. Pain, tenderness, and fever may

accompany intermittent episodes of cystitis, but men are usually asymptomatic

between episodes and the prostate examination may be normal. Non-steroidal anti-

inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) often relieve pain. If the diagnosis is uncertain or

if the patient's symptoms do not respond to therapy, consult urology. The

presence of hematuria may be a sign of carcinoma, especially in older men, and a

urology consult should be requested.

A urine culture should be performed in all patients to guide antimicrobial

therapy:

[Urine culture](orzid2-gmenu-abx-urine-culture-menu)

Chronic prostate pain syndrome should be considered in patients who have

symptoms of prostatitis but have negative urine cultures. Chronic prostate pain

syndrome is discussed elsewhere:

[Chronic prostate pain syndrome](orzid3-gmenu-chron-pros-chron-pelvic-pain-syn)

# Duration

4 weeks minimum and up to 6 weeks of treatment is required. Durations longer

than 6 weeks may be needed in treatment of resistant organisms. Treatment with

trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole requires a treatment duration of 1 to 3 months.

# Empirical treatment

Preferred:

[Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h \($\) R,DI for 4 weeks](psozid2-levofloxacin-750mg-po-qday-28d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-levofloxacin-750mg-po-qday-28d)

Alternative:

[Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h \($\) R,DI for 4 weeks](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-28days-1ds-tab-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-28days-1ds-tab-bid)
