menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU CHRONIC SINUSITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CHRONIC SINUSITIS

Diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is based on presence of at least 2 of the 4

cardinal signs/symptoms lasting >/= 12 weeks. In addition, diagnosis requires

objective evidence of mucosal inflammation using nasal endoscopy and/or CT

imaging. The initial therapy for chronic sinusitis is treatment with intranasal

corticosteroids and saline. For patients with severe nasal blockage by polyps,

treat with a short course of oral glucocorticoids. Reassess patient after 1 to 3

months of intranasal therapy or after completion of glucocorticoid therapy. If

signs/symptoms have not improved, consult surgery, ENT and Infectious Diseases

as treatment is complex.

Acute exacerbations of chronic sinusitis can be caused by discontinuing medical

therapy, viral infections, allergens, noxious inhalants and bacterial or fungal

infections. Bacterial infections should be suspected when the patient has

increased signs/symptoms persisting for more than 10 days. Refer to Severe

Sinusitis recommendations for choice of antimicrobial therapy in these patients.

Repeated use of the same agent should be avoided to prevent promotion of drug

resistant bacteria or increased fungal colonization.

[Severe Sinusitis](orzid3-gmenu-acute-sinusitis-severe)

# Cardinal Signs/Symptoms of Chronic Sinusitis

1. Anterior and/or posterior nasal mucopurulent drainage

2. Nasal obstruction/nasal blockage/congestion

3. Facial pain, pressure, and/or fullness

4. Reduction or loss of sense of smell

# Objective Evidence mucosal inflammation

1. Purulent (not clear) mucus or edema in the middle meatus or ethmoid regions

2. Polyps in the nasal cavity or the middle meatus

3. Radiographic imaging demonstrating mucosal thickening or partial or complete

opacification of the paranasal sinuses

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Chow et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012, 54(8) e72-e112

Mandell chapter: Sinusitis

Meltzer et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2004, 114(6) S155-S212.

Rosenfeld et al, Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. 2015, 152(4) 598-609

# CMV COLITIS OR ESOPHAGITIS

Infection in immunocompetent patients is rare and usually associated with

minimal or no symptoms. Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased

include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving

prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease

indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter. Treatment is complex

and requires Infectious Diseases consultation.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat for 3-6 weeks. Patients may be converted to oral therapy after initial

intravenous therapy and after clinical improvement of severe disease.

# severe disease

menus.Text:

# CMV RETINITIS AND ACUTE RETINAL NECROSIS

Infection in immunocompetent patients is rare and usually associated with

minimal or no symptoms. Patients in whom the risk for CMV disease is increased

include solid organ and bone marrow transplant recipients, persons receiving

prolonged immunosuppressive chemotherapy, and persons with advanced HIV disease

indicated by a CD4 count of less than 50 cells/microliter. Treatment is complex

and requires Infectious Diseases consultation.

For sight threatening lesions (lesions within 1500 microns of the fovea)

intravitreal infections of ganciclovir or foscarnet are recommended in addition

to systemic treatment. Contact Infectious Diseases for more information.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat retinitis for 14 to 21 days. Patients may be converted to oral therapy

after initial intravenous therapy and after clinical improvement of severe

disease. Treat acute retinal necrosis with IV therapy for at least 7 days and

until disease stabilizes then oral therapy for a minimum of 6 weeks. Maintenance

therapy after completion of treatment is indicated when CD4 count <100.

Discontinue maintenance therapy when CD4 count is >100 for 6 months.

# Treatment acute retinal necrosis or severe disease

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Treatment of mild to moderate retinitis or after clinical improvement of severe

# retinitis/acute retinal necrosis

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# COMMUNITY ACQUIRED DIARRHEA (NO RECENT TRAVEL)

Consider Clostridioides difficile infection:

[Clostridioides difficile treatment recommendations](orzid3-gmenu-cdifficile-colitis)

# Primary treatment

Hydration and electrolyte replacement

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empiric antimicrobial treatment

[Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h for 3-5 days R,DI](psozid2-ciprofloxacin-3ds-500mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-3ds-500mg-po-bid)

Alternative

[Azithromycin 1000 mg PO one-time dose M](psozid2-azithromycin-1gm-po-once)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-azithromycin-1gm-po-once)

< OR >

[Azithromycin 500 mg PO q24h for 3 days M](psozid2-azithromycin-3ds-500mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-azithromycin-3ds-500mg-po-qday)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Subacute or chronic (>/= 14 days of symptoms)

Primary treatment is hydration and electrolyte replacement. Empiric

antimicrobial therapy is not indicated. Investigate for the cause of diarrhea.

Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Diseases involvement is encouraged.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# VIRAL GASTROENTERITIS

Infectious diarrhea caused by viral pathogens such as Adenovirus, Astrovirus,

Norovirus, Rotavirus, and Sapovirus is usually self-limited. Treatment includes

supportive measures such as oral rehydration and unrestricted nutrition.

Antiviral therapy is not recommended and for most viruses is unavailable.

Antimotility agents may be used for one or two days in patients with mild to

moderate volume depletion. Antiemetic agents may be used for one or two days in

patients with vomiting.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU CONJUNCTIVITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CONJUNCTIVITIS

Conjunctivitis is associated with viral or bacterial pathogens. Viral

conjunctivitis presents with watery discharge. Bacterial infections are more

likely to present with thick exudate and conjunctival injection. Allergic

conjunctivitis typically presents with stringy mucus. If there is pus

(hypopion), corneal involvement, possible bacterial conjunctivitis, or

keratitis, consult ophthalmology.

Viral conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by adenovirus. It is self-limited

and antivirals provide no benefit. Symptomatic treatment with ophthalmic

antihistamine/decongestants and warm or cool compresses may relieve symptoms.

Bacterial conjunctivitis is most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus,

Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus spp., Moraxella catarrhalis,

Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria spp. or enteric gram-negative rods. It is

generally self-limited, but topical antimicrobials reduce duration of symptoms

and limit person-to-person spread of infection. If symptoms do not improve after

2 days of antimicrobial therapy, the patient should be seen by an

ophthalmologist.

# Treatment for acute bacterial conjunctivitis

[Trimethoprim/polymixin B ophthalmic solution 1 drop in affected eye\(s\)](psozid-trimethoprim-polymixin-b-ophth-1-drop-q3h-7d)

q3h for 7 days ($) [M]

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-trimethoprim-polymixin-b-ophth-1-drop-q3h-7d)

# Treatment for severe cases of bacterial conjunctivitis involving suppuration or

# contact lens wearers

Consult ophthalmology and begin topical antimicrobials.

[Ofloxacin 0.3% ophthalmic solution 2 drops in affected eye q2h while awake for 2](psozid2-ofloxacin-opth-2-drps-q2h-x2d-then-qid-5d)

days then 2 drops QID for 5 days ($) [M]

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ofloxacin-opth-2-drps-q2h-x2d-then-qid-5d)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

CUTANEOUS CANDIDIASIS

Cutaneous candidiasis is a superficial fungal infection of the epidermis.

Presents with red, erythematous patches, often in areas where skin contact

skin, including axillae, groin, and abdominal folds.

Keep affected areas dry and clean.

# DECUBITUS ULCERS

Decubitus ulcers are colonized with bacteria.  Antimicrobial therapy is

unnecessary unless the patient has infection of surrounding tissues signified by

erythema, warmth, local tenderness, or purulent discharge.  Rectal or groin

decubitus ulcers with surrounding infection need broad spectrum antimicrobials.

Ulcers located in other sites are usually treated with antimicrobials for

staphylococci and streptococci.

# Duration of therapy: 5 - 7 days, but adjust to clinical response

Use treatment durations for soft tissue infection even in the presence of

osteomyelitis if managed without plastic surgery. Treatment with prolonged

antibiotics for osteomyelitis is typically reserved for when patients are

managed with surgical debridement, bone biopsy, and/or wound closure. ID consult

recommended.

For deep abscesses away from the rectal area, obtain material for Gram stain and

culture and treat with:

# Treatment for Mild to Moderate Infections:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h x 7days R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

menus.Text:

# DEEP OROPHARYNGEAL INFECTIONS

Deep oropharyngeal infections may threaten life and must be treated immediately.

Assess the risk of airway compromise and monitor the airway if it is threatened.

These infections are more common in people with diabetes mellitus and are caused

by mixed organisms including streptococcus sp., Staphylococcus aureus and

anaerobes . Perform CT scan to diagnose abscess. ENT and Infectious Diseases

consults are essential.

# Duration of therapy

If the patient's condition worsens or does not improve during the first 48 hours

of antimicrobial therapy, surgical drainage is indicated. If surgical drainage

is done, antimicrobials are usually continued for 48 hours after the procedure.

If surgical drainage is not done, 2 weeks of antimicrobial therapy until

clinical improvement is observed (e.g. resolution of fever and leukocytosis) is

appropriate.

# Empiric Treatment

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Step-down treatment after initial intravenous therapy. Adjust duration based on

# criteria above.

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h for 7 days \($\) R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

# DIARRHEA WITH ESCHERICHIA COLI

# Enteroaggretive E. coli (EAEC), Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), and

# Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)

Antibiotic therapy is not required for mild to moderate disease caused by these

organisms because diarrhea often resolves on its own. Do not use antimotility

agents in patients with bloody stool. Antimicrobial treatment in patients with

AIDS Treatment is complex, consult Infectious Diseases

Primary treatment: Hydration and electrolyte replacement

Antimicrobial treatment of severe diarrhea

[Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h for 3 days R,DI](psozid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-qday-3ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-qday-3ds)

Alternative

[Rifaximin 200 mg q8h for 3 days M](orz-set-abx-op-rifaxamin-3ds-200mg-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-rifaxamin-3ds-200mg-tid)

# Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) and Shiga Toxin-producing E. coli (STEC)

EHEC and STEC disease often presents as bloody diarrhea.

Treatment includes supportive measures such as volume repletion and

administering appropriate nutrition. Do not use antimotility or antimicrobial

agents as they can increase shiga-toxin release and increase the risk of

hemolytic uremia syndrome (HUS).

# Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)

EIEC disease typically presents as watery diarrhea, sometimes progressing to

bloody diarrhea. Refer to Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment

recommendations.

[Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli treatment recommendations](orzid3-gmenu-diarrhea-shigella)

# NON-CHOLERA VIBRIO

Non-cholera vibrio is associated with gastroenteritis, septicemia, and wound

infections. Vibrio vulnificans infections are acquired from contact with

seawater or seafood, especially raw oysters. V. vulnificans cases are more

severe than cases with other species. V. parahaemolyticus causes

gastroenteritis and milder wound infections.

Antimicrobials do not shorten the course of disease in immunocompetent patients

with mild gastroenteritis.

Hydration and electrolyte replacement

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# Doxycycline for Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (doxy PEP)

# Indications:

ECTHYMA GANGRENOSUM

Ecthyma gangrenosum lesions commonly begin as painless red macules which

rapidly evolve into areas of induration that develop into pustules and-or

bullae. Ultimately, these become gangrenous ulcers. Ecthyma lesions

typically progress rapidly within 12 to 18 hours. They are often associate

with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia, especially in neutropenic patients.

Recommend blood cultures and culture of skin exudates.

# Treatment

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ENDOPHTHALMITIS

Endophthalmitis is a medical emergency and presents with eye pain and visual

loss. It may be associated with gram positive or gram-negative bacteria,

including Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, or with fungi.

Consult ophthalmology immediately. The ophthalmologist will obtain an aqueous or

vitreous fluid sample for gram stain and culture and begin intravitreal

antimicrobials.

# Treatment with intravitreal antimicrobials

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Fungal endophthalmitis

Fungal endophthalmitis is rarely diagnosed in temperate climates and treatment

is complicated. Ophthalmology and Infectious Diseases involvement is essential.

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU EPIDIDYMITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# EPIDIDYMITIS AND EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS

Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and when testicles are involved

is referred to as epididymo-orchitis. Acute epididymitis is the most common

cause of scrotal pain in adults. Other features include scrotal erythema and

edema, pyuria, dysuria, thickened epididymis, swollen testis, and is usually

unilateral. It is primarily caused by infection but can also result from trauma

and autoimmune diseases. Testicular torsion should be ruled out before

treatment. Most cases in men aged 35 and older, those with recent urinary tract

instrumentation or surgery (e.g., prostate biopsy, vasectomy) are associated

with enteric Gram-negative rods. Most cases in men under age 35 are associated

with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Resistant organisms are more likely if

the patient has been in the hospital for more than 48 hours or received a course

of antibiotics. There is increasing resistance in urinary pathogens to

ciprofloxacin.

A urine analysis, urine culture and urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)

should be performed in all cases of suspected epididymitis before starting

treatment to guide therapy:

[Lab menu](orzid2-gmenu-abx-lab-menu)

Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for

treatment. Refer to the Urogenital section of the Antimicrobial CDSS for more

information.

Patients with bacterial epididymitis treated with antibiotics should improve

within two or three days. If no improvement is noted, other causes of scrotal

pain and referral to a urologist should be considered.

Management should include bed rest, analgesics, and scrotal elevation. Older men

should have their residual urinary volume checked. If the residual volume is

elevated, the patient should be seen by a urologist as epididymitis is unlikely

to respond if the prostate is blocking the vas deferens.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment in men who practice insertive anal intercourse

[Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once \($\) M < AND > levofloxacin 500 mg PO q24h](orz-set-abx-op-ceftr-500mg-im-x1-levoflox-500mg-qday-10days)

for 10 days ($) [R, DI]

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-ceftr-500mg-im-x1-levoflox-500mg-qday-10days)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Empirical treatment in men who do not practice insertive anal intercourse

# Age >/= 35 years or

# Recent urinary tract instrumentation or urinary tract surgery (e.g., prostate

# biopsy, vasectomy):

Preferred:

[Levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h \($\) R, DI for 10 days](psozid2-levofloxacin-10ds-750mg-po-qday)

Preferred:

Patient weighing less than 300 lbs

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU ERYSIPELAS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

ERYSIPELAS

In contrast to cellulitis, erysipelas has sharply demarcated borders and a

characteristic raised, orange-peel appearance.  Most cases are associated with

streptococcus.  In a minority of cases, especially those involving the face,

Staphylococcus aureus is also a potential pathogen.  In severe cases,

methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage must be provided

until microbiology results are available.

Treat for 5 to 10days, longer if patient is bacteremic.

# _________________________________

# Facial

# _________________________________

Sudden onset of rapidly spreading red edematous tender plaque-like skin on

face in an otherwise healthy host.

# If erysipelas-like on the face treat as if MRSA is present:

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

# _________________________________

# Non-facial

# _________________________________

# MILD TO MODERATE disease

[Penicillin VK 250 - 500 mg PO QID for 10 days  \($\) R](psozid2-penicillin-vk-10ds-250mg-po-qid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-penicillin-vk-10ds-250mg-po-qid)

ERYSIPELOID (ERYSIPELOTHRIX RHUSOPATHIAE INFECTION)

Erysipeloid is a localized cutaneous infection with Erysipelothrix rhusopathiae

It is a zoonotic infection of fisherman, fish handlers, and butchers acquired by

direct animal contact, most commonly with fish, but also with other animals

(e.g., swine). It usually affects the hand or fingers and is characterized

throbbing pain and a red rash with a purple center and an elevated border.

Localized infections can be treated with oral antimicrobials.

Severe, diffuse cutaneous infections or systemic infections with E.

rhusopathiae occur rarely after ingestion of undercooked pork or contaminated

seafood in immunosuppressed individuals.  These infections are treated

initially with intravenous antimicrobials.

# _____________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# FEVER OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN

Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is the occurrence of several episodes of fever

greater than 101 degrees Fahrenheit over a period of at least 3 weeks despite 1

week of hospital evaluation. Cases with FUO are often classified in four

categories: (1) classical, (2) neutropenic, (3) nosocomial, and (4) fever in

persons with HIV/AIDS. Empirical antimicrobial therapy is rarely indicated in

patients with FUO.

Note that FUO in neutropenic patients refers to persistent fever that has

remained undiagnosed after extensive diagnostic work and empirical antimicrobial

therapy. New fever in patients with profound neutropenia is a different syndrome

and does require empirical antimicrobial therapy. Infectious Diseases should be

involved in any case where empirical treatment for fever of unknown origin is

being considered. For more information refer to the neutropenic fever

recommendations.

[Neutropenic fever](orzid3-gmenu-neutropenic-fever)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# FIRST RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic

therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide,

etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved

or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the

diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to

antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial

therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.

# First Recurrence CDI: *The REGIMEN should be different from initial treatment.*

[Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days M](psozid-vancomycin-125mg-cap-qid-10ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-vancomycin-125mg-cap-qid-10ds)

< OR >

[Vancomycin Extended-Pulse Taper Regimen M](psozid2-vancomycin-taper-and-pulse-dosing)

(Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days, then taper and pulse with 125 mg po q12h

for 7 days, then 125mg po qday for 7 days, then 125mg every other day for 6

weeks)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-vancomycin-taper-and-pulse-dosing)

< OR >

[Fidaxomicin 200 mg po q12h for 10 days M](psozid2-fidaxomicin-200mg-po-q12h-10days)

(Fidaxomicin 200mg po bid x5days, then 200mg every other day x 20days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fidaxomicin-200mg-extended-pulse-regimen)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

FOLLICULITIS

Folliculitis is an infection of the hair follicle with purulent exudate in the

epidermis. It is usually associated with Staphylococcus aureus.

In patients exposed to swimming pools or hot tubs, follicultiis may be

assosicated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa which usually clears on its own

within a week or two.

Candida albicans can cause folliculitis in patients receiving antimicrobials

and/or corticosteroids.

For folliculitis in patients with severe acne, consult Dermatology.

For extensive folliculitis or in patients with HIV, consult Infectious Diseases.

# Treatment

Usually self-limiting. For most cases, treat with daily saline compresses until

symptoms resolve.

# For moderate to severe cases associated with Staphylococcus aureus:

[Mupirocin 2% ointment topical to affected area TID for 7 days \($\) M](psozid2-mupirocin-2-oint-top-to-affect-area-tid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-mupirocin-2-oint-top-to-affect-area-tid-7ds)

# For cases associated with Candida albicans

[Clotrimazole cream to affected area TID for 7 days \($\) M](psozid2-clotrimazole-1-crm-top-tid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-clotrimazole-1-crm-top-tid-7ds)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# DIABETES-RELATED FOOT INFECTIONS (DIABETIC FOOT INFECTIONS-DFI)

# Wound Cultures:

If there are no systemic symptoms of infection or at least 2 local symptoms

(pain, erythema > 0.5cm, purulent drainage, warmth), do not culture or treat

with abx.

Do NOT:

-Culture a wound that appears uninfected (at least 2 of following: local pain,

erythema >0.5cm, purulent drainage)

-Swab the wound to obtain a culture

-Culture without first cleaning and debriding a wound DFI Do:

-Obtain culture by deep tissue biopsy after cleaning and debriding the wound

# Imaging:

-An x-ray is recommended for all new foot ulcers in patients with diabetes to

evaluate for deformity, bony destruction, soft tissue gas, and/or foreign

bodies. Antimicrobials aren't indicated unless local cellulitis or systemic

infectious symptoms are present.

[Click here for Osteomyelitis Evaluation](orzid3-gmenu-osteomyelitis-evaluation)

# INFECTION SEVERITY (IWGDF/IDSA Classification)

# __________________________________________________________________

# Uninfected DFI (Class 1/Uninfected): Chronic ulceration without s/s infection

-if no pain, erythema > 0.5cm, purulent drainage, do not culture or treat

Do not culture wound -Do not treat with antibiotics If osteomyelitis identified

arrange for bone biopsy --hold antibiotics

# _________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 2/Mild):

At least two of the following are present: -Local swelling or induration

-Erythema >0.5cm but <2cm around wound -Local tenderness or pain -Local

increased warmth -Purulent drainage

# Primarily Outpatient Treatment:

Duration of therapy: 1-2 weeks

# Preferred Regimens:

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h x 7days R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 7 days R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

# Treatment with previous MRSA infection or severe PCN allergy:

[Beta-lactam Reaction Assessment](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO bid x 7days R,DI](psozid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-po-bid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-po-bid-7ds)

< OR >

[Linezolid 600 mg PO BID for 7 days DI,O](psozid2-linezolid-600mg-po-bid-x7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-linezolid-600mg-po-bid-7days)

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 3/Moderate):

-Erythema extending >2cm from the wound margin, and/or -Tissue deeper than skin

and subcutaneous tissues (e.g., tendon, muscle, joint, and bone)

# Outpatient/Often Hospitalized Treatment:

Oral or IV with change to PO with improvement ***See CDSS Inpatient for IV

treatment*** Duration of therapy: 1-3 weeks

# Preferred Treatments:

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125mg po bid R for 7 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-7ds-po-bid)

# Treatment with history of previous MRSA infection:

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg po BID R <AND> doxycycline 100 mg PO](orz-set-abx-op-amox-clav-875-bid-doxy-100mg-7days)

bid [DI] for 7 days

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-amox-clav-875-bid-doxy-100mg-7days)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg PO bid R <AND> trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole](orz-set-abx-op-amox-clav-875-bid-tmp-sulfa-1ds-7days)

1 DS tablet PO bid [R,DI] for 7 days

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-amox-clav-875-bid-tmp-sulfa-1ds-7days)

# Treatment with Severe PCN allergy:

[Beta-lactam Allergy Assessment](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Levofloxacin 500mg PO qdayR,DI <AND> metronidazole 500mg PO bid DI](orz-set-abx-op-levoflox-500mg-qd-metro-500mg-7days)

for 7 days

[Non VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-levoflox-500mg-qd-metro-500mg-7days)

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 4/Severe):

Infection with associated systemic manifestations as indicated by 2 or more of

the following: -Fever, Tachycardia, Leukocytosis, Hypotension, Sepsis,

Necrotizing infection

# Managed exclusively in the Inpatient setting

***See CDSS Inpatient for treatment recommendations***

# __________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

FOOT ULCERS WITHOUT INFECTION OF SURROUNDING TISSUES

Clinically uninfected wounds do not need antibiotic treatment.

Topical antimicrobials are not helpful, are associated with allergic reactions,

and select for resistant organisms.  In general, local treatment should consist

of dressings with frequent changes, soaks, and debridement.Patients with

edema or impaired venous return should keep the limb elevated.  Wound care and

improved control of diabetes can improve outcomes of infection and prevent

future complications.

# Diabetes-Related Foot Infections (Diabetic Foot Infections-DFI)

# Wound Cultures:

Do NOT:

-Culture a wound that appears uninfected

-Swab the wound to obtain a culture

-Culture without first cleaning and debriding a wound

-Order blood cultures in patients with mild-moderate DFI

Do:

-Obtain culture by deep tissue biopsy after cleaning and debriding the wound

-Obtain blood culture in patiens with signs of sepsis or severe DFI

# Imaging:

-An x-ray is recommended for all new foot ulcers in patiens with diabetes

to evaluate for deformity, bony destruction, soft tissue gas, and/or

foreign bodies.

either soft tissue abscess or osteomyelitis.

[<Click here> Osteomyelitis Evaluation](orzid3-gmenu-osteomyelitis-evaluation)

-Local swelling or induration

-Erythema >0.5cm but <2cm around wound

# __________________________________________________________________

# Infected DFI (Class 3/Moderate):

-Erythema extending >2cm from the wound margin, and/or

-Tissue deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissues

(e.g., tendon, muscle, joint, and bone)

# Outpatient/Often Hospitalized Treatment:

***See CDSS Inpatient for IV treatment***

Duration of therapy: 1-3 weeks

# Preferred Treatments:

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125mg po bid \($\) R for 14 days](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-14ds-po-bid)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ASPERGILLUS SPECIES

-Aspergillus species are ubiquitous, but invasive aspergillosis occurs primarily

in immunocompromised hosts. Neutropenia and glucocorticoid use are the most

common predisposing factors. Optimal management involves early diagnosis and

early initiation of antifungal treatment.

-The most common clinical manifestation of invasive aspergillosis is pulmonary

disease, but other manifestations include central nervous system infection,

rhinosinusitis, endocarditis, gastrointestinal disease, annd others.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy:

Duration of therapy should be a minimum of 6 to 12 weeks, although duration

is highly dependent on degree/duration of immunosuppression, disease site, and

and evidence of disease improvement. Consult Infectious Disease.

# Severe disease:

Refer to Inpatient CDSS for treatment.

# Mild/moderate disease:

# Preferred treatment:

[Voriconazole 400 mg PO BID for 2 doses, then 200 mg PO BID \($$\) R,H,DI](psozid-voriconazole-400mg-po-bid-1day-then-200mg-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-voriconazole-400mg-po-bid-1day-then-200mg-bid)

# Alternative treatment:

Consult Infectious Disease for alternative.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# CANDIDA ALBICANS

Avoid using fluconazole empirically to treat candidal infections in patients who

have received an imidazole in the previous year.

# Treatment of thrush or oropharyngeal candidiasis

Oropharyngeal candidal disease may present in different patterns, like white

plaques in the oropharyngeal area, erythematous macules (often in patients with

dentures), or as pseudomembranes.

Thrush infection often recurs, especially in patients with AIDS. Consult MRTC

clinic or Infectious Diseases (MRTC may also be consulted in the MVAHCS) for

more information on treatment of recurrent infection.

Mild disease

[Nystatin swish and swallow QID for 7-14 days \($\) M](psozid2-nystatin-swish-swallow-5ml-qid-7d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-nystatin-swish-swallow-5ml-qid-7d)

< OR >

[Clotrimazole troche 10 mg PO 5X/day for 7-14 days \($\) M](psozid-clotrimazole-troche-10mg-po-5x-d-7d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-clotrimazole-troche-10mg-po-5x-d-7d)

Moderate to severe disease

[Fluconazole 200 mg PO QDay for 7-14 days \($\) R,DI](psozid2-fluconazole-200mg-po-qday-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-200mg-po-qday-7ds)

# Esophageal candidiasis

Esophageal infection requires systemic therapy.

Preferred treatment

[Fluconazole 400 mg PO QDay for 14-21 days \($\) R,DI](psozid2-fluconazole-400mg-qday-14-days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fluconazole-400mg-qday-14-days)

Alternative for patient who cannot swallow tablets

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

# Systemic candidal infection

Fluconazole is preferred empirical therapy in most cases. Amphotericin B should

be used empirically in patients who have received an azole antifungal drug

recently, or in patients who are critically ill.

Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Duration of therapy is dependent upon location, severity of infection,

and response to therapy. Consult Infectious Diseases for more information.

Preferred treatment

[Fluconazole 800 mg PO once then 400 mg PO QDay \($\) R,DI](psozid-fluconazole-800mg-po-once-then-400mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-fluconazole-800mg-po-once-then-400mg-po-qday)

< OR >

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for IV options

Recent azole antifungal treatment

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU FURUNCLES AND CARBUNCLES
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

FURUNCLES AND CARBUNCLES

Localized purulent infections include furuncles, carbuncles and cutaneous

abscesses. Nearly all are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. A furuncle is a

inflamed nodule that usually develops as a complication of folliculitis. A

carbuncle is a more extensive lesion that extends further into the subcutaneous

tissue.  Contact a wound care nurse for more information.

Incision and drainage is the mainstay of therapy for carbuncles, cutaneous

abscesses, and large furuncles.

The decision to administer antibiotics directed against S. aureus as an adjunct

to incision and drainage should be made based on the presence of systemic

inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) or in patients with markedly impaired

host defenses.

# For recurrent skin abscesses in addition to culture and antibiotic therapy

# recommended consider a decolonization regimen.

[Select here for Staphylococcus aureus Decolonization](orzid3-gmenu-abx-sa-decolonization)

# Mild infection: Purulent infection without systemic signs of infection

Recommend incision and drainage. No antibiotic indicated.

# Moderate Infection: Purulent infection with signs of systemic infection.

Recommend incision and drainage. Culture material and use results to guide

therapy.

Treat for 5 days and extend/modify treatment if not improved in this time.

# Preferred treatment

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO bid for 5 days \($\) R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-x5days)

< OR >

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO bid \($\) R,DI](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-5days-1ds-tab-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-5days-1ds-tab-bid)

# Alternatives

[Doxycycline 100 mg po BID \($\) DI](psozid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d)

# If methicillin-RESISTANT Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is suspected or proved

[Doxycycline 100 mg po BID \($\) DI](psozid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-5d)

[Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO BID \($\) R,DI](psozid2-tmp-sulfa-5days-1ds-tab-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-tmp-sulfa-5days-1ds-tab-bid)

[Linezolid 600 mg PO BID for 5 days \($\) DI,O](psozid2-linezolid-600mg-po-bid-5days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-linezolid-600-mg-po-bid-5days)

# Severe Infections:

Patients who have failed incision and drainage along with oral antibiotics

or those with SIRS or for infections in those with neutropenia or diminished

neutrophil function.

See Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU GENITAL HERPES
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# GENITAL HERPES

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompetent patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Treatment of the initial episode decreases the duration of pain, lesions, and

viral shedding by 1 to 2 days. Treatment of the initial episode does not

decrease likelihood of recurrent episodes.

Treatment

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID for 7-10 days \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-7days-400mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-7days-400mg-po-tid)

Alternative

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO BID for 7-10 days \($\) R](psozid2-valacyclovir-7ds-1gm-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-valacyclovir-7ds-1gm-po-bid)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Episodic therapy for relapses

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Treatment of recurrent episodes must be started within 24 hours of symptom

onset. Treatment decreases the duration of pain and lesions, and viral shedding

by 1 to 2 days. Consider suppressive treatment for patients with more than 6

episodes per year.

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID for 5 days \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-5ds-400mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-5ds-400mg-po-tid)

< OR >

[Acyclovir 800 mg PO TID for 2 days \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-2ds-800mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-2ds-800mg-po-tid)

< OR >

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO BID for 3 days \($\) R](psozid-valacyclovir-3ds-500mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-valacyclovir-3ds-500mg-po-bid)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Immunocompromised patients

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Immunocompromised patients in whom genital herpes simplex disease is often

severe include: patients with HIV infection, organ transplants, malnourishment,

eczema or severe burns, and in patients receiving immunosuppressive

chemotherapy.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Treat mild to moderate disease for 10 days. In severe disease, treat with

intravenous acyclovir for 2 to 7 days based on clinical response, then treat

with an oral antiviral for a total duration of 10 days.

# Treatment for mild to moderate disease or after clinical improvement of severe

# disease

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-10ds-400mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-10ds-400mg-po-tid)

Alternative

[Valacyclovir 1 gm PO BID \($\) R](psozid2-valacyclovir-10ds-1gm-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-valacyclovir-10ds-1gm-po-bid)

# Treatment for severe disease

Infectious Diseases consult encouraged.

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# Chronic suppressive therapy

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Suppressive therapy is indicated in patients with more than 6 episodes per

year, or in patients with less frequent episodes who are desiring to minimize

risk of transmission. Some patients may find episodic treatment more

convenient. The frequency of recurrences can decrease after 1 to 5 years, and

and suppressive therapy may be stopped every few years to see if it is

still needed.

[Acyclovir 400 mg PO BID \($\) R](psozid2-acyclovir-1yr-400mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-acyclovir-1yr-400mg-po-bid)

Alternative

*Note: Recommend increasing dose to 1000 mg per day for patients that have

breakthrough on the 500 mg dose. See recommendation below.

[Valacyclovir 500 mg PO QDay \($\) R](psozid2-valacyclovir-1yr-500mg-po-qday)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU GI LIVER ABSCESS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# LIVER ABSCESS

[Oral step-down treatment](orzid3-gmenu-abx-step-down-treatment)

Liver abscess should be suspected in all patients with fever, leukocytosis, and

a space-occupying liver lesion. Liver abscesses fall broadly into two

categories: pyogenic and amebic. In the United States, pyogenic liver abscess is

much more common. Amebic liver abscess occurs almost exclusively in travelers

and immigrants.

Infectious Diseases consultation is recommended due to prolonged treatment and

need for follow-up.

# Duration of therapy

A typical course for pyogenic liver abscess is 4 to 6 weeks based on improvement

and follow-up imaging.

# Treatment

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Mandell chapter: Infections of the Liver and Biliary System

Sanford Guide article: Hepatic Abscess

Solomkin et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2010, 50:133-64

Up-to-Date article: Pyogenic liver abscess

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU GONOCOCCAL
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# Gonococcal Infections:

-When diagnosed with sexually transmitted disease, the patient's sexual

partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually

transmitted infection.

# Uncomplicated gonococcal infections of the pharynx, cervix, urethra, or rectum:

-If chlamydial infection has not been excluded, recommend to treat for

chlamydia.

-A test-of-cure is unnecessary for uncomplicated urogenital or rectal

gonorrhea for patients treated with the recommended or alternative regimen.

-A test-of-cure is recommended for patients with pharyngeal gonorrhea.

Obtain nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) 7 to 14 days after initial

treatment, regardless of regimen used for pharyngeal gonorrhea.

# Lab test:

[Click here Place order for gonorrhea/chlamydia lab NAAT test](lrtzid-chlamydia-gc-urine-naat)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Chlamydial infection and no co-infection:

[Click here Chlamydial infection and no co-infection](orzid3-gmenu-chlamydia-urethritis-cervicitis-proctitis)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Preferred treatment for patients and no chlamydial co-infection:

# Patients weighing less than 150 kg:

[Ceftriaxone 500 MG IM x1 dose \($\) M](psjizid-ceftriaxone-500mg-im-x1-gonococcal)

# Patients weighing 150 kg or greater:

[Ceftriaxone 1 GM IM x1 dose \($\) M](psjizid-ceftriaxone-1gm-im-x1-gonococcal)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Preferred treatment with chlamydial co-infection or chlamydial infection has

# not been excluded:

# Patients weighing less than 150 kg:

[Ceftriaxone 500MG IM Once \($\) M <AND> Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7days\($\) DI](orz-set-abx-op-ceftri-500mg-im-x1-doxy-100mg-bid-7d-gonococc)

[Non-VA order for Doxycycline above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-7ds)

# Patients weighing 150 kg or greater:

[Ceftriaxone 1 GM IM Once \($\) M <AND> Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7days\($\) DI](orz-set-abx-op-ceftri-1gm-im-x1-doxy-100mg-po-bid-7d-gonococc)

[Non-VA order for Doxycycline above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-7ds)

# ______________________________________________________________________________

# Alternative treatment for beta-lactam allergy for cervix, urethra, or rectum:

For persons with a history of a beta-lactam allergy, a thorough assessment

of the reaction is recommended.

[Gentamicin 240 MG IM Once \($\) R <AND> Azithromycin 2000 mg PO Once \($\) DI](orz-set-abx-op-gentamicin-240mg-imx1-azith-2000mg-x1-gonoc)

# Alternative treatment for beta-lactam allergy for pharynx:

No reliable alternative treatments are available for pharyngeal gonorrhea.

For persons with a history of a beta-lactam allergy, a thorough assessment

of the reaction is recommended. For persons with an anaphylactic or other

severe reaction to ceftriaxone, consult Infectious Disease for alternative

treatment recommendation.

References:

St. Cyr S, et al. MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020, 69:1911-1916.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HELICOBACTER PYLORI INFECTION

H. pylori infection is associated with peptic ulcers, gastritis, gastric

adenocarcinoma, and gastric lymphoma. Antimicrobials should be given to patients

with confirmed H. pylori infection. Antisecretory therapy should be given

concurrently.

Test of cure should be completed at least 4 weeks after completion of therapy

(recommended within 4-8 weeks after completion). Any PPI therapy must be

held for 2 weeks prior to testing.

[Click here Lab H.Pylori, stool](lrtz-h-pylori-ag-stool)

Note: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) advises adult household

members of individuals who have a positive non-serological test for

H. pylori to seek testing trough their provider.

# First line treatment:

[Bismuth subsalicylate 524 mg PO q6h <AND> Tetracycline 500 mg q6h DI](orz-set-abx-op-bis524mgqid-tcn500mgqid-metro500mgqid-omep20mg)

<AND> metronidazole 500mg PO q6h [DI] <AND> omeprazole 20mg po q12h. Take

all for 14 days.

[NonVA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-bis524mgqid-tcn500mgqid-metro500mgqid-omep20mg)

# Alternative treatments:

Alternatives may have lower efficacy and higher resistances rates. Test of

cure extremely important.

***Consider referring patients who cannot take first line therapy to

GI pharmacist for treatment management and follow-up testing.***

[Click here Gastroenterology \(OP\) Consult - Pharmacists](gmrctz-gastroenterology-op)

# Rifabutin triple (Talicia):

Note: place medication order and PADR using order below

[Amoxicillin/Omeprazole/Rifabutin \(250/10/12.5MG\) 4 caps po tid x14days DI,H](orz-set-abx-op-rifabutin-triple-h-pylori-padr)

[NonVA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-rifabutin-triple-h-pylori-padr)

< OR >

# PCAB dual (Voquezna DualPak-Amoxicillin/Vonoprazan):

Note: place medication order and PADR using order below

[PCAB Dual \(vonoprazan 20mg q12h/amoxicillin 1000mg q8h\) po x14daysDI](orz-set-abx-op-pcab-dual-h-pylori-padr)

per package instructions

[NonVA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-pcab-dual-h-pylori-padr)

< OR >

# Clarithromycin Quadruple:

Resistance to clarithromycin is increasing. Do not use for patients with prior

exposure to macrolides. Consider susceptibility testing prior to use.

[Clarithromycin 500 mg PO q12h R,DI <AND> Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO q12h R](orz-set-abx-op-clar500mgbid-amox1gmbid-metro500mgbid-omep)

<AND> metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h [DI] <AND> omeprazole 20 mg PO q12h. Take all

for 14 days.

[NonVA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-clar500mgbid-amox1gmbid-metro500mgbid-omep20mg)

References:

Chey et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection.

Am J Gastroenterol, 2024, 119(9):1730-1753.

VA PBM Clinical Recommendations November 2024. Use of newer combination products

in the treatment of H.pylori infections.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HEAD LICE (PEDICULOSIS CAPITIS)

Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood. To

make a diagnosis, use a nit comb, bright light, or lens to find a louse living

on the scalp.  Dead nits may remain for months after successful treatment.  Dead

nits are usually located more than 6 mm from the scalp.

Lice are often transmitted by infected clothing and bedclothes but not by

ordinary furniture that is not typically in contact with hair or scalp.  Refer

to the following for advice on household cleaning for lice infestations:

[https://www.cdc.gov/lice/treatment/index.html](orz-gtx-abx-treat-head-lice-url)

# Treatment

Repeat if live lice are seen 7-10 days after treatment.

[Permethrin 1% lotion Apply to affected area for 10 minutes then comb out nits](psozid2-permethrin-1-lot-10min-7days)

[M]

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-permethrin-1-lot-10min-7days)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU HEPATITIS B EVALUATION ANTI-CD20 ANTIBODY
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# Hepatitis B evaluation for patients receiving Anti-CD20 Antibody Treatment

# NOTE: OUTPATIENT ORDERS

Before initiating anti-CD20 antibody treatment (rituximab, obinutuzumab,

ofatumumab) test all patients for Hepatitis B. Testing should be completed

within the last 6 months prior to the start of the initial infusion (same day

is acceptable, but not preferred). Annual Hepatitis B screening is not

necessary unless there are risk factors.

# More information at VHA Oncology SharePoint site for hepatitis B reactivation:

[Hepatitis B Oncology SharePoint](orz-gtx-abx-hepatitis-b-oncology-sharepoint)

# Order Hepatitis B Serology Panel for all patients:

[HEPATITIS B SEROLOGY PANEL](lrtz-hepatitis-b-serology-panel)

Includes hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), anti-hepatitis B core antibody

(total anti-HBcAb),and anti-hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBsAb).

# IF HBsAg or anti-HBcAb is positive, Consult GI for all services except

# Oncology:

(Includes Rheumatology, Renal, Neurology, and Dermatology)

[GASTROENTEROLOGY LIVER OUTPATIENT CONSULT](gmrctz-gastroenterology-liver-outpt)

# IF HBsAg or anti-HBcAB is positive for an ONCOLOGY patient initial orders:

a) Assess HIV status. To avoid potential HIV resistance-

refer HIV positive patients to ID for management.

[HIV RAPID TEST \(results in 1-2 hours\)](lrtzhiv-rapid-qualitative)

[CONSULT ID FOR HIV POSITIVE PATIENTS](gmrctz-infectious-disease-outpt)

b) Obtain Labs: Comprehensive Metabolic AND Phosphorus

[ORDER LABS: COMPREHENSIVE METABOLIC + PHOSPHORUS](orz-set-abx-lrtz-comprehensive-metabolic-mg-phosphorus)

c) Obtain HBV DNA level (viral load) initially

[HEPATITIS B DNA LEVEL \(VIRAL LOAD\)](lrtz-hepatitis-b-dna-level-viral-load)

d) Schedule GI Clinic Consult for co-management to order

liver imaging and follow-up as indicated.

[GASTROENTEROLOGY LIVER OUTPATIENT CONSULT](gmrctz-gastroenterology-liver-outpt)

e) Start hepatitis B antiviral treatment (see below)

# Recommended Antiviral Treatment:

Continue antivirals throughout anti-CD20 Ab therapy and for an additional

12 months to prevent hepatitis B reactivation, hepatitis, liver failure,

and death.

# Obtain HBV DNA level (viral load) every 3 months

[Hepatitis B DNA level \(viral load\)](lrtz-hepatitis-b-dna-level-viral-load)

# IF PATIENT IS CURRENTLY ON HEPATITIS B ANTIVIRAL THERAPY:

(lamivudine, adefovir, or telbivudine)

Consult the provider who ordered the antiviral and inform the

provider the patient is being initiated on Anti-CD20 antibody therapy.

# IF PATIENT IS NOT ON HEPATITIS B ANTIVIRAL THERAPY:

# Lamivudine-naive patients:

[Entecavir 0.5 mg po daily \(throughout anti-CD20 antibody therapy](psozid-entecavir-0-5mg-po-qday-hepatitis-b-anti-cd20-ab)

and for an additional 12 months after therapy completed). (Cost $$) [R,O]

# Lamivudine-experienced patients:

# Preferred Treatment:

[Entecavir 1 mg po daily \(througout anti-CD20 antibody therapy](psozid-entecavir-1mg-po-qday-hepatitis-b-anti-cd20-ab)

and for an additional 12 months after therapy completed). (Cost $$) [R,O]

< OR >

# Alternative Treatment:

IF creatinine clearance equal to or greater than 50 ml per minute

[Tenofovir 300 mg PO daily \(throughout anti-CD20 antibody therapy](psozid-tenofovir-300mg-po-qday-anti-cd20-therapy)

and for an additional 12 months after therapy completed). (Cost $$) [R,O]

References:

Terrault NA, Hepatology 2016, 63:261

Perrillo RP, Gastroenterology 2015, 148:221

Hwang JP, Journal of Clinical Oncology 2015, 33:2212

Up-to-Date

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU HIDRADENITIS SUPPURATIVA
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# HIDRADENITIS SUPPURATIVA

A chronic inflammatory condition that typically involves occlusion, rupture,

abscess formation and infection of hair follicles as well as secondary infection

of apocrine glands/surrounding tissues. Lesions most often occur in the

intertriginous areas (axillae, inguinal and anogenital) in is associated with

smoking and obesity. There is a 40% genetic predisposition for hidradenitis

suppurativa (HS) and is often accompanied by pain, malodor, and drainage.

Cultures are negative 50% of the time and often are polymicrobial with S.

epidermidis and S. aureus most isolated. The Hurley Staging System is often used

to determine severity of HS.

Therapy generally consists of treatment of comorbidities that can exacerbate HS,

avoidance of triggers, pain management, wound care, and topical/oral

antimicrobials. Hormonal agents, steroids, retinoids, and surgery can also be

used to treat certain patients. Biologics may be considered in Stage II-III HS.

# Consult Dermatology in all cases

# Hurley Staging System:

Stage I: recurrent nodules and abscesses with minimal scarring

Stage II: limited number of sinuses and/or scarring within a body region

Stage III: multiple or extensive sinuses and/or scarring

# Duration of Therapy:

Treatment is typically for 12 weeks but may require longer durations in certain

cases. Metronidazole should only be used for a maximum of 6 weeks to avoid

neurologic toxicity.

# Interventions for All Patients:

Smoking cessation, weight loss, avoidance of triggers, and pain management

should be part of all treatment plans. Consult Dermatology for use of hormonal

agents, steroids, retinoids, and surgery.

# Optional Topical Treatment, May be Used in Addition to Oral Therapies Below:

[Chlorhexidine gluconate 4% liquid topically wash affected area q24h \($\) M](psozid-chlorhexidine-gluconate-wash-q24h)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-chlorhexidine-gluconate-wash-q24h)

< OR >

[Benzoyl peroxide 10% soap topically wash affected area q24h \($\) M](psozid-benzoyl-peroxide-10-wash-topically-q24h)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-benzoyl-peroxide-10-wash-topically-q24h)

< ADD ON THERAPY FOR FLARES - MUST USE IN ADDITION TO ONE OF THE AGENTS ABOVE>

[Clindamycin 1% solution topically to affected areas q12h prn for flares \($\) M](psozid-clindamycin-1-crm-top-bid-prn)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-clindamycin-1-crm-top-bid-prn)

# Stage I-II Initial Treatment:

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks](psozid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h-12weeks)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h-12weeks)

< OR >

[Minocycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 12 weeks](psozid2-minocycline-100mg-po-q12h-12weeks)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-minocycline-100mg-po-q12h-12weeks)

# Stage III Initial Treatment and Stage I-II Failure of Oral Doxycycline:

[Clindamycin 300 mg PO q12h for 12 weeks \($\) H,O](psozid2-clindamycin-300mg-po-q12h-12weeks)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-clindamycin-300mg-po-q12h-12weeks)

# Stage II-III Failure of Oral Clindamycin:

[Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO q24h \($\)R,DI for 12 weeks <AND> metronidazole 500](orz-set-abx-op-moxi400poq12h-rifam300poq12h-12w-metro500q8h6w)

mg q8h ($) [DI] for 6 weeks <AND> rifampin 300 mg PO q12h ($) [DI,O] for 12

weeks

menus.Text:
# Alternative recommendations:

# Daily emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Descovy)

Must meet ALL of the inclusion criteria:

-MSM-TGW at substantial risk of sexual HIV acquisition

-Contraindication to Truvada (CrCl 30-59 ml/min OR

osteoporosis/osteopenia/prior stress fracture)

Must not have ANY of the exclusion criteria:

-Significant noncompliance with follow-up HIV testing

-Concomitant contraindicated medications (rifamycin deriatives,

St John's wort)

[Click here Descovy: Take one tablet by mouth daily \(#90 No Refill\)](psozid-descovy-po-qday-90days-no-refill-pcp)

# Cabotegravir injections:

If a patient meets the following criteria, they can be referred to infectious

diseases for evaluation of appropriateness for injectable HIV PrEP

Must meet 1 of the inclusion criteria:

-Intolerance to Truvada or Descovy

-CrCl < 60 ml/min or multiple risk factors for significant renal

dysfunction

-Very high-risk for HIV acquisition (e.g. MSM/TGW who engage in frequent

episodes condom-less receptive anal intercourse, have repeated episodes

of STIs, or high-risk sexual activity with partners who are known

or likely to be HIV infected)

Must not have ANY of the exclusion criteria:

-Significant noncompliance with follow-up HIV testing

-Concomitant contraindicated medications (rifamycin derivatives,

carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, or phenobarbital)

[Click here Place HIV Clinc \(MRTC\) Outpt Consult](gmrctz-mrtc-outpt)

# Indications:

- Anyone who requests HIV PrEP

- 1 or more sex partners with known HIV with unknown or detectable viral load

- 1 or more sex partners unknown HIV status

- History of bacterial STI in the past 6 months

- History injection drug use with shared equipment within the past 6 months

IMMUNOGLOBULIN DEFICIENCY (HUMORAL IMMUNE SYSTEM)

Antibody deficiency typically leads to recurrent, severe respiratory tract

infections associated with encapsulated bacteria, especially Streptococcus

pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, and to a lesser extent, Staphylococcus

aureus. Recurrent otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonia are common syndromes.

Gastrointestinal disease associated with Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or

rotavirus is also common in some patients.

# Preferred empirical treatment

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# FULMINANT CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

# Discontinue any antibiotics if possible.

# Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic therapy is still needed.

# Discontinue antacid therapy if possible.

# There are no available data supporting the use of fidaxomicin for treatment of

# fulminant CDI.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Antimicrobial therapy for CDI should be continued for 10 days. In patients being

treated with antibiotics for predisposing infections, consider continuing

treatment for 7 days after completion of those antibiotics. If patient is being

treated for CDI recurrence, pulse taper therapy is indicated after resolution of

severe disease. Refer to mild to moderate CDI treatment menu for

recommendations.

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

COMPLEMENT DEFICIENCY

Complement deficiency can be inherited or acquired complement deficiency.

Acquired defects are usually a consequence of other diseases like systemic lupus

erythematosus.  Complement deficiency leads to increased rates of infections,

usually of the upper respiratory tract, but also occasionally with bacteremia or

meningitis.  Pathogens are usually Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria

meningitidis, and Neisseria gonorrhea.

Patients presenting with fever or other symptoms suggesting systemic bacterial

infection should be treated immediately with antimicrobials active against these

pathogens.

# Preferred empirical treatment

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.

[References](orzid2-gmenu-abx-references)

Rich RR et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology

Roitt I et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

MALIGNANCY

Malignancies affect host defenses in many ways.  Hematogenous malignancies can

diminish the effectiveness of neutrophils and other cells involved in host

defense.  Tumors often disrupt mucous membranes or blood vessels and allow

contaminating organisms into hollow cavities or the bloodstream.  Chemotherapy

used to treat these malignancies often impairs mucus membranes and suppresses

neutrophil production and function.

Empirical antimicrobials are not indicated for patients with malignancy and

fever unless they have neutropenia or a specific infectious disease, except in

specific circumstances.

[Neutropenic fever](orzid3-gmenu-neutropenic-fever)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU IMMUNOCOM NEUROL DYSFUNCT
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

NEUROLOGICAL DYSFUNCTION

Several types of neurological dysfunction predispose patients to infectious

diseases.  Comatose patients are unable to keep weight off dependent tissues,

predisposing them to decubitus ulcers and pressure necrosis.  Atelectasis is

common in obtunded patients who cannot cough or breathe deeply.  When patients

require artificial ventilation, intubation compounds the risk of respiratory

infection.

Neurological dysfunction of the bladder can interfere with normal bladder

emptying and predisposes patients to bacteriuria.  The risk of bacteruria

increases if patients are catheterized.  Antimicrobial treatment is not

indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria.  It provides no benefit and increases

risk of colonization with resistant organisms.

Neurological dysfunction of the gastrointestinal or pulmonary systems

predisposes patients to aspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents.

Aspiration causes fever, inflammation, and/or pulmonary infiltrate, but does not

require antimicrobial treatment. Bacterial pneumonia occurs in a minority of

patients who experience significant aspiration, typically about 3 days later.

The patient usually improves for the first 2 days and then worsens as bacterial

pneumonia develops with increased fever, new or progressive infiltrates,

leukocytosis, and newly purulent sputum.

[Aspiration pneumonia](orzid3-gmenu-aspiration-pneumonia)

[References](orzid2-gmenu-abx-references)

Rich RR, et al, eds.  Clinical Immunology

Roitt I, et al, eds.  Immunology

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

Impetigo and Ecthyma

Impetigo is a superficial skin infection that rarely causes systemic

symptoms. Ecthyma is a skin infection characterized by crusted sores

beneath which ulcers form. It is a deep form of impetigo, as the same

bacteria causing the infection are involved. Ecthyma causes deeper

erosions of the skin into the dermis.

Gram stain and culture of the pus or exudates from skin lesions of

impetigo and ecthyma are recommended to help identify whether

Staphylococcus aureus and/or beta-hemolytic Streptococcus is the cause.

Bullous and non-bullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical

antimicrobials, but oral therapy is recommended for patients with

numerous lesions or in outbreaks affecting several people to help

decrease transmission of infection. Treatment for ecthyma should be an

oral antimicrobial.

# Treatment for impetigo with few lesions

[Mupirocin ointment to affected area TID for 5 days \($\) M](psozid-mupirocin-2-oint-tid-for-5-days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-mupirocin-2-oint-tid-for-5-days)

# Treatment for ecthyma and for impetigo with numerous lesions or

# whose symptoms have not responded to topical treatment

Treat orally for 7 days

[Cefadroxil 1000 mg PO q12h x 7days \($\) R](psozid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-bid-7days)

# Alternative for penicillin allergy

[Click here Assess Beta-lactam allergy prior to ordering alternative](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Doxycycline 100MG PO bid \($\) DI](psozid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-100mg-po-bid-7ds)

# IF MRSA confirmed or suspected:

[Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO bid \($\) R,DI](psozid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-po-bid-7ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-trimeth-sulfa-1-ds-po-bid-7ds)

# INFECTIOUS DIARRHEA / GASTROENTERITIS

Most episodes of acute diarrhea are self-limited. In most mild to moderate

cases, antimicrobial therapy does not provide benefit.

# Bloody diarrhea

Bloody diarrhea can represent hemorrhagic colitis or dysentery. Antimicrobial

therapy and antimotility agents are not recommended in most patients with bloody

diarrhea due to an increased risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome when using these

agents.

Hydration and electrolyte replacement

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU INFLUENZA CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# EARLY TREATMENT OF INFLUENZA AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS

In most cases, if a person is suspected of having been exposed to influenza,

early treatment, should signs or symptoms develop, is preferred rather than

chemoprophylaxis.

The provider should explain the early signs and symptoms of influenza to the

patient and advise the patient to immediately contact a health care provider for

evaluation and possible early treatment if these symptoms or signs develop.

Influenza-like symptoms or signs include fever, cough, sore throat, runny or

stuffy nose, body aches, headache, chills, fatigue, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Influenza can present without fever.

Health care providers should use clinical judgment regarding situations where

early recognition of illness and treatment might be an appropriate alternative

to chemoprophylaxis.

# Early treatment alternative or chemoprophylaxis may be considered:

*Persons who are part of a high-risk group and are household or close contacts

of someone with influenza-like illness Chemoprophylaxis duration: 7 days after

last known exposure

# Chemoprophylaxis recommended:

*For control of outbreaks in institutional settings (long-term care facilities

and hospitals)

Chemoprophylaxis duration: minimum of 2 weeks and continuing up to 1 week after

the last known case is identified.

Note: Antiviral chemoprophylaxis is recommended for all residents, including

those who have received influenza vaccination.

# Chemoprophylaxis considered:

*Atypical situations (such as case clusters). Contact the state health

department for consultation.

# Antiviral Prophylaxis Recommendations

Preferred:

[Oseltamivir 75 mg po q24h R](psozid2-oseltamivir-75-mg-po-qday-prophy-14-days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid3-oseltamivir-75-mg-po-qday-14d-prophy)

(See information above for length of prophylaxis)

# **Below is for information only, quick orders are not available

Alternative treatment:

Zanamivir is not recommended for patients with chronic respiratory diseases such

as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. These patients may have

bronchospasm with zanamivir. If zanamivir must be used, and patients are using

an inhaled bronchodilator, zanamivir should be taken just after the

bronchodilator.

Requires Infectious Disease Approval

# MVAHCS Vaccination Recommendations for Outpatients:

[Click here Outpatient Influenza Vaccine Guidelines](orz-gtx-abx-url-influenza-outpatient)

Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all persons aged 6

months and older without a specific contraindication.

Adjuvanted influenza vaccines - an ingredient is added to help create a

stronger immune response.

Quadrivalent influenza vaccine - made up of the four flu strains most likely

to cause the flu during the upcoming season (H1N1, H3N2, and two group

B viruses.

Eggs and latex allergies are NOT considered contraindications to receiving

the vaccine, the only contraindication to the flu vaccination is severe

allergic reaction (i.e. Anaphylactic reactions).

# Per available stock and ACIP 2022-2023 recommendations, the MVAHCS will provide:

*Standing orders - no patient specific order needed

# Recommendation for adults aged >/= 65 years:

*Adjuvanted influenza vaccine (Flu-Ad)

# Recommendation for adults aged <65 years:

*Standard quadrivalent influenza vaccine

# INITIAL EPISODE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)

Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic

therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide,

etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved

or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the

diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to

antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial

therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.

# Treatment for initial episode of CDI:

[Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID for 10 days \($\) M](psozid-vancomycin-125mg-cap-qid-10ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-vancomycin-125mg-cap-qid-10ds)

# Alternate treatment for patient at increased risk of CDI recurrence:

(e.g., age >65 years old, concomitant antibiotic use during CDI treatment,

and/or immunosuppression)

[Fidaxomicin 200 mg po q12h for 10 days M](psozid2-fidaxomicin-200mg-po-q12h-10days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-fidaxomicin-200mg-po-bid-10ds)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU KERATITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# KERATITIS

Keratitis is an emergency requiring prompt treatment to prevent vision loss.

Contact Ophthalmology immediately.

Keratitis is associated with viral or bacterial infection, trauma, foreign

bodies, or allergies. About half of cases of infectious keratitis are caused by

bacterial pathogens, most commonly Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., and

gram-negative bacilli. Viruses are the second leading cause. Fungi and parasites

have also been associated with corneal infection. Obtain corneal scrapings for

gram stain and bacterial and viral cultures and start empirical therapy

immediately.

Link to herpes keratitis page

[Herpes keratitis](orzid3-gmenu-abx-herpes-keratitis)

If bacterial keratitis is likely, contact ophthalmology to obtain a corneal

scraping and give empirical antibacterial drops immediately. Modify therapy

based on Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases recommendations. Ophthalmic

corticosteroids are contraindicated in patients with keratitis.

# Duration of therapy

Treatment should be continued until ulcer and other signs of infectious

keratitis have resolved. A minimum of two weeks and in rare cases, up to a month

of therapy may be required.

# Mild to moderate bacterial keratitis empirical treatment

[Moxifloxacin 0.5% ophthalmic drops: 1-2 drops in affected eye\(s\) q1h \($\) M](psozid2-moxifloxacin-0-5-oph-1-2-drop-s-q1h-14days)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-moxifloxacin-0-5-oph-1-2-drop-q1h-14days)

# Severe (vision-threatening) bacterial keratitis empirical treatment

[Cefazolin 50 mg/ml ophthalmic drops: 1-2 drops q1h <AND> gentamicin 15 mg/ml](orz-set-abx-op-cefaz-5-oph-gent-15mg-ml-oph-q1h-14days)

ophthalmic drops: 1-2 drops q1h ($) [M] in affected eye(s)

[Non-VA order for above](orz-set-abx-nv-cefaz-5-oph-gent-15mg-ml-oph-q1h-14days)

# Suspected MRSA

Patient may require vancomycin 50mg/mL eye drops q1h in addition to gentamicin

eye drops. Vancomycin eye drops must be specially compounded and managed by

Ophthalmology.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Lin et al., Ophthalmology. 2019,126(1):1-55

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# ACUTE NEUROLOGICAL DISEASE ASSOCIATED WITH LYME DISEASE

Neurological disease is a common manifestation of Lyme Disease that typically

occurs within weeks to months after the tick bite. Unilateral or bilateral

facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) can be treated with oral antimicrobials. Other

neurological manifestations, including meningitis, require treatment with

intravenous antimicrobials.

# Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases

# Duration of therapy

Treat for at least 14 days. Longer durations, up to 21 days for facial nerve

palsy and 28 days for other neurologic disease, may be required in severe cases.

# Treatment of isolated facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy)

Preferred:

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 14 days](psozid2-doxycycline-14ds-100mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-14ds-100mg-po-bid)

For pregnant patients or those with contraindications to doxycycline:

[Amoxicillin 500 mg PO q8h \($\) R for 14 days](psozid2-amoxicillin-14ds-500mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amoxicillin-14ds-500mg-po-tid)

# Treatment of neurological disease other than facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy)

Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# LYME DISEASE AND OTHER TICK-BORNE ILLNESSES

Patients who display signs of illness or fever within 30 days of removing an

attached tick should be evaluated for tick-borne illness. In the upper Midwest

these are Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and Powassan virus

disease. Patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick (deer tick) but

who do not display signs or symptoms of infection should not be treated with

antimicrobials. Refer to recommendations below for pathogen specific

recommendations.

[Anaplasmosis](orzid3-gmenu-path-a-phagocytophilum)

[Ehrlichioisis](orzid3-gmenu-path-e-chaffeensis)

[Babesiosis](orzid3-gmenu-parasite-babesia-spp)

Powassan virus disease - contact Infectious Diseases for more Information.

# Lyme Disease

Lyme disease results from the transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi from an

Ixodes spp. tick bite. Refer to CDC for map of endemic areas.

[CDC Lyme Disease Case Map](orz-gtx-abx-cdc-lyme-disease-case-map)

Prophylactic antimicrobial treatment may be beneficial in certain patients that

have been bitten while in endemic areas.

[Lyme Disease Prophylaxis](orzid3-gmenu-lyme-disease-prophylaxis)

Except for erythema migrans, Lyme disease is a complicated, difficult disease to

diagnose and treat. Infectious Diseases consultation is strongly encouraged.

Refer to recommendations below for

[Erythema migrans](orzid3-gmenu-lyme-erythema-migrans)

[Acute neurological disease](orzid3-gmenu-lyme-acute-neuro-disease)

[Arthritis](orzid3-gmenu-lyme-arthritis-assoc)

[Cardiac disease](orzid3-gmenu-lyme-cardiac-disease)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# LYME DISEASE PROPHYLAXIS

Patients who have been bitten while in endemic areas of New England, Mid-

Atlantic States, Minnesota, and Wisconsin where local rate of Ixodes spp. tick

infection rate with Borrelia burgdorferi in an endemic area may be treated with

prophylactic antibiotics for prevention of Lyme disease. Using a wait and see

method by monitoring for signs and symptoms of Lyme disease is also an

acceptable approach in patients who have been bitten by an Ixodes spp. tick.

# All following criteria must be met to be considered for prophylactic treatment

1. Doxycycline is not contraindicated (i.e. allergy, pregnant, lactating)

2. Attached tick is reliably identified as an adult or nymphal Ixodes spp.

[Ixodes spp. identification](orz-gtx-abx-tick-identification-link)

3. Tick is attached for greater than or equal to 36 hours based on degree of

tick engorgement with blood or likely time of exposure to tick infested area.

4. Prophylaxis must be started within 72 hours after time tick was removed.

5. Bite occurs in a highly endemic area.

[CDC Lyme Disease Case Map](orz-gtx-abx-cdc-lyme-disease-case-map)

# Prophylactic treatment if all of the above criteria are met

[Doxycycline PO 200mg once \($\) DI](psozid-doxycycline-200mg-po-once)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-doxycycline-200mg-po-once)

# ERYTHEMA MIGRANS ASSOCIATED WITH LYME DISEASE

Erythema migrans is the first manifestation of Lyme disease in 70-80% of cases.

It is typically an erythematous circular rash, 5cm or larger in diameter, with

induration and central clearing (although other patterns occur). It usually

develops at the site of the bite and/or in one or more distant locations. The

rash occurs 3 to 30 days after the bite. Rashes with onset less than 3 days

after a tick bite are not from Lyme disease.

If suspected erythema migrans is atypical, serology testing is recommended

with repeat in three weeks if negative.

[Lyme Panel, Serum](lrtz-lyme-panel)

# Treatment

Preferred:

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 10 days](psozid2-doxycycline-10ds-100mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-10ds-100mg-po-bid)

For pregnant patients or those with contraindications to doxycycline:

# MALIGNANT OTITIS EXTERNA

Those who are elderly, diabetic, immunocompromised and debilitated are at

highest risk. Most cases are associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, but other

pathogens can be involved. Obtain culture to identify etiologic agent and

susceptibilities. Obtain a CT scan to determine whether osteomyelitis is

present. ENT and Infectious Disease consultations are recommended.

# Treatment of uncomplicated disease

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Treatment of advanced disease, immunocompromised patients, or for coverage of

# fluoroquinolone resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in addition to above therapy

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS for parenteral therapy

# Treatment of early infection or step-down treatment after initial intravenous

# antimicrobial therapy. Adjust for a total duration of 6 weeks of antimicrobial

# therapy.

[Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q12h for 6 weeks \($\) R,DI](psozid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-28ds)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-ciprofloxacin-750mg-po-bid-28ds)
