# DENTAL INFECTIONS

Surgical drainage, scaling and antimicrobial treatment are essential. All

patients should be referred to the dental service for assessment and direction

of treatment. Empirical coverage for likely pathogens (streptococci,

Peptostreptococcus, Finegoldia, Bacteriodes and other oral anaerobes) is

required.

# Consult Dental Service

# Preferred:

[Amoxicillin 500 mg PO q8h for 5 days \($\) R](psozid2-amoxicillin-5ds-500mg-po-tid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-amoxicillin-5ds-500mg-po-tid)

< OR >

[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h for 5 days \($\) R](psozid2-amox-clav-875-125mg-5ds-po-bid)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# SYPHILIS

# Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Evaluation and management are complex.

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema

pallidum that can manifest as a variety of signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis

typically consists of painless ulcers or chancre at the site of infection with

regional adenopathy. Secondary syphilis often includes a skin rash (disseminated

and/or including the palms and soles), fever, malaise, mucocutaneous lesions and

lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis includes those with cardiovascular or

gummatous disease.

Latent syphilis is a period of disease when a patient does not have symptoms but

is found to be infected through serologic testing. Early latent syphilis refers

to latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year and late latent syphilis

refers to all other cases of latent syphilis. Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or

Otosyphilis, can occur at any stage of syphilis with early manifestations (e.g.

meningitis, stroke, vision or hearing loss) occurring within the first months to

years of infection and late manifestations (e.g. dementia, tabes dorsalis)

occurring after 10-30 years.

# Diagnosis

A presumptive diagnosis is made through use of a nontreponemal or serologic test

(i.e. rapid plasma reagin [RPR]) and a treponemal test (i.e. fluorescent

treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS]). Direct methods through darkfield

microscopy and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) must be used for definitive

diagnosis since T. pallidum cannot be cultured.

[Syphilis antibody test with reflex to rapid plasma reagin \(RPR\)](lrtz-syphilis-ab-w-reflex-to-rpr-w-titer)

# Management of sex partners

Persons with sexual contact with a person with primary, secondary or early

latent syphilis within the last 90 days should be presumptively treated even if

serologic test is negative.

# Primary, Secondary and Early Latent Syphilis

Preferred treatment

[Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 million units IM once \($$$\) M](psczid-benzathine-penicillin-2-4mu-im-once)

Secondary treatment for patients who are not pregnant

[Beta-lactam Reaction Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 14 days](psozid2-doxycycline-14ds-100mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-14ds-100mg-po-bid)

# Tertiary and Late Latent Syphilis

Preferred treatment

*Outpatient treatment requires a follow up appointment on day 7 and day 14 to

administer 2nd and 3rd dose respectfully. Ensure these appointments are made

when ordering this treatment regimen.

[Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 million units IM qweek \($$$\) M x3 doses](psczid2-benzathine-penicillin-2-4mu-im-qweek-x3-syphilis)

Secondary treatment for patients who are not pregnant

[Beta-lactam Reaction Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 28 days](psozid2-doxycycline-28ds-100mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-doxycycline-28ds-100mg-po-bid)

# Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or Otosyphilis

Consult Infectious Disease for treatment

# TINEA CAPITIS (RINGWORM)

Tinea capitis is a common fungal infection of the scalp and hair. It is

characterized by itchy, red, raised, scaly patches often sharply defined. Redder

margins than centers create impression of ring. Tinea capitis primarily affects

prepubescent children but can affect people of any age.

Baseline liver function test monitoring recommended. Repeat LFTs if treating for

longer than 6 weeks and there were baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver

disease, or other risks for hepatotoxicity.

# Treatment:

Treat for 4 weeks.

# TINEA PEDIS (ATHLETE'S FOOT), TINEA CORPORIS, TINEA MANUUM, OR TINEA CRURIS

Dermatophyte fungal infections are common worldwide. Dermatophytes metabolize

and subsist upon keratin in the skin, hair, and nails. Most tinea infections can

often be cured with topical therapy alone.  Systemic therapy is reserved for

severe or refractory infection, recurrent infection, or in immunocompromised

patients.

Treatment should continue for at least one week after clinical curing of

infection.

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU TINEA UNGUIUM (ONYCHOMYCOSIS)
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# TINEA UNGUIUM (ONYCHOMYCOSIS)

Obtain a fungal stain of nail sample prior to initiating treatment. Using large

nail clippers, remove as much of the unattached dystrophic nail as possible.

Place the piece of clipped nail plate in formalin jar and send to pathology for

fungal stain (PAS). Treatment should only be initiated if stain is positive for

fungal elements. Fungal culture is NOT recommended.

Systemic therapy is most likely to achieve a cure, especially with more nail

involvement. If <25% involvement topical therapy may be considered. If >50-75%

involvement systemic therapy should be considered.

Toenails take 12-18 months to grow out completely, so improvement should not be

expected to be observed for at least 6-9 months.  Continued improvement can be

experienced following treatment completion.

# Oral Treatment:

Terbinafine works about 70% of the time to cure the fungus, and reinfection is

common, so many patients will need to do more than one course of treatment.

Fluconazole pulse dosing response rate is approximately 50%. May consider

retreatment with oral therapy after one year.

Recommend Dermatology Consult for retreatment after failure of 2 courses of

terbinafine or fluconazole.

# Preferred Terbinafine first-line oral:

Toenail infections treat for 12 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to

starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were

baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for

hepatotoxicity.

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 12 weeks \(R,H,DI,O](psozid2-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday-x12-weeks-toenail)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday-x12-weeks-toenail)

Fingernail infections treat for 6 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to

starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were

baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for

hepatotoxicity.

[Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 6 weeks R,H,DI,O](psozid2-terbinafine-42days-250mg-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-terbinafine-42days-250mg-po-qday)

# Alternative oral therapy:

Toenail infections treat for at least 6 months

[Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for total of 6 months R,DI](psozid2-fluconazole-300mg-qweek-for-6-mons-toenail)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-fluconazole-300mg-qweek-for-3-6-months)

Fingernail infections treat for 3 months

[Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for 3 months R,DI](psozid2-fluconazole-300mg-po-qweek-for-3mons-fingernail)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-fluconazole-300mg-qweek-for-3-6-months)

# Topical Treatment:

Ciclopirox is a topical first-line treatment for both fingernails and toenails.

Complete resolution occurs in approximately 7 percent of patients treated daily

for 48 weeks.  Ciclopirox is a well-tolerated treatment. Potential side effects

include temporary nail changes and local skin irritation.

[Ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer: Apply once daily to affected nail\(s\)](psozid-ciclopirox-topical-qday-affected-nails)

Remove with rubbing alcohol every 7 days. [M] See accompanying medication

pamphlet for specific instructions. Treatment is continued until nail clearance

or up to 48 weeks.

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid-ciclopirox-8-nail-lacquer-fungal-nail-infection)

# Emergency Use Authorization (EUA): Tixagevimab plus Cilgavimab (EVUSHELD)

Tixagevimab plus Cilgavimab combination is available via FDA Emergency Use

Authorization (EUA) for pre-exposure prophylaxis for COVID-19 for patients

that meet specific criteria. They are not FDA approved drugs.

# Link to complete EUA documentation:

[Click here Pharmacist to complete EUA prior to dispensing medication](orz-gtx-abx-url-link-for-eua-fill-out-by-provider)

# Printable Fact Sheets for EUA:

[Click here] Fact Sheet for Patients/Caregivers EUA Evusheld

[Click here] Fact Sheet for Health Care Providers EUA Tix-Cil

# Tix-Cil (Tixagevimab plus cilgavimab)

On December 8, 2021 the FDA issued an EUA for AstraZeneca's Evusheld

(tixagevimab co-packaged with cilgavimab) for the pre-exposure prophylaxis

(prevention) of COVID-19 in certain adult and pediatric patients.

There are no adequate, approved and available alternatives to Evusheld

for the pre-exposure prevention of COVID-19 in the authorized population.

# Monoclonal antibodies are laboratory-made proteins that mimic the immune

system's ability to fight off harmful pathogens such as viruses. Tixagevimab and

cilgavimab are long-acting monoclonal antibodies that are specifically directed

against the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, designed to block the virus' attachment

and entry into human cells. Tigagevimab and cilgavimab bind to different,

non-overlapping sites on the spike protein of the virus.

# Patient Criteria for Use:

The product is only authorized for those individuals who are not currently

infected with SARS-CoV-2 virus and who have not recently been exposed to an

individual infected with SARS-CoV-2. The authorization also requires that

individuals either have:

-moderate to severely compromised immune systems due to a medical condition or

or due to taking immunosuppressive medications or treatments and may not

mount an adequate immune response to COVID-19 vaccination (examples of such

medical conditions or treatments can be found in the fact sheet for health

care providers) [see link top of page]

[ OR ]

-a history of severe adverse reactions to a COVID-19 vaccine and/or component(s)

of those vaccines, therefore vaccination with an available COVID-19 vaccine,

according to the approved or authorized schedule, is not recommended.

# Important information:

-One dose of Evusheld, administered as two separate consecutive intramuscular

injections (one injection per monoclonal antibody, given in immediate

succession), reduces the risk of developing COVID-19 for six months.

-Evusheld is NOT authorized for the treatment of COVID-19 or for post-exposure

prevention of COVID-19.

-Pre-exposure prevention with Evusheld is not a substitute for vaccination in

in individuals for whom COVID-19 vaccination is recommended.

-In patients with prior COVID-19 vaccination, at least 2 weeks are required

between the vaccination and the administration of Evusheld.

# **PBM EUA Criteria to be completed on web link:

# Answer to ALL of the following statements should be YES for administration:

1)Patient has no symptoms consistent with COVID-19, or if any symptoms, has a

a documented negative SARS-CoV-2 test within 72 hours prior to administration

2)Patient has no known recent exposure to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2

3)Patient has moderate to severe immunocompromise per the EUA definition or

a documented medical contraindication to vaccination. (Note: refusal to

be vaccinated does not constitute a contraindication for the purpose of

eligibility for this drug.)

4)In patients with prior COVID-19 vaccination (e.g. immunosuppressed) at least,

2 weeks have passed since the last dose was given (if no prior vaccination

answer YES)

5)The Fact Sheet for patients/caregivers has been made available to the patient/

caregiver prior to administration of this drug

# Note: Our staff is identifying the highest risk patients from our database

# for this medication. We will contact patients who are currently eligible

# for the limited doses currently allocated.

Minneapolis VAHCS is using the Minnesota Health Department's framework

for allocation of the medication. Our ID physicians shared in the development

of the plan and provides for consistency in the community.

[Click here] Minnesota Dept of Health-Prioritization of patients

# NOTES:

1)Providers approved to order: Dr. Klein (oncology) and ID Staff only

2)Second dose is not being scheduled/addressed at this time. We will pull

list of patients and assess the overall situation close to 6 month timeframe.

3)Administration in separate area from where COVID positive patients being seen

4)Pharmacy dispense in original kit to clinic (decrease waste/short expiration)

that meet specific criteria. They are not FDA approved drugs.

Evusheld is NOT authorized for the treatment of COVID-19 or for post-exposure

prevention of COVID-19.

# Evusheld and COVID-19 vaccine:

Patients who have received a COVID-19 vaccine, Evusheld should be administered

at least two weeks after vaccination, per Evusheld EUA.

Note: COVID-19 vaccine not required to receive Evusheld.

Per CDC: Patients who previously received antibody products as part of COVID-19

treatment, post-exposure prophylaxis, or pre-exposure prophylaxis can be

vaccinated at any time.

# Link to complete EUA documentation:

# Prioritization/eligibility of patients:

Minneapolis VAHCS is following the Minnesota Health Department's framework

for allocation of Evusheld. Our ID physicians shared in the development

of the document and allows for consistency with our local healthcare community.

[Click here Prioritization of patients \(See pages 7-8\)](orz-gtx-abx-evusheld-allocation)

# Nursing pre-screening questions prior to Evusheld administration:

-At least 2 weeks have passed since last dose of COVID-19 vaccine

(Note: COVID-19 vaccination is not required to receive Evusheld)

-No current symptoms consistent with COVID-19 or recent exposure (last 10 days)

-No hypersensitivity to any COVID-19 vaccines, polysorbate 80, or polyethylene

glycol (PEG)

-Nursing will provide hardcopy of Evusheld Patient/Caregiver Fact Sheet

to patient/caregiver prior to administration

# Evusheld administration notes:

Evusheld administered as 2 IM injections at one clinic visit, patient to

remain in clinic for 1 hour after administration, current redosing q6months

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# TRICHOMONAS VAGINITIS AND URETHRITIS

Male sexual partners of women with trichomonas vaginitis will not have symptoms

but should be treated to prevent recurrent vaginitis in the female sexual

partner.

Recommended to treat all sexual partners exposed during the last 60 days.

# Diagnosis

The discharge is purulent, malodorous, and thin. The vaginal pH is greater

than 4.5. Nucleic Acid amplification test (NAAT) for trichomonas has improved

sensitivities and specifities compared to wet mount.

# Treatment of Initial Episode WOMEN ONLY  (See below for MEN)

Pregnant women with trichomonas infection may be treated with metronidazole

during any trimester.

[Metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h for 7 days \($\) DI](psozid2-metroni-7ds-500mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-metroni-7ds-500mg-po-bid)

# Treatment of Initial Episode MEN ONLY  (See above for WOMEN)

[Metronidazole 2000 mg PO single dose DI](psozid2-metronidazole-2gram-po-single-dose-men-trichmonas)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-metronidazole-2gm-po-single-dose-male-trichomonas)

# Treatment failure

1st failure

[Metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h for 7 days \($\) DI](psozid2-metroni-7ds-500mg-po-bid)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-metroni-7ds-500mg-po-bid)

2nd failure

[Metronidazole 2000 mg PO q24h for 7 days \($\) DI](psozid2-metronidazole-7ds-2gm-po-qday)

[Non-VA order for above](pshzid2-metronidazole-7ds-2gm-po-qday)

3rd failure

Consult Infectious Disease

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU TYPHLITIS
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Opt\)](orzid3-gmenu-abx-general-information-outpatient)

# NEUTROPENIC ENTEROCOLITIS (TYPHLITIS)

[Oral step-down treatment](orzid3-gmenu-abx-step-down-treatment)

Neutropenic enterocolitis, also known as "typhlitis" or "necrotizing

enterocolitis", is a severe intraabdominal infection that occurs in neutropenic

patients, especially in those with acute leukemia.

Send stool for C. difficile testing to exclude of C. difficile infection.

[Information on C. difficile lab testing](orzid2-gmenu-abx-c-difficile-2-step-testing)

Hematology-oncology, Infectious Diseases and general surgery consults are

essential.

Broad spectrum antimicrobials that include anaerobic coverage should be

initiated promptly.

# Duration of antimicrobial therapy

Continue antimicrobial therapy until normalization of body temperature, recovery

of neutropenia (unless planning to transition back to antimicrobial

prophylaxis), recovery of thrombocytopenia, return of normal gastrointestinal

function and resolution of bacteremia if initially present. Infectious Disease

consult recommended to guide duration if perforation, abscess, or other

complicating feature present.

# Treatment

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:

# URETHRITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES

The main differential in a person who presents with dysuria is between cystitis

and urethritis. Bacterial urethritis is more likely in people with mild

dysuria, onset over a few days, or recent sexual contact.

The two most common sexually transmitted urethritis pathogens are Neisseria

gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Nucleic acid amplification tests for

these pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients

at risk for sexually transmitted urethritis.

[Chlamydia & GC PCR/LCR test](lrtzid-chlamydia-gc-urine-naat)

# For patients who have recently been treated for urethritis

[Treatment of recurrent or persistent urethritis](orzid3-gmenu-recurrent-persistent-urethritis)

# Initial treatment of patients and sex partners

Patients and partners are often infected with both N. gonorrhoeae and C.

trachomatis.

[Treatment for chlamydial or non-gonococcal urethritis](orzid3-gmenu-chlamydia-urethritis-cervicitis-proctitis)

menus.Name: ORZID3 GMENU UROLOGY CIPRO IN CLINIC
menus.Text:
# Urologic Clinic Procedures

In cases where prolonged catheterization follows a procedure, antimicrobial

therapy at the time of catheter removal may be considered, since

colonization has likely occurred. The recommendation to treat empirically

depends on host factors, the duration of catheterization, and the

potential of morbidity or mortality.

Single dose of fluoroquinolone may significantly lower incidence

of bacteriuria for patients undergoing ureteroscopy for stone removal.

[Ciprofloxacin 500 mg x1 orally \($0.10/day\) R,DI give in clinic and nurse text](orz-set-abx-urology-cipro-po-order-and-nurse-text-order)

# References

Best Practice Policy Statement on Urologic Surgery Antimicrobial Prophylaxis

(2008) (Reviewed and validity confirmed 2011, updated February 2012)

www.aua.org

# UVEITIS

Most cases are non-infectious. Most infectious cases are associated with a

pathogen causing systemic or central nervous system infection. Diagnosis of

uveitis usually must be made presumptively due to the technical difficulty of

sampling the uvea. Cases have been associated with fungi, bacteria, viruses, and

protozoa like Toxoplasma gondii.

# For treatment of posterior uveitis (retinitis) or acute retinal necrosis (ARN)

# Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

# Treatment of uveitis involves treating the underlying infection and is usually

# systemic. Refer to specific pathogen recommendations for treatment of underlyin

# infection. Contact Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases for assistance.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS BETWEEN ANTIMICROBIALS AND WARFARIN

Several antimicrobials will affect metabolism or the effect of

warfarin on a patient's clotting function. If possible, avoid using an

antimicrobial with a significant interaction with warfarin. If you

decide that an antimicrobial that interacts with warfarin is needed or

you stop an antimicrobial that could interact with warfarin, you

should determine the INR more frequently than usual and adjust dosage

accordingly. Instruct patients to inform their primary warfarin

provider whenever an antimicrobial is prescribed for them.

Antimicrobials can alter warfarin's anticoagulant effect by decreasing

intestinal synthesis or absorption of vitamin K or by affecting

distribution or metabolism of the vitamin. Some antimicrobials increase

synthesis of coagulation factors.

Antimicrobials can decrease the rate of warfarin absorption, compete

with warfarin at sites of warfarin metabolism, induce warfarin

metabolic enzymes, or inhibit the function or synthesis warfarin

metabolic enzymes. Some antimicrobials displace warfarin from protein

binding sites.

Check for warfarin-antimicrobial interactions on Lexicomp:

[Lexicomp Drug Interactions](orz-gtx-abx-lexicomp-interactions)

References

Holbrook, Anne M., et al. Archives of internal medicine 165.10 (2005): 1095-

1106

## Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) Symptomatic Therapy
Contact the CDSS Team
## Per CDC: Antibiotics Aren't Always the Answer. Be Antibiotics Aware.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses, such as colds and flu, or runny noses,
even if the mucus is thick, yellow or green. Antibiotics also won't help
some common bacterial infections including most cases of bronchitis, many
sinus infections, and some ear infections. When antibiotics aren't needed,
they won't help you, and the side effects could still hurt you. Reactions
from antibiotics cause 1 out of 5 medication-related visits to ED.

menus.Text:
## OTITIS EXTERNA
## Acute Localized Disease
Often due to furunculosis and usually associated with Staphylococcus aureus.
Treat mild cases with moist local heat. For cases with cellulitis or deep
invasion, incision and drainage as well as systemic antibiotics may be needed.
Refer to the Furuncles and Carbuncles page for antibiotic recommendations.
Furuncles and Carbuncles
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Acute diffuse and chronic otitis externa
Most commonly associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and
Staphylococcus epidermidis. Irrigate to remove cerumen, desquamated skin and
purulent material which can improve effectiveness of topical antibiotics. Avoid
products that contain neomycin if the tympanic membrane is perforated.
## Preferred treatment if tympanic membrane is intact
Neomycin-polymyxin-hydrocortisone ear drops 4 drops in affected ear(s) QID
for 7 days ($) [M]
## Alternative if tympanic membrane is perforated or allergy to preferred treatmen
Ciprofloxacin-Dexamethasone otic 4 drops in affected ear(s) BID for 7 days ($)
[M]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Complicated Cases
For cases resistant to topical therapy alone, patients with poorly controlled
diabetes mellitus, immunocompromised patients, cases where infection has spread
beyond ear canal and in those where topical therapy cannot be delivered
effectively. Culture secretions to guide therapy.
In addition to topical therapy above
< ADD > ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) [R,DI]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Mandell chapter: Otitis Externa, Otitis Media, and Mastoiditis
Rosenfeld et al., Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery. 2014, 150(2)161-168

menus.Name: pancreatitis
menus.Text:
## PANCREATITIS
Oral step-down treatment
Antimicrobials are not indicated for uncomplicated pancreatitis.
In cases of necrotizing pancreatitis without infection, antimicrobial
prophylaxis does not improve patient outcomes. Antimicrobials increase the risk
of fungal superinfection and should not be used.
Antimicrobials are indicated for cases with pancreatic abscess, infected
pancreatic pseudocyst, or infected necrotic pancreas (phlegmon). The diagnosis
of infection can be difficult and may require aspiration. Consultation with
Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Diseases is encouraged.
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Uncomplicated pancreatitis
No antimicrobials are indicated.
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic pseudocyst, or infected necrotic
## pancreas (phlegmon)
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Total duration of antimicrobial therapy is typically 2 to 4 weeks
## Treatment
Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 gm IV q6h [R]
< OR >
Meropenem 1 gm IV q8h [R,O]
Alternative:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Levofloxacin 500 mg IV q24h [R,DI] < AND > metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Mandell chapter: Pancreatic Infection
Sanford Guide article: Pancreatitis
Solomkin et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2010, 50:133-64
Up-to-Date article: Management of acute pancreatitis

## PARONYCHIA
Cutaneous infection of the hand, cuticle or fingers usually occurring near OR
around the nail.
Treatment depends on etiology. Candida spp. are commonly involved when the
patient has extensive exposure to water (e.g. dishwashers). Staphylococcus
aureus is more commonly after manicures or nail biting. Herpes simplex
(whitlow) usually follows exposure to oral mucosa (e.g. wrestlers, dentists, or
anesthetists).
## ________________________________________________________
## Treatment for paronychia associated with Candida
## ________________________________________________________
Treat for 14 days
Clotrimazole 1% apply to affected area once daily ($) [M]
## Alternative
Nystatin Cream to affected area BID ($) [M]
## ________________________________________________________
## Treatment for paronychia associated with Staphylococcus
## ________________________________________________________
Treat for 10 days
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO BID ($) [R,DI]
## Alternative
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID ($) [DI]
## ________________________________________________________
## Treatment for paronychia associated with Herpes whitlow
## ________________________________________________________

menus.Name: parotitis
menus.Text:
## PAROTITIS
Infection of salivary tissue is a relatively common disease. It is usually
caused by a stone in the parotid duct, dehydration, or a viral infection.
Sialolithiasis in elderly patients often leads to ductal obstruction and
secondary infection. Other predisposing factors for ductal occlusion include
dehydration, anticholinergic medications such as tricyclics and diphenhydramine,
general disability and trauma. Once culture results are available adjust
antimicrobial therapy based on specific etiologic organism.
For more information click on the link below
[More information on Parotitis](orzid2-gmenu-abx-parotitis-more-information)
## Duration of Therapy
Therapy duration varies based on clinical response to treatment and is typically
10-14 days.
## Suppurative Parotitis or Chronic Bacterial Parotitis Exacerbation Empiric
## Treatment
## Immunocompetent Patient
Preferred:
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) [M] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h ($) [DI]
< OR >
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) [M] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg PO q8h ($) [DI]
< OR >
Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 gm IV q6h ($) [R]
If MRSA suspected or alternative to above:
[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h ($) [DI]
< OR >
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg PO q8h ($) [DI]
## Immunocompromised Patient
<AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
## Viral Parotitis
Suspect mumps parotitis if there is fever, malaise, earache and bilateral tender
swelling of the parotid glands. For mumps parotitis treat with warm compresses
and analgesics and maintain good hydration to prevent secondary bacterial
infection. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Wilson et al., Am Fam Physician. 2014, 89(11)882-888
Mandell chapter:Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases

menus.Name: peri-assoc-w-peri-dial
menus.Text:
## PERITONITIS ASSOCIATED WITH PERITONEAL DIALYSIS
Peritonitis associated with peritoneal dialysis usually presents with abdominal
pain, fever, nausea or vomiting, and cloudy effluent. The leukocyte
concentration is greater than 100 cells/microliter of dialysate, with more than
50% neutrophils.
Obtain Gram stain, culture, and cell count with differential of dialysate before
antimicrobials are given. Nephrology consultation is essential. If cultures
show Gram-negative or mixed bacterial infection, a gastrointestinal tract
infectious source is more likely. Gram-positive organisms like staphylococci
usually result from external contamination. Fungal peritonitis is rare and
requires immediate catheter removal.
**Antimicrobial recommendations are for empirical therapy only. Regimens should
be tailored according to patient response and microbiology results in
consultation with Nephrology and/or Infectious Diseases for more information.
To prevent catheter occlusion by turbid dialysate, add 1,000 units of heparin
per dialysis bag each day until one day after the dialysate is clear.
If vancomycin is used, trough serum concentrations should be kept above 15
mcg/ml to ensure adequate intraperitoneal levels. Usually vancomycin must be
given every 3 to 7 days. Contact Nephrology and/or Pharmacy for more
information.
## Consult Nephrology in all cases.
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Antimicrobial therapy
## Duration
Duration of therapy depends on the pathogen identified. Treat staphylococcal and
streptococcal infections for 2 weeks and all other gram-positive infections for
3 weeks. In patients who have Staphylococcus isolated and had a previous
staphylococcal infection, treat for 3 weeks
## All antimicrobials below are administered via peritoneal dialysate bag over 6
## hours with the option to include heparin 1000 units.
## Empirical treatment while waiting for results of gram stain
[Cefepime 1 gm PD q24h ($$) [R]](orzid2-gmenu-pd-cefepime-1-gm-q24h)
<OR>
[Cefazolin 15 mg/kg ($) [R] <AND> gentamicin 0.6 mg/kg ($) [R,O] PD q24h](orzid2-gmenu-pd-cefazolin-15mg-kg-q24h-and-gent-0-6mg-kg-q24h)
MRSA risk factors
Vancomycin 30 mg/kg PD LD then 15 mg/kg PD every 3 to 7 days ($) [R] <AND>
cefepime 1 gm PD q24h ($) [R]
Alternative for severe penicillin or cephalosporin allergy
[Vancomycin 30 mg/kg PD LD then 15 mg/kg PD every 3 to 7 days ($) [R]](orzid2-gmenu-pd-vanco-15-30mg-kg-q5-7d) <AND>
gentamicin 0.6 mg/kg PD q24h ($) [R,O]

## PERIANAL/ANORECTAL ABSCESS
Antibiotics should typically be reserved for patients with an anorectal abscess
complicated by cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, underlying
immunosuppression, or failure to improve with drainage alone.
Cultures of abscess fluid are not routinely recommended. Consider in patients

## PERIODONTAL DISEASE
Periodontal disease, including gingivitis and periodontitis, may progress into
more severe disease or cause hematogenous spreading of bacteria if left
untreated. All patients with periodontal disease should be referred to the
dental service for assessment and direction of treatment. In the presence of
gingivitis, the most commonly isolated subgingival flora includes Prevotella
intermedia, Capnocytophaga spp, Finegoldia magna and Peptostreptococcus. In the
presence of periodontitis, flora increases in complexity to most commonly
include Porphyromonas gingivalis, P. intermedia, Aggregatibacter
actinomycetemcomitans, Tanneralla forsythensis and Treponema denticola.
## Consult Dental Service
## Non-severe periodontitis or acute simple gingivitis treatment
Chlorhexidine 0.12% oral rinse swish for 30 seconds, then spit 15 ml twice
daily for 7 days ($) [M]

## PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE (PID)
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) refers to bacterial infection of the upper
female reproductive tract. Likely bacterial pathogens include Neisseria
gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, anaerobes, enteric Gram-negative rods, and
Streptococcus agalactiae. PID should be considered in sexually active women
with pelvic tenderness and signs of lower genital tract inflammation. Signs and
symptoms may be mild or non-specific, and providers should have a low threshold
to initiate treatment. All women who are diagnosed with acute PID should be
tested for N. gonorrohoeae, C. trachomatis, and HIV. Male sex partners of
patients with PID should be examined and treated (see below) if they had sexual
contact within the 60 days before onset of the patient's symptoms.
Judge severity of infection based on clinical signs and symptoms, including
blood pressure, pulse, mental status, and degree of fever.

days ($) [DI]

menus.Name: pneumocystis-jirovecii
menus.Text:
## PNEUMOCYSTIS JIROVECII DISEASE
Diagnosis and treatment are complex, consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.
Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly termed Pneumocystis carinii) in an ubiquitious
organism that causes disease in people with compromised cell-mediated immunity.
Disease is exceedingly rare in people with intact host defenses. Pneumonia is
the usual manifestation but P. jirovecii can infect extrapulmonary sites,
especially in patients who have been receiving prophylaxis with aerosolized
pentanmidine. P. jirovecii disease occurs most commonly in people with AIDS and
fewer than 200 CD4 T lymphocytes/microliter.
The abbreviation PCP is often used for Pneumocystis pneumonia. It was derived
from the old species name, Pneumocystis carinii.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) is the treatment of choice for P.
jirovecii disease, including disease that occurs despite TMP-SMZ prophylaxis.
Corticosteriods should be prescribed for patients with AIDS and P. jirovecii
pneumonia and an arterial oxygen tension <70 torr or an alveolar-arterial oxygen
gradient of >35 torr.
LINK to Prophylaxis for Pneumocystis Jirovecii
## Preferred treatment for mild to moderate disease or step-down treatment once
## disease has stabilized
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 2 DS tablets PO q8h for 21 days ($)[R,DI]
< OR >

PO QDay ($)[DI] for 21 days
Alternative

for 21 days
< OR >
Atovaquone 750mg PO BID for 21 days ($)[M]
## Preferred treatment for severe disease

($$)[R,DI]
Alternative

for 21 days
< OR >
Requires ID Approval: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV q24h ($$$)[DI]
## Prednisone for patient WITH AIDS
Prednisone 40mg PO twice daily for 5 days, then 40mg PO daily for 6 days,
then 20 mg daily for 10 days.

menus.Name: pneumocystis-jirovecii-prophylaxis
menus.Text:
## PNEUMOCYSTIS JIROVECII PROPHYLAXIS (PCP Prophylaxis)

Indications for primary prophylaxis of P. jirovecii include:
1) HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 count <200 cells/microliter
2) Hematopoietic or organ transplantation patients during immunosuppression
3) Patients receiving Alemtuzumab, temozolomide or fludarabine
4) Patients receiving >/= 20mg equivalent of prednisone per day for over 1 month
5) Patients with acute lymphocytic leukemia, rheumatologic disease receiving
immunosuppressive therapy and certain primary immunodeficiencies (e.g. severe
combined immunodeficiency, idiopathic CD4 T-lymphocytopenia, hyper-IgM
syndrome)
Dose and duration of prophylaxis varies with the indication. Please contact
Infectious Diseases or Hematology/Oncology for more information.
Prophylaxis should be discontinued when host defenses are restored. In persons
with AIDS on highly active antiretroviral therapy, Prophylaxis should be
discontinued when the CD4 cell concentrations remain over 200 cells/microliter
for 3 to 6 months in patients, except that prophylaxis should be continued for
life in those who have had P. jirovecii disease.

## Recommended FIRST-LINE prophylaxis:

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet q day ($) [R,DI]
< OR >
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 SS tablet q day ($) [R,DI]

## Alternative when trimethoprim/sulfa is poorly tolerated or contraindicated:

\*\*Patient should be tested for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6-PD)
deficiency before starting dapsone. Individuals deficient in G6-PD
show about a 2-fold increase in sensitivity toward dapsone-induced hemolytic
anemia.
G6-PD lab test are resulted the same day or next day. May be add on lab.
G6-PD lab result should be "normal" to start dapsone therapy.

Dapsone 100mg PO q day ($) [DI]

(e.g. patients with SLE, hematologic concerns, G6PD deficiency)

menus.Name: positive-blood-culture-coag-neg-staph
menus.Term1: POSITIVE BLOOD CULTURE COAG NEG STAPH
menus.Text:
Inpatient/ Outpatient ## BLOOD CULTURE POSITIVE FOR COAGULASE NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CNS)
CNS are the most common contaminants isolated from blood cultures. When CNS
isolated from blood cultures represent true bacteremia, the blood is usually
obtained from a patient with plastic or metal in the body. The most common
source of coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia is an infected
intravascular catheter.
When CNS are isolated from blood, the physician should carefully assess the
patient to decide whether the isolation represents disease or colonization.
Colonization is more likely if a single bottle is positive or both bottles from
a single blood draw are positive. If multiple bottles are positive from separate
blood draws, it is more likely that the isolates reflect disease or colonization
of an intravascular device. Isolates from contaminated bottles often take
several days to become positive. If the patient has risk factors for true
coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia, catheter-related blood stream
infection and/or the patient is severely ill, antimicrobials should be given
(see below). If there is a plastic or metal prosthesis in the body, the
physician should evaluate the site for possible infection. If the isolates are
likely to represent contamination and the patient does not seem ill with CNS,
antimicrobial therapy would not be helpful and should not be given.
[Treatment of CNS Bacteremia](orzid2-gmenu-bacteremia-coag-neg-staph)
Treatment of CNS Infected Intravascular Catheters
References
Mandell chapter: Staphylococcus epidermis and Other Coagulase-Negative
Staphylococci
Mermel et al, Clin Infect Dis, 2009, 49

menus.Text:
## POSTSEPTAL CELLULITIS (ORBITAL CELLULITIS)
Postseptal cellulitis (orbital cellulitis) is often preceded by sinusitis and
requires immediate consultation with otolaryngology and ophthalmology. Urgent
surgical drainage may be necessary. The most common pathogenic organisms in
adults are streptococci, Haemophilus influenzae, anaerobes, and Staphylococcus
aureus. Broad-spectrum empirical antimicrobials should be used until a pathogen
can be identified from the drainage fluid.
## Duration of treatment
Orbital cellulitis should be treated until all signs of infection have resolved.
Uncomplicated orbital cellulitis should be treated for minimum of 2 weeks and
complicated orbital cellulitis (severe ethmoid sinusitis and bony destruction of
sinus) should be treated for at least 4 weeks.
## Empiric treatment
Preferred:
<AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
Alternative:
[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) [M] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h ($) [DI]
<AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
## Step-down treatment after initial intravenous therapy. Base selection on cultur
## results. Adjust duration based on criteria above.
Preferred:
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID ($) [R] < AND >
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 2 DS PO BID ($) [R,DI] for 7 days
Alternative:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Cefdinir 300 mg PO q12h ($) [R] < AND > trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 2 DS PO
q12h ($) [R,DI] for 7 days

## PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS
Preseptal cellulitis involves soft tissues in front of the orbital septum and
the eyelids and is often preceded by sinusitis. Infection does not involve the
orbital contents. The most common pathogenic organisms in adults are
streptococci, Haemophilus influenzae, anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus.
Treat under the guidance of ophthalmology and/or otolaryngology. Intravenous
antimicrobials are indicated initially for treatment of moderate to severe
disease. Switch to oral antimicrobials when the patient's symptoms improve and
the patient can tolerate oral medications.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is often given to patients likely to have profound,
prolonged neutropenia. Profound neutropenia is less than 100 neutrophils and
bands per microliter, and such neutropenia is considered prolonged when it is
expected to last more than 7 days. Most patients who should receive prophylaxis
have received stem cell transplants or are undergoing induction chemotherapy for
acute leukemia.

## PREVENTION OF FUNGAL INFECTIONS IN A PATIENT WITH MALIGNANCY
Antifungal chemoprophylaxis is often given to patients undergoing induction
chemotherapy for acute leukemia expected to have profound neutropenia (less than
100 neutrophils and bands per milliliter) for more than 10 days and for patients
receiving allogeneic stem cell transplantation. For most other patients the
expected benefits do not outweigh the risks of adverse effects and selection of
resistant fungi.
Antifungal is usually given until the absolute neutrophil concentration
increases to more than 500 cells/microliter in patients undergoing induction
chemotherapy for leukemia. Duration is 100 days for patients undergoing stem
cell transplantation. Some physicians continue prevention after 100 days if
corticosteroids are part of the immunosuppressive regimen.
Recommend posaconazole prophylaxis for patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
Contact Hematology Oncology or Infectious Disease for more information.
Patients who have had invasive fungal infection in the recent past and who are
about to become neutropenic may require chemoprophylaxis. Contact Hematology-
Oncology or Infectious Disease for more information.
## If antifungal prophylaxis is indicated:
Duration of therapy: during period of expected neutropenia
Fluconazole 400 mg po q24h ($) [R,DI]

Requires Infectious Disease approval:
Posaconazole 300mg Tablets twice daily on day 1, then 300mg once daily on
day 2 and thereafter. Continue for 7 days after the neutrophil count
rises above 500/mm3. ($$$$) [DI]

menus.Name: prev-of-bact-endocarditis
menus.Text:
## PREVENTION OF BACTERIAL ENDOCARDITIS
Bacteremia occurs several times a day during daily activities like eating and
brushing teeth and rarely results in endocarditis, even in people with abnormal
valves. While bacteremia might occur following dental or other procedures, most
cases of endocarditis are from the millions more episodes of transient
bacteremia a person experiences per year from ordinary daily activities. There
is no evidence that antimicrobial prophylaxis prevents endocarditis after
procedures. The best available evidence suggests that prophylactic
antimicrobials confer more risks than benefits in most situations. A decision
about whether to administer antimicrobial prophylaxis should be based on both
the risk of endocarditis conferred by the patient's cardiac defect and the risk
of bacteremia from a planned dental or surgical procedure.
## Minneapolis VAHCS SOP antimicrobial prophylaxis for dental surgery:
SOP for dental surgery antimicrobial prophylaxis
## Determine the need for prophylaxis through the 2-step process outlined
## below.
## Step 1. Assess the risk of endocarditis for your patient
Prophylaxis is recommended if a patient has any of the following conditions:
o Prosthetic cardiac valve or material including: Presence of cardiac
prosthetic valve, transcatheter implantation of prosthetic valves (e.g. TAVR
cardiac valve repair with devices (e.g. annuloplasty, rings, or clips), left
ventricular assist devices or implantable heart
o A history of infective endocarditis
o Certain specific congenital heart conditions - refer to the full SOP
(link above) or consult Cardiology for more detailed recommendations
o Cardiac transplant that develops a problem in the heart valve
## Step 2. Assess the risk of bacteremia from the planned procedure
Prophylaxis is indicated for these procedures:
o All dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the
periapical region of teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa.
o Procedures on the respiratory tract that involve incision or biopsy of the
respiratory mucosa, such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy. Prophylaxis is
recommended for bronchoscopy when procedure involves incision of the respir.
tract mucosa.
o Procedures that involve incision through infected skin, skin structures, or
musculoskeletal tissue.
o Dermatologic procedures that breach the oral mucosa.
## Prophylactic Antimicrobials select below:
Patients undergoing dental or oral mucosa procedures

menus.Text:
## PREVENTION OF PERTUSSIS
## Immunization
Give a single dose of tetanus-diphtheria acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap) in
adults regardless of interval between most recent Td vaccine. One dose of Tdap
vaccine is given to pregnant women during each pregnancy.
## Postexposure prophylaxis in adults
Household contacts with symptomatic coughing should be treated as if they have
pertussis. Consult Infectious Diseases for all suspected cases of pertussis and
exposure to pertussis.
CDC recommends postexposure prophylaxis in household contacts within 21 days
after exposure to pertussis regardless of immunization history. Non-household
contacts who are at high risk of severe illness or who have close contact with
high-risk individuals should receive post exposure prophylaxis within 21 days of
exposure. Those at high risk of severe illness are infants less than one year of
age, women in third trimester of pregnancy and those with preexisting health
conditions that may be exacerbated by pertussis (e.g. immunosuppressed and
asthmatic individuals).
A single dose of Tdap should be administered in those who are not up to date.
Preferred:
Azithromycin 500mg po day 1, then 250mg q24h for days 2-5 [O]
Alternative for macrolide intolerant or allergic patients:
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet PO q12h [R,DI] for 7 days

## PUBIC LICE (PEDICULOSIS PUBIS)
Lice are parasitic insects. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood.
To make a diagnosis, use a nit comb, bright light, or lens to find a louse
living in pubic hair.
The presence of nits on a hair shaft, especially when they are located more
than 6 mm from the skin, does NOT indicate active infestation. Nits may remain
present for months after successful treatment.
Household contacts and persons who may have come into contact with personal
belongings of an infested individual should be examined for evidence of lice
and discarded or cleaned if contaminated.
## Treatment
A repeat application may be used if live lice are seen 7-10 days after
treatment.
Permethrin 1% lotion. Apply to affected area for 10 minutes then comb out
nits ($) [M]
References
Sanford keyword: lice
Up-to-date website

menus.Name: react-prim-infect-zoster
menus.Text:
## REACTIVATION OF PRIMARY INFECTION (ZOSTER OR SHINGLES)
Zoster represents reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. After primary
infection, virus remains latent in the sensory dorsal root ganglia.
Reactivation syndrome is characterized by painful, unilateral, vesicular,
dermatomal rash.
## Prevention
Vaccinate all adults greater than or equal to 50 years of age with the
recombinant zoster vaccine regardless of past episode or receipt of the live
zoster vaccine.
Give recombinant zoster vaccine x2, 2nd dose 2-6 months after the first
## ________________________________
## Immunocompetent patients
## ________________________________
## Treatment in persons <50 years
Treatment is not beneficial, none is recommended.
## Treatment in persons >=50 years
Treatment with antivirals can shorten duration of pain and rash in patients over
50 years old. Treatment must be started within 72 hours of onset.
Valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h for 7 days ($) [R]
There is evidence that addition of corticosteroids to antiviral
therapy decreases pain and duration of rash and improves quality of life
modestly during the acute shingles episode. Corticosteroids do not decrease the
incidence of post-herpetic neuralgia. Some authorities recommend addition of
corticosteroid therapy to antiviral therapy for patients over age 50 years.
Corticosteroids are not recommended for patients at greater risk for steroid
toxicities (e.g., insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peptic
ulcer disease) or for immunocompromised patients.
Optional Recommendation:
Prednisone 60 mg daily for 7 days then 30 mg daily for 7 days, then 15 mg
daily for 7 days. ($)
## ________________________________
## Immunocompromised patients
## ________________________________
## Treatment
Immunocompromised patients at increased risk for complications of VZV disease
include: patients with malignancy, current immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV
infection. Treatment with antivirals shortens duration of symptoms and reduces
incidence of complications. In immunocompromised patients, treatment is
recommended to be started at any point during an active infection.
## Treatment for mild to moderate disease
Valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h for 7 days ($) [R]
## Treatment for severe disease or progression from mild to moderate disease in
## patients <=65 years
Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h for 7-14 days ($$) [R]
## Treatment for severe disease or progression from mild to moderate disease in
## patients >65 years
Acyclovir 7.5 mg/kg IV q8h for 7-14 days($$) [R]
References:
Kim et al. Annals Intern Med. 2018, 168(3):210-220
Sanford keyword: Varicella-Zoster Virus
Mandell chapter: Chickenpox and Herpes Zoster (Varicella-Zoster Virus)

## Outpatient

Guidance
## Treatment in persons >=50 years
Valacyclovir 1000 mg PO TID for 7 days ($) [R]

menus.Name: retinitis
menus.Text:
## RETINITIS AND ACUTE RETINAL NECROSIS
Retinitis is a subset of uveitis, is rare in immunocompetent people: in these
individuals it is usually caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV) or herpes
simplex virus (HSV). Retinitis is more common in immunocompromised patients and
cytomegalovirus being the most common pathogen in these patients. Other
retinitis pathogens include Toxoplasma gondii, Bartonella henselae, Histoplasma
capsulatum, and Treponema pallidum. In most cases, patients have other
neurological symptoms or signs. Patients with candidemia may present with 1-3
mm white punctate retinal lesions called cotton-wool spots. These may only be
visible on fundus examination. Treatment of candidal retinitis is systemic
antifungal therapy. Consult Ophthalmology, Infectious Diseases, or Neurology for
help.
VZV and HSV cause nearly all cases of acute retinal necrosis (ARN), with a small
number being caused by cytomegalovirus. ARN is a rapidly progressing retinitis
that occurs primarily in immunocompetent people and can cause vision loss.
Treatment with intravenous acyclovir or valacyclovir is essential to halt
progression of ARN.
Ophthalmology and Infectious Diseases consultation is essential
## Treatment of Non-viral Retinitis or ARN
Refer to specific pathogen treatment recommendations of the CDSS to treat
underlying infection
## Treatment of Retinitis or ARN due to CMV:
Link to Treatment of CMV Retinitis and ARN
## Treatment of VZV Retinitis
Acyclovir 800 mg PO 5x/d for 5-7 days ($) [R]
< OR >
Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h for 7 days ($$) [R]
Alternative
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q8h for 5 days ($) [R]
## Treatment of HSV Retinitis
Acyclovir 400 mg PO q8h for 7-10 days ($) [R]
< OR >
Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV q8h ($$) [R]
Alternative
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q12h for 7-10 days ($) [R]
## Treatment of VZV and HSV Acute Retinal Necrosis
Ophthalmologist involvement is essential for treatment including
corticosteroids, vitrectomy, or laser therapy. Intravitreal foscarnet in
addition to a systemic antiviral may provide added therapeutic efficacy.
Duration
Treat with intravenous therapy for a minimum of 7 days until disease has
stabilized then treat with or therapy for a minimum of 6 weeks
Treatment
Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h for 7 days ($) [R]
< Optional add-on therapy > Foscarnet 2.4mg/0.1 mL intravitreal injection STAT
($$$$) [R,O]
< THEN >
Valacyclovir 1 gm PO q8h for 42 days ($) [R]
## _______________________________________________________________________________

Lau et al, Ophthalmology. 2007, 114(4)756-762

## SCABIES
Scabies is an infestation of the skin by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei.
It is transmitted by skin to skin contact. Outbreaks occur in nursing
homes, day care centers, and residential institutions. Scabies is highly
contagious and meticulous infection control is needed.
Treatment is a single application of permethrin cream. Some experts recommend a
second application 7-10 days after the first application if the patient is still
symptomatic or if live mites are found at that time. Contact Dermatology or
Infectious Diseases for more information.
Treat family members and other close contacts to prevent spread and recurrence.
## Treatment
Repeat application 7-10 days after the first application if patient is still
experiencing symptoms, or if lives mites are found.
Permethrin 5% cream apply from head to feet, leave on for 8-14 hours, then
wash cream off with soap and water ($) [M]
References

Complicated Intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) include any infectious process
that extends from an intra-abdominal organ into a sterile space and is
associated with peritonitis with or without abscess.
Community-acquired cIAI: patients without recent procedure related to site of
perforation or abscess
Healthcare-associated cIAI: patients developing a new infection > 48 hours after
an incident intra-abdominal procedure
## Primary therapy: abscess drainage
CT or US-guided percutaneous or surgical drainage should be considered in all
cases for diagnostic confirmation, microbiologic evaluation, and therapy.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Adequate source control: 4 days after source control
Incomplete source control and no abscess: 5-7 days tailored to improvement.
Re-evaluate need for source control if ongoing signs/symptoms of infection
beyond 7 days
Abscess: 2-6 weeks depending on resolution on repeat imaging. ID Consult
recommended.
## Community-acquired infection without severe illness or immunosuppression
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h for 5 days [M] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
Alternative:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h [R,DI] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
## Healthcare-associated infection, severe illness, or immunosuppression
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h [R]
Alternative:
Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
Alternative for severe beta-lactam reaction:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q8h [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
Consider vancomycin for enterococcal coverage in critically ill or
immunosuppressed patients:
<ADD> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h [R] to one of the regimens above

## SECOND RECURRENCE OF CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)
Discontinue implicated antibiotic(s). Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic
therapy is still needed. Avoid antiperistaltic agents (narcotics, loperamide,
etc.). Avoid antacid therapy without clear indication. If diarrhea has improved
or resolved prior to starting C. difficile treatment, consider re-assessing the
diagnosis before initiating therapy. C. difficile infection usually responds to
antimicrobial therapy. If symptoms do not respond to appropriate antimicrobial
therapy, re-consider the diagnosis.
## Second Recurrence CDI:
Vancomycin Extended Pulse-Taper Regimen [M]
(Vancomycin 125 mg PO q6h for 10 days, then taper and pulse with 125 mg po q12h
for 7 days, then 125mg po qday for 7 days, then 125mg every other day for 6
weeks)
< OR >
If fidaxomicin not previously used:
Fidaxomicin 200 mg po q12h for 10 days [M]
< OR>
If fidaxomicin extended-pulse regimen not previously used:
Fidaxomicin Extended-Pulse Regimen [M]
(Fidaxomicin 200mg po bid x5days,then 200mg every other day x20days)
## Third or more recurrence: Consult Gastroenterology or Infectious Disease

menus.Name: sepsis-and-shock
menus.Text:
## SEPSIS AND SEPTIC SHOCK
Per the Sepsis-3 task force, sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ
dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection.
Septic shock is a subset of sepsis in which profound circulatory, cellular, and
metabolic abnormalities occur. Septic shock requires vasopressor therapy and is
associated with in-hospital mortality greater than 40%.
Early intervention is crucial to prevention of death from sepsis. Antimicrobials
active against likely pathogens, based on source infection, and supportive
treatment to maintain vascular perfusion should be initiated immediately (within
the first hour of patient presentation). Reassess antimicrobial therapy daily to
narrow therapeutic spectrum when culture and susceptibility data are available.
## Sepsis/septic shock management bundles based on patient location (includes
## empiric antimicrobial treatment)
Intensive Care Unit (ICU)
Hospital ward

menus.Name: severe-sinusitis
menus.Text:
## SEVERE SINUSITIS
Community-acquired bacterial sinusitis is most often due to Streptococcus
pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza or Moraxella catarrhalis. Group A
Streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes are isolated less frequently.
For patients who present with severe symptoms (high fever (>/= 102 degrees
Fahrenheit, >/= 39 degrees Celsius) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4
consecutive days or facial pain lasting for at least 3-4 consecutive days at the
beginning of illness), initiate empiric antimicrobials and obtain CT of sinuses
to determine the extent of infection. If the CT shows extension of sinusitis
infection into surrounding structures (i.e. the cranium or orbit) consult ENT
immediately. Closely monitor all patients who present with severe signs and
symptoms to ensure that signs and symptoms improve within 72 hours.
## Outpatient

Treatment
Preferred:
Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h ($) [R] for 7 days
Alternatives:
[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)
Cefdinir 300 mg PO q12h ($) [R] for 7 days
< OR >
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID ($) [DI] for 7 days
## Treatment of hospitalized patient
Preferred:
Ampicillin-sulbactam 3gm IV q6h ($) [R] for 7 days
Alternative:
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h ($) [M] for 7 days
## Treatment failure
If symptoms worsen or no improvement is seen after 3-5 days of treatment,
broaden coverage, switch to different antimicrobial class and treat 10 days. If
symptoms continue to worsen or there is no improvement after 3-5 more days of
treatment, obtain CT to investigate non-infectious or suppurative causes. ENT
consultation is recommended. If sinuses are aspirated, specimens should be
cultured.
Preferred
for 7 days

## Daily Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Asplenia
The need for daily antibiotic prophylaxis and its duration is typically
determined individually based on patient age, immune status, history of
infection, potential for adverse drug reactions and other factors.
## Consider Prophylaxis:
1) Approximately 1 year prophylaxis for all patients following splenectomy.
2) Lifelong prophylaxis for patients with history of sepsis or other severe
infections caused by encapsulated organisms.
3) Prophylaxis for as long as the patient is immunocompromised or for life
for patients with concurrent immunocompromising conditions (e.g. hematologic
malignancy, hypogammaglobulinemia, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver
disease, or HIV infection).

## Asplenia Functional or Anatomical
Following a splenectomy there is considerably increased risk of developing
septicemia from invasive encapsulated organisms, namely Streptococcus pneumonia,
Haemophilus inluenza type b and meningococcus. Key measures to prevent
such infections include education, vaccination, prophylactic antimicrobial
therapy in selected patients, and early empirical therapy for febrile
epsisodes. It is critically important to educate patients regarding the
lifelong risk of postsplenectomy sepsis, the importance of vaccinations,
and the need for urgent action in response to a febrile episode.
## Inpatient

## [Management of an Episode of Fever in an Asplenic Patient](orzid2-gmenu-abx-management-of-febrile-episode-asplenia)

elective splenectomy. Where this is not possible they can be given up to
two weeks before or at least two weeks post-splenectomy.

SBP is infection of the peritoneal cavity in the absence of apparent trauma or
other obvious cause. SBP occurs primarily in people with end-stage liver disease
and ascites. The diagnosis is made when a peritoneal fluid sample has >/= 250
polymorphonuclear leukocyte cells per microliter, or when bacterial pathogens
are isolated.
Long-term SBP prophylaxis is indicated for patients who experience a first
episode of SBP.

## SPOROTRICHOSIS
Sporotrichosis occurs most often in people who have had significant outdoor
exposure to soil. In immunocompetent people, disease is usually limited to the
skin. In people with decreased host defenses (eg, HIV/AIDS, alcoholism,
diabetes mellitus, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) sporotrichosis
often disseminates to bones, joints, or lungs. Consult Infectious Diseases or
Dermatology
## ____________________________________________________________________________
## Cutaneous infection in a patient without HIV infection
## ____________________________________________________________________________
Itraconazole 200 mg PO q12h continue for 2-4 weeks after all lesions
resolved, usually for a total of 3-6 months ($) [DI]
## Alternative
Consult Dermatology or Infectious Diseases.
## ____________________________________________________________________________
## Extracutaneous infection or any infection in a patient with HIV/AIDS
## ____________________________________________________________________________
Consult Dermatology or Infectious Diseases.

Kaufman CA Clin Infect Dis 2000, 30: 684

menus.Name: ssti-purulent-infections
menus.Text:
## PURULENT SKIN/SOFT TISSUE INFECTIONS
Includes furuncles/boils, carbuncles and cutaneous abscesses with or without
surrounding inflammation. The predominant pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus
(MSSA or MRSA).
Incision and drainage are recommended whenever feasible. Adjunctive antibiotics
are typically recommended. Incision and drainage alone are reasonable based on
patient preferences when abscess is smaller, limited surrounding inflammation,
no systemic signs of infections, and/or limited comorbidities.
## For recurrent skin abscesses in addition to culture and antibiotic therapy
## recommend considering a decolonization regimen.
[for Staphylococcus aureus Decolonization](orzid2-gmenu-abx-staphylococcus-aureus-decolonization)
## Preferred oral therapy:
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 DS tablet BID for 5 days [R,DI]
< OR >
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 5 days [DI]
## Preferred IV therapy:
Vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q 12 hours [R]
## Alternative:
Reserve for contraindication, precaution, failure to preferred options, or for
patient where parenteral antibiotics would be otherwise be selected.
Linezolid 600 mg PO BID for 5 days [DI,O]
## _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Name: staph-scalded-syndrome
menus.Text:
## STAPHYLOCOCCAL SCALDED SKIN SYNDROME (RITTER'S DISEASE)
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) presents with severe skin
blistering and exfoliation resulting from toxins produced by Staphylococcus
aureus. SSSS is usually found in children and rarely in older adults. Obtain
a skin biopsy to differentiate between SSSS and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Initiate anti-staphylococcal therapy and obtain cultures and susceptibilities.
Empiric therapy active against both MRSA and MSSA until results available.
If cultures reveal methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), change
to nafcillin or cefazolin for better antimicrobial activity.
## Empirical treatment
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
## Treatment if MSSA is isolated
Nafcillin 2 gm IV q4h ($$) [DI]
< OR >

## PLASTIC SURGERY
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for most clean procedures in
patients without additional postoperative infection risk factors.
Risk factors that increase the risk of postoperative infectious complications
for plastic surgery procedures include implants, skin irradiation before the
procedure, and procedures below the waist.
Antimicrobial prophylaxis is recommended for clean-contaminated procedures,
breast cancer procedures, and clean procedures with risk factors. A single
preoperative dose is recommended.

menus.Name: tinea-capitis-ringworm
menus.Text:
## TINEA CAPITIS (RINGWORM)
Tinea capitis is a common fungal infection of the scalp and hair. It is
characterized by itchy, red, raised, scaly patches often sharply defined. Redder
margins than centers create impression of ring. Tinea capitis primarily affects
prepubescent children but can affect people of any age.
Baseline liver function test monitoring recommended. Repeat LFTs if treating for
longer than 6 weeks and there were baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver
disease, or other risks for hepatotoxicity.
## Treatment:
Treat for 4 weeks.
Terbinafine 250 mg PO QDAY [R,H,DI,O]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Up-to-date website
Sanford keyword: Tinea Capitis, Ringworm

menus.Name: tinea-pedis-athlete-s-foot
menus.Text:
## TINEA PEDIS (ATHLETE'S FOOT), TINEA CORPORIS, TINEA MANUUM, OR TINEA CRURIS
Dermatophyte fungal infections are common worldwide. Dermatophytes metabolize
and subsist upon keratin in the skin, hair, and nails. Most tinea infections can
often be cured with topical therapy alone. Systemic therapy is reserved for
severe or refractory infection, recurrent infection, or in immunocompromised
patients.
Treatment should continue for at least one week after clinical curing of
infection.
## Treatment
Terbinafine 1% cream apply to affected area BID x 2-4 weeks [M]
## Alternative
Clotrimazole 1% cream apply to affected area BID x 4 weeks [M]
## Systemic treatment
Fluconazole 150 mg q week x 2-4 weeks [R,DI]
< OR >
Terbinafine 250 mg PO QDAY x 2 weeks [R,H,DI,O]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
References:
Up-to-date website
Sanford keyword: Tinea Corporis, Cruris, Pedis
Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2007 Jul 18:2007(3):CD001434
Am Fam Physician. 2002 May 15:65(10):2095

menus.Name: tinea-unguium-onychomycosis
menus.Text:
## TINEA UNGUIUM (ONYCHOMYCOSIS)
Obtain a fungal stain of nail sample prior to initiating treatment. Using large
nail clippers, remove as much of the unattached dystrophic nail as possible.
Place the piece of clipped nail plate in formalin jar and send to pathology for
fungal stain (PAS). Treatment should only be initiated if stain is positive for
fungal elements. Fungal culture is NOT recommended.
Systemic therapy is most likely to achieve a cure, especially with more nail
involvement. If <25% involvement topical therapy may be considered. If >50-75%
involvement systemic therapy should be considered.
Toenails take 12-18 months to grow out completely, so improvement should not be
expected to be observed for at least 6-9 months. Continued improvement can be
experienced following treatment completion.
## Oral Treatment:
Terbinafine works about 70% of the time to cure the fungus, and reinfection is
common, so many patients will need to do more than one course of treatment.
Fluconazole pulse dosing response rate is approximately 50%. May consider
retreatment with oral therapy after one year.
Recommend Dermatology Consult for retreatment after failure of 2 courses of
terbinafine or fluconazole.
## Preferred Terbinafine first-line oral:
Toenail infections treat for 12 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to
starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were
baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for
hepatotoxicity.
[Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 12 weeks (R,H,DI,O]](psjzid-terbinafine-250mg-po-qday)
Fingernail infections treat for 6 weeks. Obtain baseline liver enzymes prior to
starting. Repeat LFTs if treating for longer than 6 weeks and there were
baseline abnormalities, pre-existing liver disease, or other risks for
hepatotoxicity.
Terbinafine 250 mg PO qday for 6 weeks [R,H,DI,O]
## Alternative oral therapy:
Toenail infections treat for at least 6 months
Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for total of 6 months [R,DI]
Fingernail infections treat for 3 months
Fluconazole 300 mg PO q week for 3 months [R,DI]
## Topical Treatment:
Ciclopirox is a topical first-line treatment for both fingernails and toenails.
Complete resolution occurs in approximately 7 percent of patients treated daily
for 48 weeks. Ciclopirox is a well-tolerated treatment. Potential side effects
include temporary nail changes and local skin irritation.
Ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer: Apply once daily to affected nail(s)
Remove with rubbing alcohol every 7 days. [M] See accompanying medication
pamphlet for specific instructions. Treatment is continued until nail clearance
or up to 48 weeks.

menus.Name: tinea-versicolor
menus.Text:
## TINEA VERSICOLOR
Topical antifungals can be used for limited disease. For disease that involves
nails or does not respond to topical therapy, use oral antifungals.
Return of normal skin color often takes several weeks after the treatment course
is finished.
## Treatment limited disease:
Ketoconazole 2% shampoo apply to the affected area QDAY for 3 days. Apply to
damp skin, lather, leave on 5 minutes, and rinse.
< OR >
Ketoconazole 2% cream to affected area QDAY for 14 days [M]
< OR >
Terbinafine 1% cream apply to affected area QDAY for 7 days [M]
< OR >
Selenium sulfide lotion 2.5% apply to affected area, leave on for 10 minutes,
then rinse/shower thoroughly QDAY for 7 days [M]
## Treatment extensive disease:
Fluconazole 300 MG PO weekly for 2 weeks [R]

menus.Name: toxic-megacolon
menus.Text:
## FULMINANT CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE INFECTION (CDI)
## Discontinue any antibiotics if possible.
## Narrow antibiotic spectrum if antibiotic therapy is still needed.
## Discontinue antacid therapy if possible.
## There are no available data supporting the use of fidaxomicin for treatment of
## fulminant CDI.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Antimicrobial therapy for CDI should be continued for 10 days. In patients being
treated with antibiotics for predisposing infections, consider continuing
treatment for 7 days after completion of those antibiotics. If patient is being
treated for CDI recurrence, pulse taper therapy is indicated after resolution of
severe disease. Refer to mild to moderate CDI treatment menu for
recommendations.
## Inpatient

## Treatment if ileus is present
General Surgery consult is essential for ileus or megacolon. Recommend
Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Disease consults for fulminant CDI. Deliver
antimicrobials by intravenous, oral, and rectal routes.
Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI] <AND> vancomycin 500 mg PO q6h [M]
<AND> vancomycin enema 500 mg in 100 ml normal saline q6h [M]
**ONLY for Vancomycin NG administration**
Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI] <AND> vancomycin 500 mg NG soln q6h [M]
<AND> vancomycin enema 500 mg in 100 ml normal saline q6h [M]

Gastroenterology and/or Infectious Diseases consults are recommended.
Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI] <AND> vancomycin 500 mg PO q6h [M]
**ONLY for Vancomycin NG administration**

menus.Name: toxic-shock-syndrome
menus.Text:
## TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) can be associated with either staphylococci or
streptococci. Antimicrobial treatment and supportive care is urgent. Click one
of the links below for diagnostic criteria.
[Link to Diagnosis of Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome](orzid2-gmenu-strep-toxic-shock-syndrome)
[Link to Diagnosis of Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome](orzid2-gmenu-staph-toxic-shock-syndrome)
## _________________________________________________
## Treatment of Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome
## _________________________________________________
## Preferred treatment
Penicillin 4 million units IV q4h ($) [R] <AND> clindamycin 900 mg
IV q8h ($$) [H,O]
## Alternative for penicillin allergy
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R] <AND> Clindamycin 900 mg IV
q8h ($$) [H,O]
## _________________________________________________
## Treatment of Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome
## _________________________________________________
Use vancomycin initially in case methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is
present. If cultures reveal methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus
(MSSA), change to nafcillin or cefazolin for better antimicrobial activity.
## Empirical treatment
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R] <AND> Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h ($$) [H,O]
## Treatment if MSSA is isolated
Nafcillin 2 gm IV q4h ($$) [H,O]) [R] <AND> Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h ($$
Cefazolin 2 gm IV q8h ($) [R] <AND> Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h ($$) [H,O]
References
MMWR 1990, 39(RR-13):1
Up-to-Date website
Sanford: Staphylococcal toxic shock
Lappin E, Lancet Infect Dis 2009, 9:281
Stevens DL Clin Infect Dis 2014, 59: 147

menus.Name: trich-vaginitis
menus.Text:
## TRICHOMONAS VAGINITIS AND URETHRITIS
Male sexual partners of women with trichomonas vaginitis will not have symptoms
but should be treated to prevent recurrent vaginitis in the female sexual
partner.
Recommended to treat all sexual partners exposed during the last 60 days.
## Diagnosis
The discharge is purulent, malodorous, and thin. The vaginal pH is greater
than 4.5. Nucleic Acid amplification test (NAAT) for trichomonas has improved
sensitivities and specificities compared to wet mount.
## Treatment of Initial Episode WOMEN ONLY (See below for MEN)
Pregnant women with trichomonas infection may be treated with metronidazole
during any trimester.
Metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) [DI]
## Treatment of Initial Episode MEN ONLY (See above for WOMEN)
## Treatment failure
1st failure
Metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h for 7 days ($) [DI]
2nd failure
Metronidazole 2 gm PO q24h for 7 days ($) [DI]
3rd failure
Consult Infectious Disease
## ________________________________________________________________________

menus.Name: typhlitis
menus.Text:
## NEUTROPENIC ENTEROCOLITIS (TYPHLITIS)
Oral step-down treatment
Neutropenic enterocolitis, also known as "typhlitis" or "necrotizing
enterocolitis", is a severe intraabdominal infection that occurs in neutropenic
patients, especially in those with acute leukemia.
Send stool for C. difficile testing to exclude of C. difficile infection.
[Clostridioides difficile infection](orzid2-gmenu-abx-assoc-colitis)
Hematology-oncology, Infectious Diseases and general surgery consults are
essential.
Broad spectrum antimicrobials that include anaerobic coverage should be
initiated promptly.
## Duration of antimicrobial therapy
Continue antimicrobial therapy until normalization of body temperature, recovery
of neutropenia (unless planning to transition back to antimicrobial
prophylaxis), recovery of thrombocytopenia, return of normal gastrointestinal
function and resolution of bacteremia if initially present. Infectious Disease
consult recommended to guide duration if perforation, abscess, or other
complicating feature present.
## Treatment
## Inpatient

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h [R]
< OR >
Cefepime 2 gm IV q8h [R] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
## Alternative
Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h [R,DI] <AND> metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h [DI]
## _______________________________________________________________________________
## Outpatient

Refer to the Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS References:
Mandell chapter: Diverticulitis and typhlitis

menus.Name: urethritis-assoc-std
menus.Text:
## URETHRITIS ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES
The main differential in a person who presents with dysuria is between cystitis
and urethritis. Bacterial urethritis is more likely in people with mild
dysuria, onset over a few days, or recent sexual contact.
The two most common sexually transmitted urethritis pathogens are Neisseria
gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Nucleic acid amplification tests for
these pathogens are more sensitive than culture and should be used for patients
at risk for sexually transmitted urethritis.
Chlamydia & GC PCR/LCR test
## For patients who have recently been treated for urethritis
Treatment of recurrent or persistent urethritis
When dysuria is from a sexually transmitted disease, the patient's sexual
partner(s) during the previous 60 days should be evaluated for sexually
transmitted infection.
If diagnostic tests for the cause of urethritis are not feasible, therapy for
both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be given to partners.
## Initial treatment of patients and sex partners
Patients and partners are often infected with both N. gonorrhoeae and C.
trachomatis. Treat for both pathogens unless one is ruled out by lab test.
Treatment for gonococcal urethritis
Treatment for chlamydial or non-gonococcal urethritis
References:
St. Cyr S, et al. MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2020, 69:1911-1916.
Mandell chapter: Urethritis
