menus.Name: vaginitis
menus.Text:
## BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS
Vaginitis usually presents with discharge, itching, irritation, odor, or pain.
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common form of vaginitis. Normal hydrogen
peroxide and lactic acid producing vaginal flora, including Lactobacillus
species, is reduced and high concentrations of anaerobic bacterial pathogens are
present. Pathogenic bacteria commonly include Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma
hominis, Nobiluncus, Prevotella and other Gram-negative anaerobes.
Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the
microscope for identification of clue cells (epithelial cell coated with
bacteria). In bacterial vaginosis the vaginal pH is high (> 4.5), the discharge
is homogenous and gray-white, and the specimen has a positive amine or whiff
test characterized by a fishy odor before or after addition of 10% KOH.
Bacterial vaginosis nucleic acid amplification tests are available for common
pathogens to aide in identification of pathogen(s).
Bacterial vaginosis may be transmitted sexually. Patients at risk of sexually
transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment.
Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Exposure
## Treatment
## Inpatient

Preferred:
Metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for 7 days
< OR >
Metronidazole vaginal gel 0.75%, contents of 1 applicator intravaginally qhs ($)
[DI] for 5 days
< OR >
Clindamycin phosphate vaginal cream 2%, contents of 1 applicator
intravaginally qhs ($) [H,O] for 7 days
Alternative:
Clindamycin 300 mg PO q12h ($) [H,O] for 7 days

## DISKITIS AND VERTEBRAL OSTEOMYELITIS

When possible, obtain diagnostic cultures before starting empiric therapy.
Obtain blood cultures and image guided aspirates or surgical bone biopsy.
Definitive therapy is based on culture and susceptibility test results.

## Recommended duration of therapy:

Treat for at least 6 weeks of pathogen directed IV/PO therapy for high risk
including MRSA infection, ESRD, or undrained abscess or device implantation.
Once culture and susceptibility testing is available switch to pathogen directed
therapy.

## Previously healthy patients (i.e. no comorbidities):

congestive heart failure, malignancy, alcoholism, asplenia, immunosuppressing
conditions, or use of immunosuppressing drugs)
Preferred:
Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h [DI] for 5 days
< OR >
Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO q8h [R] for 5 days
## Patients with comorbidities:
(WITH chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, renal failure, congestive
heart failure, malignancy, alcoholism, asplenia, immunosuppressing conditions or
use of immunosuppressing drugs)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO Q12H [R] for 5 days <AND> azithromycin po
once on day 1, then 250 mg PO QDAY for 4 days [M]
< OR >
Cefdinir 300 mg PO Q12H [R] for 5 days <AND> azithromycin once on day 1, then
250 mg PO QDAY for 4 days [M]
< OR >
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO Q12H [R] for 5 days <AND> doxycycline 100
mg PO Q12H for 5 days [DI]
< OR >

days [DI]

menus.Text:
# ANTIMICROBIAL RESTRICTION POLICY

Medication orders placed using the CDSS system will NOT require Infectious

Disease approval. Because prescribing advice within the system has been

developed with input from a broad, representative group of clinicians and the

recommendations that have emerged are based on site-specific susceptibility

patterns, clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines,

INFECTIOUS DISEASE APPROVAL FOR RESTRICTED ANTIMICROBIALS WILL NOT BE NEEDED at

participating VA sites. Clinicians are still encouraged to seek advice from

Infectious Diseases whenever it would be helpful.

Restricted antimicrobials ordered outside the CDSS system will continue to need

ID approval.

menus.Name: how-to-find-alt-abx
menus.Text:
# HOW TO FIND AN ALTERNATIVE ANTIMICROBIAL WITHIN THE CDSS

The CDSS has been developed locally with input from a broad, representative

group of clinicians. All antimicrobial recommendations within the Antimicrobial

CDSS are reviewed by a clinical pharmacist and an Infectious Diseases Medical

Specialist. Recommendations provided are based on local susceptibility patterns,

clinical evidence, local preferences, and national guidelines. In rare cases,

the recommended antimicrobials and listed alternatives may not be preferred for

the patient you are treating (e.g. isolate resistance, allergies, etc.). In

these cases, a broader set of alternative antimicrobials may be ordered through

the Antimicrobial CDSS. Like other antimicrobial orders in the CDSS,

antimicrobials ordered through the Alternative Antimicrobials menu do on require

a prior authorization or ID approval.

To access the Alternative Antimicrobials menu, navigate to the menu containing

antimicrobial recommendations for the infectious disease you are treating.

At the top of the menu, select:

#2 Help legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more

Then select- Alternative Antimicrobials to CDSS Recommendations

Select the reason an alternative antimicrobial is required then the Alternative

Antimicrobial menu will display.

The Alternative Antimicrobial menu contains antimicrobial regimens that have

been deemed appropriate for use as alternatives to recommended antimicrobials by

the Antimicrobial P&T Subcommittee. If the list does not contain the preferred

antimicrobial, contact or consult Infectious Diseases.

The regimens provided in the Alternative Antimicrobial menu are not tailored for

a specific infectious disease. The dose, frequency, and duration must be changed

based on the infectious disease you are treating as well as for patient specific

factors. The usage of alternative antimicrobials are monitored by the

Antimicrobial CDSS team for appropriateness and to identify infectious diseases

for addition to the system.

menus.Text:
# ASSESSMENT OF BETA-LACTAM REACTION AND ALTERNATIVE TREATMENT

# Streamlined Version (PDF form)

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction CLICK HERE](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

This guide is intended to aid clinicians in assessment of beta-lactam

reactions and selection of appropriate alternative therapy. It is not a

substitute for clinical judgment and should not be used as a sole resource when

selecting antimicrobial therapy.

[Important Beta-Lactam Allergy Facts and Obtaining a Detailed Reaction History](orzid2-gmenu-abx-important-beta-lactam-allergy-facts)

# Reaction Assessment and Selection of an Alternative Beta-lactam

- If the same or a different beta-lactam was subsequently tolerated without

reaction, that beta-lactam may be used.

- If reaction was intolerance (e.g. headache, GI symptoms), family history of

reaction, or if the patient denies allergy, any beta-lactam may be used.

- See below for treatment based on type of reaction (severe vs non-severe).

- If reaction is unknown and patient denies any severe reactions (see below for

list of severe reactions), reaction is considered non-severe.

- If patient is in a suitable care setting, observation during the first 15

minutes to 1 hour after first dose of therapy may be performed to monitor for

signs/symptoms of an allergic reaction.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# SEVERE REACTION TO BETA-LACTAM:

# _______________________________________________________________________________

If the patient experienced a known severe reaction (use link below for severe

reaction list), AVOID ALL Beta-Lactam Antibiotics. If beta-lactam therapy is

ideal, contact Infectious Diseases for desensitization or alternative.

Severe Reaction Examples:

- Anaphylaxis

- Reaction needed medical intervention

- Mucosal, cardiovascular or respiratory system involvement

- Hemolytic anemia

- Immune hepatitis

- Interstitial nephritis

- Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)

- Skin desquamation

- Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

- Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)

- Generalized exanthematous pustulosis

- Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# NON-SEVERE REACTION TO BETA-LACTAM:

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Select an alternative non-cross-reactive beta-lactam for therapy based on

beta-lactam class patient had a reaction to. Refer to PDF document above for

detailed cross-reactivity chart.

# PENICILLIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Amoxicillin, ampicillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, oxacillin,

penicillin, piperacillin, ticarcillin)

# Use: Cefazolin, cefdinir, cefuroxime, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cefepime,

# ertapenem, imipenem, or meropenem

# 1ST GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Cefadroxil, cefatrizine, cefazolin, ceftezole, cephalexin, cephalothin,

cephapirin)

# Use: Dicloxacillin, nafcillin, cefazolin (unless reaction was to cefazolin)

# cefdinir, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, cefepime, ertapenem, imipenem,

# or meropenem

# 2ND GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Cefaclor, cefamandole, cefonicid, cefotetan, cefoxitin, cefprozil,

cefuroxime)

# Use: Amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, piperacillin,

# cefadroxil cefazolin, cefdinir, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cephalexin, cefepime,

# ertapenem imipenem, or meropenem

# 3RD-5TH GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Cefdinir, cefditoren, cefepime, cefiderocol,cefixime, cefpirome,

cefoperazone, cefotaxime, cefpodoxime, ceftaroline, ceftazidime, ceftibuten,

ceftizoxime, ceftolozane, ceftriaxone)

# Use: Amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, penicillin,

# piperacillin, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cephalexin, ertapenem, imipenem, or

# meropenem

# CARBAPENEM CLASS REACTION

(e.g. Ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem)

# Use: Amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, penicillin,

# piperacillin, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cephalexin, cefdinir, ceftazidime,

# ceftriaxone, or cefepime

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Name: vanco-mrsa-nares-information
menus.Text:
# Information on adding MRSA nares screening with new IV Vancomycin starts:

MRSA nares screening will be ordered on all new IV Vancomycin starts.

MRSA nares may be a helpful tool in identifying patients with low risk of

MRSA infection in whom empiric vancomycin may not be required.

A negative MRSA nares does not definitively rule out the presence of MRSA

elsewhere and is one factor to consider in the de-escalation of vancomycin

(and other anti-MRSA antimicrobials).

# References

Parente DM, Cunha CB, Mylonakis E, Timbrook TT. The Clinical Utility of

Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) Nasal Screening to Rule

Out MRSA Pneumonia: A Diagnostic Meta-analysis With Antimicrobial  Stewardship

Implications. Clin Infect Dis. (2018) 67(1):1-7

doi: 10.1093/cid/ciy024. PMID: 29340593.

Jones BE, Ying J, Stevens V, et al. Empirical Anti-MRSA vs Standard Antibiotic

Therapy and Risk of 30-Day Mortality in Patients Hospitalized for Pneumonia.

JAMA Intern Med. (2020) 180(4):552-560. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.7495

menus.Name: esbl-kpc-etc
menus.Text:
# Gram-Negative Bacilli Drug Resistance

In some Gram-negative bacilli, potent bacterial enzymes have emerged that

inactive many newer broad-spectrum beta lactam drugs. These include extended-

spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), serine carbapenemases, metallo-beta-

lactamases, AmpC beta-lactamases and oxacillinases. These enzymes are most

common in strains of Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Escherichia coli,

Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella, and Serratia

marcescens. The enzymes can be latent under many circumstances. However, in

patients receiving beta lactam antibiotics, the enzymes can be expressed and

contribute to treatment failure. Because of this, and since the enzymes continue

to evolve, they are difficult to detect in clinical microbiology laboratories.

Bacteria carrying these enzymes are often also resistant to many other commonly

used antimicrobials, including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, and

others, through different mechanisms. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas and

Acinetobacter are increasingly resistant to all antimicrobials.

Clinicians must be aware that these enzymes may not be detected in all strains

that carry them. If a Gram-negative infection is not responding to therapy with

a beta lactam drug, consider adding or switching to a drug that is not a beta

lactam and appears active in the susceptibility report.

If a patient is suspected of having a Gram-negative infection and is likely to

be colonized with bacteria carrying these enzymes, empirical therapy with

alternative drugs that are not inactivated by them should be considered.

# Risk factors for colonization or infection with resistant gram-negative bacilli

1. Travel to Asia

2. Central venous catheters and other indwelling tube and drains

3. Recent surgical procedures

4. Recent antibiotic therapy

5. Long-term care facility residence

6. Multiple, severe chronic illnesses

7. Ventilator assistance

8. Hemodialysis

9. Long hospital or ICU stay.

# AmpC beta-lactamases alternative antimicrobials

Inactivate many cephalosporins, most penicillins, and beta-lactam inhibitor

combinations. Alternatives include aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cefepime and

colistin.

# ESBLs alternative antimicrobials

Inactivate most cephalosporins, monobactams, and penicillins. Alternatives

include aminoglycosides, carbapenems and colistin.

# Serine carbapenemases, metallo-beta-lactamases and oxacillinases alternative

# antimicrobials

Confer resistance to all beta-lactams. Most strains are also resistant to most

other antibiotic classes. Alternatives include aminoglycosides and colistin.

Infectious Diseases consultation is recommended.

# Additional alternative antimicrobials

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and quinolones are non-beta-lactam alternative

antimicrobials, especially useful for IV to PO conversion. Gram negative bacilli

co-resistance to these antimicrobials is common however. Tigecycline (restricted

to ID) and ceftazidime-avibactam (non-formulary) are also potential options for

susceptible isolates. Infectious Diseases consultation is required for their

use.

References

Mandell chapter: Molecular Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance in Bacteria

Up-to-Date article: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases

Up-to-Date article: Overview of carbapenemase-producing gram-negative bacilli

Rodrï¿½guez-Bano et al. Clinical microbiology reviews, 2018, 31(2): e00079-17

Sanford guide keyword: Gram Negative Bacilli, Drug Resistance, Overview

# CONDITIONS NOT BENEFITTED BY ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY

Several common conditions associated with inflammation or

microorganisms do not benefit from antibiotic therapy in most or all cases.

Yet, antimicrobials are frequently prescribed for these conditions leading to

unnecessary toxicity and costs, rare deaths, and the relentless increase in

antimicrobial resistance. Please review these conditions and do not give

antimicrobials for these conditions unless there are extraordinary

circumstances that make your situation different. If you have any questions,

please contact the infectious disease physician on call.

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# CDC MPOX TREATMENT WITH TPOXX

# Eligibility:

o Consent: Must have documented consent by patient or legally authorized

representative in paper or i-Med consent

o Primary/empiric treatment: Confirmed diagnosis or suspected infection based

on exposure and/or symptoms while testing is pending.

o Secondary Treatment: Complications from replication competent vaccinia

infection from vaccination, secondary transmission, or other exposure. TPOXX may

be used after VIGIV treatment or in conjunction with VIGIV and/or with other

therapies based on clinical judgement.

o Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): May be considered on a case-by-case basis in

consultation with the CDC. Eligibility for PEP use depends on high risk exposure

confirmed or probable case and alternative or complement to PEP vaccination

is needed based on clinical judgment (e.g. vaccine allergy, immunocompromise).

o Dosage and duration: Weight based dosing for 14 days. But it may be longer

based on clinical progress but not to exceed 90 days. Oral tecovirimat capsule

should be taken by mouth with a full glass of water within 30 minutes after

eating a full meal of moderate or high fat (ideally about 600 calories and 25

grams of fat).

o CDC Case Reports Forms:  To be completed and returned to CDC by treating

physicians per IND protocol.

[CLICK HERE for link to required documents \(MPox Taskforce Teams group\)](orz-gtx-abx-tpoxx-documents-link)

# Exclusions:

o Patient or legally authorized representative unwilling to sign an informed

consent and refuse tecovirimat treatment

o  Known allergy to tecovirimat and/or excipients of tecovirimat

o  Upon negative test results for orthopoxvirus whose treatment was initiated

based on clinical manifestations prior to laboratory results.

o For IV tecovirimat only: patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine

clearance <30 mL/min)

# Oral Treatment:

Patients 40kg to < 120 kg

[INV-Tecovirimat 600 mg \(3 capsules\) orally q12h for 14 days](orz-set-abx-inv-tecovirimat-600-mg-orally-q12h-14-days)

*Places medication orders for inpatient and outpatient (included in order set)

Patients 120 kg and Above

[INV-Tecovirimat 600 mg \(3 capsules\) orally q8h for 14 days](orz-set-abx-inv-tecovirimat-600-mg-orally-q8h-14-days)

*Places medication orders for inpatient and outpatient (included in order set)

# Intravenous Treatment:

o Very ill hospitalized patients who are unable to take oral therapy or for whom

there is a concern that oral drug absorption may be altered.

o IV tecovirimat should not be administered in patients with severe renal

impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min) and should be used with caution in

patients with moderate (creatinine clearance 30-49 mL/min) or mild (creatinine

clearance 50-80 mL/min) renal impairment.

o IV tecovirimat should be switched to the oral formulation as soon as patients

can take oral medications and/or gastrointestinal disfunction impacting

absorption has resolved.

Patients 35 kg to < 120 kg

# Guidance on managing Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS)

# CRS GRADE & DEFINING SYMPTOMS

# MANAGEMENT

# GRADE 1 CRS (Floor patients)

# Administer symptomatic treatment:

# Symptoms require symptomatic treatment only.

# Note: Acetaminophen order below placed with Bispecific medication order.

# If temperature >/=100.4 F or headache or rigors,

[Acetaminophen 650mg PO q6h prn Temp>/=100.4 F or headache or rigors](psjizid-acetamin-650mg-po-q6h-prn-temp-100-4-ha-rigors-crs)

# without hypotension or hypoxia.

Give and then NOTIFY Inpatient Medicine Provider.

# GRADE 2 CRS (Floor patients)

# In addition to Grade 1 treatment above:

# Symptoms require and respond to moderate intervention.

[Sodium Chloride 0.9% 1000 ml IV initial bolus over 2 hours for hypotension](psjizid-sodium-chloride-0-9-first-bolus-crs)

# -Fever greater than or equal to 100.4F

[Sodium Chloride 0.9% 1000 ml IV bolus over 2 hours \(2nd bolus for hypotension\)](psjizid-sodium-chloride-0-9-second-bolus-crs)

# -Hypoxia requiring oxygen therapy, AND/OR

# If hypotension not responsive to 2 liters NS, administer dexamethasone:

# -Hypotension responsive to fluids not requiring

[Dexamethasone 8MG IV x1 STAT for CRS Grade 2](psjzid-dexamethasone-8-mg-iv-x1-crs-grade-2)

# vasopressors.

# If patient not responding to interventions above, call a rapid response to

# transfer patient to ICU.

# Note: Tocilizumab may be given on 3D if delay in transferring patient to ICU.

# GRADE 3 AND 4 CRS (ICU patients)

# In addition to GRADE 2 treatment above:

# Severe symptoms defined as temperature >/=100.4F with:

[Transfer Patient to ICU](orz-set-pcm-transfer-to-micu)

# -Hemodynamic instability requiring a vasopressor (with or

# without vasopressin) OR

# Provider must order EACH dose of Tocilizumab as needed:

# -Worsening hypoxia or respiratory distress requiring high-flow

May repeat q8h if no improvement, no more than 3 doses/24hours and 4 doses total

# oxygen.

Maximum for each dose 800MG

Tocilizumab may be given with corticosteroids.

[Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#1 \(Grade 3-4 CRS\)](psjizid-tocilizumab-8mg-kg-iv-once-dose-1)

[Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#2 \(Grade 3-4 CRS\)](psjizid-tocilizumab-8mg-kg-iv-once-dose-2)

[Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#3 \(Grade 3-4 CRS\)](psjizid-tocilizumab-8mg-kg-iv-once-dose-3)

[Tocilizumab 8 MG/KG IV STAT DOSE#4 \(Grade 3-4 CRS\)](psjizid-tocilizumab-8mg-kg-iv-once-dose-4)

# VASOPRESSORS: use ICU specific orders/order sets

# Reference:

Lee D., et al. ASTCT Consensus Grading for Cytokine Release Syndrome

and Neurologic Toxicity Associated with Immune Effector Cells

Biology of Blood and Marrow Transplantation (2018) 25:625-638

menus.Text:
# Guidelines for management of neurologic toxicity, including ICANS

# (Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome)

# Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy (ICE) Score

[Click here Calculate ICE Score](orzid2-gmenu-ice-assessment-for-icans)

# ICANS GRADE & DEFINING SYMPTOMS

# MANAGEMENT

# Grade 1

-ICE score 7-9 with no depressed level of consciousness

-Supportive care

# Grade 2

-ICE score 3-6 and/or

-Supportive care

-Mild somnolence awaking to voice

[Click here to order Dexamethasone 10mg IV ONCE STAT](psjzid-dexamethasone-10mg-iv-once-stat)

[Click here to order Dexamethasone 10mg IV q12h](psjzid-dexamethasone-10mg-ivp-q12h)

-Monitor neurologic symptoms and consider consultation with neurologist

and other specialists for further evaluation and management.

# Grade 3

-ICE score 0-2 and/or

-Recommend intensive monitoring ICU

-Depressed level of consciousness awakening only to tactile stimulus and/or

-Consider mechanical ventilation for airway protection

-Any clinical seizure focal or generalized that resolves rapidly or

[Click here to order Dexamethasone 10mg IV q6h](psjzid-dexamethasone-10mg-iv-q6h-no-stop-date)

-Nonconvulsive seizures on EEG that resolve with intervention and/or

-Consider repeat neuroimaging (CT or MRI) q 2-3 days if patient has persistent

-Focal or local edema on neuroimaging

Grade >/=3 neurotoxicity

-Consult neurology for seizure control.

# Grade 4

-ICE score 0 (patient is unarousable and unable to perform ICE) and/or

-ICU care

-Stupor or coma and/or

-Consider mechanical ventilation for airway protection

-Life threatening prolonged seizure (>5minutes) or

[Click here to order High dose Methylpred 500mg IV q12h x3days THEN taper](psjzid-methylpred-high-dose-icans-with-taper)

-Repetitive clinical or electrical seizures without return to baseline

[Taper: 250mg IV q12hx2days, then 125mg IV q12hx2days, then 60mg IV q12hx2days]

in between and/or

-Consider repeat neuroimaging (CT or MRI) every 2-3 days if patient has

-Diffuse cerebral edema on neuroimaging, decerebrate or decorticate posturing

persistent Grade >/=3 neurotoxicity

or papilledema, cranial nerve VI palsy, or Cushing's triad

-Treat convulsive status epilepticus (ICU)

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# BACTEREMIA ASSOCIATED WITH ENTEROCOCCI

Enterococcus faecalis is almost always susceptible to penicillins locally,

ampicillin is more effective than vancomycin in susceptible isolates.

Enterococcus faecium is typically resistant to some beta-lactams,

aminoglycosides, and vancomycin. Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.

Refer to cardiovascular section for suspected infectious endocarditis.

[Approach to Endocarditis](orzid2-gmenu-abx-appro-to-endocarditis)

# Duration of treatment

For uncomplicated infections where blood cultures are sterile after 24 hours of

treatment, treat for 7-14 days. A longer duration is needed if infection is

complicated or repeat blood cultures are positive.

# Treatment of susceptible E. Faecalis (Van A/B negative)

[Ampicillin 2 gm IV q4h \($$\) R](psjizid-ampicillin-2-gm-iv-q4h)

# Treatment of susceptible E. Faecium (Van A/B negative)

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R](orz-set-abx-vanco-new-start-15mg-kg-q12h-mrsa-nares-screening)

# Treatment of resistant enterococcus (Van A/B positive)

[Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h \($$$$\) DI](psjizid-linezolid-600mg-iv-q12h)

# _______________________________________________________________________________

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# BACTEREMIA ASSOCIATED WITH STREPTOCOCCI

Bacteremia is typically caused by S. pyogenes (Group A), S. agalactiae (Group B)

and S. pneumoniae. If other streptococcal species are isolated contamination is

likely. Treat only if greater than one blood culture is positive. Identification

and treatment of the source of infection, in addition to antimicrobial therapy,

is crucial for resolution of infection.

For patients with toxic shock syndrome refer to those recommendations.

[Toxic Shock Syndrome](orzid2-gmenu-toxic-shock-syndrome)

# Duration of treatment

Treatment duration is not well established. Treat for 7 -14 days depending on

source control and response to treatment. Consult ID for more information.

# Treatment of S. pyogenes (Group A), S. agalactiae (Group B) and S. pneumoniae

[Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h \($$\) R](psjizid-penicillin-g-4-million-units-iv-q4h)

# Treatment of other streptococcal isolates with 2 of 2 blood cultures positive or

# alternative to above

[Assessment of beta-lactam reaction CLICK HERE](orz-gtx-abx-beta-lactam-reaction-pdf)

[Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h \($\) M](psjizid-ceftriaxone-2gm-iv-q24h)

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# NATIVE VALVE ENDOCARDITIS--EMPIRICAL THERAPY

# Empirical treatment in a non-intravenous drug user

Wait for identification of pathogen before initiating antimicrobial therapy in

most cases. If empiric antimicrobial treatment is necessary, due to hemodynamic

instability or other severe disease, use:

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h \($\)](orz-set-abx-vanco-15-mg-kg-iv-q12h-ceftriax-2gm-iv-q24h)

< OR >

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV q8h \($\)](orz-set-abx-van-15-mg-kg-iv-q12h-gent-1-mg-kg-iv-q8h)

[R,O]

# Empirical treatment in an intravenous drug user

Staphylococcus aureus is the most likely pathogen, followed by streptococci and

enterococci. However, gram negative pathogens are often associated with

endocarditis in these patients. Culture results are key for appropriate therapy.

Consult Cardiology and Infectious Diseases for more information.

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV q8h \($\)](orz-set-abx-van-15-mg-kg-iv-q12h-gent-1-mg-kg-iv-q8h)

[R,O]

[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# MYOCARDITIS

Myocarditis is most commonly associated with enterovirus or coxsackie virus

infection. Less common pathogens include pyogenic bacteria, rickettsia,

toxoplasmosis, and fungi.

Empirical antimicrobial treatment is not indicated. Supportive care and

treatment of CHF are essential. Consult Cardiology and/or Infectious Diseases

for more assistance.

Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) and corticosteroids in

these patients, as the use of NSAIDs in myocarditis has been associated with

worse outcomes.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Mandell chapter: Myocarditis and Pericarditis

Up-To-Date article: Treatment and prognosis of myocarditis in adults

menus.Name: pericarditis
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# PERICARDITIS

Most cases arise from non-infectious causes or are associated with viruses.

Antimicrobial therapy is not indicated unless pericardial fluid is purulent. If

fluid is purulent, pericardial drainage is required in most cases. Modify

antimicrobial regimen and narrow coverage based on results of culture and

susceptibility tests.

Cardiology consultation is essential for management of therapy. Infectious

Diseases consultation is recommended if an infectious origin is suspected.

# Duration of therapy

Duration is based on patient specific factors such as resolution of fever and

clinical signs of infection. Generally, duration is 2 to 4 weeks depending on

how adequacy  of drainage of pericardial fluid and susceptibility of infectious

organism.

# Empirical Treatment

Preferred:

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q24h \($\) R,DI](orz-set-abx-vanco-15-mg-kg-iv-q12h-ceftriax-2gm-iv-q24h)

Alternative:

[Assessment of beta-lactam reaction CLICK HERE](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h \($\) R <AND> piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm](orz-set-abx-pip-taz4-5gm-ne-extinf-ci-cefep-metro-vanco15mg-kg)

IV q6h ($$) [R]

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Adler et al., European Heart Journal 2015, 36.2921-2964

menus.Text:
# ANTIMICROBIAL COST INFORMATION

Cost is represented as dollar ($) signs in parenthesis following the antibiotic.

The number of $ signs represent the cost ranges below:

$ = Less than 10 dollars per day

$$ = 10-50 dollars per day

$$$ = 51-100 dollars per day

$$$$ = 101-400 dollars per day

$$$$ = Greater than 400 dollars per day

The displayed cost of an antibiotic is an estimate based on usual daily doses

for an 80kg patient. Costs may change frequently due to VA contract negotiations

as well as supply and demand effects. Antibiotic cost and formulary are reviewed

by members of the Antimicrobial Subcommittee annually.

# INFLUENZA VACCINATION RECOMMENDATIONS

[Influenza Vaccine Outpatient and Inpatient Guidelines](orz-gtx-influenza-info)

Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all persons aged 6 months and

older without a specific contraindication.

Eggs and latex allergies are NOT considered contraindications to receiving the

vaccine, the only contraindication to the flu vaccination is severe allergic

reaction (i.e. Anaphylactic reactions).

# Recommend observing all patients for 15 minutes after receiving any influenza

# vaccine. A previous severe allergic reaction to influenza vaccine, regardless of

# the component suspected of being responsible for the reaction, is a

# contraindication to future receipt of ANY influenza vaccine.

menus.Name: syphilis
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# SYPHILIS

# Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases. Evaluation and management are complex.

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the spirochete Treponema

pallidum that can manifest as a variety of signs or symptoms. Primary syphilis

typically consists of painless ulcers or chancre at the site of infection with

regional adenopathy. Secondary syphilis often includes a skin rash (disseminated

and/or including the palms and soles), fever, malaise, mucocutaneous lesions and

lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis includes those with cardiovascular or

gummatous disease.

Latent syphilis is a period of disease when a patient does not have symptoms but

is found to be infected through serologic testing. Early latent syphilis refers

to latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year and late latent syphilis

refers to all other cases of latent syphilis. Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or

Otosyphilis, can occur at any stage of syphilis with early manifestations (e.g.

meningitis, stroke, vision or hearing loss) occurring within the first months to

years of infection and late manifestations (e.g. dementia, tabes dorsalis)

occurring after 10-30 years.

# Diagnosis

A presumptive diagnosis is made through use of a nontreponemal or serologic test

(i.e. rapid plasma reagin [RPR]) and a treponemal test (i.e. fluorescent

treponemal antibody absorbed [FTA-ABS]). Direct methods through darkfield

microscopy and direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) must be used for definitive

diagnosis since T. pallidum cannot be cultured.

[Syphilis antibody test with reflex to rapid plasma reagin \(RPR\)](lrtz-syphilis-ab-w-reflex-to-rpr-w-titer)

# Management of sex partners

Persons with sexual contact with a person with primary, secondary or early

latent syphilis within the last 90 days should be presumptively treated even if

serologic test is negative.

# Primary, Secondary and Early Latent Syphilis

Preferred treatment

[Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 million units IM once \($$$\) M](psjzid-benzathine-penicillin-2-4mu-im-once)

Secondary treatment for patients who are not pregnant

[Beta-lactam Reaction Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 14 days](psjzid-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h)

# Tertiary and Late Latent Syphilis

Preferred treatment

[Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 million units IM qweek \($$$\) M x3 doses](psjzid2-benzathine-penicillin-2-4mu-im-qweek-x3-syphilis)

Secondary treatment for patients who are not pregnant

[Beta-lactam Reaction Assessment](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h \($\) DI for 28 days](psjzid-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h)

# Neurosyphilis, Ocular syphilis or Otosyphilis

Consult Infectious Disease for treatment

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

CDC STD Treatment Guidelines MMWR (2021) 70.4

Mandell Chapter: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum)

menus.Name: mastoiditis
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# MASTOIDITIS

# Acute Mastoiditis

Acute mastoiditis most commonly occurs as a suppurative complication of acute

otitis media. Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and culture of

drainage. Antibiotics and drainage of middle ear are sufficient treatment in

most cases. Mastoidectomy is necessary if abscess has formed in the mastoid

bone. If complication of first episode of acute otitis media, etiologies

typically include Streptococcus pneumonia (most common), Streptococcus pyogenes,

or Staphylococcus aureus. If secondary to chronic otitis media, etiologies

typically include Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Patients

usually too ill for outpatient therapy. ENT consultation recommended. Obtain

cultures of auditory canal or middle ear fluid (preferred).

# Empirical Treatment

Preferred:

[Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q6h \($$\) R](orz-set-abx-pip-taz4-5gm-ne-extinf-ci-cefep-metro-vanco15mg-kg)

<AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q 12 hours ($) [R] for 7 days

Alternative:

[Assessment of Beta-lactam Reaction](orzid2-gmenu-abx-beta-lactam-allergy-assesment)

[Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q 12 hours \($\) R < AND > cefepime 2 gm IV q12h \($$\) R](orz-set-abx-cefepime-2-gm-iv-q12h-vanco-15mg-kg-q12h)

for 7 days

# Step down treatment after initial intravenous antibiotic treatment in patients

# who can tolerate oral therapy. Base selection on culture results. Adjust for a

# total duration of 7 days of antimicrobial therapy.

[Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875-125 mg PO q12h for 7 days \($\) R](psjzid-amox-clav-875-125mg-po-q12h)

< OR >

[Cefuroxime 500mg PO q12h for 7 days \($\) R](psjzid-cefuroxime-500mg-q12h)

< OR >

[Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h for 7 days \($\) DI](psjzid-doxycycline-100mg-po-q12h)

# __________________________________________________________________

# Chronic Mastoiditis

Chronic mastoiditis is usually the result of chronic otitis media with

perforation of the tympanic membrane. There is often associated formation of a

cholesteatoma (keratoma). Diagnosis is supported by CT or MRI imaging and

culture of drainage. Long term treatment with topical antimicrobials is first

line therapy. Infection is often polymicrobial, including Staphylococcus aureus,

Pseudomonas aeruginosa and anaerobes. Treatment should be managed in

collaboration with otolaryngology and includes topical antimicrobials, care of

external auditory canal, and is some cases mastoidectomy. If possible, withhold

therapy until a pathogen is identified by culture of drainage to direct therapy.

Specific drug choice dictated by culture results.

# Empirical Treatment

Preferred:

[Ciprofloxacin-Dexamethasone otic 4 drops in affected ear\(s\) BID for 4 weeks \($\)](psjzid-ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone-otic-4-drps-bid)

[M]

Alternative:

[Neomycin-polymyxin-hydrocortisone ear drops 4 drops in affected ear\(s\) QID for 4](psjzid-neomycin-polymixin-hc-otic-4-drps-qid)

weeks ($) [M]

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

Mandell chapter: Otitis Externa, Otitis Media, and Mastoiditis

Loh et. al., The Journal of Laryngology & Otology. 2018, 132(2)96-104.

Sanford keyword: Mastoiditis

Up-to-Date article: Chronic otitis media, cholesteatoma, and mastoiditis in

adults

menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# PERIOCULAR INFECTIONS

# Eyelid infections

Patients with moderate or severe eyelid infections should be referred to

ophthalmology.

# __________________________________________________________________

# Blepharitis

Wash margins with baby shampoo daily and use warm compresses daily.

Antimicrobials have no benefit.

# __________________________________________________________________

# Hordeolum (stye)

For external disease (involving the gland of Zeis), daily hot pack massage

encourages drainage and relieves symptoms. For internal disease (involving

Meibomian glands) ophthalmology consult is encouraged, as the infection seldom

drains without intervention.

# __________________________________________________________________

# Lacrimal infections

Refer cases of lacrimal infection to ophthalmology, including infections of the

lacrimal gland (dacryoadenitis), lacrimal sac (dacrocystitis), or tear ducts

(canaliculitis).

# _______________________________________________________________________________

# UVEITIS

Most cases are non-infectious. Most infectious cases are associated with a

pathogen causing systemic or central nervous system infection. Diagnosis of

uveitis usually must be made presumptively due to the technical difficulty of

sampling the uvea. Cases have been associated with fungi, bacteria, viruses, and

protozoa like Toxoplasma gondii.

# For treatment of posterior uveitis (retinitis) or acute retinal necrosis (ARN)

# due to Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) or herpes simplex virus (HSV) or

# Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

[VZV or HSV retinitis and ARN](orzid2-gmenu-retinitis)

[CMV retinitis and ARN](orzid2-gmenu-abx-cmv-retinitis)

# Treatment of uveitis involves treating the underlying infection and is usually

# systemic. Refer to specific pathogen recommendations for treatment of underlyin

# infection. Contact Ophthalmology and/or Infectious Diseases for assistance.

# _______________________________________________________________________________

References:

menus.Name: chronic-sinusitis
menus.Text:
[Help, legend, allergy info, consults, alternative antimicrobials and more \(Inpt\)](orzid2-gmenu-abx-general-information-inpatient)

# CHRONIC SINUSITIS

Diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is based on presence of at least 2 of the 4

cardinal signs/symptoms lasting >/= 12 weeks. In addition, diagnosis requires

objective evidence of mucosal inflammation using nasal endoscopy and/or CT

imaging. The initial therapy for chronic sinusitis is treatment with intranasal

corticosteroids and saline. For patients with severe nasal blockage by polyps,

treat with a short course of oral glucocorticoids. Reassess patient after 1 to 3

months of intranasal therapy or after completion of glucocorticoid therapy. If

signs/symptoms have not improved, consult surgery, ENT and Infectious Diseases

as treatment is complex.

Acute exacerbations of chronic sinusitis can be caused by discontinuing medical

therapy, viral infections, allergens, noxious inhalants and bacterial or fungal

infections. Bacterial infections should be suspected when the patient has

increased signs/symptoms persisting for more than 10 days. Refer to Severe

Sinusitis recommendations for choice of antimicrobial therapy in these patients.

Repeated use of the same agent should be avoided to prevent promotion of drug

resistant bacteria or increased fungal colonization.

[Severe Sinusitis](orzid2-gmenu-severe-sinusitis)

# Cardinal Signs/Symptoms of Chronic Sinusitis

1. Anterior and/or posterior nasal mucopurulent drainage

2. Nasal obstruction/nasal blockage/congestion

3. Facial pain, pressure, and/or fullness

4. Reduction or loss of sense of smell

# Objective Evidence mucosal inflammation

1. Purulent (not clear) mucus or edema in the middle meatus or ethmoid regions

2. Polyps in the nasal cavity or the middle meatus

3. Radiographic imaging demonstrating mucosal thickening or partial or complete

opacification of the paranasal sinuses

# _______________________________________________________________________________

Chow et al, Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012, 54(8) e72-e112

occurs in immunocompetent hosts. Drainage is essential. Consult ENT and

Infectious Disease.

# PREVENTION OF INFECTION IN PATIENTS WITH NASAL PACKING

Antimicrobial prophylaxis to prevent infection and toxic shock syndrome in

patients with nasal packing is not recommended. Antibiotics increase the risk of

adverse events in patients with nasal packing with no proven effectiveness in

preventing infection.
